card.oneLiner: Some things are certain, some impossible — most sit in between, and you can put a number on it.

sections.idea: Roll a die twice and you may get different numbers, or the same one. You cannot know the next roll. That is chance. Chance is not a mystery. You can name it with a number between 0 and 1. Zero means never. One means always. A coin landing heads is 0.5. Naming chance with numbers is how machines handle everything they are not sure about.

sections.inTheStudio: "Will it rain on the site visit?" is a chance question. So is "will this tool give me the same image twice?" The answer to the second one is: almost never. Soon you will know why.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking "random" means "anything can happen." A die never rolls a seven. Chance always works inside limits.
sections.tryIt: Roll one die twenty times and tally the results. Then predict: if you rolled it six hundred times, roughly how many times would 4 appear?
sections.proveIt: Explain to a friend, with one example, what a chance of 0.5 means, and why a chance of 0 and a chance of 1 are not really chance at all.
sections.howItWorks: The proper name for this is probability, and you will study it in maths class. On this map it sits under one big idea: every answer a generative machine gives is one draw from many possible answers.

sections.idea: A machine does not see a picture the way you do. To the machine, the picture is numbers. So is a word. So is a song. Everything a machine "knows" is data that people collected and gave it. Its world is that data, plus whatever you give it in the moment. Nothing else exists for it.
sections.whyItMatters: If the data is the machine's world, then whoever chose the data chose the world.
sections.inTheStudio: A machine that has only seen data about city houses knows nothing about your village house. It is not being unfair. Your house is simply not in its world.

Later ideas on this map — where data comes from, who is in it, who is missing from it — all grow from this one. Later still, you will learn that a machine can also be handed data while it works: a photo you upload, a document it looks up. That is a different channel from the training data, and a card higher up this map keeps the two apart.

sections.idea: Many AI systems are not given a rule for every situation. Instead, they are shown a very large number of examples. The machine finds patterns in those examples, and then makes guesses about things it has never seen. The examples matter. What is missing, repeated, or wrongly labelled changes what the machine learns.
sections.whyItMatters: If the examples are the teacher, then bad examples teach badly. That one idea explains most of what goes wrong with AI.
sections.inTheStudio: A tool that has seen a million photos of glass towers and very few brick courtyards will keep offering you glass towers. It is not being stubborn. It is showing you its diet.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking the machine "knows" things the way you do. It has patterns from examples — not experience, not understanding.
sections.tryIt: Show a friend ten photos of cats and none of dogs. Then show them a husky and ask what the machine would say. Talk about why.

sections.howItWorks: This way of building software is called machine learning. The examples together are called training data. The patterns the machine keeps are called a model. Later ideas on this map — bias, provenance, whose work taught the machine — all begin right here, in the diet of examples.
sections.lineage: For decades, people tried writing rules for machines by hand: if this, then that. The rule books grew huge and still missed too much. Learning from examples took over because the world holds more examples than anyone can write rules for.

card.oneLiner: A machine fails in its own strange ways — and does not know it failed.

sections.idea: A machine only knows what it was shown. Bad examples, or missing examples, lead to wrong answers, and the machine gives them with full confidence. AI is not magic. It is maths on data. sections.watchForThis: Believing an answer because it came fast and looked neat. Machines are wrong just as fast and just as neatly as they are right.

topics.name: You are a child in the data law

grounding.ref: PRS India, The Digital Personal Data Protection Bill, 2023
The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 — text, hosted by PRS
PRS India, Monthly Policy Review, November 2025

topics.description: India's data law calls everyone under eighteen a child, and says a parent must agree before a company uses a child's data — a rule that is still being switched on. India has a law about personal data: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. It says a child is anyone who has not completed eighteen years.
evidence: Pick one app you use. Find the age it asks you to be. Then ask a parent: did anyone ask you before I signed up? Write the two answers next to each other.
Say what the law calls a child, what a company needs before it uses a child's data, and whether that rule has started yet.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to say what the law calls a child, what a company needs before it uses a child's data, and whether that rule has started yet.

card.oneLiner: India's data law calls everyone under eighteen a child, and says a parent must agree before a company uses a child's data — a rule that is still being switched on.

sections.idea: India has a law about personal data: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. It says a child is anyone who has not completed eighteen years. If you are at school, the law is talking about you. Before a company uses a child's personal data — stores it, studies it, shares it — it needs checkable consent from a parent or guardian. Companies must not track what children do or aim advertisements at them. The Act was passed in August 2023. The Rules came in November 2025, and the duties on companies are scheduled to start in May 2027.
sections.whyItMatters: Every app you sign up for asks for something — a name, a birthday, a photo. Today most of them ask you, not your parent. The law says that should change. Knowing the rule is how you notice when it is not being followed.
sections.inTheStudio: Your class is using an image tool for a model-making project. The sign-up page asks for your date of birth. You type it in. Nobody asks your parents anything. Under the Act, the tool is supposed to get a parent's consent first. From May 2027 that rule is scheduled to have teeth.
sections.watchForThis: Hearing "the law protects you" and thinking "so I am protected today". The law was passed in 2023. The duties on companies start in 2027. In between, the habit from YOUR DATA still does the work: think before you upload.
sections.tryIt: Pick one app you use. Find the age it asks you to be. Then ask a parent: did anyone ask you before I signed up? Write the two answers next to each other.
sections.proveIt: Say what the law calls a child, what a company needs before it uses a child's data, and whether that rule has started yet.
sections.howItWorks: The Act defines a child in section 2(f): an individual who has not completed eighteen years. Section 9 does three things. A company that handles your data (the law calls it a Data Fiduciary) must get verifiable consent from the parent or lawful guardian before processing a child's personal data. It must not process that data in a way likely to harm the child's well-being. And it must not track children, monitor their behaviour, or target advertising at them. The Rules of November 2025 say how a parent's consent is checked — from identity details the company already holds, from details the parent gives, or from a digital token issued by an authorised provider — and they exempt some people, such as schools and doctors, for specific purposes. Section 1(2) of the Act lets the government start different parts on different dates. The Rules give companies eighteen months from publication for their duties, which lands in May 2027. That is why this card is EVOLVING: the words are settled, the start date is ahead of us, and a date can move. Check the law as it stands, not this card's note about it.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Rules that draw: the kolam

grounding.ref: Krithivasan, A View of India through Kolam Patterns and their Grammatical Representation
Siromoney, Siromoney & Krithivasan, Array Grammars and Kolam (1974)
Reddy, Kambi Kolam as Algorithmic Pattern (2023)

topics.description: A grid of dots and a rule make endless valid patterns — an algorithm run by hand at the doorstep. Every morning, at doorsteps across Tamil Nadu and South India, someone draws a kolam. Kolam is a living practice with many regional forms; the pulli kolam starts from a grid of dots (pulli), and in the kambi kolam a line weaves round them.
evidence: Draw a 3×3 grid of dots. Make up one rule — for example, loop around every dot and never let the line cross itself. Draw it. Give the same grid and the same rule to a friend, and compare: you will probably get two different valid kolams. Then tighten the rule until only one drawing is possible, and notice what that costs.
Draw a kolam on a small grid while saying your rule out loud, step by step, so a friend could draw it without seeing yours.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to draw a kolam on a small grid while saying your rule out loud, step by step, so a friend could draw it without seeing yours.

card.oneLiner: A grid of dots and a rule make endless valid patterns — an algorithm run by hand at the doorstep.

sections.idea: Every morning, at doorsteps across Tamil Nadu and South India, someone draws a kolam. Kolam is a living practice with many regional forms; the pulli kolam starts from a grid of dots (pulli), and in the kambi kolam a line weaves round them. The hand follows rules: go round every dot, keep the line moving, let it close on itself. Keep them and a valid pattern appears — and one grid admits many valid patterns, so two people keeping the same rules draw different kolams. A set of steps anyone can follow is an algorithm; this is one, run by hand.
sections.whyItMatters: Rules can make form. You have watched it happen before breakfast. Knowing that is the start of understanding how machines make things.
sections.inTheStudio: A paving pattern, a jali screen, a brick bond. Each is a small rule repeated across a surface. Before you draw a single tile, you can write the rule; the rule then draws the rest.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking the pattern is "just decoration" because a hand drew it. The hand is running a procedure. Computer scientists in Madras wrote kolam rules down as formal grammars in 1974. The rules were always there. And the opposite mistake: thinking kolam is only this. The pulli and kambi families are the ones the mathematicians took up; the practice is wider, and it is not a textbook exercise.
sections.tryIt: Draw a 3×3 grid of dots. Make up one rule — for example, loop around every dot and never let the line cross itself. Draw it. Give the same grid and the same rule to a friend, and compare: you will probably get two different valid kolams. Then tighten the rule until only one drawing is possible, and notice what that costs.
sections.proveIt: Draw a kolam on a small grid while saying your rule out loud, step by step, so a friend could draw it without seeing yours.
sections.howItWorks: Kolams come in families. In one, a single continuous line weaves around the dots and closes; in another, the dots are joined by straight strokes (kambi). Researchers have written the rules as formal grammars — array grammars in 1974, and later L-systems, the same kinds of rule systems used to describe programming languages and the growth of plants. A grammar that can generate a kolam is a small program, and most such grammars describe a whole family of valid kolams rather than a single drawing. People at their doorsteps were running them long before computers did.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Early algorithms: the Sulba Sutras

grounding.ref: Price, Applied Geometry of the Sulba Sutras

topics.description: The Sulba Sutras give step-by-step rules for geometric construction, some exact, some approximate — procedure as knowledge, centuries before the word "algorithm". Before the word "algorithm" existed, Indian priests needed altars of set shapes: a square of a given area, a square twice another, a circle close in area to a square. The Sulba Sutras — texts attached to the Vedas, the earliest usually dated to around 800 BCE — give the steps: peg, cord, arc, mark.
evidence: With a cord and two pegs (string and two pencils will do), construct a square using only arcs and straight lines, never the markings on a ruler. Write your steps as a numbered list. Hand the list to a friend and see whether they get a square.
Construct a square with string and pegs, explain each step, and say which step would go wrong if you skipped it.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to construct a square with string and pegs, explain each step, and say which step would go wrong if you skipped it.

card.oneLiner: The Sulba Sutras give step-by-step rules for geometric construction, some exact, some approximate — procedure as knowledge, centuries before the word "algorithm".

sections.idea: Before the word "algorithm" existed, Indian priests needed altars of set shapes: a square of a given area, a square twice another, a circle close in area to a square. The Sulba Sutras — texts attached to the Vedas, the earliest usually dated to around 800 BCE — give the steps: peg, cord, arc, mark. Some are exact; the circle-and-square ones are good approximations, and the texts do not say which is which. One rule gives the square root of two to five decimal places. A rule that reliably produces a result is knowledge, even when nobody has written why it works.
sections.whyItMatters: Knowing how to do something, step by step, is a kind of knowledge. Machines run on exactly this kind. So did builders nearly three thousand years ago.
sections.inTheStudio: On site, a mason sets out a right angle with a 3-4-5 rope triangle. No protractor, no theorem recited, only a procedure that works. The Sulba Sutras carry the same knowledge. The procedure is the knowledge.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking a step-by-step rule is "lower" than an explanation. The texts give no proofs, and they mix exact methods with approximations without saying which is which. That is a fair warning about every rulebook, including the ones inside machines. And do not call these "the oldest" algorithms: Mesopotamian procedures are older. The Sulba Sutras are an early and remarkable example, and that is enough.
sections.tryIt: With a cord and two pegs (string and two pencils will do), construct a square using only arcs and straight lines, never the markings on a ruler. Write your steps as a numbered list. Hand the list to a friend and see whether they get a square.
sections.proveIt: Construct a square with string and pegs, explain each step, and say which step would go wrong if you skipped it.
sections.howItWorks: "Sulba" means cord or rope. The four main texts — Baudhayana, Apastamba, Manava, Katyayana — open with geometric and arithmetic constructions and end with instructions for building altars. The constructions include the rule we now call the theorem of Pythagoras, stated as a procedure rather than a proof, and a value for the diagonal of a unit square: 1 + 1/3 + 1/(3×4) − 1/(3×4×34), which is 577/408, the square root of two to five decimal places. Historians date the texts between roughly 800 and 200 BCE; as with most texts of that age, the dates are uncertain.

topics.description: Sun, wind, rain and heat at your site already exist as numbers a machine can read. You feel the climate of a place: the afternoon heat, the wind off the sea, the rain in July. Weather stations have been recording the same things as numbers for decades — temperature, humidity, wind, sunshine — hour by hour.

card.oneLiner: Sun, wind, rain and heat at your site already exist as numbers a machine can read.

sections.idea: You feel the climate of a place: the afternoon heat, the wind off the sea, the rain in July. Weather stations have been recording the same things as numbers for decades — temperature, humidity, wind, sunshine — hour by hour. Put a year of those numbers in one file and you have a weather file. India's National Building Code uses records like these to sort the whole country into five climate zones: hot-dry, warm-humid, composite, temperate and cold. To a machine, your site's climate is that file of numbers.
sections.whyItMatters: Once climate is a file, a machine can read it before you draw a line. Every environmental tool on this map starts from that file.
sections.inTheStudio: A tutor asks, "Which way does the hot wind come from on this site?" One student points the way they remember from the visit. Another opens the weather file for the nearest station and draws a wind rose. Both may be right. Only one can be checked.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking the file is the site. A weather file comes from a station, often at an airport, kilometres away and in the open. Your plot sits in a lane, behind a wall, under a tree. Start from the file, then correct it for your plot.
sections.tryIt: Find the climate zone for your town under the National Building Code. Then find out where the nearest weather station is, and how far it is from your school. Write down one thing about your school's own microclimate that the station cannot know.
sections.proveIt: Explain to a friend what a weather file holds, where the numbers come from, and one reason the numbers at your site might differ from it.
sections.howItWorks: A typical weather file holds 8,760 rows — one for each hour of a year — with temperature, humidity, wind speed and direction, and solar radiation in each row. Free tools such as Ladybug read them and draw sun paths, wind roses and comfort charts. India's National Building Code uses long-run records like these to place every town in one of its five climate zones, and the zone is the first thing a design should respond to. Later cards on this map — climate numbers, the surrogate, simulate-then-trust — run on exactly these files. A model that predicts your building's heat needs this data. Without it, it has nothing to work from.

topics.description: One unit, a set of ratios, and a figure correct within its canon at any size — the rule system this map is named for. Tālamāna is the name for the Indian systems of proportion for sculpted figures, set out in the śilpa texts and the Āgamas; there are several, not one. Tāla means the palm of the hand, fingertip to wrist, taken as equal to the face.
evidence: Measure your own face from hairline to chin. Call that one tāla. Measure your height in tālas. Now draw a figure at twice your size using the same count. The proportions hold; only the unit changed.

card.oneLiner: One unit, a set of ratios, and a figure correct within its canon at any size — the rule system this map is named for.

sections.idea: Tālamāna is the name for the Indian systems of proportion for sculpted figures, set out in the śilpa texts and the Āgamas; there are several, not one. Tāla means the palm of the hand, fingertip to wrist, taken as equal to the face. Māna means measure. A system divides that unit into aṅgulas (finger-breadths) and states every part of the figure as a count of them. Give a sculptor the tāla and the class of figure, and the whole body follows at any size. This map is named for that idea: a rule carrying proportion inside it.
sections.whyItMatters: A proportion rule is somebody's judgment written down so it can be repeated. Once you see that, you can ask of any rule — a byelaw, a grid, a model's defaults — whose judgment it carries.
sections.inTheStudio: A column order, a door-to-room ratio, a brick module. Architects also work from a unit and a set of ratios. Change the unit and the building scales; the relationships hold. Talamana does the same for the human figure.
sections.watchForThis: Treating the system as one neat formula. The texts give some thirty sets of proportions in ten classes, and the highest deities, the goddesses, Ganapati and children each get a different set. The scholar who compiled the system in English in 1920, T. A. Gopinatha Rao, also noted that the class names do not match a simple count of tālas. A real rule system has rough edges.
sections.tryIt: Measure your own face from hairline to chin. Call that one tāla. Measure your height in tālas. Now draw a figure at twice your size using the same count. The proportions hold; only the unit changed.
sections.proveIt: Explain what tāla means, what aṅgula means, and how a sculptor could carve a figure at two different sizes from the same set of numbers.
sections.howItWorks: The sets of proportions are grouped in ten classes, each in three grades: uttama (superior), madhyama (middling) and adhama (inferior). The classes are named as if by a count of tālas — daśa (ten), nava (nine), ashṭa (eight) and so on down to children and dwarfs — but Rao shows the names do not match the arithmetic: the uttama-daśa-tāla figure, 124 aṅgulas in total height, does not work out to ten of its own tālas. Different texts — the Agamas, the Shukranīti, the Shilparatna — give slightly different tables. The standard English account is Rao's *Tālamāna or Iconometry*, Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India No. 3 (1920), free to read online.

Each of these sentences puts a mind inside the machine. The Lab's rule is plain: do not use a mind-word when a mechanism-word will do.
evidence: For one day, every time you or a friend says "it knows / thinks / decided / wants" about a machine, rewrite the sentence with predicts / matches / produces / is set to. Keep the list. Notice which rewrites change what you would do next.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: "it knows, thinks, decided" puts a mind in the machine. Say prediction, pattern, output.

sections.position: "The AI knows." "It thinks." "It decided." Each of these sentences puts a mind inside the machine. The Lab's rule is plain: do not use a mind-word when a mechanism-word will do. A model predicts. It matches patterns. It produces an output. Those verbs are true of every system on this map, and they keep the machine the right size. This is a discipline of language, held on purpose. It is not a finding about what machines can or cannot have inside.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The words you use decide the questions you ask. "Why did it decide that?" has no answer you can check. "What pattern produced that output?" has one. And a student who says "it decided" has already handed over authorship before the jury asks a single question.
sections.strongestObjection: Whether words like understanding, representation, reasoning and knowledge can properly be applied to computational systems is contested across AI research, cognitive science and philosophy, and it is not settled in the Lab's favour. Some researchers use "knows" and "represents" as technical terms for things they can measure inside a model. Forbidding the words may make students miss real questions about what these systems do inside — and it may be the Lab's preference dressed as a fact.
sections.revisionCondition: If the field arrives at measured, agreed meanings for these words as applied to models — so that "the model represents X" becomes a claim a student can check — the Lab will allow the technical senses and keep the rule only for the loose, everyday ones. We watch the interpretability literature for that every edition.
sections.inTheStudio: A jury asks why your massing looks the way it does. "The AI chose it" hands your authorship to a pattern-matcher. "I generated options and selected this one, for these reasons" is an answer an architect can give.
sections.watchForThis: Your own shortcuts. "It understood my brief" — it matched your brief. "It got confused" — it produced an unlikely output. The shortcuts feel natural because the machine talks like a person. That is exactly why they are a trap.
sections.tryIt: For one day, every time you or a friend says "it knows / thinks / decided / wants" about a machine, rewrite the sentence with predicts / matches / produces / is set to. Keep the list. Notice which rewrites change what you would do next.
sections.proveIt: Take three sentences that give the machine a mind and rewrite each so it says what the machine actually did.
sections.howItWorks: Models are trained to continue patterns: words after words, pixels toward a description. Products are then tuned to sound helpful, which makes mind-language feel natural. Researchers call the habit anthropomorphism. It is old and human, and these tools are built in a way that invites it. UNESCO's AI competency framework for students puts a "human-centred mindset" first for the same reason: the person acts, the system produces.

topics.name: What Indian cities are actually facing

grounding.ref: NITI Aayog, Composite Water Management Index (2019)

topics.description: The Lab's position: heat, water and the city are the measured forces to design against first — with sources and dates; AI maps them, it does not solve them. The Lab puts three forces first for a young Indian architect: heat, water and the city itself. Not because nothing else matters — seismic risk, air, land, money and carbon all do — but because these three are measured, dated and public, and they decide the section of almost every building here.
evidence: Pick your own city. Find one number about its heat from the IMD, one about its water from NITI Aayog's index or your city's water board, and one flood map from Bhuvan. Write each with its source and its date. Then take one claim you heard this year — "it was the hottest May ever", "we had a heat wave all week" — and check it against the IMD's own published station data and its criteria: did the numbers meet the rule, or not? Three lines and one check, and you have the start of a site dossier.

topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to name the three forces the Lab puts first, say why they are the Lab's choice rather than a fact, and for one of them show a number, where it came from, and when it was measured.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: heat, water and the city are the measured forces to design against first — with sources and dates; AI maps them, it does not solve them.

sections.position: The Lab puts three forces first for a young Indian architect: heat, water and the city itself. Not because nothing else matters — seismic risk, air, land, money and carbon all do — but because these three are measured, dated and public, and they decide the section of almost every building here. The India Meteorological Department declares heat waves by published criteria. NITI Aayog's water index reported that, as of 2014, no major Indian city supplied water round the clock to all its people. Floods are mapped from satellites. AI tools can map these layers. Designing against them is still your job.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A claim with a source can be checked and built on; a slogan like "the planet is burning" gives you nothing to draw. Three forces with public data behind them give a first-year student something to draw against on the first day, and the habit they teach — which report, which year, which number — transfers to every other force later.
sections.strongestObjection: "Three" is a curricular choice, not a fact about India. Seismic zoning, air pollution, land and tenure, ecology, affordability, infrastructure, material supply, regulation and embodied carbon could each claim a place on the list, and in Guwahati, Delhi or Bhuj a different three would be truer. A tidy trio risks teaching students to stop counting at three.
sections.revisionCondition: If the Lab's own site dossiers, across regions, show a fourth force deciding more sections than one of these three — seismic in the north-east, air in the Indo-Gangetic plain — the list changes, and the card with it. We check the dossiers every edition.
sections.inTheStudio: A first-year site in Hubballi. One student writes "the site is very hot" on the sheet. Another writes the climate zone, the months the IMD issued heat warnings for the district last year, and where the afternoon sun falls on the plot — then draws the shade to match. The jury can argue with the second sheet. The first sheet only says it was hot.
sections.watchForThis: Asking a chatbot "is my city water-stressed?" and taking the fluent paragraph as a fact. Ask instead: which report, which year, which number. If it cannot name them, it is only repeating the usual paragraph.
sections.tryIt: Pick your own city. Find one number about its heat from the IMD, one about its water from NITI Aayog's index or your city's water board, and one flood map from Bhuvan. Write each with its source and its date. Then take one claim you heard this year — "it was the hottest May ever", "we had a heat wave all week" — and check it against the IMD's own published station data and its criteria: did the numbers meet the rule, or not? Three lines and one check, and you have the start of a site dossier.
sections.proveIt: Name the three forces the Lab puts first, say why they are the Lab's choice rather than a fact, and for one of them show a number, where it came from, and when it was measured.
sections.howItWorks: Heat, water and flood data come from different bodies. Temperature comes from the IMD's station network, and the heat-wave criteria are published in its own FAQ. The IMD sets thresholds by station type, by absolute temperature and by departure from normal. A station qualifies only if its maximum reaches at least 40 °C on the plains or 30 °C in the hills; at the coast a departure of 4.5 °C counts once the maximum reaches 37 °C. On the plains, then, a departure of 4.5 to 6.4 °C above normal is a heat wave and more than 6.4 °C a severe one; or, whatever the normal, an actual maximum of 45 °C is a heat wave and 47 °C a severe one. The IMD declares it when the criteria are met at two or more stations in a meteorological sub-division on two consecutive days. Water comes from state and city boards, gathered nationally in NITI Aayog's Composite Water Management Index, whose 2019 edition notes that five of the world's twenty largest cities under water stress are in India. Flood extent comes from satellites, served on ISRO's Bhuvan portal. AI tools can fetch, join and map these layers quickly, and a language model can help you write the steps — the maps-as-data card shows how. The figures are measured again every season and the reports are reissued. That is why this card is marked EVOLVING: the forces stay, the figures change.

topics.subject: Foundations
topics.name: Same input, same output?

grounding.ref: Gopalan & VanLeeuwen, A Topological Approach to Creating any Pulli Kolam (2015)

topics.description: A fully written-out rule gives the same pattern every time. A generative model gives a draw. Two different machines. Write a rule out completely — every step fixed — and ten people following it produce ten copies of the same drawing. That is deterministic generation: same input, same output, every time.
evidence: Run one fully written-out rule three times on paper — a kolam rule tightened until only one drawing fits. Then run one image prompt three times. Lay the six results in two rows. Write one sentence on what stayed the same in each row, and why.
Explain, with one hand-drawn example and one generated example, the difference between same-input-same-output and same-input-different-output, and which of the two you would trust without looking.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain, with one hand-drawn example and one generated example, the difference between same-input-same-output and same-input-different-output, and which of the two you would trust without looking.

card.oneLiner: A fully written-out rule gives the same pattern every time. A generative model gives a draw. Two different machines.

sections.idea: Write a rule out completely — every step fixed — and ten people following it produce ten copies of the same drawing. That is deterministic generation: same input, same output, every time. Loosen it into a rule system and it defines a space of valid outputs: one pulli grid admits many valid kolams. A generative AI model is a third thing. Give it the same prompt ten times and you get ten cousins, each a draw from a range of likely answers: probabilistic generation. A rule is checked by reading it. A draw is checked by looking at what came out.
sections.whyItMatters: Most confusion about AI in design comes from treating a draw as if it were a rule. Knowing which machine you are holding tells you how to check its work.
sections.inTheStudio: A Grasshopper definition rebuilds the same façade every time you open it. An image model given "a brick façade with deep windows" gives you a new one each run. One is a recipe. The other is a roll of the dice. You keep the recipe. You take several rolls and compare them.
sections.watchForThis: "The AI decided on this design." A draw is not a decision. And the reverse trap: expecting a rule system to surprise you. It cannot, and that is its strength.
sections.tryIt: Run one fully written-out rule three times on paper — a kolam rule tightened until only one drawing fits. Then run one image prompt three times. Lay the six results in two rows. Write one sentence on what stayed the same in each row, and why.
sections.proveIt: Explain, with one hand-drawn example and one generated example, the difference between same-input-same-output and same-input-different-output, and which of the two you would trust without looking.
sections.howItWorks: Deterministic systems — a fully specified kolam procedure, Sulba constructions, talamana tables, CAD, parametric scripts — carry their result in their rules. Run them twice and nothing changes unless a rule changes. Rule systems such as the kolam grammars sit between: they fix what counts as valid and leave the choice among valid patterns to the hand. Probabilistic systems hold a spread of possible outputs with a likelihood for each, and a sampler picks one. Settings can narrow the spread, and some tools offer a fixed "seed" that makes a run repeatable, but the machine is still choosing from a distribution rather than following a recipe. This idea sits under THE DRAW and the two "generatives" elsewhere on this map.
sections.lineage: Three Indian rule systems open this strand on purpose — the kolam, the Sulba constructions, the talamana tables. They show that rules making form is old, familiar and done by hand, so that the probabilistic machine can be met as a new kind of machine rather than as magic.

sections.idea: Some models sort things that already exist: this is a chair, this façade is Art Deco. Others make something that was not there before: a new image, a new paragraph. Sorting can be checked against a label: the façade is Art Deco or it is not, even where the edges of "Art Deco" are arguable. Making has no single answer sheet. card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: same word, two different machines — one searches a space you defined, one predicts from its data.

sections.position: Generative design and generative AI are not synonyms, and the Lab keeps them apart. Generative design is an umbrella over several lineages — search and optimisation, shape and graph grammars, agent-based systems — and what they share is that a designer sets up the space: the rules, the goals, the scoring. Every result traces back to that setup. Generative AI predicts plausible results from patterns in its training data, with no goals and no scoring unless you bring them. The shared word hides that difference, and the difference decides how each is checked.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Clients and juries mix these up constantly, and a designer who can separate them in one sentence can lead the conversation. The two are verified differently. A generative-design result is checked against the goals and rules you wrote. A generative-AI result is checked by looking, against criteria you bring afterwards. A student who confuses the two either distrusts an honest search or over-trusts a likeness.
sections.strongestObjection: The clean split is already leaking from both sides. "Generative design" is not one machine, and some of what sits under it — evolutionary solvers, learned surrogates, agent systems — is as opaque as any model. Meanwhile generative AI is being wrapped in goals, constraints and scoring: a diffusion model inside an optimisation loop is both machines at once. Calling them "opposite" may teach students a boundary the tools no longer respect.
sections.revisionCondition: When mainstream design tools ship generative AI inside a scored, constrained search as the default rather than the experiment, so that "which machine is this?" has no single answer for most tools a student meets, we rewrite this card around a different question: which parts are searched against goals, which parts are predicted, and how is each checked. We test this every edition against what the tools actually ship.
sections.inTheStudio: A structural layout tool that minimises steel tonnage under your loads is generative design. The tonnage number defends the result. An image model's "efficient structure" is a picture of what efficient structures look like. One is engineering. The other is a summary of how such structures look.
sections.watchForThis: The phrase "the computer optimised it" attached to a generated image. Optimisation needs a measurable goal. Without a goal there is no optimisation, only likeness.
sections.tryIt: Write one design goal as a number (daylight hours, steel weight, travel distance). Ask: which of my tools can actually score against this? That question separates the two machines at once.
sections.proveIt: Explain to a junior the difference between a tool that searches your goals and a tool that predicts its data, with one honest use for each.
sections.howItWorks: Most generative design belongs to the search family — define, search, score, rank — with grammar-based and agent-based cousins beside it. You can usually see every step. Generative AI belongs to the prediction family you have met across this ring. Hybrids are arriving that wrap one inside the other. If you know the parts, you can read the hybrids too.

card.oneLiner: Gather, train, test, deploy — and each step can fail in its own way.

sections.idea: A model is built in steps. Gather data. Train on it. Test what was learned. Put it to work. Each step has its own failure: gathering can bake in gaps, training can memorise instead of learn, testing can miss what the test never asked, deployment can meet a world the data never showed. When a tool misbehaves, the useful question is: which step is showing?
sections.whyItMatters: "The AI is wrong" is a dead end. "The gathering step missed our building type" is a diagnosis, and sometimes a fix.
sections.inTheStudio: A plan-reading tool fails on your hand-drawn survey. It was probably never shown one at the gathering step. That is not stupidity. That is its diet.
sections.watchForThis: Test scores quoted without asking what the test contained. A model can pass its own exam and fail in your studio, because its makers set the exam.
sections.tryIt: Pick one tool you use. Try to find one fact about each step: what data, trained by whom, tested how, deployed where. The steps you cannot find out about are worth noticing too.
sections.proveIt: Walk through the four steps for any real system and name one way each step can fail.
sections.howItWorks: Professionals split the steps further — cleaning, labelling, validation splits, fine-tuning, monitoring — but the four-step skeleton holds. Later ideas on this map attach a failure to each step: bias at gathering, memorisation at training, benchmark traps at testing, drift at deployment.

card.oneLiner: Human choices run through the whole system — including the last one: yours.

sections.idea: Human choices run all the way through these systems. People gathered and labelled the data. People tuned the model by rating better and worse answers. People decided where it ships and what it refuses. And a person receives the output. "The machine did it alone" is never the whole story. There are people at every joint of the loop, whether you see them or not.
sections.whyItMatters: Wherever there is a person, responsibility can sit. Finding the people in the loop is how you find who answers for what.
sections.inTheStudio: Your rendering tool refuses certain content, prefers certain styles, softens certain edges. Each of those is a person's decision, shipped to millions of users. You are working with strangers through the tool.
sections.watchForThis: The passive voice: "the image was flagged," "the answer was filtered." Someone built the flag. Someone tuned the filter. The grammar hides the people.
sections.tryIt: Take one refusal or odd behaviour from a tool you use, and write down which human decision most likely produced it. You will rarely be sure. Notice that too.
sections.proveIt: Trace one output you received through the loop: whose choices touched it before it reached you, and where your own choice enters.
sections.howItWorks: The tuning step has a name worth knowing: reinforcement learning from human feedback. Thousands of people rate answers, and their preferences are trained into the model's manners. Labelling and rating is real work by real people, and most of it is invisible. What this ring adds to PEOPLE is that the people are specific jobs — labellers, raters, red-teamers, policy writers, evaluators — and each job is a place where a decision can be questioned. The ethics strand of this map returns to them.

card.oneLiner: Old software follows written rules. These systems picked up patterns instead.

sections.idea: Older design software follows rules a person wrote by hand. It can search, solve and simulate, but somewhere a programmer can point to the line that did it. The systems on this map are different. Nobody wrote their behaviour line by line. They were shown enormous numbers of examples and kept the patterns. That is why they can surprise you, and why nobody, including their makers, can list exactly what they will do.
sections.whyItMatters: There is no rulebook to look up. To work with these tools you test them, because there is no manual to read.
sections.inTheStudio: CAD snaps a line to a grid because a programmer wrote that rule. An image model puts a shadow where shadows usually go in photographs. One follows a rule. The other follows a habit.
sections.watchForThis: Asking "why did it do that?" and expecting a clean answer. Pattern-machines often cannot show their reasons the way rule-machines can.
sections.tryIt: Give the same simple request to a calculator and to a chatbot, five times each. One never varies. One drifts. That difference is the whole idea.
sections.proveIt: Explain the difference between rule-following software and pattern-learning software, with one example of each from your own toolbox.
sections.howItWorks: Training adjusts millions of internal numbers until the machine's outputs match its examples well. What is stored is not sentences of knowledge but weights: numbers that say how strongly each part connects to the next. The behaviour lives in the weights. It is real, but it is not written down anywhere.
sections.lineage: Hand-written rules ran computing for fifty years, and still run most of it. Learning took over wherever there were too many rules to write: seeing, speaking, and making pictures of the world.

topics.name: A picture of a plan is not a plan

grounding.ref: MDN, Image file type and format guide

topics.description: A raster image is a grid of colours, a CAD drawing is lines with lengths, a BIM object is a wall that knows it is a wall — and a generated image is only the first. A plan can be stored three ways. A raster image — a JPEG, a PNG, a screenshot — is a grid of tiny coloured squares: no lines, no lengths, only colours in positions.
evidence: Draw a small room in any CAD tool: four walls, one door. Export it three ways — as a DWG or DXF, as a PDF, and as a PNG screenshot. Open each and try to measure the door. Then, in the CAD file, select one wall and list what the software knows about it. If your college has a BIM tool, do the same with a wall there and compare the two lists.
Explain the difference between a raster image, a vector drawing and a BIM object using one wall, and say which of the three a generated image is.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain the difference between a raster image, a vector drawing and a BIM object using one wall, and say which of the three a generated image is.

card.oneLiner: A raster image is a grid of colours, a CAD drawing is lines with lengths, a BIM object is a wall that knows it is a wall — and a generated image is only the first.

sections.idea: A plan can be stored three ways. A raster image — a JPEG, a PNG, a screenshot — is a grid of tiny coloured squares: no lines, no lengths, only colours in positions. A CAD drawing is vector: each line is stored as geometry, with a start, an end and a length, so it can be measured. A BIM model stores a wall as an object that knows it is a wall, with thickness, material and openings. An image generator makes the first kind only. A generated plan cannot be measured: a raster has nowhere to keep a length.
sections.whyItMatters: Once you know which of the three kinds a file is, you know what can be asked of it. You can ask a raster what it looks like. You can ask a vector what it measures. You can ask a BIM object what it is.
sections.inTheStudio: A client sends a photograph of a plan on WhatsApp and asks you to "just pull the dimensions". You cannot. The photo has pixels where the drawing had lines. You redraw it, and you measure the real room to check, because the pixels never held the number. A generated plan is that photograph, with no original behind it.
sections.watchForThis: A generated image that looks like a drawing. Clean black lines on white, a north arrow, a scale bar. Every one of those is painted. The scale bar is a picture of a scale bar. Nothing in the file is 1:100.
sections.tryIt: Draw a small room in any CAD tool: four walls, one door. Export it three ways — as a DWG or DXF, as a PDF, and as a PNG screenshot. Open each and try to measure the door. Then, in the CAD file, select one wall and list what the software knows about it. If your college has a BIM tool, do the same with a wall there and compare the two lists.
sections.proveIt: Explain the difference between a raster image, a vector drawing and a BIM object using one wall, and say which of the three a generated image is.
sections.howItWorks: A raster stores colour values in a grid; zoom in and the squares show. A vector format stores drawing commands — lines, arcs, shapes — as numbers in real units, so the same file renders sharp at any size. A BIM model stores building elements as objects with properties and relationships. In the open IFC standard, for instance, a wall is an IfcWall: a vertical construction that may bound or subdivide spaces, with its openings attached to it as objects of their own. Today's image generators work in pixels: diffusion models, and most other image generators in wide use, produce a grid of colour values, and DIFFUSION on the Generative Mechanics strand shows how. A model can be asked to draw something that resembles a plan, and with a control input it can be held close to a plan you supply, but the output file is still a raster. The machine does not lack a ruler so much as a place to keep a length. Turning a raster back into geometry — vectorising a scan, reading a plan from a photograph — is a separate task, and current benchmarks find models well behind people at it. NO RULER, READ A PLAN and BIM MEETS AI on this map each start from this card.

topics.name: Prediction, not understanding
topics.description: The machine continues patterns. It does not know what they mean. Many language models generate by predicting the next token, again and again, from patterns in their data. Image models built on diffusion work differently: they turn noise into a picture step by step, steered by your words.

card.oneLiner: The machine continues patterns. It does not know what they mean.

sections.idea: Many language models generate by predicting the next token, again and again, from patterns in their data. Image models built on diffusion work differently: they turn noise into a picture step by step, steered by your words. Neither kind knows what is true, wants anything, or has stood on a site. Each produces what is likely. When the output is right, that is the pattern working. When it is wrong, that is the pattern working too.
sections.whyItMatters: Once you see every output as a prediction, you stop asking "does it know?" and start asking the useful question: "is this prediction good enough for my purpose, and how would I check?"
sections.inTheStudio: Ask for "a section through a courtyard house" and you get what sections of courtyard houses tend to look like, not a section of any house that could stand. Likely is not the same as true.
sections.watchForThis: The words "it understands me." It matched your words. From the outside, matching looks like understanding.
sections.tryIt: Ask a chatbot something about your street that only a local would know, once in English and once in Kannada. Watch it produce a confident, likely, wrong answer in both, and notice whether the Kannada one is thinner. That is prediction without any knowledge of the place.
sections.proveIt: Explain to a classmate why a model can be fluent about a place it knows nothing about, and why that fluency is not a fault but the way the machine works.
sections.howItWorks: During training a language model plays a guessing game billions of times: hide the next piece, predict it, adjust. A diffusion model plays a different game: add noise to a picture, learn to take it away. What comes out of either is a machine that produces what is likely. Meaning, checking and responsibility were never part of the game. They arrive when you do.

sections.idea: The same prompt can give you a different result each time, because each output is one pick from a range of possibilities. A draw, not an answer. Turn the randomness setting down and the picks repeat; turn it up and they scatter. What the machine really holds is the whole range. Every single output is just one visit to it.

sections.howItWorks: At each step the model holds a spread of likely continuations, each with a probability. A sampler picks from that spread; settings like temperature widen or narrow the picking. sections.idea: Before any AI there is data: site readings, surveys, costs, climate numbers. Reading data means asking three questions. What does it actually say? What was measured, by whom, when? card.oneLiner: Retrieval returns what exists. Generation makes new output. One answer can do both, and confusing them is expensive.

sections.idea: Retrieval brings back things that already exist, and each result has an address: you can go there and check. Generation makes a new output that may look exactly as trustworthy and have no address at all. A generated answer is not a lie; it can be correct, and it can be built from retrieved material. But the two feel the same in a text box, and one answer can be both at once. Underneath, they are different operations.
sections.whyItMatters: "Where did this come from?" has an answer for search and often none for generation. Professional work depends on that question.
sections.inTheStudio: A search for IS-code ventilation requirements returns documents you can cite. A chatbot's answer about the same code may be a fluent blend of many codes. You cannot cite it, and you can only check it by opening the real code.
sections.watchForThis: Tools that mix both modes in one box: retrieved facts and generated filler in a single smooth paragraph. You cannot see the joins.
sections.tryIt: Ask the same factual question to a search engine and a chatbot. For each claim in the chatbot's answer, try to find its address. Some claims will have none.
sections.proveIt: Explain the difference between a result you can trace and an output that was generated, and why a generated answer can still be correct.
sections.howItWorks: Modern systems increasingly join the two together: retrieve real documents first, then generate an answer from them. Done well, the answer carries addresses with it. Done badly, you cannot see the joins. A card higher up this map keeps apart the four places a system's knowledge can come from: its weights, the context you give it, what it retrieves, and what the product stores. topics.description: Data used to learn, data used to tune and data used to judge must stay in three separate piles, or the score lies. A model is taught on one pile of data. It is tuned on a second pile: the builders try settings, look at the results on this pile, and adjust.
evidence: Take twenty reference photographs of one building type. Work out a rule for recognising the type from the first fourteen. Then test your rule on the remaining six, and separately on the same fourteen. Write both scores down. The gap between them is what the separate piles are for.
Explain why a model must be judged on data it never learned from, and say what goes wrong with the score when the two piles mix.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain why a model must be judged on data it never learned from, and say what goes wrong with the score when the two piles mix.

card.oneLiner: Data used to learn, data used to tune and data used to judge must stay in three separate piles, or the score lies.

sections.idea: A model is taught on one pile of data. It is tuned on a second pile: the builders try settings, look at the results on this pile, and adjust. Then it is judged on a third pile it has never met. The three piles must stay separate. If the judging pile leaks into the teaching pile, the model has seen the exam before it sits it. The score goes up, and the model has not got better. That is why a published score can be higher than the model deserves, and a studio test much lower.
sections.whyItMatters: Every score you will ever be shown was produced on some pile. Whether that pile was truly separate decides whether the number means anything.
sections.inTheStudio: A plan-reading tool is sold with a high score on a set of floor plans. You try it on your studio's plans and it misreads half of them. One likely reason: the test plans came from the same archive as the training plans, so the exam was full of drawings the model had already seen. Your plans were not in either pile.
sections.watchForThis: Checking your own work against the examples you learned from. You practise on ten past jury sheets and then judge yourself on the same ten. You will look good. That is the same leak, done by hand.
sections.tryIt: Take twenty reference photographs of one building type. Work out a rule for recognising the type from the first fourteen. Then test your rule on the remaining six, and separately on the same fourteen. Write both scores down. The gap between them is what the separate piles are for.
sections.proveIt: Explain why a model must be judged on data it never learned from, and say what goes wrong with the score when the two piles mix.
sections.howItWorks: The textbook names are training set, validation set and test set. Google's course suggests a rough split of about 70, 15 and 15 per cent, and warns that the more often you use the test pile to make decisions, the less it can tell you about new data. Two failures live here. Overfitting: the model memorises the teaching pile instead of learning a pattern from it, so it does well on what it has seen and badly on anything new. Leakage: items from the test pile, or near-copies of them, sit in the training pile, so the test is no longer a test. For large models trained on much of the public internet, leakage is hard to rule out, because a benchmark published online may already be in the training data. That is one reason the benchmarks idea on this map asks what a score actually measured.

grounding.ref: OpenAI, How your data is used to improve model performance

topics.description: The model learned before you arrived. When you ask it something, it is being used, not taught. A model has two separate times. Training is when its weights were set: a long run over a huge pile of data, finished before you ever opened the app.
evidence: Tell a chatbot a made-up fact about yourself — say, that your studio is on the fourth floor. In the same chat, ask about it: it will remember, because the fact is still in front of it. Now open a brand-new chat with memory turned off and ask again. It has no idea. Nothing you said reached the weights.
Explain, in two sentences, why correcting a model today does not make it right tomorrow, and say what a provider's "we may train on your data" line actually means.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain, in two sentences, why correcting a model today does not make it right tomorrow, and say what a provider's "we may train on your data" line actually means.

card.oneLiner: The model learned before you arrived. When you ask it something, it is being used, not taught.

sections.idea: A model has two separate times. Training is when its weights were set: a long run over a huge pile of data, finished before you ever opened the app. Inference is the moment you ask it something: the weights are read, an answer comes out, and the weights are exactly as they were. Your conversation does not change them. It cannot. So when the tool gets your project right on Monday and wrong on Tuesday, it did not forget. It never learned. Training happens once, elsewhere. Using happens now, with you.
sections.whyItMatters: Most of the false hopes and the false fears about these tools come from mixing the two times up. "It will learn our studio's style from our chats" is a hope from the wrong time. "It is learning from me right now" is a fear from the wrong time.
sections.inTheStudio: You spend an hour correcting a chatbot's idea of a Mangalore tile roof. Next week, a new chat, and it is wrong again in the same way. You taught nobody. The weights were set months ago in a data centre. What you typed stayed in that one conversation.
sections.watchForThis: The line "your data is used to improve our models" in a provider's terms. That is real, and it is not the same as learning from you now. The provider may keep your chats and use them in a future training run, weeks or months later, for a future model. That is a privacy question about where your words go, not a sign that this model is learning. Some products train on consumer chats unless you opt out; business and API accounts often do not by default. Read the setting for the product you use.
sections.tryIt: Tell a chatbot a made-up fact about yourself — say, that your studio is on the fourth floor. In the same chat, ask about it: it will remember, because the fact is still in front of it. Now open a brand-new chat with memory turned off and ask again. It has no idea. Nothing you said reached the weights.
sections.proveIt: Explain, in two sentences, why correcting a model today does not make it right tomorrow, and say what a provider's "we may train on your data" line actually means.
sections.howItWorks: Training adjusts the weights, a little at a time, over billions of examples, until the model's guesses match its data well. That run costs machines, electricity and weeks. When it ends, the weights are frozen and copied to the servers that answer questions. Inference is one pass through those frozen weights per token. Nothing in that pass writes anything back. The things that seem like learning — the tool remembering your site, picking up your phrasing, knowing your last upload — are context and memory features added by the product, and FOUR PLACES on this map sorts them out. Fine-tuning is real learning, but it is a separate training run that a developer sets up on purpose, not something a conversation does; FINE-TUNE on the Generative Mechanics strand is about that. And the provider's right to keep and train on your chats is the third thing again: a future training run, on a future model, governed by your settings and the company's terms. TWO CLOCKS, beside this one, follows the two times to the cut-off date; TWO BILLS on Ethics & Provenance follows them to the energy bill.

sections.idea: A model lives on two clocks. Training is when its weights were set: pretraining on huge data, then post-training and fine-tuning, finished before you arrived at great cost in machines and energy. Inference is the moment it answers your prompt: the weights are read, not changed. Inference is usually cheaper per use, but not always cheap — long reasoning, video and agent runs burn real compute. The line that matters is this: nothing you type changes the weights. What you type, upload or have retrieved changes only what the model is given in the moment.
sections.whyItMatters: Once you know the two clocks, two puzzles clear up: why the model does not know yesterday's news, and why correcting it today changes nothing tomorrow.

sections.idea: Machines learn in four main ways. From labelled examples: here is a photo, here is its name. From raw patterns: here is everything, find the structure yourself. From the data itself: hide the next word or the next patch, predict it, check against what was hidden. No person labelled anything, and this is how the large models were built. From reward: try, get scored, try again. Most tools you use mix these. Knowing which mix built a tool tells you what it is likely to be good at, and where its blind spots are.
sections.whyItMatters: "How was it trained?" is the professional's first question about any tool, because the training method shapes how the tool behaves.

sections.watchForThis: Assuming a polite tool is an accurate tool. Politeness was trained in by reward. Accuracy was not necessarily trained in at all.
sections.tryIt: Ask a chatbot to disagree with an obviously weak idea of yours. Note how gently it tries. That gentleness is reward learning, and you can see it.
sections.proveIt: Name the four ways machines learn and match one real tool to each.
sections.howItWorks: The textbook names are supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised, and reinforcement learning. Modern chatbots stack them: self-supervised learning on huge amounts of text first, then tuning from human preferences on top. That second step is exactly where their agreeable streak comes from.

card.oneLiner: An AI system can know a thing from four different places, and each place has its own rules.

sections.idea: When a chatbot seems to know something, that knowledge came from one of four places. The weights: what the model learned in training, fixed before you arrived. The context: what sits in front of it right now — your message, the file you attached, the chat so far. Retrieval: what the product fetched from outside for this answer, such as a web search or a document lookup. Memory: notes the product stored about you from earlier chats. Only the first one is the model. The other three are added around it, and they differ from product to product.
sections.whyItMatters: "The AI knows my project" is four different claims. Which place the knowledge sits in decides whether it will still be there tomorrow, whether you can check it, and whether you can delete it.
sections.inTheStudio: You describe your site on Monday. On Tuesday the tool remembers the plot is in Hubballi. Nothing changed in the model. Either the product saved a memory note, or Monday's chat is still in the context. Test it: open a fresh chat and ask. If the site is gone, it was context. If it is still there, it was memory.
sections.watchForThis: Believing a fact is "in the AI" when it was in your own upload. The model read your brief in context and gave it back in clean sentences. That is your knowledge, returned to you. It was never learned.
sections.tryIt: Ask a chatbot three questions: one about a famous building such as the Taj Mahal (that is in the weights), one about today's weather in your city (it needs retrieval, or it will guess), and one about something you told it last week (it needs memory). For each answer, name the place it came from. Then open the product's settings and find the memory page, if it has one.
sections.proveIt: Name the four places an AI system can know something from, and give one example of each from a tool you use.
sections.howItWorks: The weights are the trained model: millions or billions of numbers set during training and then frozen. Your conversation never changes them. The context is what the model reads on every turn — the context window is its size, and CONTEXT WINDOW on this map is about that budget. Retrieval is a product step that runs before the model answers: a search, a database lookup, a file read, with the results pasted into the context. The research paper that joined a fixed model to a live document store called the two halves parametric and non-parametric memory, which is the weights and the retrieved text in plainer words. Product memory is different again: both ChatGPT and Claude describe it as stored notes drawn from your past chats, given to the model along with your new message, and both say you can view it, edit it, turn it off or delete it. So memory is a feature of the app, not of the model. The reason this matters for a designer: a model's habits come from its weights, and a grounded answer comes from context or retrieval. THE DIET, CLOSED WORLD and RAG on this map each take one of these places further.

sections.idea: A benchmark is a fixed exam: a set of questions, a marking scheme, and a number at the end. Benchmarks make progress visible and comparable, and the field runs on them. But an exam only measures what its setters thought to ask. A model can be trained on material close to the exam, tuned until its score rises, and still fail on work the exam never contained. A score tells you how a model did on that paper, on that day. It does not tell you how it will do on your brief.
sections.whyItMatters: Scores travel in headlines and sales decks. Knowing what a score is, and what it is not, stops a leaderboard from making a studio decision for you.
sections.inTheStudio: A model "scores 90 per cent on a reasoning benchmark" and is sold to your office on that basis. Then it reads a floor plan and mistakes a staircase for a corridor. The exam had no floor plans in it. Researchers who built a plan-reconstruction benchmark found leading models far below people, several at or below a random baseline; the exam that asked the studio's question returned a very different number.
sections.watchForThis: Goodhart's trap: once a score becomes the target, it can stop measuring what it was meant to measure. And watch for the benchmark you never see: the one that went unpublished because the model did badly on it.
sections.tryIt: Take any published benchmark score for a model you use. Find the benchmark's own description: what tasks, how many, who wrote them. Then write three questions from this week's studio work and check whether anything like them is in the exam.
sections.proveIt: Explain what a benchmark score does measure, what it cannot, and how you would decide whether a given score applies to your work.
sections.howItWorks: Benchmarks are datasets with answers. They can leak into training data, become saturated, or reward the exam's style rather than the underlying skill; the idea train · validate · test, beside this one, shows how a score can lie before the exam is even sat. Raji and colleagues have argued that treating a handful of benchmarks as measures of "general" capability has no sound basis. Well-made task-specific benchmarks are still the best public evidence we have. Blueprint-Bench and AECV-Bench are two built for the built environment, and they are why several cards on this map can say "measured" instead of "probably". sections.idea: The name "artificial intelligence" was put on paper on 31 August 1955, in a proposal for a summer workshop at Dartmouth College, New Hampshire. Four researchers — John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon — proposed a study on the conjecture that "every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it." The workshop met in summer 1956, and the field dates itself from it. The dream is far older; 1955 gave it a name, 1956 a group and a programme.
sections.whyItMatters: A field seventy years old has had seventy years of promises, failures and recoveries. Knowing that stops the present from feeling like magic, or like the end of the story.
sections.inTheStudio: The Dartmouth conjecture — that intelligence can be described precisely enough to be simulated — is the same bet a parametric script makes about a façade. The question for your studio is which parts of design can be described that precisely, and which cannot be yet.
sections.watchForThis: "AI" spoken of as one recent invention. The name was written down in 1955 and the field dates from the 1956 workshop; the methods behind today's tools come from several later decades; the tools on your phone are from the last few years. Three different ages, one word.
sections.tryIt: Read the first page of the 1955 proposal; it is short and free. Underline every goal the four proposers set. Mark which ones a tool you use today can do, which it cannot, and which you cannot tell.
sections.proveIt: Say where and when the name "artificial intelligence" came from, who proposed it, and one thing they hoped to do that still is not done.
sections.howItWorks: The proposal set out to find how to make machines "use language, form abstractions and concepts, solve kinds of problems now reserved for humans, and improve themselves." The workshop did not deliver these. It founded a community that spent decades trying, mostly by writing rules and logic by hand — the approach this map calls programmed rather than learned. The learning approach that dominates today also existed in early forms in the 1950s, but it needed data and computing power that did not yet exist.
sections.lineage: Alan Turing asked "Can machines think?" in print in 1950, six years before the name. The question is older than the field, and the field is older than the tools.

Everything in the model's weights is second-hand, limited, and fixed at the moment training stopped. What is frozen is the learned parameters; what the model is given in the moment — your prompt, an upload, a retrieved document — is not.

card.oneLiner: The weights are second-hand, limited, and fixed at training's end — and they never stood on your site.

sections.idea: Everything in the model's weights is second-hand, limited, and fixed at the moment training stopped. What is frozen is the learned parameters; what the model is given in the moment — your prompt, an upload, a retrieved document — is not. But the weights are where its habits live, and they have never stood on a site, felt a monsoon, or heard a client change their mind. That world is closed. Yours is not. The value you add starts at that boundary, because you are the one in the open world.
sections.whyItMatters: Half of professional judgment is knowing what the tool cannot know. The closed world is the permanent list of what it cannot know.
sections.inTheStudio: The model can describe "a narrow plot in a hot climate." It cannot know that your plot's neighbour built to the boundary last month, that the owner's mother must live on the ground floor, that the byelaw changed in March. Most of what is true about any project sits outside the closed world.
sections.watchForThis: Letting fluent general knowledge stand in for absent local knowledge. The model fills your silence with the world's averages, and an average has never built a building.
sections.tryIt: List ten facts your current project depends on. Tick the ones a model could possibly have. The ones left unticked are your open-world advantage, written out.
sections.proveIt: Explain the closed world in one sentence, and name three kinds of project truth that live permanently outside it.
sections.howItWorks: Retrieval, uploads, and live search pass open-world facts into the model's context for one conversation. That is what grounding means on this map, and the idea weights · context · retrieval · memory, beside this one, names the channels. Facts passed in are visitors, not residents. The model weighs them against its fixed habits, and the habits are heavy.

topics.name: The compute story

grounding.ref: Sevilla et al., Compute Trends Across Three Eras of Machine Learning (2022)

topics.description: Capability has tracked data, chips and money — and who owns compute shapes who owns capability. Capability in this field has tracked three things together: data, chips and money. Researchers who measured it found that the computing power used to train the largest models doubled roughly every six months after 2010 — far faster than the older pace of about twenty months — with a separate era of very large training runs from around 2015–16.
evidence: Look up the reported training compute or cost of one well-known model. Then look up the electricity demand of data centres in the IEA report. Write down which numbers you found, who reported them, and which you could not find. The gaps are part of the story.
Explain, in plain terms, why capability rose when it did, and name the three inputs it has tracked.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain, in plain terms, why capability rose when it did, and name the three inputs it has tracked.

card.oneLiner: Capability has tracked data, chips and money — and who owns compute shapes who owns capability.

sections.idea: Capability in this field has tracked three things together: data, chips and money. Researchers who measured it found that the computing power used to train the largest models doubled roughly every six months after 2010 — far faster than the older pace of about twenty months — with a separate era of very large training runs from around 2015–16. Compute is one large part of why capability jumped when it did — data, methods, engineering and money are the others — and it is why capability sits where the chips are. Compute costs money and burns electricity, so whoever owns compute shapes capability.
sections.whyItMatters: A tool's power does not come from nowhere. It was bought, with chips, data centres and capital. Knowing that lets you read AI news as industrial news, which is mostly what it is.
sections.inTheStudio: The render you get in twelve seconds ran on hardware you will never see, in a building you could one day be asked to design. The data centre is now a building type, and a client.
sections.watchForThis: Treating doubling curves as laws of nature. They are measurements of what companies chose to spend. Spending can slow, chips can be rationed, and efficiency gains can bend the curve. That is why this card is marked EVOLVING.
sections.tryIt: Look up the reported training compute or cost of one well-known model. Then look up the electricity demand of data centres in the IEA report. Write down which numbers you found, who reported them, and which you could not find. The gaps are part of the story.
sections.proveIt: Explain, in plain terms, why capability rose when it did, and name the three inputs it has tracked.
sections.howItWorks: Training compute is counted in floating-point operations; the doubling times above come from Sevilla and colleagues' 2022 survey of landmark models, which found a pre-2010 era tracking Moore's law at roughly twenty months, a deep-learning era at roughly six, and a large-scale era from late 2015 using ten to a hundred times more compute than the trend. On the energy side, the International Energy Agency's 2025 report *Energy and AI* gives the measured and projected electricity demand of data centres. Quote the report, not a headline. EVOLVING because the curve, the chips and the policy around them are all moving this year.

topics.name: Confident is not correct
topics.description: The smoothness is a fact about the writing, not about the world. A model sounds smooth and sure because it picks the most likely words. That confidence is a property of the writing, not evidence about the world.
evidence: Ask a model ten factual questions you can check. Before checking, mark how confident each answer sounded (1–5). Then check. Plot sound against truth. Study the mismatches.
Explain why a model's certainty of tone carries no information about correctness, and name the one thing that does.
topics.critPrompt: When a student trusts an answer, ask what they are trusting: its confidence, or a source they checked.

grounding.ref: Guo et al., On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks, 2017
IFLA, How to Spot Fake News
Xiong et al., Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (2023)

card.oneLiner: The smoothness is a fact about the writing, not about the world.

sections.idea: A model sounds smooth and sure because it picks the most likely words. That confidence is a property of the writing, not evidence about the world. Researchers who asked models to say how sure they were found them over-confident more often than not. Treat the tone as styling. You only get to the truth by checking.
sections.whyItMatters: People read confidence as competence. That reflex is older than machines, and these tools trigger it millions of times a day. The only fix is a habit: separate how an answer sounds from whether it is true.
sections.inTheStudio: Two answers about a building code: one hedged and right, one fluent and wrong. In a hurry, which gets pasted into the report? The fluent one. That is the whole danger, in one office moment.
sections.watchForThis: Your own relief when the answer arrives polished. Relief is not checking. The polish cost the machine nothing.
sections.tryIt: Ask a model ten factual questions you can check. Before checking, mark how confident each answer *sounded* (1–5). Then check. Plot sound against truth. Study the mismatches.
sections.proveIt: Explain why a model's certainty of tone carries no information about correctness, and name the one thing that does.
sections.howItWorks: Three things are easy to confuse here: the probability a model assigns inside, the confidence it states in words, and how assertive its prose sounds. Calibration — whether a stated or internal confidence matches the actual hit-rate — is its own measured thing, and the idea uncertainty has more than one meaning, higher on this map, takes it apart. This card is about the third thing: the tone. The judgment strand of this map builds the professional response: test before you trust.

grounding.ref: Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks (NIPS 2012)

topics.description: ImageNet, graphics cards, and the moment learning from examples overtook hand-written rules. In 2012 a neural network built by three researchers in Toronto — Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton — won the ImageNet competition, a yearly test of sorting over a million photographs into a thousand categories, by a margin that shocked the field. It had been given no rules for recognising cats or cars.
