card.oneLiner: AI reads images as well as makes them — and reading is the everyday work: surveys, audits, sorting, at a scale no hand can match.

sections.idea: Reading images is a different job from making them, and often the more useful one. A vision model can find objects, sort photographs, count windows, classify a building type from a street view, or flag where shade appears in each frame of a time-lapse. That is a large part of visual site documentation, at a scale no hand can match. It is not site analysis. Site analysis also needs time of day, access, where water collects, who uses an edge, regulation, and what a photograph leaves out. You choose what the tool looks for. You answer for what it misses.
sections.whyItMatters: Making images gets the attention. Reading them does the everyday work: surveys, audits, mapping. A student who can only generate has half the toolbox.
sections.inTheStudio: Two hundred photographs from a site walk along a bazaar street. A vision tool sorts them by shopfront type, counts awnings, flags every hand-painted sign. It also labels a chai stall's tarpaulin as "tent" and misses the temple gopuram behind the cables entirely.
sections.watchForThis: Trusting counts you did not spot-check. A vision model's error rate on your street is unknown until you measure it on your street.
sections.tryIt: Run fifty of your own site photos through any image-tagging tool. Check twenty tags by hand. Write down the error rate and the kind of thing it got wrong.
sections.proveIt: Name two site-analysis jobs an image-reading tool could speed up, and say what such a tool is likely to miss on an unfamiliar Indian street.
sections.howItWorks: Vision models learn from labelled images, or from image–text pairs in the CLIP family. NAME OR MAKE on Foundations sets out why a reader can be checked against truth while a maker cannot. Coverage follows the data. The well-photographed world reads well and the under-photographed world reads badly. DENSE, SPARSE applies here too.
sections.lineage: For decades, machine vision ran on features people designed by hand — edge detectors, corner finders, colour histograms. It worked only where the hand-written feature happened to fit. Convolutional networks changed that. The network learns its own features from labelled images, layer by layer, from edges up to parts and then objects. The 2012 ImageNet result, where a convolutional net beat hand-built methods by a wide margin, is usually taken as the moment the field turned. The current form is the vision-language model — CLIP and its descendants. It learns from image–text pairs rather than hand-assigned labels, so it can name things it was never explicitly taught. Each step widened what the machine could read, and each inherited the data problem from the step before. *(lineage as of Aug 2026)*

topics.name: Images out of noise
topics.description: The picture is not fetched; it forms, step by step, out of static. A diffusion model starts with a square of pure noise, like an untuned television. Step by step it removes a little noise.
evidence: Find a tool or demo that shows the intermediate steps (the Diffusion Explainer does this in the browser). Watch one image form. Note the step where you first recognise a building, and the step where the first wrong detail appears.
Talk through the denoising steps in plain words using a row of images from noise to finished picture, then explain why every detail can look believable while none of it is actually correct.

grounding.ref: Ho, Jain & Abbeel, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

card.oneLiner: The picture is not fetched; it forms, step by step, out of static.

sections.idea: A diffusion model starts with a square of pure noise, like an untuned television. Step by step it removes a little noise. At each step the prompt steers what the cleaner image should look like. After tens of steps, a picture stands where the static was. The picture was not pulled from a library, and no photograph was copied in. It formed, guided by patterns the model learned about how pictures tend to look. That is why a generated image can look right everywhere and still be made up in every part.
sections.whyItMatters: "Where did it get this image?" has no answer. The image has no source, only a process. Knowing that changes how you can use it and what you can claim about it.
sections.inTheStudio: A render shows a staircase that starts in the courtyard and leads into a wall. Nobody drew that stair. At each denoising step, "stair-like" and "wall-like" were both likely, and the process settled on both. That is not a bug. That is the process, with nobody checking it.
sections.watchForThis: Asking why the model "chose" a detail. It did not choose. Every detail is where a noisy path ended, not a decision.
sections.tryIt: Find a tool or demo that shows the intermediate steps (the Diffusion Explainer does this in the browser). Watch one image form. Note the step where you first recognise a building, and the step where the first wrong detail appears.
sections.proveIt: Talk through the denoising steps in plain words using a row of images from noise to finished picture, then explain why every detail can look believable while none of it is actually correct.
sections.howItWorks: Training adds noise to real images and teaches a network to predict that noise. Generation runs the prediction backwards, starting from pure noise. Text steers through a text encoder — often a CLIP-style one (SHARED SPACE) — and, in many pipelines, a setting called guidance (GUIDANCE on this strand). EVOLVING: diffusion is the dominant engine for images and video today, but some recent image systems generate differently — token by token, as language models do — and the field moves fast. The lesson holds for both: no source, only a process.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: call the unconditioned use of a generator a dreaming engine — best at mood and what-ifs, dangerous when "new" looks "finished".

sections.position: Some uses of a generative model are meant to invent freely, with nothing held to a real input: mood, atmosphere, what-ifs, images you could not have drawn. The Lab calls these dreaming engines — our name for one end of a continuum, not a kind of machine. The continuum runs: text only → a reference image → image-to-image at rising strength → an edge or depth map → generation conditioned on real geometry. This card is the free end. Its strength: it takes you somewhere you would not have gone. Its danger: the new place can look finished when nothing was designed.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Because students need a word for the moment, and the field's words — "unconditioned", "text-to-image" — name the setting, not the moment. Early in a project, with a question in hand, dreaming is research. Late, with a deadline, it stands in for design. Naming the two ends has, in our teaching, made students say which end they were at before they showed a picture.
sections.strongestObjection: "Dreaming engines" and "grounded generators" are not accepted technical categories, and naming them as a pair can hide what is actually true: the same model, with the same settings, sits at every point of one continuum, and the difference between the two ends is a conditioning input and its strength. A student who learns two species may look for two tools. The honest teaching is the continuum itself, and this card's name is a convenience laid over it.
sections.revisionCondition: If students taught the pair turn out to reason less well about conditioning strength than students taught the continuum alone, the names go and the continuum stays. If the field settles on its own word for the free end, we adopt it. Reviewed every edition.
sections.inTheStudio: Week one of a library brief: "what would a reading room feel like under a deep stone roof in the monsoon?" — twenty images, no plan, and a conversation about light. Week eight, the same prompt, dropped onto the sheet as "the concept". Same engine. Only the first was design.
sections.watchForThis: Presenting a dream as a scheme. If you cannot say which question the image answered, it was not a study.
sections.tryIt: Make a study with a dreaming engine. Before you generate, write the question you are asking in one line. After, write one line on whether the images answered it. Keep both lines with the images.
sections.proveIt: Name the moments in a project where free invention is the right tool, and show one study where you can say what question you asked it.
sections.howItWorks: Technically, a dreaming engine is any generator run without conditioning beyond text: pure text-to-image, high denoising strength, no control image. The same model becomes a GROUNDED generator the moment you hold it to a plan or a photograph (TWO STARTS and CONTROL INPUT are the mechanisms). The pair names two ends of one continuum of conditioning, not two kinds of machine. Sahil's essay on the two families makes the case; this card states it as the Lab's position.

topics.name: Embeddings, meaning as coordinates
topics.description: A token becomes a list of numbers, and in that space near means similar in use — the first of several number-spaces AI uses, each for a different job. AI uses several different number-spaces for different jobs. Here is the first.
evidence: Ask a model for the ten words closest in meaning to "verandah", then to "otla" or "thinnai" (or your region's word for the same thing). Notice where the list thins or drifts. That shows you how well the space covers your region's words.
Using the map-and-distance picture, explain why the model treats "threshold" and "entry" as neighbours — without reaching for a dictionary.

grounding.ref: Mikolov et al., Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
Pinecone, What is a Vector Database?

card.oneLiner: A token becomes a list of numbers, and in that space near means similar in use — the first of several number-spaces AI uses, each for a different job.

sections.idea: AI uses several different number-spaces for different jobs. Here is the first. Inside a language model, each token becomes a list of hundreds or thousands of numbers — an embedding — and as the model reads, that list is reshaped to carry the token's meaning in its sentence. In such a space, close means similar in use. "Courtyard" sits near "atrium" and far from "loading dock". Nobody told the model that; it learned the positions from which words appear together in training. Separate embedding models do the same for whole documents, which is what search runs on. Three more spaces follow.
sections.whyItMatters: When a tool treats two ideas as neighbours that you never paired, it is not confused. It is reporting a distance in its space. That distance tells you how the model holds your vocabulary.
sections.inTheStudio: You write "threshold" and get entrance steps and a door frame. In the model's space, "threshold" and "entry" are close. The spatial idea you meant — the pause between outside and inside — is a weaker neighbour, so you have to name it.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking there is one space. A language model's token embeddings, a search index's document embeddings, a CLIP-style text–image space and a diffusion model's latent are four different objects with four different jobs; the next three cards take them in turn. And thinking the space is a dictionary. There are no definitions at the points, only positions. "Similar" means "appeared in similar company", which is not the same as "means the same thing".
sections.tryIt: Ask a model for the ten words closest in meaning to "verandah", then to "otla" or "thinnai" (or your region's word for the same thing). Notice where the list thins or drifts. That shows you how well the space covers your region's words.
sections.proveIt: Using the map-and-distance picture, explain why the model treats "threshold" and "entry" as neighbours — without reaching for a dictionary.
sections.howItWorks: Early word embeddings (word2vec) were learned by predicting a word from its neighbours. The famous result was that directions in the space carried meaning. Inside a transformer the embedding is only the first layer; every layer after it reshapes the representation in context, so the same word carries a different list of numbers in a different sentence. A CLIP-style model learns a separate space in which images and captions can be compared (SHARED SPACE). A diffusion model works in yet another, its latent (LATENT). A multimodal chat model converts image patches into its own token space (ONE STREAM). Coverage is uneven in all of them, and DENSE, SPARSE takes that up.

card.oneLiner: Many products rest on a few model families — so tools that look unrelated can share strengths and blind spots, and a product can be several models at once.

sections.idea: A foundation model is trained once, on a very broad diet, then adapted to many jobs: chat, code, captioning, drafting. Many products rest on one of a few such model families, with an interface on top and often other parts — retrieval, OCR, a vision encoder, filters, tools. So tools that look unrelated can share strengths, manners and blind spots from one family. But a product can also be a system of several models, and its behaviour cannot be read off the headline model alone. A small model for one narrow task is different: cheaper, narrower, easier to test.
sections.whyItMatters: When two tools make the same mistake, the likely reason is that they share a model, not that the mistake is true. If you know which model sits under a tool, you know which other tools will make the same errors.
sections.inTheStudio: A "brief assistant" and a "spec writer" from two different companies both confuse plinth with skirting. That is not a coincidence. One model family under two products, one gap.
sections.watchForThis: Taking a second tool's agreement as confirmation. If both rest on the same model, you have asked one source twice.
sections.tryIt: Pick three AI tools you use. Find out which model is underneath each; it is usually one search away. Draw the map: how many model families, how many products — and which products turned out to be several models working together?
sections.proveIt: Explain why many different-looking tools can share the same weakness, say why a product's behaviour can still differ from its headline model's, and tell a foundation model apart from a small tool built for one narrow task.
sections.howItWorks: The term was coined in 2021 to name the shift from many task-specific models to a few general ones, adapted by prompting, fine-tuning or retrieval. Adaptation changes behaviour at the edges. The core habits come from pre-training. FINE-TUNE and RETRIEVE FIRST on this strand are the two main ways a foundation model is fitted to a studio.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Grounded generators
topics.description: The Lab's position: call the conditioned use of a generator a grounded generator — held close to a real input, worth it only if the input is. A grounded generator is held to a real input: a plan, a site photograph, a massing model, a control image. This is the conditioned end of the continuum DREAMING opens — reference → image-to-image strength → edge or depth map → real geometry.
evidence: Take one idea. Run it once free (text only) and once grounded (the same prompt plus your drawing as control). Put them side by side and list what stayed the same. That list is what your drawing actually decided.
Explain what a control input holds close and what it still leaves free, using your own two runs — and say why "holds close" is the honest phrase rather than "locks".
topics.critPrompt: Is the student grounding on inputs that carry real design thinking, or just dressing up a weak drawing in a strong style?

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: call the conditioned use of a generator a grounded generator — held close to a real input, worth it only if the input is.

sections.position: A grounded generator is held to a real input: a plan, a site photograph, a massing model, a control image. This is the conditioned end of the continuum DREAMING opens — reference → image-to-image strength → edge or depth map → real geometry. Its strength is that it stays close to what exists. Conditioning raises adherence to your plan or photograph; it does not make the geometry invariant, so you check it. The catch: the input has to be worth staying close to. Grounding adds no design thinking. It keeps whatever the input carries and dresses it up. A weak drawing comes back well-lit.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Grounding is the difference between a picture of a building and a picture of your building. It is also the easiest way to give a weak idea a finished face. Naming this end of the continuum makes the student ask, before the render, whether the drawing underneath has been judged.
sections.strongestObjection: No control mechanism warrants "the walls stay where you put them". Conditioning increases adherence; it does not lock geometry, and adherence varies with the conditioning scale, the pre-processing, the model, the prompt and the sampler. A category called "grounded" invites a student to trust the geometry because the input was real, which is the one thing a generated image never earns. The same objection as DREAMING also applies: this is a name for one end of a continuum, not a kind of engine, and the honest teaching is the continuum.
sections.revisionCondition: A conditioning method that provably preserves the input geometry — a render path rather than a generator — would make "grounded" a literal description and this card a FACTUAL one. Evidence that the name makes students trust conditioned output more than they should would make us drop the name and keep only the continuum. Reviewed every edition.
sections.inTheStudio: A plan with a 900 mm corridor and a bedroom that cannot take a bed, rendered through a control image into a warm, populated interior. The jury sees the warmth first. The plan is unchanged.
sections.watchForThis: Grounding on a drawing you have not yet judged. The render will not judge it for you.
sections.tryIt: Take one idea. Run it once free (text only) and once grounded (the same prompt plus your drawing as control). Put them side by side and list what stayed the same. That list is what your drawing actually decided.
sections.proveIt: Explain what a control input holds close and what it still leaves free, using your own two runs — and say why "holds close" is the honest phrase rather than "locks".
sections.howItWorks: Grounding is implemented as conditioning. Image-to-image starts from your picture (TWO STARTS). Control methods feed edges, depth or a plan alongside the prompt at every step (CONTROL INPUT). A written instruction — "keep the walls where they are" — asks; the conditioning input and its strength are what enforce, and even they enforce adherence, not a lock. The same model dreams or grounds depending on what you hold it to. The pairing with DREAMING comes from Sahil's essay on the two families; this card states it as the Lab's position.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: The joint text-image space
topics.description: In a CLIP-style model, a photo of a courtyard and the words "a photo of a courtyard" land at almost the same address — one family's space, built for comparison. In a CLIP-style model, an image encoder and a text encoder are trained together so that a caption and its picture come out close, and a caption and the wrong picture come out far apart. Across hundreds of millions of pairs, a courtyard photograph lands near the sentence "a photograph of a courtyard".
evidence: Upload one reference with no text. Then the same reference with one line naming the single quality you want. Compare. The difference is the text moving the address.
Describe what it means that, in a CLIP-style model, an image and its caption are trained to line up, and explain how a reference image and a text prompt get compared inside that space.
topics.critPrompt: When a student uploads a reference, can they say what the model really does with it, which is find its coordinate, instead of 'it looks at my image'?

grounding.ref: Radford et al., Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision (CLIP), 2021

card.oneLiner: In a CLIP-style model, a photo of a courtyard and the words "a photo of a courtyard" land at almost the same address — one family's space, built for comparison.

sections.idea: In a CLIP-style model, an image encoder and a text encoder are trained together so that a caption and its picture come out close, and a caption and the wrong picture come out far apart. Across hundreds of millions of pairs, a courtyard photograph lands near the sentence "a photograph of a courtyard". This is the second number-space on this strand; its job is comparison: is this image like that text? Many image generators read your prompt through such an encoder, which is partly why "make it like this reference" works. It is one family's space, not every model's.
sections.whyItMatters: In a pipeline built on this space, uploading a reference does not "show" the model anything. It hands the model a coordinate. What the coordinate captures — mood, palette, typology — is what you get back. What it does not capture is lost.
sections.inTheStudio: You upload a photo of a Chettinad house for its courtyard proportion. The result gives you its colours and columns instead. In a CLIP-style space, palette and ornament dominated the photo's address. Proportion was a smaller part of it.
sections.watchForThis: Saying "the model looked at my image". In a CLIP-style pipeline it found the image's coordinate, so say in words what you want from the reference as well, so that both addresses point the same way. And taking this for the space in which images are made. Generation happens in a different space — LATENT, next.
sections.tryIt: Upload one reference with no text. Then the same reference with one line naming the single quality you want. Compare. The difference is the text moving the address.
sections.proveIt: Describe what it means that, in a CLIP-style model, an image and its caption are trained to line up, and explain how a reference image and a text prompt get compared inside that space.
sections.howItWorks: The method is contrastive training (CLIP). An image encoder and a text encoder learn together, so that matching pairs score high and mismatched pairs score low. Many diffusion-based generators read the prompt through a text encoder of this kind; some newer ones use a language model's encoder instead. A multimodal chat model is a different design again. It does not drop your picture into this space; it converts image patches into tokens and feeds them in beside your words — ONE STREAM on this strand.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Latent space, the field of possibilities
topics.description: A latent diffusion model works in a compressed version of the image — not in pixels, and not in the embedding space either. Many image generators do not work in pixels. An autoencoder first compresses an image into a much smaller grid of numbers — its latent — and can expand a latent back into a picture.
evidence: Run one prompt eight times and lay the results out. Circle what every image shares. Then change one word and run eight more. What moved, and what stayed, shows you what your prompt decided and what the model's habits decided.
Explain what a latent is, why a diffusion model works in one instead of in pixels, and why two prompts close in wording give similar-looking images — without using a map picture.
topics.critPrompt: When every result has the same look, can the student name the corner of latent space they are stuck in, and say what small change to the prompt would move them out?

grounding.ref: Rombach et al., High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models

card.oneLiner: A latent diffusion model works in a compressed version of the image — not in pixels, and not in the embedding space either.

sections.idea: Many image generators do not work in pixels. An autoencoder first compresses an image into a much smaller grid of numbers — its latent — and can expand a latent back into a picture. The diffusion process runs on that small grid: it starts from noise there, is denoised there, and the result is decoded to pixels at the end. This is the third number-space on this strand. Its job is compression, so that generation is fast enough to use. It is not a map you walk about in, and a prompt is not a pin. The prompt steers each denoising step.
sections.whyItMatters: When every result looks the same, the model's learned habits are steering every run the same way. Change what steers it — a different anchor, a reference, a control input — rather than the number of words.
sections.inTheStudio: Ten runs of "a contemporary house in Goa" all give white render, laterite accent, pool, palms. That is a well-worn habit of the model. Change one anchor — "monsoon verandah, no pool, pitched Mangalore tile" — and the steering changes.
sections.watchForThis: Writing a longer prompt when you want a different result. Length does not change the steering. A different anchor does.
sections.tryIt: Run one prompt eight times and lay the results out. Circle what every image shares. Then change one word and run eight more. What moved, and what stayed, shows you what your prompt decided and what the model's habits decided.
sections.proveIt: Explain what a latent is, why a diffusion model works in one instead of in pixels, and why two prompts close in wording give similar-looking images — without using a map picture.
sections.howItWorks: Latent diffusion (Rombach et al.) compresses images with an autoencoder and runs the denoising inside that compressed space, then decodes back to pixels. Compression is what makes generation fast enough to use. The space is learned, so it is uneven (DENSE, SPARSE on this strand), and it has no measuring tape in it (NO RULER on Foundations). Some newer generators use other latents, or none; the lesson holds for all of them — generation is a learned transformation of noise, not a walk across a map.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Reasoning models think slow
topics.description: Some models answer straight off; a newer kind is trained to spend compute on intermediate working first — know which you are holding, and what the working proves. Some models predict the reply straight off. A newer kind is trained to spend more compute at answer time producing intermediate working — text that looks like planning, checking and backtracking — before it replies.
evidence: Give one genuinely hard design problem — a staircase that must fit a given well, under the code's riser and tread rules — to a fast model and a reasoning model. Compare the working, not the answers. Which one can you actually check?
Explain, with a design example, the difference between a fast one-shot answer and a slow, step-by-step reasoned one, and say when you would pay for the slow one.
topics.critPrompt: When a task is genuinely hard, can the student say why they would reach for a reasoning model and still check its working, rather than take the first reply?

grounding.ref: Generative AI’s Shift From Thinking Fast to Thinking Slow — generative-ais-shift-from-thinking
OpenAI, “Learning to reason with LLMs” / “Introducing OpenAI o1-preview”, Sept 2024 — AIME 2024: o1 83% (consensus of 64 samples; 74% on a single sample) vs GPT-4o 13%

card.oneLiner: Some models answer straight off; a newer kind is trained to spend compute on intermediate working first — know which you are holding, and what the working proves.

sections.idea: Some models predict the reply straight off. A newer kind is trained to spend more compute at answer time producing intermediate working — text that looks like planning, checking and backtracking — before it replies. It costs more. On hard problems with checkable answers it does much better. Two cautions. The working is generated too, so it is not proof the answer is right. And the product may show you a summary of it, or none. Knowing which kind you hold tells you how to treat the first answer: a draft to test, or a result whose working you read.
sections.whyItMatters: The wrong match wastes effort either way. A reasoning model for a caption is slow for no reason. A fast model for a structural logic question gives you fluent nonsense quickly.
sections.inTheStudio: "Can a 4.5 m span in 230 mm brick carry a first floor with a 1.2 m cantilever?" A fast model answers in a paragraph. A reasoning model sets out assumptions, checks them against each other, and says where it is unsure. You still open the code and do the sum. But now you have working to check.
sections.watchForThis: Treating the visible "thinking" as proof. It is generated too. It is better evidence than a bare answer, but it is still something to read and check, not a stamp of approval — and some products show you a tidied summary rather than the working that actually ran.
sections.tryIt: Give one genuinely hard design problem — a staircase that must fit a given well, under the code's riser and tread rules — to a fast model and a reasoning model. Compare the working, not the answers. Which one can you actually check?
sections.proveIt: Explain, with a design example, the difference between a fast one-shot answer and a slow, step-by-step reasoned one, and say when you would pay for the slow one.
sections.howItWorks: Reasoning models are post-trained (PRETRAINING / POST-TRAINING on this strand) to produce and use a chain of intermediate steps before the final answer, and to spend more compute at answer time on hard problems. That training improves results on verifiable tasks; it does not establish that the model reliably plans or checks in the human sense, and the displayed chain is not guaranteed to be a faithful record of the internal computation. The fact behind the shift: on the 2024 AIME — a hard American maths competition, one stage in selecting the United States team for the International Mathematical Olympiad — OpenAI reported its o1 model at 83% against 13% for GPT-4o on the same consensus-of-64 measure, and 74% on a single attempt (OpenAI, September 2024). EVOLVING: the category is new, every major lab now ships one, and how much of the gain carries over to design work is unmeasured.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Seed, temperature, and re-runs
topics.description: The seed fixes the start, temperature sets the boldness — a repeat on the same setup is a control you hold, not a guarantee. Two settings explain most re-runs. The seed is the number that fixes the random starting point — the exact pattern of noise, or the exact random draw in a text model.
evidence: Fix a seed. Run a prompt. Change one word and run again. Then unfix the seed and change the same word. Lay the four results in a square and describe what each pair shows.

Explain why fixing the seed lets you repeat a result on the same setup while re-rolling only gives a different one, say what else has to stay fixed for the repeat to hold, and describe what turning temperature up does to how spread-out the results get.
topics.critPrompt: When a student wants the 'same image but change one thing', do they fix the seed first, or just press regenerate and hope?

card.oneLiner: The seed fixes the start, temperature sets the boldness — a repeat on the same setup is a control you hold, not a guarantee.

sections.idea: Two settings explain most re-runs. The seed is the number that fixes the random starting point — the exact pattern of noise, or the exact random draw in a text model. A fixed seed makes a run repeatable on the same setup: same model, sampler, software and hardware. Change any of those and the same seed may give a different result. Temperature reshapes the spread the sampler draws from. Low, and the likeliest option wins almost every time. High, and the draw wanders further. Re-rolling without the seed fixed gives a different result you did not steer.
sections.whyItMatters: "Same image but change the roof" is impossible without the seed. With it, you change one thing and see one thing change.
sections.inTheStudio: You finally get a massing you like, change "brick" to "stone", and the whole building is different. You re-rolled. Fix the seed, then change the word.
sections.watchForThis: Tools that hide the seed. Many consumer apps do. If you cannot fix it, you cannot run a controlled comparison. Note that before you draw conclusions from two runs.
sections.tryIt: Fix a seed. Run a prompt. Change one word and run again. Then unfix the seed and change the same word. Lay the four results in a square and describe what each pair shows.
sections.proveIt: Explain why fixing the seed lets you repeat a result on the same setup while re-rolling only gives a different one, say what else has to stay fixed for the repeat to hold, and describe what turning temperature up does to how spread-out the results get.
sections.howItWorks: Generation needs random numbers. The seed is the starting value of the generator that supplies them, so the same seed gives the same sequence again. Temperature reshapes the probability spread before the draw — SAMPLING on this strand, THE DRAW on Foundations, seen from the sampler's side. Different tools use different samplers and step counts, so the same seed rarely matches across tools, and PyTorch's own documentation says results are not guaranteed to match across releases, platforms, or CPU and GPU, even with identical seeds. Record the model version and settings with the seed, or the seed alone records nothing.

topics.name: Synthetic data

grounding.ref: Shumailov et al., The Curse of Recursion: Training on Generated Data Makes Models Forget

topics.description: Models increasingly learn from material that other models made, and learning from echoes changes what a model can imagine. Training data used to mean things people made: photographs, drawings, sentences. Now a growing share of what models learn from is synthetic, meaning text and images produced by earlier models.
evidence: Generate "a traditional Indian house" ten times and save the set. Use three of those images as references and generate ten more. Compare the second set to the first, and both to a photograph of a real one. Describe what narrowed.
Explain why a model trained on model output tends to lose its rare cases, and name one situation where synthetic data is the right choice anyway.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain why a model trained on model output tends to lose its rare cases, and name one situation where synthetic data is the right choice anyway.

card.oneLiner: Models increasingly learn from material that other models made, and learning from echoes changes what a model can imagine.

sections.idea: Training data used to mean things people made: photographs, drawings, sentences. Now a growing share of what models learn from is synthetic, meaning text and images produced by earlier models. Some is made on purpose, to fill gaps. Some arrives by accident, because the open web is filling up with generated material. Synthetic data is useful. It can be made to order and labelled exactly. It also has a known danger. A model trained mostly on model output drifts towards the average of the average. Rare things — the unusual house, the minority building culture — fade first.
sections.whyItMatters: The question "where does the model's world come from?" now has a second answer: partly from other models. A designer who works from generated references, using tools that were trained on generated references, is looking at copies of copies.
sections.inTheStudio: A student's moodboard is twelve generated courtyards. Each looked plausible because it was built from the average of photographed courtyards. The next model, trained partly on images like those, learns an even narrower idea of a courtyard. The real one in the student's own town — with its odd proportions and its tulsi plant — is now two steps further from anything a tool will offer.
sections.watchForThis: Assuming synthetic data is always a problem, or never one. Carefully made synthetic data is how some models get good at rare cases. Unfiltered model output is how they lose them. The question is who made it, and whether anyone was checking.
sections.tryIt: Generate "a traditional Indian house" ten times and save the set. Use three of those images as references and generate ten more. Compare the second set to the first, and both to a photograph of a real one. Describe what narrowed.
sections.proveIt: Explain why a model trained on model output tends to lose its rare cases, and name one situation where synthetic data is the right choice anyway.
sections.howItWorks: Researchers trained models on their own output again and again, generation after generation, and measured the tails of the data — the rare cases — disappearing. They named the effect model collapse. In practice, labs now mix synthetic data deliberately with curated human data and filter what they scrape. So the pure case is a warning, not a forecast. How much of the open web is generated, and how well filtering works, are both moving numbers. That is why this card is EVOLVING.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Text-to-image vs image-to-image
topics.description: One starts from pure noise; the other starts from your picture, partly noised — you choose how much survives. In a diffusion or flow pipeline, text-to-image starts the denoising loop from pure noise, so layout, massing and viewpoint are invented fresh every run. Image-to-image starts from a noised-up version of a picture you supply.
evidence: Take one sketch. Run image-to-image at low, middle and high strength. Lay the three beside the sketch. Mark, on each, what survived and what was invented.
Explain why image-to-image keeps the layout that text-to-image makes up fresh each time, and describe what you give up as you turn denoising strength up.
topics.critPrompt: When a student wants to keep a building's massing but change the mood, can they say why image-to-image, not a fresh text prompt, is the right choice?

card.oneLiner: One starts from pure noise; the other starts from your picture, partly noised — you choose how much survives.

sections.idea: In a diffusion or flow pipeline, text-to-image starts the denoising loop from pure noise, so layout, massing and viewpoint are invented fresh every run. Image-to-image starts from a noised-up version of a picture you supply. The less noise you add, the more of your picture's structure survives. The more noise, the freer the model gets. The setting that controls this is usually called denoising strength. Choosing between the two modes is really choosing how much of your source to keep. Keep the massing and change the mood, or keep almost nothing and take a fresh look.
sections.whyItMatters: Most "it ignored my sketch" complaints come from a strength setting that is too high. Most "it just traced my sketch" complaints come from the same setting, too low.
sections.inTheStudio: You have a massing screenshot and want it at dusk, in brick, with people. Text-to-image gives you a different building. Image-to-image at moderate strength keeps your masses and repaints the rest.
sections.watchForThis: Using image-to-image on a weak drawing and expecting it to be redesigned. It keeps what you gave it. A wrong plan, lit beautifully, is still a wrong plan.
sections.tryIt: Take one sketch. Run image-to-image at low, middle and high strength. Lay the three beside the sketch. Mark, on each, what survived and what was invented.
sections.proveIt: Explain why image-to-image keeps the layout that text-to-image makes up fresh each time, and describe what you give up as you turn denoising strength up.
sections.howItWorks: Image-to-image adds noise to your picture part of the way along the same path training used, then denoises from there. The idea was set out in a method called SDEdit. It is the simplest form of grounding. CONTROL INPUT on this strand is the stronger form, where edges or depth are fed alongside the prompt at every step rather than only as a starting point. Other generator families — autoregressive image models, for one — have no denoising loop and do "start from my picture" differently; this card describes the diffusion and flow family.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Why 'left of' fails
topics.description: Models fumble "left of" partly because captions rarely say it — one measured cause among several, not a mystery. Ask for "a stair left of the door" and many image models give you a stair and a door in any arrangement. The captions the models learned from rarely say where things are.

People write "a stair and a door", not "a stair to the left of a door". Spatial words are rare in training data, so the model has had little practice. topics.name: Can the model read a plan?
topics.description: It reads the labels well, judges the space unevenly, and fails at the symbols — "saw" is not "understood". Reading a floor plan means holding three things at once: the geometry of the rooms, the connections between them, and the symbols — door swings, window breaks, stair arrows, the drawing's own notation. Current multimodal models have been tested on exactly this.
evidence: Give a model one of your plans and test three things in turn: read the labels; judge two adjacencies; count the doors. Score each against the drawing. If your sheet carries Kannada labels, run the label test twice — once on the Kannada sheet, once on an English copy — and score the difference. Keep the score sheet, dated, for the next model.
Show one thing a model reads on a plan and one thing it cannot, from your own test — and explain the gap between reading text on a drawing and understanding the drawing.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student show one thing a model reads on a plan and one thing it cannot, from their own test?

card.oneLiner: It reads the labels well, judges the space unevenly, and fails at the symbols — "saw" is not "understood".

sections.idea: Reading a floor plan means holding three things at once: the geometry of the rooms, the connections between them, and the symbols — door swings, window breaks, stair arrows, the drawing's own notation. Current multimodal models have been tested on exactly this. On AECV-Bench (2026) they read the text on a drawing well, reason about space unevenly, and do worst at the symbols — counting doors, windows and rooms — with wide differences between models and tasks. "It saw my plan" is true. "It understood my plan" is, on that evidence and today, mostly not true.
sections.whyItMatters: A model that reads your title block and room names will sound as if it has read your plan. Its fluent summary can hide that it never counted the doors.
sections.inTheStudio: You upload a hostel floor plan and ask for a fire-exit check. The model names the rooms from their labels, then reasons about travel distance from rooms it has not located, past doors it has not counted. The reply reads like a checker's report. It is a guess built from the labels.
sections.watchForThis: A plan summary that mentions every labelled room and no unlabelled one. That is the sign that it read the words, not the drawing.
sections.tryIt: Give a model one of your plans and test three things in turn: read the labels; judge two adjacencies; count the doors. Score each against the drawing. If your sheet carries Kannada labels, run the label test twice — once on the Kannada sheet, once on an English copy — and score the difference. Keep the score sheet, dated, for the next model.
sections.proveIt: Show one thing a model reads on a plan and one thing it cannot, from your own test — and explain the gap between reading text on a drawing and understanding the drawing.
sections.howItWorks: AECV-Bench tests how well current models read built-environment drawings: it finds them strong on document-style questions and weak on counting architectural objects, with door and window counts the worst, and the gap varying by model. That fits PHOTOS, NOT PLANS on Foundations: the training data was photographs, not drawing notation. PIXELS ARE NOT GEOMETRY on this strand gives the deeper reason — the model is reading a raster, not lines. EVOLVING because the benchmark exists to be re-run and drawing-trained models are an active line of work. This card carries its review date for that reason.

topics.name: Conditioning and control inputs
topics.description: Feed the model a depth map, an edge map or a plan alongside the prompt, and the output is held much closer to that geometry — closer, not locked. Generation does not have to run on text alone. You can condition it on structural inputs as well: an edge map, a depth map, a pose, a reference image, a line drawing of your plan.
evidence: Extract an edge map from one of your own elevations; most tools do it in a click. Generate three materials with the same control and seed. Then run the same prompts with no control. Lay the six out and describe what the control gave you.

Explain what a structural control input holds close and what it leaves free, and why a control image keeps the walls near their place when you change the prompt — and why "near", not "fixed", is the honest word.

grounding.ref: Zhang et al., Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion Models (ControlNet), 2023

card.oneLiner: Feed the model a depth map, an edge map or a plan alongside the prompt, and the output is held much closer to that geometry — closer, not locked.

sections.idea: Generation does not have to run on text alone. You can condition it on structural inputs as well: an edge map, a depth map, a pose, a reference image, a line drawing of your plan. In ControlNet-style diffusion systems the control input is read at every denoising step and constrains the output towards its geometry. Adherence rises a great deal; it is not guaranteed, and it varies with control strength, model and prompt. The prompt stays free to decide material, light and mood. The walls mostly stay where the edge map put them when "brick" becomes "glass". Check.
sections.whyItMatters: Conditioning separates what you have decided from what you are still exploring. That separation is the core skill in using these tools for design rather than for pictures.
sections.inTheStudio: You have a sketch elevation and want to see it in three materials. Edge-map control keeps the openings and proportions fixed across all three; only the prompt changes. Without control, you would get three different buildings.
sections.watchForThis: Conditioning on a drawing that carries no decisions — a box with holes — and reading the result as a design. The control holds the box. It was still a box. And writing "preserve the geometry" in the prompt instead of supplying a control: a written instruction asks; the control input and its strength are what enforce — and even they enforce adherence, not a lock.
sections.tryIt: Extract an edge map from one of your own elevations; most tools do it in a click. Generate three materials with the same control and seed. Then run the same prompts with no control. Lay the six out and describe what the control gave you.
sections.proveIt: Explain what a structural control input holds close and what it leaves free, and why a control image keeps the walls near their place when you change the prompt — and why "near", not "fixed", is the honest word.
sections.howItWorks: ControlNet, the best-known method, attaches a trained copy of part of the diffusion network. That copy reads the control image and feeds its influence into each step, scaled by a conditioning strength you can set. The base model is untouched. Other methods bring reference images in as extra tokens, and non-diffusion generators condition in their own ways. All of them are conditioning — an input that shapes every step. Image-to-image is different: it only sets the starting point (TWO STARTS). PIXELS ARE NOT GEOMETRY on this strand explains why even a well-held edge map is still a picture of lines, not lines.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Dense and sparse territory
topics.description: The Lab's position on why some prompts obey and others quietly drift — the shared space is not filled evenly. The learned spaces are not filled evenly. Styles photographed, published and captioned a great deal form dense territory; there, the model can be steered with small moves.
evidence: Choose two references: one canonical (a famous modernist house) and one local (a house from your town that has never been in a magazine). Predict which will steer cleanly. Run both. Then rescue the local one with an anchor photograph instead of more words. Then test the assumption itself: try a second regional type — a Chettinad house, a nalukettu, a Goan house — and see whether "regional" drifts as one thing or as several.
When your local-style prompt drifted, did you write a longer prompt, or did you recognise sparse territory and change the anchor image? Show both runs.
topics.critPrompt: When your local-style prompt drifted, did you write a longer prompt, or did you recognise sparse territory and change the anchor image? Show both runs.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position on why some prompts obey and others quietly drift — the shared space is not filled evenly.

sections.position:
The learned spaces are not filled evenly. Styles photographed, published and captioned a great deal form dense territory; there, the model can be steered with small moves. Styles with thin documentation sit in sparse territory; there, the model interpolates, fills gaps from its neighbours, and drifts. Which styles are sparse is uneven and has to be tested, not assumed: a Kerala nalukettu, a Chettinad house, a Ladakhi house and an ordinary Hubballi street differ enormously in how much has been photographed and captioned. We hold that this density map, not prompt skill, explains most of why prompts obey or fail.
> A prompt in sparse territory is an address in a town with no streets.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Because it predicts. Given two references, a student who knows the density map can say in advance which will steer cleanly and which will drift, and is usually right. It also changes the fix. In sparse territory a longer prompt does nothing. A good anchor image — a photograph of the actual vernacular — gives the model coordinates it never learned.
sections.strongestObjection: Prompt obedience does not reveal dataset density directly. What looks like sparse representation may come from several hidden parts of the system — how often a style appeared, how well it was captioned, what was filtered out, how the tokeniser splits its name, how the text and image encoders were aligned, what post-training did — and those are confounded. A style can be photographed often and captioned badly; another can be rare and still strongly encoded through its neighbours. Without access to those processes we cannot attribute a failure to data scarcity alone, so the position may be naming a symptom and calling it a cause. And the map is moving: a style that drifted last year may steer this year.
sections.revisionCondition: A measured coverage tool — a way to read, before generating, how well a style or region is represented in a given model — would turn this position from an inference into an instrument, and we would rewrite the card around it. So would a controlled study that separates frequency from caption quality and alignment and finds that density explains little of the steering failure. The Lab intends to run an Indian-typology benchmark after launch; this card and INDIA, NOW on Foundations will be re-read against its results. Reviewed every edition.
sections.tryIt: Choose two references: one canonical (a famous modernist house) and one local (a house from your town that has never been in a magazine). Predict which will steer cleanly. Run both. Then rescue the local one with an anchor photograph instead of more words. Then test the assumption itself: try a second regional type — a Chettinad house, a nalukettu, a Goan house — and see whether "regional" drifts as one thing or as several.
sections.takeItToCrit: When your local-style prompt drifted, did you write a longer prompt, or did you recognise sparse territory and change the anchor image? Show both runs.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Guidance, how hard it steers
topics.description: Too low and the image wanders off the brief; too high and it burns — the work lives between. Keep the seed and the prompt fixed. Run a low guidance value, a middle one and a high one.
evidence: Three images, one seed, one prompt, three guidance values. Label each with its value and write one word under it. Keep the sheet. It is your calibration for that tool.
Shown an image that is either blurred or burnt, trace the fault to the guidance setting rather than the wording, and say clearly what guidance controls and what the seed controls.
topics.critPrompt: Shown an image that is either mush or scorched, can the student trace it to the guidance setting rather than the wording of the prompt?

grounding.ref: Cho et al., Diffusion Explainer, IEEE VIS 2024

card.oneLiner: Too low and the image wanders off the brief; too high and it burns — the work lives between.

sections.whenToUse: Whenever a diffusion or flow tool exposes a guidance setting (often called "CFG", for classifier-free guidance) and the result is either a soft blur that ignores your prompt or a stiff, over-saturated image that looks shouted. If the tool hides the setting, this card does not apply to it.
sections.method: Keep the seed and the prompt fixed. Run a low guidance value, a middle one and a high one. The tool's documentation gives the usual range. Lay the three out. Low gives a soft, loose image that drifts from the words. High gives hard edges, burnt colour and repeated details. Pick the zone between, where the image follows the prompt and still looks natural. Note the value. Only then change the prompt or the seed. Guidance controls how closely the image follows the prompt. The seed controls the starting point. Change one at a time.
sections.watchForThis: Rewriting the prompt when the fault is guidance. A burnt image is not over-described. It is over-steered. A vague image is not always under-described. It may be under-steered.
sections.tryIt: Three images, one seed, one prompt, three guidance values. Label each with its value and write one word under it. Keep the sheet. It is your calibration for that tool.
sections.proveIt: Shown an image that is either blurred or burnt, trace the fault to the guidance setting rather than the wording, and say clearly what guidance controls and what the seed controls.
sections.howItWorks: At each denoising step the model makes two predictions, one with your prompt and one with no prompt. Guidance pushes the result further along the difference between them. More push means the image follows the prompt more closely, until the push overshoots and produces artefacts. This is a mechanism of particular diffusion and flow pipelines, not a law of image generation: some newer, distilled models build guidance in and hide the setting, and "too high and it burns" is a habit of today's pipelines rather than a durable principle. Where the setting is hidden you cannot calibrate it, and this method does not apply.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Models have temperaments
topics.description: The Lab's position: brief for a model's behavioural profile under the version you are using, rather than assume every model listens the same way. Different models show recognisably different behavioural profiles under a given version and configuration, and you get more by briefing for that profile than by assuming every model listens the same way. "Temperament" is our shorthand for the profile.
evidence: Give the same brief to two models and describe how their default manner differs, without claiming one is simply better
Adjust a prompt to suit a model’s disposition and show what improved
topics.critPrompt: Did you treat the model's temperament as something to brief for, or expect every model to respond the same way? Show the same brief in two models, and the adjustment you made.

grounding.ref: Prompt Personalities: How to Collaborate With ChatGPT and Claude — prompt-personalities-how-to-collaborate

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: brief for a model's behavioural profile under the version you are using, rather than assume every model listens the same way.

sections.dilemma: You have a brief that worked beautifully in one model. You paste it into another and get a flatter, more literal, or oddly cautious result. Do you conclude the second model is worse, rewrite the brief for it, or stop using one brief for all?
sections.choices: Rank the models and keep the "best". Keep one brief and blame the model that did not suit it. Or treat each model as a collaborator with a disposition — one wants a crisp task, another wants to know why first, a third pushes back on ambiguity — and adjust the brief to the disposition before judging the output.
sections.consequence: Rank the models, and you mistake fit for quality and lose the model that would have been right for the next task. Blame the model, and you learn nothing. Brief for disposition, and you pay a little time per model and get each one's strengths. You also risk reading personality into what is really a mixture of training data, system prompt and sampling.
sections.theCase: A studio asks two models for a design-intent statement for a school in a hot-dry town. One returns a crisp five-point list, on target but thin. The other asks two questions about the site before it writes, then produces a paragraph that reads like a colleague. The intern reports that the second "is better". The senior reruns the first with the two questions answered in the brief. The list becomes a paragraph too.
sections.takeItToCrit: Did you treat the model's temperament as something to brief for, or expect every model to respond the same way? Show the same brief in two models, and the adjustment you made.
sections.position: Different models show recognisably different behavioural profiles under a given version and configuration, and you get more by briefing for that profile than by assuming every model listens the same way. "Temperament" is our shorthand for the profile. It is real enough to plan for, even though it comes from training choices, system prompts and sampling rather than from a character — and it is measured on your tasks, never inferred as personality.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: In teaching, the students who adjusted for the profile got better work from every model. The students who ranked models got good work from one and gave up on the rest. The habit carries over when the models change.
sections.strongestObjection: "Temperament" may not be a stable thing at all. What the word bundles together — system prompt, sampling settings, refusal training, routing between models, context length, verbosity defaults, which tools are available, the interface — can each vary independently, and often do, release by release. If they vary independently there is no single underlying disposition to brief for; there is a list of settings, and the student has learned to read character into a configuration. Briefing for "the model's temperament" may then be less useful than briefing for the specific settings, and less honest.
sections.revisionCondition: If the profile differences between the major models shrink to noise on studio tasks, or if the components above are shown to vary so independently that a profile measured in March predicts nothing in June, or if wrappers expose the configuration directly so that "brief for the model" becomes "set the settings", the card retires into CHATBOT on Foundations. Reviewed every edition, with the same paired-brief test.
sections.howItWorks: Labs now deliberately shape a model's behaviour during post-training, and some describe how they do it. Add a system prompt and a sampler on top and you have a behavioural profile. It is stable within a release and configuration and unstable across them, so record the model version and settings beside any profile you measure. The review date in the status strip is doing real work here.

topics.name: One window, both modalities
topics.description: A vision encoder and a projector feed image tokens in beside your words — one attention stream, no translator in between. In many current multimodal chat models, a vision encoder turns your uploaded image into patches, a small trained projector turns them into tokens the language model can accept, and they enter the same sequence as your words. One set of attention weights then runs over the mixed stream, weighing a patch of the plan against a word in your question.
evidence: Upload a plan and ask one question that needs only the text on it (what is the room labelled at top-left?), one that needs only the geometry (how many doors open onto the corridor?), and one that needs both. Note which fail.

Explain, without using a "translator" picture, how a model reasons over an uploaded plan and a written question together — and tell apart a CLIP-style comparison space (SHARED SPACE) from image tokens entering a language model's window.

grounding.ref: Liu et al., Visual Instruction Tuning (LLaVA), 2023

card.oneLiner: A vision encoder and a projector feed image tokens in beside your words — one attention stream, no translator in between.

sections.idea: In many current multimodal chat models, a vision encoder turns your uploaded image into patches, a small trained projector turns them into tokens the language model can accept, and they enter the same sequence as your words. One set of attention weights then runs over the mixed stream, weighing a patch of the plan against a word in your question. That is why such a model can answer a question needing picture and words together, and why it can get both wrong at once. This is the fourth number-space: a conversion into the language model's own tokens.
sections.whyItMatters: Everything you know about attention now applies to your image as well as your text. A large image is a lot of tokens competing with your question.
sections.inTheStudio: You upload a ground-floor plan and ask "which rooms get morning light?" The model reads "north" from your title block, picks out windows from the patches, and reasons across both. When it is wrong, it is often because the patch it weighed was the wrong one, not because "the image side" failed.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking in the translator picture: "it describes the image to itself, then answers." Some older systems did that, and some pipelines still do. The stronger models reason over the mixed stream directly. The difference shows on questions that need spatial detail.
sections.tryIt: Upload a plan and ask one question that needs only the text on it (what is the room labelled at top-left?), one that needs only the geometry (how many doors open onto the corridor?), and one that needs both. Note which fail.
sections.proveIt: Explain, without using a "translator" picture, how a model reasons over an uploaded plan and a written question together — and tell apart a CLIP-style comparison space (SHARED SPACE) from image tokens entering a language model's window.
sections.howItWorks: Visual instruction tuning (LLaVA was an early open example) runs the image through a vision encoder, projects the features into the language model's token space with a small trained layer, and trains on image–question–answer data. Newer models train on mixed streams from the start. EVOLVING: architectures differ — projectors, cross-attention, native mixed training — and which design dominates changes year to year. The lesson about attention over a mixed stream holds across all of them.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: The perspective can lie
topics.description: Parallel lines that never meet, vanishing points that disagree — a convincing scene can be impossible. A generated render arrives, polished and atmospheric. Every surface looks real.
evidence: Trace the perspective lines on a generated render and find where they fail to converge
Show one image that looks convincing but whose vanishing points disagree
topics.critPrompt: Handed a slick render, did you test its perspective construction before trusting the space? Show the traced lines.

grounding.ref: Diffusion — How AI Paints from Noise

card.oneLiner: Parallel lines that never meet, vanishing points that disagree — a convincing scene can be impossible.

sections.dilemma: A generated render arrives, polished and atmospheric. Every surface looks real. Do you trust the space it shows — its depth, its heights, its room sizes — or do you spend ten minutes with a ruler on lines the client will never look at?
sections.choices: Trust it, because it looks right and time is short. Test it: trace the edges of floors, lintels and parapets, extend them, and see whether lines that are parallel in the world meet at one vanishing point on one horizon. Or generate the render with a control input that fixes the perspective from your own model, so the test is built in.
sections.consequence: Trust a broken perspective and the space you present does not exist. The room reads deeper than it could be, the ceiling higher, the street wider. Someone will measure it later — a client, a contractor, a jury with a scale rule — and the error becomes yours. Test it and you lose ten minutes and gain a checking habit. Build it in and you give up some freedom for a scene that holds together.
sections.theCase: A final-year student presents a generated interior of a double-height library. The juror asks for the section. Drawn against the render, the gallery's floor line vanishes to a point a metre above where the ground-floor window heads vanish. The two storeys were painted in two different rooms. The student had not traced a single line.
sections.takeItToCrit: Handed a slick render, did you test its perspective construction before trusting the space? Show the traced lines.
sections.howItWorks: Diffusion models learn what perspective looks like locally — edges that recede, shadows that lengthen — but they have no single camera model for the whole image. So separate regions of one image can follow different cameras. Work such as ControlVP adds vanishing-point constraints to generation. That is evidence that the failure is common, and a sign that it is being engineered away. EVOLVING for that reason.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Retrieval as context allocation
topics.description: The Lab's position: a studio's memory problem is a retrieval problem, not a window-size problem. Retrieval-augmented generation — RAG — pulls the few most relevant pieces from an archive and places them in the prompt, where attention can still reach them. A small, well-chosen set usually beats pasting in a million tokens, because capacity is not the same as attention.
evidence: Take a question your studio asks often. Answer it once by pasting the whole project folder as context, and once by retrieving the two or three documents that actually bear on it. Compare not only the answers but where each went wrong.
You keep pasting the same background into every session. Name the retrieval step that should replace it — and say what would have to be true of your archive for that step to work.
topics.critPrompt: You keep pasting the same background into every session. Name the retrieval step that should replace it — and say what would have to be true of your archive for that step to work.

grounding.ref: retrieval beats a bigger context window (RAG / Studio-Stack essay)
Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
Liu et al., Lost in the Middle

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: a studio's memory problem is a retrieval problem, not a window-size problem.

sections.position:
Retrieval-augmented generation — RAG — pulls the few most relevant pieces from an archive and places them in the prompt, where attention can still reach them. A small, well-chosen set usually beats pasting in a million tokens, because capacity is not the same as attention. Usually, not always: when evidence is spread across a whole archive, or the question cannot predict what will matter, a long context can beat a poor retriever. We also hold the stronger claim: a studio's memory problem is first a retrieval problem, not a window-size problem. The question is "what deserves the model's attention for this task?"
> Retrieval is the discipline of choosing context before the model spends intelligence on it.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Bigger windows keep arriving and the complaint does not change. The model "forgot" the material standard, the client's constraint, last week's decision. Lost-in-the-middle research explains why: position and crowding decide what gets used. Retrieval puts the right piece in the right place on purpose. It also keeps the archive editable. Fix a document, and every future answer inherits the fix.
sections.strongestObjection: A studio's memory problem is not a retrieval problem. It is also a problem of authority, provenance, versioning, access and time. If three specifications exist, retrieval can find all three perfectly and still not say which supersedes which. If a junior should not see the tender file, excellent semantic retrieval is a security failure. If the fire consultant issued Revision 6 yesterday, similarity does not establish what is current. The position reduces a governance problem to a search problem, and a studio that builds the search without the register will retrieve the wrong document with full confidence. Separately, long-context models keep improving, and for a small studio whose whole archive fits, "paste it all in" may be the less fragile system.
sections.revisionCondition: We already concede the governance half: retrieval has to sit inside a system that records which document is current and who may see it, and a retriever that consults no such register is not the system we mean. And measured evidence that current long-context models use material evenly across the window, for archives of studio size, would shrink it further, to "retrieval when the archive outgrows the window". Write a prompt with three or four named elements in stated positions: "courtyard left of the entry, service block behind, water tank on the roof to the right". Design a small test that proves where a model's spatial placement breaks, scored on relation and count rather than presence alone, and show the first-object bias by changing which element you name first.

card.oneLiner: Name several things in stated positions and score the model — a benchmark you can run yourself.

sections.whenToUse: Before you rely on any image model to place things where you say — and whenever a new version arrives and someone claims it "handles layout now".
sections.method: Write a prompt with three or four named elements in stated positions: "courtyard left of the entry, service block behind, water tank on the roof to the right". Generate ten images from ten different seeds. For each image, score each element on four things. Present? Relation satisfied — actually left of the entry, actually behind? Count right — one tank, not three? Viewpoint lets you judge the relation at all? If the viewpoint does not, mark that element unjudgeable, not wrong. Tally per element and per relation, as a rate over the ten seeds. Then swap the order you name things — put "service block" first — and run ten more. If the tally shifts towards whatever you named first, you have found first-object bias. Write the scores down with the model's name, version and the date.
sections.watchForThis: Scoring presence when you meant to score relation. A model can put all four things in the wrong places and pass a presence tally. And scoring by "looks about right". Score each element, each relation, each image. A test without a tally is only an impression.
sections.tryIt: Run the twenty images today on whatever tool you use. Keep the sheet. Run the same twenty on the next version. Now you can say "improved" with a number instead of a feeling.
sections.proveIt: Design a small test that proves where a model's spatial placement breaks, scored on relation and count rather than presence alone, and show the first-object bias by changing which element you name first.
sections.howItWorks: Public benchmarks do exactly this at scale. VISOR scores objects and their stated relations. T2I-CompBench++ covers spatial and other kinds of composition. Both report that current models struggle with prompts that place several objects. Your ten-image version is the same logic at studio scale. EVOLVING: the scores move with every release. “Promenade architecturale” is Le Corbusier’s term (c.1929, Villa Savoye), per Fondation Le Corbusier — not Charles Correa’s; today’s models demonstrate subject/character consistency, not navigable spatial coherence
OpenAI, Video generation models as world simulators

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: subject consistency is not spatial persistence — the promenade is the test.

sections.position: Today's image models can keep a subject looking consistent across separate images: the same chair, the same fluted timber, the same person. That is subject consistency, and it is real progress. It is not a room you can walk through. Ask to step past the door and the space changes. The window that was on the left is gone, the ceiling height changes, the corridor leads somewhere new. We hold that the test for a spatial designer is the promenade — Le Corbusier's promenade architecturale. Does one room still anchor the next as you move? A single striking view cannot pass that test. A consistent subject cannot pass it. Only a space that is held can.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Architecture is experienced in sequence. A tool that produces beautiful, unconnected views is a tool for pictures of buildings, not for buildings. Naming the promenade as the bar keeps the profession's own standard in view when a demonstration of consistency is presented as a demonstration of space.
sections.strongestObjection: We may be applying a world-state test to a system that was never built to hold a world. A single-image generator's job is to produce independent 2D samples. When it fails the promenade, that is not evidence that it is bad at its task; it shows that 2D subject consistency and persistent 3D scene state are different capabilities, and we are testing one tool for the other's job. "The model forgets the room" then says less about the model than about which tool we asked. The systems actually built to hold a scene — video models, world models — are the ones the test should be run on, and on those the bar is moving quickly. A designer can also supply the persistence the model lacks, by using a 3D massing as the control input for every view.
sections.revisionCondition: Two things, separately. If the objection holds — if the promenade is being asked of tools that never claimed it — the position narrows to "run the promenade on systems that claim scene state, and do not read a consistent subject as a held space", which keeps the test and drops the complaint. And a repeatable promenade test passed by such a system alone — a sequence of views through one interior, generated without a 3D control, in which adjacency, openings, heights and materials hold across every step, as judged by architects — makes this a history card. Reviewed every edition. We run the test ourselves.
sections.tryIt: Generate a view of a room. Then ask for the view from the doorway on the left of that room, then from the next room looking back through the door. Lay the three in sequence. Mark every element that changed. Then do it again with a massing model as control and compare.
sections.takeItToCrit: Tell subject consistency apart from true spatial persistence in your own sequence, and name the promenade as the harder test. Did your sequence pass it?
sections.howItWorks: Subject consistency is achieved by conditioning on reference images or identity embeddings. It keeps the thing, not the scene. Holding a scene needs a representation of space that the model carries between frames. That is what HOLDING TIME and WORLD MODELS on this strand are about, and why they are harder.
sections.lineage: The promenade architecturale is Le Corbusier's phrase, from the Villa Savoye years. It means movement organised so that spaces and views unfold as you advance. Charles Correa later wrote about movement through space in the Indian context, and the two are sometimes confused — including in the Lab's own essay on spatial memory, which credits Correa. The term is Le Corbusier's. The test works under either name.
