topics.name: Upscaling and the resolution question
topics.description: The upscaler cannot recover what was never captured — it infers detail that fits the small image, and where the evidence runs out, it invents. Models make images at a working resolution, then add detail in upscaling passes. An upscaler cannot know what was lost at the small size.
evidence: Take one generated image. Upscale it. Put the two at the same screen size and zoom into the same 200 mm of wall on each. List what the upscaler added. Then ask: would anyone downstream read that as information?
Explain why an upscaled render can gain a lot of detail that means nothing, and show, on one blown-up image, where inference consistent with the source ends and invented detail begins.
topics.critPrompt: Handed a crisp 4K render, can the student spot the upscaled detail that looks sure of itself but is made up?

card.oneLiner: The upscaler cannot recover what was never captured — it infers detail that fits the small image, and where the evidence runs out, it invents.

sections.idea: Models make images at a working resolution, then add detail in upscaling passes. An upscaler cannot know what was lost at the small size. It infers detail consistent with the small image, and where several answers fit, it picks a plausible one: grain in the stone, joints in the brick, letters on a signboard you never asked for. So a 4K render can look sharper and more certain than the model ever was. Some of the sharpness is honest inference. Some is new invention over the old invention, at a finer grain, and nothing in the image tells you which.
sections.whyItMatters: Detail reads as evidence. A contractor, a client or a juror will trust a crisp joint line more than a soft one, though neither was designed. Higher resolution raises confidence without adding any truth.
sections.inTheStudio: The upscaled street view shows a shop sign in something like Kannada, a tile pattern on the plinth, a meter box by the door. Zoom in. The letters are not letters, the tiles change size halfway up the wall, and the meter box floats. Each of these was invented in the pass that made the image "print-ready".
sections.watchForThis: Sending an upscaled image for material approval. The texture the client approves does not exist as a specification.
sections.tryIt: Take one generated image. Upscale it. Put the two at the same screen size and zoom into the same 200 mm of wall on each. List what the upscaler added. Then ask: would anyone downstream read that as information?
sections.proveIt: Explain why an upscaled render can gain a lot of detail that means nothing, and show, on one blown-up image, where inference consistent with the source ends and invented detail begins.
sections.howItWorks: Modern upscalers are themselves generative networks, trained on pairs of degraded and clean images to infer a likely clean image from a degraded one. Where the small image genuinely constrains the answer, the inference is faithful; where it does not — the fine texture, the lettering — the network supplies a plausible answer, not the true one. Diffusion-based upscaling runs another denoising pass at the larger size, with all the freedom that brings.

topics.description: Because meaning lives at coordinates, "find the most similar" becomes "find the nearest points". If every document, drawing and photograph has coordinates in a space where near means similar, then "find me projects like this brief" becomes a measurement. Which stored points sit nearest to the point of my query?

grounding.ref: Pinecone, What is a Vector Database?, 2024

card.oneLiner: Because meaning lives at coordinates, "find the most similar" becomes "find the nearest points".

sections.idea: If every document, drawing and photograph has coordinates in a space where near means similar, then "find me projects like this brief" becomes a measurement. Which stored points sit nearest to the point of my query? That is vector similarity search. A vector database stores the coordinates of each item alongside the item, and answers nearest-neighbour questions quickly, even over millions of items. It is the basic operation that retrieval runs on. It lets a studio search its own archive by intent, climate or building type instead of by filename.
sections.whyItMatters: A folder finds what you named. A vector search finds what you meant, including things you named badly in 2019. That changes how you can use your own past work.
sections.inTheStudio: "Narrow plot, hot-dry, courtyard, low budget" returns a 2017 house whose folder was called `Final_FINAL_v3`. The filename never said courtyard. The embedding did.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking nearest means best. Nearest means nearest in the model's sense of similar, which may weigh a photograph's palette more than your brief's climate logic. Read the results. Do not trust the ranking.
sections.tryIt: Write three short descriptions of past studio projects. Ask a model which two are most similar and why. Then ask which two a client would call similar. The answers will differ, and the difference is what "similar" means in the space.
sections.proveIt: Explain how "find projects like this brief" becomes a distance measurement in the space, and describe what a vector database stores that plain folders cannot.
sections.howItWorks: Each item is embedded once and stored. A query is embedded the same way, and the database returns the items at the smallest distance (or the highest cosine similarity). Exact search over millions of items is slow, so real systems use approximate indexes that trade a little accuracy for speed. RAG on this strand is what happens next: the nearest pieces are handed to the model as context.

topics.name: 3D and world models
topics.description: Systems that build geometry you can move through, or learn how a space behaves as you act in it — the frontier aimed at architecture, and the least agreed upon. Beyond flat images sit two more kinds of system. 3D generators produce a representation of shape and appearance — a mesh, a point cloud, a radiance field, a splat — that you can orbit and, for a mesh, section and measure.

grounding.ref: OpenAI, Video generation models as world simulators (Sora), 2024
Google DeepMind, Genie 3: a new frontier for world models

card.oneLiner: Systems that build geometry you can move through, or learn how a space behaves as you act in it — the frontier aimed at architecture, and the least agreed upon.

sections.idea: Beyond flat images sit two more kinds of system. 3D generators produce a representation of shape and appearance — a mesh, a point cloud, a radiance field, a splat — that you can orbit and, for a mesh, section and measure. A world model is something else: a learned model of an environment's state and how that state changes over time or under an action. It may never show a picture. Some recent systems render an interactive scene you can move through, but that is one use, not the definition. A splat is not a world model.
sections.whyItMatters: The day a model can hold a room is the day this whole strand changes. Knowing how far off that day is, and what people mean when they claim it has arrived, is part of being literate.
sections.inTheStudio: A text-to-3D tool gives you a mesh of a pavilion you can open in your modelling software. It is watertight nowhere and its roof is a skin with no structure. It is still the first generated thing on this strand you can put a scale to. A "world" demo lets you walk down a generated street. In many demos, turn round and the street behind you has been invented again; the newest hold it for minutes. Ask how long, and what happens after.
sections.watchForThis: The word "world" doing marketing work. A video model that produces believable motion is not, because of that, holding a world. Ask: can I go back to where I was and find it unchanged?
sections.tryIt: Generate one object three ways: as an image, as a 3D mesh, as a short video. For each, write what you can measure, what you can move through, and what stays put when you look away.
sections.proveIt: Explain the difference between a generated image, a generated 3D model and a simulated world you can walk through, and name one thing a world model would offer a spatial designer that image generation never can.
sections.howItWorks: 3D generation usually lifts 2D generative priors into geometry, or trains directly on 3D data, which is scarce. A radiance field (NeRF) or a Gaussian splat stores appearance from many viewpoints; it is not a watertight solid you can section like a BIM model. "World model" has two meanings in use. The older research sense is a learned internal simulator that an agent plans with. The newer product sense is a generative system that renders consistent, explorable scenes — Google DeepMind's Genie 3 (August 2025) is described by its makers as a general-purpose world model whose environments stay largely consistent for several minutes as you move. CONTESTED: OpenAI framed its video model as a "world simulator". Many researchers dispute that predicting believable pixels amounts to modelling a world, and argue that a genuine world model must represent state, not appearance. This card names the disagreement rather than settling it.

topics.description: A model inside a loop with some authority to choose its next action — planning, tools, memory and self-checks are parts it may have, and it needs checking from outside. An agentic system is a model placed inside a loop with some authority to choose its next action from the result of the last one. Give it a goal and it works towards it over several steps.

card.oneLiner: A model inside a loop with some authority to choose its next action — planning, tools, memory and self-checks are parts it may have, and it needs checking from outside.

sections.idea: An agentic system is a model placed inside a loop with some authority to choose its next action from the result of the last one. Give it a goal and it works towards it over several steps. Planning, tool calls, stored state and self-checks are parts it may have; none alone makes it an agent, and a fixed sequence of model calls laid down in code — a workflow — is not one either. An agent acts over time, which buys reach and costs reliability: errors add up. So checking is built in: runtime gates where a human approves.
sections.whyItMatters: When a machine acts over several steps, responsibility is no longer a single moment. You have to decide in advance where the human gate sits, because afterwards is too late.
sections.inTheStudio: "Prepare the area statement for the municipal submission." The agent opens the model file, pulls areas, formats the table, checks totals against the byelaw limit, drafts the cover note — and pauses before filing. That pause is the design, and it is a permission gate in the runtime, not a sentence in the goal. "Stop before filing" written in the brief asks; the runtime's gate enforces. The closer a step comes to a signature, a payment or something that cannot be undone, the stronger the gate should be.
sections.watchForThis: An agent that reports success in fluent prose. The report is generated like everything else. Read the artefact, not the summary.
sections.tryIt: Take one studio task and write out its loop by hand: goal, first tool call, what state must be kept, what self-check runs, where a human must approve. Then decide which step you would never automate, and say why.
sections.proveIt: Explain the difference between asking a model a question and handing an agent a goal, name the parts of the loop for one studio task — goal, tool call, memory, self-check — and say which of them that task actually needs, and where the gate sits.
sections.howItWorks: The loop is orchestration code around the model. It supplies tools (TOOL USE on this strand), stores intermediate state, and feeds results back as context. Practitioner guidance distinguishes workflows, where code fixes the path, from agents, where the model directs its own process, and favours the simplest form that does the job; it treats permissions as the real design decision, and they live in the runtime, not in the prompt. EVOLVING: agent frameworks and their reliability are moving fast. What counts as "built-in checking" this year may be standard plumbing next year.

card.oneLiner: Judge a model by your briefs, your building types and what a mistake costs — not by a leaderboard.

sections.dilemma: Two models, one decision. One tops the leaderboards this month. The other is cheaper, runs locally, and nobody is talking about it. The studio needs one for reading survey reports and drafting design statements. How do you choose?
sections.choices: Pick the leader, because everyone does. Pick the cheap one, because cost is real. Or build a small test set from your own work — twenty survey reports, ten briefs, the kind of mistake that actually hurts you — run both models on it, and read where each holds and where each breaks.
sections.consequence: Pick by leaderboard and you inherit a ranking built on tasks that are not yours, possibly gamed, possibly out of date. Pick by cost and you may save money on a tool that invents survey figures. Build the test and you spend a day. In return you have a reusable instrument that tells you, for every future model, whether it fits your work.
sections.theCase: A practice adopts the top-ranked model for reading geotechnical reports. It is excellent at summarising and, twice in a month, confidently misreads a bearing-capacity table. The unfashionable model, tested later on the same twenty reports, misreads none — and is worse at prose. The leaderboard had measured prose.
sections.takeItToCrit: When you picked a model, can you show evidence from your own task behind the choice — or only point to what is popular? Bring the test set.
sections.howItWorks: Public benchmarks measure general tasks under conditions you do not control, and the rankings themselves have been shown to be distorted by how labs test and what they disclose. A studio test set is small, specific and honest: your inputs, your error costs, your judges. THE PIPELINE on Foundations names the trap. A model can pass its own exam and fail in your studio.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Fine-tune or retrieve
topics.description: The Lab's position: to make a model speak your studio's language, retrieve first and train last. For most studios the honest first move is retrieval, not training. Knowledge that changes, that must be cited, or that lives in documents belongs in an archive you retrieve from.
evidence: Take a real studio need and frame it as a fine-tune-or-retrieve choice, with the trade-offs on each side
Explain which kinds of knowledge belong in the weights and which belong in an archive you can retrieve from
topics.critPrompt: When a studio said it wanted the model to "know our work", did you reach for training out of habit, or weigh retrieval first and say why? Show the split.

grounding.ref: no-training / retrieval-first default (Training-Data and RAG essays)

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: to make a model speak your studio's language, retrieve first and train last.

sections.dilemma: The studio wants the model to "know our work". There are two roads. Fine-tune, so the knowledge lives inside the weights. Or retrieve, so the knowledge stays in an archive you can edit and is fed in at the moment you ask. Which do you reach for first?
sections.choices: Train. You get a model that carries your manner without being told each time. It costs rights work and compute, and it freezes your archive at training day. Retrieve. You get an archive you can correct tomorrow, answers that can cite their source, and no training. It costs a retrieval pipeline that must be built well, and the model still sounds like itself. Or split the two: retrieve for facts and precedents, and train only for a visual signature that words cannot carry.
sections.consequence: Train first and you own a model that knows last year's studio, cannot say where an answer came from, and must be retrained when the archive changes. Retrieve first and you can show your working, fix your sources and switch base models freely. But a weak retriever hands the model the wrong document with full confidence. The split takes more thought, and it is usually the honest answer.
sections.theCase: A twelve-person practice wants "our standard details and our way of writing specs" in the model. The knowledge is documents: details, specifications, past reports. Retrieval serves it at once, with citations to the detail sheet. Six months later they want renders in the house visual language. Words do not carry it, and fifty cleared images do. That is the moment for a LoRA, and not before.
sections.takeItToCrit: When a studio said it wanted the model to "know our work", did you reach for training out of habit, or weigh retrieval first and say why? Show the split.
sections.position: For most studios the honest first move is retrieval, not training. Knowledge that changes, that must be cited, or that lives in documents belongs in an archive you retrieve from. Training is reserved for what words cannot carry — a visual signature — and only after the zero-training paths are exhausted. We hold this as studio policy: a default order for a practice with limited time and rights, not a ranking of the techniques.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Retrieval keeps the studio's knowledge editable, inspectable and portable across models. Training buries it in the weights. In our teaching, the studios that trained first took on upkeep they had not priced. The ones that retrieved first kept their citations and their options.
sections.strongestObjection: Retrieval and fine-tuning are not first and last answers to one problem. They change different things. Retrieval supplies information at the moment you ask. Fine-tuning changes behaviour — format, domain habits, how the model selects tools, its manner, its style. Sometimes the right architecture is retrieval, sometimes fine-tuning, sometimes examples in the prompt, sometimes two together, and the published comparisons show task-dependent results rather than a universal order. So "retrieve first, train last" is defensible as a studio policy and not as a technically privileged sequence — and a card that presents policy as mechanism teaches the wrong kind of reason. A practice whose value is a way of reasoning rather than a set of documents may be delayed by the policy from the one thing that would work.
sections.revisionCondition: Measured evidence, on real studio tasks, that the default order is the wrong default: that a light fine-tune for behaviour plus retrieval for facts beats retrieval alone often enough that "retrieve first" costs studios more than it saves. Or training becoming cheap, rights-clean and reversible enough that the upkeep cost that justifies the policy disappears. Reviewed every edition.
sections.howItWorks: Retrieval (RAG on this strand) places the archive's nearest pieces in context. Fine-tuning (FINE-TUNE) shifts the weights. The two can be combined, and many serious systems retrieve into a lightly tuned model. Sahil's essays on training data and on the studio stack set out the zero-training-first ladder this position rests on.

topics.description: Fine-tuning and LoRA adapt a model on your own work — a style, a domain, a behaviour — when the work is worth it. Audit the archive first. Which images actually carry the signature — typology, light, composition — and which are noise?
evidence: Choose fifty images of your own work. Before training anything, write down what you expect the model to learn from them. Then write down what it cannot learn from pictures: why you made each choice. Keep both lists for afterwards.
Explain what a fine-tune can change in a model and what it cannot, and make the case for when your own body of work is worth training on and when prompting is enough.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say what fifty images of their own work would teach a model, and what it would still not know about their judgment?

grounding.ref: Hu et al., LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

card.oneLiner: Fine-tuning and LoRA adapt a model on your own work — a style, a domain, a behaviour — when the work is worth it.

sections.whenToUse: When you have tried prompting, conditioning and reference images, the model still cannot produce your studio's visual language, and you hold enough rights-cleared, consistent work to teach it.
sections.method: Audit the archive first. Which images actually carry the signature — typology, light, composition — and which are noise? Caption each one carefully. The captions are a large part of what the model learns to associate with the images; the learning comes from the pairing of each example, its caption and the parts of the model being adapted. Start with the lightest method the tool offers before any full fine-tune. Today that is usually a LoRA: a small adapter trained beside a frozen model. Train, then test on prompts the model never saw in training. Judge on work near your own typology. The signature carries best where the target is close to the training set. Record what the trained model can now do and what it still cannot.
sections.watchForThis: Training to fix what a reference image would have fixed. Most studios should use up the zero-training paths first: conditioning, references, retrieval. Training is a commitment. It needs rights, compute and upkeep, and the model ages.
sections.tryIt: Choose fifty images of your own work. Before training anything, write down what you expect the model to learn from them. Then write down what it cannot learn from pictures: why you made each choice. Keep both lists for afterwards.
sections.proveIt: Explain what a fine-tune can change in a model and what it cannot, and make the case for when your own body of work is worth training on and when prompting is enough.
sections.howItWorks: Fine-tuning adjusts the weights on new data. LoRA freezes the base model and trains small low-rank matrices inside selected layers beside it, which is cheaper and keeps the base intact. It is a general adaptation method — used for a language model's behaviour, a domain, a task or a format as much as for an image style; this card takes the image case because that is usually a studio's first need. Either method shifts what the model treats as likely. Neither adds judgment, and neither carries a signature over to a typology the training set never held. EVOLVING: LoRA is today's standard lightweight method and the tooling changes yearly. The reasoning about when to train is the durable part.

topics.name: Open-weights or API
topics.description: Weights you can run and fine-tune yourself, or a model you reach through a provider — a structural trade, not a brand; and open weights, open source, local and private are four different things. Some models give you their weights. You can download them, run them, fine-tune them, and — if the inference, the logging and every service around them also run on your machines — keep your data in-house.
evidence: Take one real studio need with a privacy constraint. Write the two paths side by side: what runs where, who sees the data, what it costs per month, what you cannot do on each. Defend the pick in five lines.

List what open-weights access lets you DO that an API does not — run locally, fine-tune, keep data in — and the reverse; tell open weights, open source, local and private apart; then match a studio's privacy and control needs to one path and defend it.
topics.critPrompt: When a studio worries about client-data privacy, can the student reason from how open-weights and API models actually work, instead of naming a favourite product?

grounding.ref: OSI, The Open Source AI Definition 1.0

card.oneLiner: Weights you can run and fine-tune yourself, or a model you reach through a provider — a structural trade, not a brand; and open weights, open source, local and private are four different things.

sections.idea: Some models give you their weights. You can download them, run them, fine-tune them, and — if the inference, the logging and every service around them also run on your machines — keep your data in-house. You can look at the weights; that does not let you read off what the model knows or why it behaves as it does. Others you reach only through a provider's API: your prompt travels to their servers and the answer comes back. Open weights give you control and the option of privacy. An API gives you ease and often the strongest models.
sections.whyItMatters: "Can we put the client's drawings into it?" is answered by the architecture, not the brand. Where the model runs decides where the drawings go.
sections.inTheStudio: A hospital client's contract forbids their plans leaving the studio network. An API tool, however good, is out unless the provider's terms and hosting satisfy the contract. An open-weights model on a studio machine is in. The price is a machine, a person to run it, and a model a step behind the best.
sections.watchForThis: "Open" used loosely. Released weights are not released training data, and some "open" licences restrict commercial use. Read the licence, not the adjective.
sections.tryIt: Take one real studio need with a privacy constraint. Write the two paths side by side: what runs where, who sees the data, what it costs per month, what you cannot do on each. Defend the pick in five lines.
sections.proveIt: List what open-weights access lets you DO that an API does not — run locally, fine-tune, keep data in — and the reverse; tell open weights, open source, local and private apart; then match a studio's privacy and control needs to one path and defend it.
sections.howItWorks: An API call sends your context to the provider's servers, and the provider's terms govern how long it is kept and whether it is used for training. Open weights run wherever you can supply the hardware, and can be fine-tuned locally (FINE-TUNE). The Open Source Initiative's definition of open-source AI asks for more than weights: the freedom to use, study, modify and share, with enough detail to rebuild the model. Most "open" releases do not fully meet it. EVOLVING: the capability gap between open and closed models moves every quarter, and so do the terms.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: The surrogate model
topics.description: A fast model trained to approximate something slower or costlier to compute — right inside its training range, and silent outside it. A surrogate is a model trained to approximate something slower or more expensive to compute. In architecture that is usually a physics simulation — daylight, energy, wind, heat — though the original can be an experiment or any costly calculation.
evidence: Find any fast performance tool you use — a daylight or energy quick-check. Find out what it was trained or calibrated on. If you cannot find out, write that down as the answer.
Explain what a surrogate imitates and why it is faster than the real simulation, and name the validity limit that must be stated whenever a surrogate's answer is used.
topics.critPrompt: When a student quotes a fast AI performance figure, do they also state the range the surrogate was trained on?

grounding.ref: Risk-aware early-stage building heating/cooling surrogate workflow with explicit validity limits (PMID: 42362706, 2025)
ML daylight/visual-comfort prediction at early stage (arXiv:2109.06450, 2021)

card.oneLiner: A fast model trained to approximate something slower or costlier to compute — right inside its training range, and silent outside it.

sections.idea: A surrogate is a model trained to approximate something slower or more expensive to compute. In architecture that is usually a physics simulation — daylight, energy, wind, heat — though the original can be an experiment or any costly calculation. The simulation is run many times to make training data. The surrogate learns the mapping from inputs to results, then answers in seconds what the original takes far longer to compute. The catch is where it learned. Inside the range of the training runs it is usually close. Outside that range it still answers, just as quickly, and is not close.
sections.whyItMatters: A surrogate makes performance questions fast enough to ask at sketch stage, which is when they matter. It also makes a wrong number fast enough to put on a jury sheet.
sections.inTheStudio: A daylight surrogate trained on rectangular rooms with side windows gives a crisp daylight factor for your courtyard scheme with a clerestory. The number is confident. The courtyard was never in its training set. Nothing in the output says so.
sections.watchForThis: Quoting a surrogate's figure without its range. "Daylight factor 2.8%" means nothing on its own. "2.8%, from a surrogate trained on side-lit rooms, and our scheme is top-lit" means something. What it means is: run the real simulation.
sections.tryIt: Find any fast performance tool you use — a daylight or energy quick-check. Find out what it was trained or calibrated on. If you cannot find out, write that down as the answer.
sections.proveIt: Explain what a surrogate imitates and why it is faster than the real simulation, and name the validity limit that must be stated whenever a surrogate's answer is used.
sections.howItWorks: Surrogates are ordinary regression models — neural networks, gradient-boosted trees — trained on simulation outputs. Good practice builds in an applicability-domain check that flags inputs outside the training range and reports uncertainty with each prediction. Recent building-performance work does exactly this. FIND OR INVENT on Foundations is the related idea: a surrogate predicts, it does not look up.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: Tool use, reaching the world
topics.description: A model only predicts text — it proposes a tool call, the runtime checks and runs it, and the result comes back as text. On its own, a language model only predicts text. Tool use is how a system lets it reach the world anyway.
evidence: Read the tool description of any tool a model you use can call; many apps show them. Rewrite it badly — vague inputs, no stated purpose — and watch how the model's use of it changes. The description is the brief.

Explain how a model that only predicts text ends up "using" a calculator or an API, give the sequence — model proposes, runtime checks and runs, result returns, model continues — and say why the permission belongs at the runtime step.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student explain why handing the model your existing studio software as tools is different from replacing that software, and why that difference protects human judgment?

card.oneLiner: A model only predicts text — it proposes a tool call, the runtime checks and runs it, and the result comes back as text.

sections.idea: On its own, a language model only predicts text. Tool use is how a system lets it reach the world anyway. Each tool — a climate API, a code library, a calculator — is described to the model in words: what it does and what inputs it takes. When the job needs a tool, the model writes a structured request instead of an answer: which tool, with which inputs. The runtime — the software around the model — checks that request, runs the tool, and hands the result back. The model never runs anything itself. It proposes; the runtime executes. Permissions live there.
sections.whyItMatters: Tool use is how your existing studio software becomes something the model can consult rather than something it replaces. The calculation is still done by the calculator. The judgment of which tool to reach for, and whether to trust the result, is now shared. You should know where each part of that judgment sits.
sections.inTheStudio: "What is the basic wind speed for Belagavi?" Without tools: a confident number from memory, possibly wrong. With a code-lookup tool described to it: a call, a result with a clause reference, an answer you can check. Same model. The tool gave it somewhere to look.
sections.watchForThis: A model that describes using a tool when no call happened. Check the log. "I consulted the code" can be predicted text like anything else.
sections.tryIt: Read the tool description of any tool a model you use can call; many apps show them. Rewrite it badly — vague inputs, no stated purpose — and watch how the model's use of it changes. The description is the brief.
sections.proveIt: Explain how a model that only predicts text ends up "using" a calculator or an API, give the sequence — model proposes, runtime checks and runs, result returns, model continues — and say why the permission belongs at the runtime step.
sections.howItWorks: Models are trained to write tool requests in a fixed format when given tool descriptions, and to read tool results as ordinary context. The conventions for describing tools are converging across vendors. Because the runtime executes and the model only proposes, the runtime can refuse, sandbox, log or ask a human before anything runs. Put the permission there: a line in the prompt — "never send without asking" — asks; the runtime's gate enforces. Read-only tools run freely. Tools that write, spend or send wait for a human.

topics.subject: Generative Mechanics
topics.name: How video generation holds time
topics.description: Many frames, one world — keeping light, material and shape steady as the camera moves is the hard part. A video model must do what an image model never has to: keep the world the same from one frame to the next. Light must stay where the sun put it.
evidence: Generate a ten-second walkthrough of a simple building. Extract a frame every second. Pin them up. Circle what changed that should not have.
Explain why a generated clip can shift in material or lighting from one frame to the next, and name what temporal coherence asks a model to hold that a single still never has to.
topics.critPrompt: Watching a generated walkthrough, can the student point to the frame where the building stops being the same building?

grounding.ref: OpenAI, Video generation models as world simulators (Sora), 2024
Diffusion — How AI Paints from Noise

card.oneLiner: Many frames, one world — keeping light, material and shape steady as the camera moves is the hard part.

sections.idea: A video model must do what an image model never has to: keep the world the same from one frame to the next. Light must stay where the sun put it. Materials must not move. A column must not become two when the camera turns. That steadiness is called temporal coherence, and it is one of the places these systems break — alongside physics, cause and effect, camera geometry and object permanence: a brick wall that turns to render mid-pan, a window that slides along a façade. Generation runs across many frames at once, trying to hold one scene through time.
sections.whyItMatters: For architecture, a walkthrough is a claim about a space. If the building at second four is not the same building as at second one, the clip shows no space at all. It only shows the appearance of one.
sections.inTheStudio: A generated approach to a school: gate, forecourt, verandah. Watch the columns. Frame by frame, the bay count changes, the verandah depth shifts, and the courtyard that should appear through the entrance never resolves. The clip looks good. The building has not been held.
sections.watchForThis: Judging a clip at playback speed. Coherence failures hide in motion. Scrub it, or pull stills every half-second and lay them in a row.
sections.tryIt: Generate a ten-second walkthrough of a simple building. Extract a frame every second. Pin them up. Circle what changed that should not have.
sections.proveIt: Explain why a generated clip can shift in material or lighting from one frame to the next, and name what temporal coherence asks a model to hold that a single still never has to.
sections.howItWorks: Current video models extend diffusion across space and time. They denoise a block of frames together, so that attention runs between frames as well as within them, often in a compressed latent space. That is what buys coherence, and the coherence is still partial. EVOLVING: this is one of the fastest-moving corners of the field, and a year changes which failure is the visible one.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The right word does real work
topics.description: "Nice" makes your reader guess. An exact word chooses for them. "Nice" tells your reader you approve. It does not say what you approve of.
evidence: Write down five "nice" things in your school. Replace each "nice" with a word that says what kind of nice. Swap lists with a friend and see whether they can picture what you meant.
Take two words that are nearly the same — "narrow" and "tight", or "bright" and "glaring" — and explain to someone what different room each one makes you picture.
topics.critPrompt: What exact word would carry this better than “nice”?

grounding.ref: mt_WzOyJFKDIu, mt_OLwNsTI6C7, mt_MlmIrLb_7x (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)
NCERT English syllabus, vocabulary — connotation and denotation (upper secondary), India

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: "Nice" makes your reader guess. An exact word chooses for them.

sections.idea: "Nice" tells your reader you approve. It does not say what you approve of. A nice room could be bright, or quiet, or big, or cosy, and your reader has to guess which one you meant. An exact word chooses for them. Say "airy" and they picture light and space. Say "snug" and they picture a low ceiling and a warm corner. The two words are close, and the two rooms are different. A stock of exact words is a tool, not decoration. You will use it on a drawing, in a letter, and in a brief to a machine.
sections.whyItMatters: A machine that reads your words cannot ask what you meant. It takes the word you gave it. A vague word lets it guess.
sections.inTheStudio: Two students describe the same verandah. One says "nice and open." The other says "a deep, shaded verandah, open on three sides, its floor one step above the garden." Only the second could be drawn by someone who was never there.
sections.watchForThis: Words that sound like praise but describe nothing: nice, good, cool, modern. If a word could be said about almost any room, it is not describing this one.
sections.tryIt: Write down five "nice" things in your school. Replace each "nice" with a word that says what kind of nice. Swap lists with a friend and see whether they can picture what you meant.
sections.proveIt: Take two words that are nearly the same — "narrow" and "tight", or "bright" and "glaring" — and explain to someone what different room each one makes you picture.
sections.howItWorks: Your English class calls the exact meaning of a word its denotation, and the feeling it carries its connotation. "Narrow" and "tight" point at the same measurement and carry different feelings. Later on this map, briefing a machine comes down to the same thing: choosing words that carry the right measurement and the right feeling at once.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Who is it for, and why
topics.description: The same message is written differently for different readers and different jobs. You tell the same news three ways in one day: to your grandmother, to your best friend, to your class teacher. The facts do not change.
evidence: Write one line inviting people to your school's annual day. Now rewrite it for a five-year-old, then for the chief guest. Notice what you had to add and what you had to drop.
Pick any poster in your school and say who it is for and what it is trying to make them do.
topics.critPrompt: Who is this for, and what is it trying to do?

grounding.ref: NCERT English syllabus, writing for purpose and audience (upper secondary), India

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: The same message is written differently for different readers and different jobs.

sections.idea: You tell the same news three ways in one day: to your grandmother, to your best friend, to your class teacher. The facts do not change. The words, the order, and how much you explain all change, because each reader knows different things and wants different things. Every piece of writing has a purpose (what it is trying to do), an audience (who it is for), and a context (where and when it will be read). Name all three before you write and the writing gets easier. Name them while you read and you understand the writer better.
sections.whyItMatters: When you later write instructions for a machine, the machine is your audience. It has read more than any person and knows nothing about you. Writing for it is this same skill.
sections.inTheStudio: An architect explains one house three times in a day: to the family who will live in it, to the mason who will build it, and to the municipal office that must approve it. Same house. Three different documents.
sections.watchForThis: Writing for yourself by mistake. You already know what you mean, so you skip the parts your reader needed most.
sections.tryIt: Write one line inviting people to your school's annual day. Now rewrite it for a five-year-old, then for the chief guest. Notice what you had to add and what you had to drop.
sections.proveIt: Pick any poster in your school and say who it is for and what it is trying to make them do.
sections.howItWorks: Writers call this purpose, audience and context, and it sits in your English syllabus. On this map it becomes the first layer of every brief: who the reader is decides what must be said and what can be left out. A machine is an unusual reader. It has seen most of what people have written and has never met you, so everything about your project has to be said.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Scale, ratio, and proportion
topics.description: On a 1:100 drawing every length is one-hundredth of the real one — a two-metre door is two centimetres, and so is everything else. Architects draw buildings small and build them big. A plan at 1:100 means every length is one-hundredth of the real length.
evidence: Measure your bedroom with a tape. Draw it on squared paper, one square for every half metre. Then draw your bed and your desk by the same rule. Does everything fit where it really is?
Draw a door two metres wide at 1:100, then at 1:50. Explain why the two drawings are different sizes and the door is not.
topics.critPrompt: If you shrink this drawing, what has to stay the same?

grounding.ref: mt_1badik7iKJ, mt_2OtRUM_0zW, mt_5mIcmKRCgA, mt_yK51ZnKA8m (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)
NCERT Mathematics syllabus, Comparing Quantities — Ratio & Proportion (Classes 6–8), India

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: On a 1:100 drawing every length is one-hundredth of the real one — a two-metre door is two centimetres, and so is everything else.

sections.idea: Architects draw buildings small and build them big. A plan at 1:100 means every length is one-hundredth of the real length. A door two metres wide is drawn two centimetres wide, and every wall and step follows the same rule, so you can measure the drawing and know the building. That is scale. A photograph of your house on a phone is small too, but it has no single rule: things near the camera look big, things far away look small. Proportion is the relationship between the parts. Change one part alone and the thing stops being itself.
sections.whyItMatters: Scale is the promise that the drawing and the building agree. A mason measures the drawing and trusts the number. Later you will meet machines that make pictures of buildings with no scale at all, and you will know what is missing.
sections.inTheStudio: A two-metre door on a 1:100 plan is two centimetres on paper. A classmate draws it four centimetres "to make it clear." The door is now four metres wide. The drawing says something false, and it does not look wrong.
sections.watchForThis: Making something bigger so it looks important. On a scaled drawing, bigger means bigger. There is no "just for show."
sections.tryIt: Measure your bedroom with a tape. Draw it on squared paper, one square for every half metre. Then draw your bed and your desk by the same rule. Does everything fit where it really is?
sections.proveIt: Draw a door two metres wide at 1:100, then at 1:50. Explain why the two drawings are different sizes and the door is not.
sections.howItWorks: Ratio is the maths under this: a comparison of two quantities, written 1:100 or 1:50. Your maths class teaches it as comparing quantities. A resized photograph keeps its proportions, but it is not a scale drawing, because nothing in it can be measured by one rule. On this map ratio returns as the thing a generated picture does not have. A generated building looks right at any size. That means it has no size at all.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Naming what you see
topics.description: Threshold, datum, grain, mass, aperture — exact words for the parts of space most people only feel. Architects have exact words for the parts of space that most people only feel. A threshold is where you cross from one kind of space into another: a doorstep, a gate, a change in floor level.
evidence: Take one photograph of a space you know: a temple corridor, a school verandah, a railway platform. Describe it in ten exact spatial words. Hand the description, without the photo, to a friend and ask them to sketch it.
Replace "nice," "modern," and "cool" in a description of your own room with three words that tell a builder what to build.

grounding.ref: standard architectural pedagogy (e.g. Ching, Architecture: Form, Space & Order)

card.oneLiner: Threshold, datum, grain, mass, aperture — exact words for the parts of space most people only feel.

sections.idea: Architects have exact words for the parts of space that most people only feel. A threshold is where you cross from one kind of space into another: a doorstep, a gate, a change in floor level. A datum is a line or level that everything else is measured against. Grain is the direction a place runs in, the way wood does. Mass is the solid bulk of a building; an aperture is any opening cut into it. These words are not decoration. They let you describe a space to someone who cannot see it: a builder, a client, a machine.
sections.whyItMatters: A brief to a machine is made of words. If all you have is "nice" and "modern," that is all you can ask for.
sections.inTheStudio: In crit, a student says the entrance "feels good." The tutor asks why. Once the student can say "a low, dark threshold that opens into a tall, bright court," the feeling has become a design move — something that can be kept, changed, or drawn.
sections.watchForThis: Using the words to sound clever rather than to say something. "Datum" earns its place only if you can point at the line.
sections.tryIt: Take one photograph of a space you know: a temple corridor, a school verandah, a railway platform. Describe it in ten exact spatial words. Hand the description, without the photo, to a friend and ask them to sketch it.
sections.proveIt: Replace "nice," "modern," and "cool" in a description of your own room with three words that tell a builder what to build.
sections.howItWorks: The classic textbook for this vocabulary is Francis Ching's *Architecture: Form, Space and Order*, on most first-year reading lists. Its words run through this whole map. When you brief an image model, the words you choose are the instructions, so the more exact words you have, the more control you have. Parti — the organising idea of a scheme, drawn in one small sketch — is the word you will meet next.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Briefing in your own language
topics.description: You can brief in Kannada or Hindi — if you know what it costs on the system you are using, and where that system supports English better. When you write in Kannada, Hindi, Marathi or Tamil, two things can happen. The tokeniser — the part that chops text into pieces before the model reads it — may cut your script into far more pieces than English, so the same sentence costs more and fills the window faster.
evidence: Write one short brief in English and the same brief in your own language. Run both. Compare how faithful each output is to what you meant, and where each one drifted. Then try a third version: your language for the idea, English for the constraints. If your tool shows a token count, write the same Kannada sentence once in Kannada script and once in Roman letters, and compare what each one costs.
Name one design idea from your own region that a model handles poorly, and explain, using tokens and training data, why it handles it poorly — on the model you tested, not on models in general.
topics.critPrompt: Does the student choose the brief's language on purpose, knowing where their own tongue adds meaning and where it loses precision?

grounding.ref: Petrov et al., Language Model Tokenizers Introduce Unfairness Between Languages
Tokens, Context, and Why AI Forgets

card.oneLiner: You can brief in Kannada or Hindi — if you know what it costs on the system you are using, and where that system supports English better.

sections.idea: When you write in Kannada, Hindi, Marathi or Tamil, two things can happen. The tokeniser — the part that chops text into pieces before the model reads it — may cut your script into far more pieces than English, so the same sentence costs more and fills the window faster. And the model may have seen less writing in your language, so its habits there are thinner. Both gaps vary by language and tokeniser, so test the model you are using. You can still brief in your own language, and sometimes you should: a *jagali* has no clean English name.
sections.whyItMatters: Your own language carries design ideas that English flattens. Where a system supports English better, that is a limit of the system, not of your language. A good brief often uses both, on purpose.
sections.inTheStudio: A student briefs a house "with a jagali" — the raised plinth-seat along the front of a Karnataka house. Translated as "a porch," it returns a Western porch with a swing. The word was right. The model simply knew very little about it. Name it, then describe it: "a raised masonry seat along the front wall, under the eave, where visitors sit before entering."
sections.watchForThis: Assuming that a fluent answer in your language is a correct one. A model sounds fluent before it is right, in every language. Less training data makes that gap wider.
sections.tryIt: Write one short brief in English and the same brief in your own language. Run both. Compare how faithful each output is to what you meant, and where each one drifted. Then try a third version: your language for the idea, English for the constraints. If your tool shows a token count, write the same Kannada sentence once in Kannada script and once in Roman letters, and compare what each one costs.
sections.proveIt: Name one design idea from your own region that a model handles poorly, and explain, using tokens and training data, why it handles it poorly — on the model you tested, not on models in general.
sections.howItWorks: Researchers have taken the same text in different languages and counted the tokens. The counts differ several times over, and the languages the tokeniser saw least pay the most. The gap is tokeniser-specific: a newer tokeniser can cut the same Kannada sentence into far fewer pieces than an older one did. How much of any one model's training was in your language is usually not disclosed, so "trained mostly on English" is a reasonable guess about many systems, not a fact you can check for yours. This card is EVOLVING because both things are changing: newer models train on more multilingual data, and tokenisers are being rebuilt. The gap is what we measure today, not a fixed fact.

The model is good at sorting text into named fields and at noticing contradictions you read past. It is poor at knowing which contradiction matters, because that depends on a site, a client and a budget it has never met. sections.position: This card is about one distinction: purpose against deliverable. "Draw a diagram" tells the receiver what to produce. "Compare the two access strategies so we can choose one" tells the receiver why — and the diagram follows from it. Both may end in the same drawing, but only the second tells the model, and you, what a good answer looks like. We hold that the purpose comes first, in the first line, every time, and the deliverable after it. THE BRIEF, the next card, builds the full structure on this one move.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A model fills whatever you leave unsaid with its own assumption. If you name only the deliverable, it guesses the purpose, and its guess shapes the work instead of yours. Naming the purpose also gives you a test: the output either serves it or it does not. "Draw a diagram" has no way to fail, so it also gives you no way to judge the result.
sections.strongestObjection: In exploratory design the purpose may not yet be knowable. Drawing, modelling and making images are sometimes how the question gets discovered; the purpose arrives after the artefact, not before it. Requiring a stated purpose can close an open study too early and turn an exploration into a task. A student taught to always state the job may invent one to satisfy the rule, and then design against the invention.
sections.revisionCondition: Evidence from studio that open, deliverable-first runs in early exploration lead to stronger questions than purpose-first briefs do, judged blind on the work that follows — or models that reliably infer the purpose from the artefact request alone. We already teach that the dreaming register stays open on purpose; if that openness serves early design better than a stated job, this card moves to "name the job once you can." We test it against student work every edition.

topics.description: Two operations, not one: change one thing to learn what the brief is sensitive to; hold everything and run again to learn what the change actually did. Two operations, and they answer different questions. Diagnosis: keep the brief that produced the result, copy it, change one thing — one constraint, one reference, one word of intent — and run it.
evidence: Take one brief that gave a poor result. Make three copies. In each, change a different single thing: the intent line, one constraint, one reference image. Run each copy three times, and the original three times. Which change moved the result most, across all its runs? That is where the brief was weakest — and where one run alone would have misled you.

Show a chain of at least four changes, each run more than once with the settings held, with the observation for each — and name the change that mattered most and the one that turned out to be the random draw.

card.oneLiner: Two operations, not one: change one thing to learn what the brief is sensitive to; hold everything and run again to learn what the change actually did.

sections.whenToUse: Every time an output is wrong and you are about to revise the brief. Especially when you are tempted to rewrite the whole thing.
sections.method: Two operations, and they answer different questions. **Diagnosis:** keep the brief that produced the result, copy it, change one thing — one constraint, one reference, one word of intent — and run it. This tells you what the brief is sensitive to. It does not prove the change caused the difference, because a generative tool is stochastic: the same brief, run twice, can differ. **Comparison:** hold the model, its version and every setting constant; fix the seed where the tool allows; run each version several times, not once; and compare the tendencies across the runs, not one image against another. Write down what you held, what you changed, and what moved. A brief revised in five places at once, run once, gives you a new result and no knowledge. One change, run once, gives you a suspicion. One change, run five times against five unchanged runs, gives you something you can say in crit.
sections.watchForThis: Trusting one before-and-after pair. On image tools, the difference you see can come from the random draw rather than from your edit. And changing one thing at a time cannot show you when two things only work together — a material word that matters only once the light is set. When you suspect a pair, test it together as well as apart, and say so in the note.
sections.tryIt: Take one brief that gave a poor result. Make three copies. In each, change a different single thing: the intent line, one constraint, one reference image. Run each copy three times, and the original three times. Which change moved the result most, across all its runs? That is where the brief was weakest — and where one run alone would have misled you.
sections.proveIt: Show a chain of at least four changes, each run more than once with the settings held, with the observation for each — and name the change that mattered most and the one that turned out to be the random draw.
sections.labNote: Isolate to diagnose, repeat to compare: this is the Lab's discipline for briefing, carried over from the science class and corrected by it. Changing one factor at a time is the beginner's experiment, and it misses what factors do together; repeated runs with settings held are what let you say anything about a tool that answers differently each time. The Judgment strand's on-ramp card teaches the first half to younger students; this card adds the second.
sections.howItWorks: This is the controlled comparison, applied to a stochastic tool. Holding everything constant and varying one factor is what lets you attribute a difference; repeating the run is what lets you see the difference through the noise. Generative tools make both cheap — a run costs seconds — and that cheapness is the trap, because it invites changing everything every time. The six-layer brief names the layers you can vary; the versioned brief keeps the record, including the model and settings that produced each output. Together they turn prompting from guesswork into something you can learn from.

card.oneLiner: "Dramatic light" is an impression. "Low west sun at four, deep shadow on the far wall" is a condition — and a condition is what a reader or a model can act on.

sections.idea: Material and light are where a brief goes vague first. "Warm materials, dramatic light" are impressions: they say how you want the image to feel, and leave every decision to the reader. A condition names the decision itself. "Low sun from the west an hour before sunset, deep shadow on the opposite wall" is a condition. "Oiled teak beside honed Kota stone" is a condition. Raking, overcast, tungsten, matte, specular, patina are useful because each names a condition. Write the condition and two readers picture the same wall. Write the impression and each reader, and each model, invents their own.
sections.whyItMatters: A reader can ask what you meant by "dramatic". A model cannot; it fills the impression with whatever its training most often attached to the word. A condition leaves it less to fill.
sections.inTheStudio: The same laterite wall, three times. "Raking evening sun from the west," and every pit in the stone throws a shadow. "Monsoon overcast," and the wall goes flat and dark red. "Tungsten from a single bulb inside," and it turns orange at the window and black everywhere else. Three images, one wall. Each brief named a condition, and each image followed it.
sections.watchForThis: Stacking adjectives instead of naming conditions. "Beautiful, warm, soft, golden light" is four words of mood. "Low west sun, one hour before sunset" is one condition a model can act on. The same test works for material: "warm" is an impression; "oiled teak" is a decision.
sections.tryIt: Take a brief you have written and underline every impression: dramatic, warm, soft, moody, natural. Rewrite each as a condition — a direction, a time, a weather, a named material and its finish. Run both. Then check: could two readers draw the same surface from your conditions? Could they from your impressions?
sections.proveIt: Write a material-and-light description made only of conditions, precise enough that two classmates, working apart, sketch the same surface. Put the two sketches side by side.
sections.howItWorks: Photographers and lighting designers built this vocabulary long before image models existed, and the models learned it from photo captions, where conditions are named far more often than impressions. "Raking light" sits beside many photographs of raking light; "dramatic" sits beside almost anything. How strongly any one word pulls differs by model, version and the rest of the brief — there is no fixed list of the words that change an image most, which is why this card is EVOLVING. What holds is the habit: name the condition. The seven-slot brief on this map gives material and light a slot each.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: a prompt is not a wish. It is a brief you hand a machine, and it obeys the same discipline.

sections.position:
A prompt is not a wish. It is a brief handed to a machine, and it needs the same discipline as a brief handed to a consultant or a junior: intent, constraints, exclusions, criteria. When an image comes back plausible and empty, do not assume the model failed before you have examined the brief — most of the time it read exactly what it was given, and what it was given was thin. And do not assume a better brief can beat a capability limit: a model that cannot count bays will not count them for a better sentence. Writing the programme before the form is the oldest skill in practice. It is now the first step in using the newest tool.
> The tool is not the problem. The programme is.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: William Peña made the argument in 1969: programming is problem seeking, design is problem solving, and most design failures are programme failures. Drawing used to absorb a vague programme — you sketched your way to clarity. A model cannot do that. It returns the most probable version of what you wrote. With AI, Peña's fifty-year-old argument now runs inside the machine: a thin programme returns a thin result.
sections.strongestObjection: The junior-architect analogy anthropomorphises the model. A junior asks questions back, reads your silences, knows the office, and carries responsibility for the answer. A model does none of that, and it reacts to things no human brief contains: word order, token position, the statistical weight of a phrase. Teaching students to brief it "like a junior" may teach them to credit the receiver with understanding, intention and professional responsibility it does not have. The same briefing discipline does not make the two readers alike, and calling the prompt a brief may hide how strange the reader is. Some practitioners argue that "prompt engineering" is the honest name for exactly that strangeness.
sections.revisionCondition: Models that reliably ask the clarifying questions a good consultant asks — questioning a thin brief instead of filling it. If the machine starts doing the programme's work for you, the skill moves again, and this card moves with it. We check it against what the tools actually do, every edition.
sections.tryIt: Take a one-line wish: "a contemporary house with natural light and warm materials." Run it. Now rewrite it as a brief — the spatial type, the material logic, where the light enters and when, the sequence of arrival, the moment, what must not appear. Run that. Put the two outputs side by side and name what the second has that the first could not. Then brief the same room twice more — once in Kannada, once in English, same content — and compare which output is closer to the room you meant, and where each one drifted.
sections.takeItToCrit: Shown a weak output, did the student reach for the re-roll or for the brief — and can they point to the missing part of the brief that caused the failure, or say honestly that the brief was sound and the tool could not do it?
sections.howItWorks: Large generative models do not work out what you left unsaid. They compute a probable answer from what you wrote and what they learned in training. So a vague prompt returns a probable house, not your house. A thin brief is the commonest cause of an empty image; it is not the only one — spatial relations, counts and geometry can fail under a sound brief, and the spatial-check card on this map is how you tell the two apart. Every other card in this strand is a part of the brief — the words (space, material, light, conventions), the structures (six layers, seven slots), and the discipline around them (criteria, exclusions, versions, the crit loop).
sections.lineage: Peña's *Problem Seeking* (1969; fifth edition with Parshall, 2012) established architectural programming as a discipline separate from design. The profession has written programmes for clients, teams, planning departments and contractors ever since. AI is a new audience for a document architecture already knows how to write.

card.oneLiner: A reference image is a dense brief — but the model reads what it shows, and cannot know a reason for choosing it that you never stated.

sections.idea: A reference image is a dense brief. One picture carries light, material, proportion, mood and a dozen things you never noticed. But a model reads what the image shows; it cannot know why you pinned it unless you say. You chose that photograph for the way the stair turns. The model sees the stair, the railing, the floor tile, the window, the colour grade and the cat, all at once and with no ranking. Unless you say which quality you want carried over, it borrows whatever is loudest.
sections.whyItMatters: In most reference failures the model did not copy badly. It copied the wrong thing, and copied it well.
sections.inTheStudio: You attach a photo of a Goan house for its deep verandah shadow. The output arrives with the verandah, and the laterite, the red-oxide floor, the Portuguese balusters and the tiled roof. You wanted one quality. You received the whole house. The brief never said which part was the point.
sections.watchForThis: Two references that look alike to a model and mean opposite things to you. A monastery corridor and a hotel corridor can share proportion, light and material and carry opposite intent. A model can see proportion, and it can guess at intent when your words give it a lead. It cannot know an intent you never stated.
sections.tryIt: Take one reference you have actually used. Make two columns: what a model would read from it (everything visible), and why you picked it (usually one or two things). The gap between the columns is what your brief must say out loud.
sections.proveIt: Show two references a model would read as similar, and explain, in words a model could act on, which quality each is there to contribute.
sections.howItWorks: Modern multimodal systems put images and text in one shared space. The technique most people first met as CLIP, in 2021, showed how such a space is learnt by matching millions of photographs to their captions. Today's image-reasoning systems are built differently and do more with a reference than CLIP could, including inferring a plausible reason for it when your text gives them a lead. When you upload a reference, it lands in the window beside your words, and attention looks for what satisfies both. The image brings everything in it at once. Only your words can rank one quality above another. EVOLVING: image-reasoning models are getting better at taking instructions about a reference ("keep the proportion, not the material"), so how much you need to spell out is changing. Measured today; reviewed each edition.

card.oneLiner: Rooms, areas and adjacencies as a structured list — the oldest brief, and now a machine-friendly one.

sections.whenToUse: Whenever a brief needs to carry rooms, areas and relationships, which is the moment a project stops being a mood and becomes a building. Use it before any plan-making, whether the reader is a person or a model.
sections.method: Write the programme as a structured list, not a paragraph. Put each room on its own line: name · area in square metres · who uses it · when. Then write the adjacencies as plain pairs: "kitchen — adjacent to — dining"; "clinic waiting — visible from — reception"; "bedrooms — not adjacent to — street". Then the quantities that govern everything: total built-up area, floors, the plot. A list like this is the oldest form of the brief. It is also machine-friendly: a model can read an adjacency pair and reason about it. It can do nothing useful with "open plan, flowing spaces." Machine-readable in the strict sense asks for one step more — the same named fields for every room, explicit units, and a way to detect a missing value — which is a schema, and belongs further along this map.
sections.watchForThis: Atmosphere in the area column. "Generous living room" is not a programme line; "Living — 32 m²" is. Mood belongs in the brief, in its own slot — not in the place of a number.
sections.tryIt: Write a small programme, six to eight rooms, with areas and adjacencies a model could act on. Then turn a paragraph of client wishes into the same structured form, and notice which wishes had to become questions because they carried no quantity.
sections.proveIt: Show a programme that gives the model relationships and quantities to work with — then show the spatial checks you ran on what came back.
sections.howItWorks: Architectural programming in Peña's sense is problem seeking: stating the problem in precise written terms before any form is attempted. The structured list is its classic artefact. Current models read such lists well and reason about them. Producing a valid plan from one is a separate and weaker skill, which is why the spatial-check card sits beside this one. A programme tells the model what must be true. It does not make the model able to draw it.

card.oneLiner: For every brief and every source, sort each line into what was stated, what you inferred, what is unknown, and what you have assumed so the work can go on.

sections.whenToUse: Every time a brief, a survey, a client email or a generated draft arrives and you are about to design from it. Especially when a model has written part of it, because a model writes its guesses in the same tone as its facts.
sections.method: Four labels, one per line of the document. **Stated:** the client or the source said it, and you can point to where. **Inferred:** nobody said it, but it follows from something that was said, and you can show the step. **Unknown:** it matters and nobody has said it. **Assumed:** it is unknown, you need a value to proceed, so you have chosen one for now and written the choice down. Then apply one rule. If an unknown would change the design, it is asked, not invented. Do not invent north. Do not invent occupancy. Do not invent the budget. Take those to the client as questions. Keep the four labels on the document, because a brief whose lines are unlabelled turns its assumptions into facts within a week.
sections.watchForThis: An inferred line that has lost its step. "Family of four" became "three bedrooms" became "no study", and nobody can now say where the third bedroom came from. If you cannot show the step, the line is assumed, not inferred. Label it so.
sections.tryIt: Take a generated brief, or a real client email. Write the four labels down the margin, one per line. Count each label. Then pick the three unknowns that would change the plan most and write them as questions to the client. Most first attempts find that the stated column is short, and that at least one assumed line was about to become a wall.
sections.proveIt: Show one brief with every line labelled, and the list of unknowns you sent to the client instead of inventing them.
sections.labNote: The four labels are the Lab's method, and the rule about north and occupancy is ours. It sat inside the generate-the-brief card and we have lifted it out, because it applies to every source, not only to a generated one. Other studios keep a single assumptions list, which is a good habit. We think the list must also say which lines were inferred, and from what, or the assumptions spread.
sections.howItWorks: A model asked to complete a brief completes it with the most probable content: probable plot sizes, probable budgets, probable orientations. The four labels are a way of reading that output without being fooled by its tone. They also describe every human brief. Peña's problem seeking is, among other things, the discipline of finding out what is not yet known before you design, and a list of open questions is one of the things it produces. The red-pen habit on this map is the same method applied to one kind of document. This card is the general form.

topics.name: Style words and substance words
topics.description: The Lab's position: style words leave the decisions to the model; substance words make them. "Contemporary, warm, natural light" are style words. They name a preference and leave every decision to the model.
evidence: Take a real brief you have sent. Split every descriptive word into two columns: style (mood, era, adjective) and substance (a space, a material, a direction, a count, a sequence). Most first attempts run nine to one. Rebalance toward substance and run both.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: style words leave the decisions to the model; substance words make them.

sections.position: "Contemporary, warm, natural light" are style words. They name a preference and leave every decision to the model. "Single-storey courtyard house, board-marked concrete, north skylight, compressed entry through a low corridor" are substance words. They name spaces, materials, directions and sequences — decisions. Style words return a house. Substance words return something much closer to your house. We hold that most weak briefs fail here, and that the fix is more programme, not more adjectives.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A model has no way to know what "warm" means to you. It has a learned tendency for what images described as "warm" tend to look like, and it follows that tendency wherever you leave the decision open. Substance words are the parts of an architectural programme — type, material logic, light with direction and time, sequence, moment. They leave less open. They do not guarantee geometry: a named courtyard can still come back wrong, and the spatial check on this map exists for that. But a brief made of substance can be checked line by line. A brief made of mood can only be liked.
sections.strongestObjection: "Style" and "substance" are not stable categories, in architecture or in how a model is steered. "Kerala vernacular" looks like a style word and carries roof geometry, material system, climate response, spatial order and craft at once — and it can steer harder than a paragraph of geometry. Meanwhile a supposedly substantive instruction — "courtyard house", "compressed entry" — may be obeyed only at the surface. The split teaches specificity well. Taught as a rule about which words control appearance and which control architecture, it teaches a false map.
sections.revisionCondition: If blind studio comparisons showed that precisely named traditions match substance-rich briefs on the outputs students can defend in crit, we would rewrite the card around vague against precise and drop the style/substance line. We already accept that a named tradition is substance in disguise. The open question is whether the split still helps a beginner more than it misleads them. We check it against evidence each edition.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Briefing for reading, not making
topics.description: Asking a model to read, compare or extract needs a different brief from asking it to make — and most students only know the making brief. Five parts. The material: paste or attach it, and say what it is.
evidence: Take one real document — a competition brief, a municipal notice. Brief a model to extract every date, number and named obligation into a table, with the page or line each came from. Check five entries against the source. Count the ones that are wrong or invented.
Write one analysis brief with all five parts labelled, run it on a document you know well, and mark which answers you could trace and which you could not.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to write one analysis brief with all five parts labelled, run it on a document you know well, and mark which answers you could trace and which you could not.

card.oneLiner: Asking a model to read, compare or extract needs a different brief from asking it to make — and most students only know the making brief.

sections.whenToUse: Whenever you hand a model material to read rather than a thing to make: a client email to summarise, two bye-law clauses to compare, a survey to pull numbers from, a transcript to extract decisions from.
sections.method: Five parts. **The material:** paste or attach it, and say what it is. **The question:** one job, stated plainly — extract, compare, summarise or classify; not all four. **The form of the answer:** a table, a list with page references, a paragraph of fixed length. **The rule for gaps:** "if it is not in the material, say so; do not fill from general knowledge." **The check:** ask for the exact words or location behind every claim, and open them. The gap rule asks the model not to fill; the check you make against the material is what catches it when it does. An analysis brief is judged by whether its answers can be traced back into the material. A making brief is judged by whether the result suits. That is the whole difference.
sections.watchForThis: Letting the model mix what the document says with what it knows. Without the gap rule, a summary of your client's brief will quietly contain sentences the client never wrote — plausible ones, which are the hardest to catch.
sections.tryIt: Take one real document — a competition brief, a municipal notice. Brief a model to extract every date, number and named obligation into a table, with the page or line each came from. Check five entries against the source. Count the ones that are wrong or invented.
sections.proveIt: Write one analysis brief with all five parts labelled, run it on a document you know well, and mark which answers you could trace and which you could not.
sections.labNote: The five-part analysis brief is the Lab's scaffold, built because students arrived knowing only how to brief for images. It is not the only workable shape. It is the one where, when an answer fails, we can point to the part that was missing.
sections.howItWorks: A model reading a document is still predicting the next tokens. But now the document sits in its context window, and the likeliest continuation of "what does clause 4 say" is usually something close to clause 4. The brief's job is to keep it there: to make quoting the text more likely than drifting from it. This card is the way in to the whole beyond-image part of the map — codes, quantities, climate numbers, minutes — where the model reads more than it draws.
