topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Criteria, or only plausibility
topics.description: Without stated criteria the model aims at what looks right. With them, it returns an assessment against your lines — which you then verify yourself. Criteria belong in the brief, written before generation. Naming how you will judge the answer gives the model a target other than plausibility, and gives you a test you can run on what comes back.
evidence: Add clear success criteria to a brief you have already run. Run it again, and show how the reply shifted from describing the scheme to assessing it — then show one criterion where you checked the model's assessment against the drawing, and say whether it was right.

Before generating, could the student state the criteria that would make the result usable or not — did they judge the outputs against those criteria rather than first impression — and did they check the model's own assessment against the drawing?
topics.critPrompt: Before generating, could the student state the criteria that would make the result usable or not — did they judge the outputs against those criteria rather than first impression — and did they check the model's own assessment against the drawing?

grounding.ref: Prompt Literacy for Architects: Briefing GPT‑5.2 Like a Studio Team
Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI

card.oneLiner: Without stated criteria the model aims at what looks right. With them, it returns an assessment against your lines — which you then verify yourself.

sections.dilemma: The brief is ready to run: type, constraints, materials, all of it. One thing is missing — how you will judge the answer. Writing criteria takes five more minutes and forces you to say what "good" means before you have seen anything. Leaving them out is faster, and the model will return something that looks right.
sections.choices: Run it now and judge the outputs by first impression. Or stop, write the criteria — "must keep the view axis from living room to court", "must not add a wet area", "must improve cross-ventilation" — and run it with the criteria inside the brief.
sections.consequence: Without criteria, the model aims for plausibility, because that is the only target it has. You get a description and grade it on feel. With criteria, you get an assessment: the model checks its answer against the lines you drew, and so can you. That assessment is a first pass, not a verdict. The model that made the scheme shares the blind spots of the model now checking it, so you confirm each check yourself, on the drawing. The second path is slower. It is also the only one that gives you a result you can defend when someone asks "why this one?"
sections.theCase: Two schemes for a school on a tight urban plot. Scheme A looks better on the screen. The criteria said: every classroom cross-ventilated, no dead-end corridors, the playground visible from the staff room. Scheme B meets all three — confirmed on the plan, not on the model's say-so. Scheme A meets one. Without the written criteria, A goes to the jury — and the jury finds the dead-end corridor in four minutes.
sections.takeItToCrit: Before generating, could the student state the criteria that would make the result usable or not — did they judge the outputs against those criteria rather than first impression — and did they check the model's own assessment against the drawing?
sections.position: Criteria belong in the brief, written before generation. Naming how you will judge the answer gives the model a target other than plausibility, and gives you a test you can run on what comes back. A written criterion asks; it does not verify. The check that counts is made by something independent of the generator — you on the drawing, a measurement, the CAD geometry.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: It is the layer students skip most, and the one that changes the reply most: from description to assessment. It is also the layer that carries the designer's judgment into the machine's work, and that is where we think authorship lives — provided the judgment stays with the designer and is not handed back to the machine as "it checked itself."
sections.strongestObjection: A model assessing its own output against your criteria is not an independent tester. It can misread the output, misapply the criterion, or rationalise a failure it cannot see, because the evaluator shares the generator's ways of being wrong. Explicit criteria can therefore create the look of verification without any. "Does the kitchen open onto the courtyard?" may be answered by the same model that misdrew the kitchen. If students learn that criteria make the model a tester of its own work, the card has taught the opposite of what it meant.
sections.revisionCondition: If self-assessment against stated criteria turned out, on student work, to catch the errors an independent check catches — measured, not felt — we would let the model's check stand as verification. Until then the criteria go in the brief and the verification stays outside the model. We also watch the older objection: if criteria-first briefs measurably narrow student work without a matching gain in defensibility, we would teach criteria as the second pass, not the first. Reviewed against studio output each edition.
sections.proveIt: Add clear success criteria to a brief you have already run. Run it again, and show how the reply shifted from describing the scheme to assessing it — then show one criterion where you checked the model's assessment against the drawing, and say whether it was right.
sections.howItWorks: A reasoning model plans before it answers, and its plan is built from whatever the brief supplies. Criteria give it a target to check against while planning. That is why the answer changes shape and not only content. What the criteria do not supply is an independent eye: a written instruction asks; the system's own controls enforce, and the control here is a check the generator did not make — yours, a measurement, a separate tool. The six-layer brief on this map gives criteria a layer of its own for exactly this reason.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Briefing a dreaming engine
topics.description: The Lab's position: atmosphere and photographic language steer what we call a dreaming engine. They should not be relied on to fix geometry. What the Lab calls a dreaming engine — a diffusion-led image tool used for atmosphere — is briefed in the language of photography and weather: light quality, time of day, lens, film stock, a named sensibility. Those words steer mood with real precision.
evidence: Write a dreaming brief for a space you are designing that sets light, atmosphere and camera and says nothing about the plan. Run it five times. Which qualities held across all five? That is what this register can carry. Which wandered? That belongs in another brief.
Does the student's dreaming brief chase atmosphere on purpose, or does it leak precision the engine cannot honour — and do they know which of their words did which job?

grounding.ref: Diffusion — How AI Paints from Noise

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: atmosphere and photographic language steer what we call a dreaming engine. They should not be relied on to fix geometry.

sections.position: What the Lab calls a dreaming engine — a diffusion-led image tool used for atmosphere — is briefed in the language of photography and weather: light quality, time of day, lens, film stock, a named sensibility. Those words steer mood with real precision. They should not be relied on to fix geometry. Asking a dreaming brief to hold a plan, a room count or a structural grid gives the register a job it was not built for. Then you blame the tool for failing.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Used this way, these tools improvise. Their value is in what they open up: the courtyard you did not ask for, the light you had not imagined. Open, charged language releases that value. Instruction-language shuts it down. Geometry belongs to the grounded register and to drawing. Most of the skill is knowing which register you are in. The split into dreaming and grounded is the Lab's working taxonomy, not a fact about the machines.
sections.strongestObjection: "Dreaming engine" may not describe an engine at all. It increasingly describes one mode of use inside hybrid systems that reason, generate, edit, retrieve and condition on geometry through a single interface; the same product that dreams from a phrase will hold a plan if you hand it one. Teaching dreaming and grounded as different engines may teach students this year's products instead of the transferable distinction underneath — open-ended generation against structurally conditioned generation — and leave them under-briefing tools that could have held the geometry.
sections.revisionCondition: When the tools we call dreaming engines hold counts, adjacencies and a supplied plan reliably under an atmospheric brief — measured on student work, not on demos — the register split softens into a dial, and this card is rewritten around open against conditioned generation rather than around two engines. Reviewed each edition against what the tools ship.
sections.tryIt: Write a dreaming brief for a space you are designing that sets light, atmosphere and camera and says nothing about the plan. Run it five times. Which qualities held across all five? That is what this register can carry. Which wandered? That belongs in another brief.
sections.takeItToCrit: Does the student's dreaming brief chase atmosphere on purpose, or does it leak precision the engine cannot honour — and do they know which of their words did which job?
sections.howItWorks: Diffusion models learn from photographs and their captions, and photographic vocabulary is dense in those captions. "Golden hour, 35 mm, Portra grain" sits beside thousands of images that share those qualities, so the words pull hard. "Three bedrooms off a central court" rarely appears in a caption, so the words pull weakly. The pull comes from the training data, not from your sentence.

topics.description: Put your facts into the brief — attached, retrieved, cited — and the answer can be traced, if you trace it; leave them out and the model fills the gap from its default. Three moves. Attach: put the actual source in — the site survey, the bye-law extract, the client's email, the photograph — once you have checked what may leave the studio (the four-risks card on this map: privacy, confidentiality, copyright, security).
evidence: Ask a model about the permitted height on a real plot, with nothing attached. Save the answer. Now attach the relevant pages of the actual regulation and ask again with the cite rule. Put the two answers side by side and mark where the first one was invented.

Show one grounded brief — sources attached, cite rule stated — and the answer it produced, with every claim traced by you to its source or flagged as unsupported, and one citation the model attached to a claim the source did not make.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one grounded brief — sources attached, cite rule stated — and the answer it produced, with every claim traced by you to its source or flagged as unsupported, and one citation the model attached to a claim the source did not make.

card.oneLiner: Put your facts into the brief — attached, retrieved, cited — and the answer can be traced, if you trace it; leave them out and the model fills the gap from its default.

sections.whenToUse: Any brief whose answer must be true about a particular place, project, document or person. In a studio, that is most briefs.
sections.method: Three moves. **Attach:** put the actual source in — the site survey, the bye-law extract, the client's email, the photograph — once you have checked what may leave the studio (the four-risks card on this map: privacy, confidentiality, copyright, security). **Retrieve:** where the source is too large, pull out the relevant pieces — a page, a clause, a table — and put those in, near the top of the brief. **Cite:** instruct the model to mark every claim with the attached source it came from, and to say plainly when a claim comes from nowhere you supplied. Then read the answer by tracing each claim back to your sources. The cite rule asks; your tracing is the control. A model can ignore an attached source, blend it with what it already believes, or pin a citation to a claim the source does not make — so a citation is a pointer to check, not a proof. A claim with no source is a claim to check or discard.
sections.watchForThis: Grounding for show. If you attach a survey and then ask a question the survey does not answer, you still get an answer — generated from the model's default, and carrying the survey's authority. Ground the brief, then ask only what the sources can actually answer.
sections.tryIt: Ask a model about the permitted height on a real plot, with nothing attached. Save the answer. Now attach the relevant pages of the actual regulation and ask again with the cite rule. Put the two answers side by side and mark where the first one was invented.
sections.proveIt: Show one grounded brief — sources attached, cite rule stated — and the answer it produced, with every claim traced by you to its source or flagged as unsupported, and one citation the model attached to a claim the source did not make.
sections.labNote: Attach, retrieve, cite is the Lab's briefing-side habit for the retrieval idea in the Mechanics strand. The engineering has other names and bigger machinery; this is the version a student can run by hand, tomorrow, on one document.
sections.howItWorks: Retrieval-augmented generation is the engineering form of this: a system searches a store of documents, puts the best-matching passages into the context, and the model answers from them. Grounding the brief by hand is the same structure at the scale of one conversation. The Mechanics strand explains why retrieval is really a way of spending the context budget. This card is the briefing habit that uses it.

topics.name: Name the drawing convention
topics.description: The Lab's position: name poché, fine-line elevation, orthographic severity — and a capable model can follow the look. Whether it cut the right thing is yours to check. After the words for space and the words for material and light, there is a third vocabulary: the discipline's own drawing conventions. Poché on the cut wall.
evidence: Take a vague, mood-based prompt for a section or an elevation. Rewrite it naming three drawing conventions: the cut, the beyond, the presentation register. Run both. Then check the convention-led output against the plan: does the poché sit where the section plane actually cuts? Then try a convention from your own region's drawing tradition and find out whether the model knows it.

topics.critPrompt: When the brief drifted, did the student reach for the discipline's drawing conventions or for more adjectives — and did they check what the named convention drew against the plan it was cut from?

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: name poché, fine-line elevation, orthographic severity — and a capable model can follow the look. Whether it cut the right thing is yours to check.

sections.position: After the words for space and the words for material and light, there is a third vocabulary: the discipline's own drawing conventions. Poché on the cut wall. Beyond in fine-line elevation. Orthographic severity. Editorial presentation, not photoreal. Name these in a brief and a capable model can steer toward them, where the convention is represented in what it learned. Stay at the level of mood and it falls back on its default — extra trees, soft gradients, generic tastefulness. A named convention asks for the look. It does not make the model understand the rule behind the look.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Poché is not black shading. Hand-drafted ink-over-watercolour is not watercolour illustration. A convention packs a hundred decisions into one term; an adjective packs none. When a brief drifts, the instinct is to add adjectives. The better move is to name the convention that already contains what the adjectives were reaching for. This is architecture's real advantage in prompting: the field has a vocabulary most other prompters do not. One line to keep beside it: a written instruction asks; the system's own controls enforce. The convention in the brief steers the look. What the section actually cuts is checked against the plan it was cut from, by you.
sections.strongestObjection: Even where a convention is heavily represented, reproducing its look is not evidence that the model understands the rule that gives it meaning. A wall rendered black is not proof the model knows what the section plane cuts; a dimension string is not proof the dimensions agree. A model can mimic an architectural drawing and fail architecturally inside it, and the better the mimicry, the harder the failure is to see. The regional problem stands too: conventions thin in the training data return a costume. But the deeper objection is this — the model may know exactly what our convention looks like without knowing what it means.
sections.revisionCondition: Evidence that named conventions steer no better than well-chosen adjectives on the plates students actually make — or that the look they produce comes so often with wrong geometry that the steering is worth less than the check it demands. We already teach the check; if the check turns out to be the whole lesson, this card folds into the spatial check and stays only as vocabulary. Reviewed each edition.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: What must remain visible together
topics.description: A drawing's frame follows what it must communicate. Decide what has to be seen together, and set the proportion from that — not from the drawing's type, and not from the platform. Start from the drawing's job, not its type. Ask what must remain visible together for the drawing to make its argument.
evidence: Take one drawing you are making and write the sentence: what must be seen together. Generate it once at the tool's default and once at the proportion the sentence asks for. Put them side by side and list what the default cost: which rooms, which ground line, which end of the argument.
Defend a drawing's proportion in crit from what it had to show, with the default-shaped version beside it for comparison.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student defend a drawing’s aspect ratio as a design decision, not a platform default?

card.oneLiner: A drawing's frame follows what it must communicate. Decide what has to be seen together, and set the proportion from that — not from the drawing's type, and not from the platform.

sections.whenToUse: Before you generate any drawing-type image — a section, an elevation, a street, a plan — and before you crop one for a platform.
sections.method: Start from the drawing's job, not its type. Ask what must remain visible together for the drawing to make its argument. A section through a long terrace, where the point is the continuity of the ground line, may need 3:1. A section through an atrium, where the point is the stack of air rising through six floors, may need 2:3. A façade may be long, square or tall depending on the building. Write the answer as a sentence: "the reader must see the ground line and both end walls in one view." Then set the aspect ratio as a slot in the brief to match that sentence — not the tool's default square. Generate at that proportion. If a platform later wants a square, crop a copy and keep the framed one as the record.
sections.watchForThis: Two errors, opposite in direction. Accepting the default because it is the default: most tools open at a square or a 16:9, which is the shape of a feed, not of an argument. And assuming a drawing type has a shape: "a section is wide" is false — a tower section is tall, a transverse section through a narrow house is nearly square. The proportion belongs to what this drawing must show, not to the word "section".
sections.tryIt: Take one drawing you are making and write the sentence: what must be seen together. Generate it once at the tool's default and once at the proportion the sentence asks for. Put them side by side and list what the default cost: which rooms, which ground line, which end of the argument.
sections.proveIt: Defend a drawing's proportion in crit from what it had to show, with the default-shaped version beside it for comparison.
sections.labNote: A method, not a law. Platforms have real constraints, and a square crop for a carousel is sometimes the right call. Our claim is narrower: the frame is set from the drawing's argument, that version is the record, and the crop is made from it, never the other way round. Others teach "design for the platform first"; we think that order loses the drawing.
sections.howItWorks: A drawing is read by moving through it, and the frame decides what the eye can hold at once. A long ground line read in one sweep makes one argument; the same ground line cut into a square and scrolled makes a different, weaker one. A tall atrium section works the same way in the other direction. For years image tools forced drawings into social-media formats, because those were the shapes their training images came in. Aspect ratio is now a slot you can set in most tools. That makes a drawing's shape your decision again, and leaving it to the default is still a decision.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Exclusions are design decisions
topics.description: What you forbid shapes what you get. An exclusion is the negative space of the brief. Run the brief once without exclusions. Read the output for what arrived uninvited: people, planting, warm fairy lights, a second storey, a glass balustrade.
evidence: Take a brief you have run. Add three exclusions chosen from what the first output added on its own. Run it again and mark what changed. Then remove one exclusion and watch the default return.

card.oneLiner: What you forbid shapes what you get. An exclusion is the negative space of the brief.

sections.whenToUse: Every image brief, and any text brief where the model keeps adding something you did not ask for. Exclusions are the last slot of the seven-slot brief and the one most often left empty.
sections.method: Run the brief once without exclusions. Read the output for what arrived uninvited: people, planting, warm fairy lights, a second storey, a glass balustrade. Name each one and forbid it: "no people", "no planting", "no artificial light". Put the exclusions on their own line, not buried in the description. Run again. Keep the exclusions that changed something. Record them with the brief, because each one is a decision about what your building is not.
sections.watchForThis: Some image tools, especially older diffusion pipelines, read the noun in an exclusion as the thing itself: "no trees" can add trees. Many tools therefore give exclusions their own field, often called a negative prompt. Where that field exists, use it: a "no" in the prose asks; the negative-prompt field is the control the tool actually reads. Test how your tool handles a "no" before you trust one.
sections.tryIt: Take a brief you have run. Add three exclusions chosen from what the first output added on its own. Run it again and mark what changed. Then remove one exclusion and watch the default return.

sections.howItWorks: Every slot you leave open, the model fills with its most probable content. Exclusions close slots. That is why they carry design intent: "no glass balustrade" is a decision about material, just as "brick parapet" is. The card is marked EVOLVING because how tools handle negation is changing — image-reasoning models increasingly read "no" the way a person does, while older diffusion pipelines still need a separate negative field. The method works either way.

topics.name: Negotiating the model's defaults
topics.description: Every blank slot gets the model's default — a learned tendency, tilted the way its data and training are tilted. Briefing is talking it down. Every slot you leave blank, the model fills with its default. The default is not an average of its data.

grounding.ref: Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas

card.oneLiner: Every blank slot gets the model's default — a learned tendency, tilted the way its data and training are tilted. Briefing is talking it down.

sections.dilemma: Every slot you leave blank, the model fills with its default. The default is not an average of its data. It is a learned tendency, shaped by what the data contained most, by how the model was trained and tuned afterwards, by the system's own instructions and by how it samples — and it is tilted the way all of those are tilted. You cannot fill every slot; there are always more than you can name. So you have to choose which defaults to fight and which to accept.
sections.choices: Accept the default where it does not touch your argument. Fight it where it does, by naming what you mean before the model decides. Or fight everything, and write a brief so long that the model attends to none of it.
sections.consequence: Accept the wrong default and a decision you never made appears in your work looking like yours: the glass tower the model prefers, the Western porch, the extra trees. Fight every default and you lose what a generator offers, which is speed and surprise. The skill is predicting the default before you see it, so the fight happens in the brief and not in the re-roll.
sections.theCase: "A house in Dharwad" returns a house that has never seen Dharwad: a pitched tiled roof from somewhere else, a lawn, no compound wall, no jagali. Each is a default. The student decides: the roof matters — fight it, "flat RCC roof with a parapet"; the compound wall matters — fight it; the lawn does not matter for this study — accept it, or exclude it. Three lines in the brief, and the house moves from the model's default to the student's street.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student name the defaults their brief quietly accepted, say which ones they chose to fight, and show that the fight happened in the brief rather than in forty re-rolls?
sections.proveIt: Before you run a minimal prompt, write down the defaults you predict it will impose. Run it. Score your predictions. Then write the brief that overrides the ones that matter.
sections.howItWorks: A generative model returns a probable completion of what it was given. Where the brief is silent, "probable" follows the model's learned tendency, and that tendency over-represents the photographed, the published and the Western, because the data did and the later training did not correct for it. There is no villain here, and there is no "average" being looked up. The default is simply what the system leans toward when nothing pushes back, and it will be chosen for you unless you choose first. The exclusions card on this map is the tool; this card is the judgment about when to use it.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The seven-slot brief
topics.description: Subject · composition · material · light · view · mood · exclusions. Seven slots to inspect before you generate — an unexamined slot is a decision handed to the model. Write seven lines, one per slot. Each slot is a decision: subject (what the image shows — type, scale, point in time) · composition (framing, point of view, foreground to background) · material (every named surface) · light (time, weather, direction, quality) · view (focal length, format, a camera sensibility) · mood (the affective register — a named photographer or film stock if it helps) · exclusions (what must not appear).
evidence: Write a seven-slot brief for a space you are designing, marking which slots you filled and which you left open and why. Then take a classmate's brief and mark the slots they left empty. Run theirs, and find in the output each decision the model made for them — and ask which of those were left open on purpose.
For any image you show, produce the seven-slot brief behind it and defend each slot as a decision you made — including the ones you chose to leave open.
topics.critPrompt: For any image the student shows, can they produce the seven-slot brief behind it, and defend each slot as a decision?

card.oneLiner: Subject · composition · material · light · view · mood · exclusions. Seven slots to inspect before you generate — an unexamined slot is a decision handed to the model.

sections.whenToUse: Any brief to an image engine where the output has to be yours: a design study, a client image, a plate you will present. Not for a throwaway mood test.
sections.method: Write seven lines, one per slot. Each slot is a decision: **subject** (what the image shows — type, scale, point in time) · **composition** (framing, point of view, foreground to background) · **material** (every named surface) · **light** (time, weather, direction, quality) · **view** (focal length, format, a camera sensibility) · **mood** (the affective register — a named photographer or film stock if it helps) · **exclusions** (what must not appear). Inspect all seven. Fill the ones that must be controlled; leave open, on purpose, the ones you want the engine to explore — and write down which is which. An unexamined slot is not neutral. It is a decision you have handed to the model without noticing.
sections.watchForThis: Filling material and mood and leaving composition blank by accident. The model then chooses the view, and the view decides what the image is about. The opposite error is filling every slot out of habit: if the material palette is the question, specifying every material in advance ends the experiment before it starts.
sections.tryIt: Write a seven-slot brief for a space you are designing, marking which slots you filled and which you left open and why. Then take a classmate's brief and mark the slots they left empty. Run theirs, and find in the output each decision the model made for them — and ask which of those were left open on purpose.
sections.proveIt: For any image you show, produce the seven-slot brief behind it and defend each slot as a decision you made — including the ones you chose to leave open.
sections.labNote: Seven slots is the Lab's scaffold. It is written for architectural photography, because that is the register most built-environment image work borrows. It is a checklist to inspect, not seven boxes to fill: a daylight study may leave mood open on purpose, and an input image may already fix the composition. It is not the only structure that works; we use a five-slot version in crowded rooms, and other teachers divide the same ground differently. It is the one we can defend slot by slot.
sections.howItWorks: Most prompting tutorials teach two or three things — subject, style, medium — and leave the rest unsaid. Architectural photographs are described in more ways than that, and image models learned from those descriptions. The seven slots name the qualities the captions usually carry. Exclusions is the slot that matters most: beginners skip it, and without it an image drifts in ways they cannot explain. This is the image twin of the six-layer reasoning brief elsewhere on this map.

topics.name: Tables are not prose

grounding.ref: Dziri et al., Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
Gao et al., PAL: Program-aided Language Models

topics.description: A model reads a table as fluently as a paragraph and adds it up far less reliably — numbers need checking machinery, not trust. A language model handles a table the way it handles a sentence: as a sequence of tokens to continue. It reads a schedule of areas beautifully.
evidence: Give a model a twenty-row table of rooms with areas. Ask for the total. Then ask it to write the formula or a short script instead, and run that. Then add the column yourself. Compare all three. Repeat with a harder ask — a weighted cost — and note where the plain answer failed.
Explain why a model that reads a table fluently can still add it wrongly, and describe the working method that makes the number checkable.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain why a model that reads a table fluently can still add it wrongly, and describe the working method that makes the number checkable.

card.oneLiner: A model reads a table as fluently as a paragraph and adds it up far less reliably — numbers need checking machinery, not trust.

sections.idea: A language model handles a table the way it handles a sentence: as a sequence of tokens to continue. It reads a schedule of areas beautifully. Asked to total the column by continuing the tokens, many current models make errors, confidently. Language generation is not arithmetic execution. Many products now hand the sum to code or a spreadsheet behind the scenes; find out whether yours does, and ask for the working either way. Brief the calculation: source data, units, the formula, the tool, the working, the result, the check. Read with the model. Count with a machine built for counting.
sections.whyItMatters: Areas, quantities and costs are where a design meets money and law. An error in prose embarrasses you. An error in a quantity schedule can become a contract dispute. The same shape of brief carries FSI, costing, occupancy and embodied carbon.
sections.inTheStudio: You paste a room schedule and ask for the total carpet area and the FSI consumed. The answer arrives in two seconds with a neat table. One room was counted twice; the FSI figure uses a ratio the model assumed. A spreadsheet would have got both right, because you would have seen the formula.
sections.watchForThis: A total that arrives without the working. If you cannot see the sum being done, treat the number as a sentence: plausible, unverified.
sections.tryIt: Give a model a twenty-row table of rooms with areas. Ask for the total. Then ask it to write the formula or a short script instead, and run that. Then add the column yourself. Compare all three. Repeat with a harder ask — a weighted cost — and note where the plain answer failed.
sections.proveIt: Explain why a model that reads a table fluently can still add it wrongly, and describe the working method that makes the number checkable.
sections.howItWorks: Research on how transformers handle multi-step tasks such as multi-digit multiplication found them matching patterns from training rather than carrying out the procedure: good on familiar sizes, failing as the steps stack up. The standard repair is program-aided: the model writes code, and an interpreter does the computing. Many products now do this behind the scenes. That is why this card is EVOLVING: the raw weakness remains, the tools increasingly route around it, and you need to know whether yours does.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Three prompt families, three registers
topics.description: The Lab's position: one brief discipline, three registers — reasoning, dreaming, grounded. Prompting is not one skill. The Lab works in three registers, and briefs the same design intent three ways.
evidence: Take one project of yours. Write three briefs for it, one per engine, so that each reads as unmistakably different. Hand all three, unlabelled, to a classmate and ask which engine each is for. If they cannot tell, the registers have not separated.
Can the student write three genuinely different briefs for one project and justify each against its engine — rather than the same brief in three costumes?
topics.critPrompt: Can the student write three genuinely different briefs for one project and justify each against its engine — rather than the same brief in three costumes?

grounding.ref: Prompt Personalities: How to Collaborate With ChatGPT and Claude

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: one brief discipline, three registers — reasoning, dreaming, grounded.

sections.position: Prompting is not one skill. The Lab works in three registers, and briefs the same design intent three ways. To a reasoning model, in layers: intent, context, constraints, criteria, output form, iteration. To a dreaming engine, in atmosphere: light, lens, mood, a charged open phrase. To a grounded generator, in instructions: what to preserve, what to label, what format to return. One discipline of briefing, three registers of language. Give the reasoning model a dreaming brief and you get poetry with no plan. Give the dreaming engine an instruction brief and you get obedience with no life. These are working registers — a way of approaching the machine — not three species of machine.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The jobs differ in character, not only in interface. One plans, one improvises, one complies. Language that suits one is wasted on the others. A student who learns one register on one tool can brief that tool and is stuck with everything else. A student who writes three registers for one project has a skill that survives when the tools change.
sections.strongestObjection: Reasoning, dreaming and grounded are not three categories of the same kind. Reasoning names a capability; dreaming names a generative mode; grounded names a relationship to supplied information or constraints. One system can be all three at once — reasoning over a grounded image, then generating a speculative one — and a single interface increasingly routes to whatever engine fits. Taught as studio shorthand the split works. Taught as a taxonomy of AI systems it is wrong, and students at this age are old enough to mistake a memorable framework for how the systems are actually classified. "Write one clear brief and let the system route it" may become the honest advice.
sections.revisionCondition: When a single brief, written once, reliably produces the reasoning, the atmosphere and the grounded plate without the student changing register — judged on studio work — the three families become one brief with three outputs, and this card is rewritten as history. Reviewed each edition against what the tools do.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Millimetres, north, datum, grid

grounding.ref: Bureau of Indian Standards, National Building Code of India 2016 (SP 7:2016)

topics.description: Put the drawing's fixed facts into the brief — units, orientation, datum, floor level, scale, grid — or the model chooses them for you. Before the design content, write the anchors, one per line. Units: "all dimensions in millimetres" — the convention on an Indian working drawing, where a wall is 230, not 0.23.
evidence: Take a plan study you have briefed before. Run it as written. Then add six anchor lines at the top: units, north, datum, scale, origin, grid. Run it again. Measure the second output against the anchors: is the grid 7.2 m, is north where you said, is the ground floor at ±0.000. Record which anchors held and which the model quietly dropped.
Show one brief with its anchors written before the design content, and the check you ran on each anchor after the run.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one brief with its anchors written before the design content, and the check you ran on each anchor after the run.

card.oneLiner: Put the drawing's fixed facts into the brief — units, orientation, datum, floor level, scale, grid — or the model chooses them for you.

sections.whenToUse: Any brief where the output must line up with real drawings: a plan study, a section, a massing that has to sit on a surveyed plot, a request to read or redraw a drawing. Not for a mood image.
sections.method: Before the design content, write the anchors, one per line. **Units:** "all dimensions in millimetres" — the convention on an Indian working drawing, where a wall is 230, not 0.23. **Orientation:** "north is up on the attached survey", or "north is to the top-left, as marked". **Datum and floor level:** "±0.000 is the finished floor level of the ground floor; the road is at −0.450". **Scale, where it applies:** "the attached plan is at 1:100". **Coordinate origin:** "the origin is the south-west corner of the plot". **Dimensional anchors:** "preserve the 7.2 m structural grid"; "the plot is 12 m by 18 m". Each anchor is one line. Each one removes a choice the model would otherwise make for you. After the run, check each anchor against the output, one by one. The spatial-check card gives that method.
sections.watchForThis: Writing "12 by 18" and letting the model decide whether that is metres or feet. Many Indian sites are still described in feet on the ground and in millimetres on the drawing. Put the unit on every number, and say once which system the whole brief uses. Watch also for an orientation with no reference: "north is up" means nothing unless you say up on what.
sections.tryIt: Take a plan study you have briefed before. Run it as written. Then add six anchor lines at the top: units, north, datum, scale, origin, grid. Run it again. Measure the second output against the anchors: is the grid 7.2 m, is north where you said, is the ground floor at ±0.000. Record which anchors held and which the model quietly dropped.
sections.proveIt: Show one brief with its anchors written before the design content, and the check you ran on each anchor after the run.
sections.labNote: Putting the anchors first is the Lab's method. The conventions themselves are not ours: millimetres, a north point, a ±0.000 datum and a structural grid are how Indian working drawings have been read for decades, and the National Building Code of India sits behind that practice. What we add is the order, anchors before content, and the insistence that each anchor is checked after the run. Other teachers put precision in the constraints layer and leave it there. We think it belongs at the top, in the drawing's own language.
sections.howItWorks: A model has no ruler and no compass. It has text and pixels. An anchor line turns a fact about the drawing into text the model can follow, and into a test you can run afterwards. A raster image can hold the look of a grid and still not hold a 7.2 m dimension. That is why these anchors work best with reasoning models and grounded generators, and why a plan that must be accurate is drawn in CAD or BIM from what the model returns, never exported from its image. The conventions come from practice: millimetres are the usual unit on Indian working drawings, a north point is marked on plans, and levels are given from a stated datum, usually the finished floor of the ground floor as ±0.000. The National Building Code of India 2016, published by the Bureau of Indian Standards, is the code those drawings answer to.

topics.name: Working a long document

grounding.ref: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle
Tokens, Context, and Why AI Forgets

topics.description: A long document is easy to misread at length — work it in pieces, demand page-true citations, and make the model show you where it says that. Start by asking the model for the document's structure — sections, headings, page ranges — and check it against the real contents page. Then work one section at a time, naming the section each turn.
evidence: Upload a long regulation. Ask for the rule on one specific matter, with page and quoted sentence. Open the page. Do this five times across the document — early, middle, late. Note where it was right and where it drifted.
Show one set of claims extracted from a long document where every line carries a page reference you personally opened — and one line you caught that was wrong.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one set of claims extracted from a long document where every line carries a page reference you personally opened — and one line you caught that was wrong.

card.oneLiner: A long document is easy to misread at length — work it in pieces, demand page-true citations, and make the model show you where it says that.

sections.whenToUse: Any document longer than a few pages: a development control regulation, a tender, a conservation report, a thesis you are reviewing.
sections.method: Start by asking the model for the document's structure — sections, headings, page ranges — and check it against the real contents page. Then work one section at a time, naming the section each turn. Demand page-true citations: every claim carries a page number, and "show me the sentence" is a question you ask often. Quote rather than paraphrase wherever a word matters — a bye-law's "shall" is not "should". Keep your own running note of what has been verified. When the conversation grows long, start a fresh one with the section you need, rather than trusting the model to hold the whole file.
sections.watchForThis: A page number that looks exact and is not. Models produce citations the way they produce everything: plausibly. A page-true citation is one you opened. Watch the middle of a long file too — on some models, material there is recalled less reliably than the start and the end; test yours rather than assume it.
sections.tryIt: Upload a long regulation. Ask for the rule on one specific matter, with page and quoted sentence. Open the page. Do this five times across the document — early, middle, late. Note where it was right and where it drifted.
sections.proveIt: Show one set of claims extracted from a long document where every line carries a page reference you personally opened — and one line you caught that was wrong.
sections.labNote: Map first, one section at a time, page-true or nothing: this is the Lab's way of working a long document, arrived at by watching page numbers drift in student work. Other methods will do; this is the one we teach and can defend line by line.
sections.howItWorks: The document becomes tokens in the context window, and attention spreads unevenly across them. Measured work on 2023 models found recall weakest for material in the middle; newer models have narrowed that gap, and how much remains depends on the model and the task. Working section by section keeps each turn short enough that the answer does not depend on the curve at all. Some products add retrieval — they search the file and pass only the matching passages into the window. That helps, and it also means the model may never have "read" the page you assume it did.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: Brief spatially, verify spatially
topics.description: Every spatial clause you brief needs a matching check on the output — two halves of one loop. Before you run the brief, write one check for each spatial clause in it. "Three bays": count the bays.
evidence: Write a brief with three spatial clauses and, beneath it, the three checks. Run and check. Most first attempts find at least one dropped clause. Re-anchor it and run again.
Catch one spatial instruction the model dropped, using a check you wrote before you saw the output.
topics.critPrompt: For every spatial thing the student asks for, can they show the matching test they ran on what came back?

grounding.ref: Chatterjee et al., 2024 — Getting it Right / SPRIGHT (arXiv:2404.01197)

card.oneLiner: Every spatial clause you brief needs a matching check on the output — two halves of one loop.

sections.whenToUse: Any brief with a spatial clause: a count ("three bays"), a relation ("the kitchen opens onto the court"), an adjacency, a left/right/above/below. That is nearly every architectural brief.
sections.method: Before you run the brief, write one check for each spatial clause in it. "Three bays": count the bays. "Kitchen opens onto the court": find the kitchen, find the court, find the opening. Run the brief. Run the checks one by one on the output itself, not on your impression of it. Record which clauses held and which the model dropped. Put the dropped ones back into the brief, stated again — or move them into a grounded step that can hold them. A spatial clause in the brief asks; the check you run on the output is what enforces it.
sections.watchForThis: Checking the image for beauty and forgetting to check it for truth. An image can be compelling and have four bays where you asked for three. The eye forgives counts. A client's surveyor does not.
sections.tryIt: Write a brief with three spatial clauses and, beneath it, the three checks. Run and check. Most first attempts find at least one dropped clause. Re-anchor it and run again.
sections.proveIt: Catch one spatial instruction the model dropped, using a check you wrote before you saw the output.
sections.labNote: The weakness is measured; the loop is ours. Benchmarks establish that current image models drop spatial clauses. Writing the check before you generate, and running it on the output rather than on your impression of it, is the Lab's method for living with that — not the only one. Others check afterwards, or move every spatial clause into a conditioned step from the start. Ours is the one that leaves a record of which clause failed.
sections.howItWorks: Benchmarks built to test spatial language in image generation show current models failing often on exactly these clauses: relative position, counting, several objects placed together. Part of the cause is the training data. Captions rarely say where things sit in relation to each other, so the models learned how things look better than how they are arranged. Re-captioning images with clear spatial language improves the results. The numbers will move: the weakness is measured today and is being worked on. The loop — brief spatially, verify spatially — holds whatever the numbers do.

topics.subject: The Brief
topics.name: The brief-to-crit loop
topics.description: Output, crit, revised brief, again. A crit that only judges the image stalls; a crit that produces a next action — most often a rewritten brief — iterates. The studio loop closes through the brief: output, crit, revised brief, again. A crit must produce a next action, and most often that action is a change to the document, not a choice between images.
evidence: Show one full loop — an output, the crit notes on it, the brief rewritten from those notes, and the next output — where the crit changed the brief and not just the image you selected.
After critiquing the output, did the student go back to the brief or to the re-roll button — and can they show one crit finding that became a specific edit in the next version of the brief?
topics.critPrompt: After critiquing the output, did the student go back to the brief or to the re-roll button — and can they show one crit finding that became a specific edit in the next version of the brief?

card.oneLiner: Output, crit, revised brief, again. A crit that only judges the image stalls; a crit that produces a next action — most often a rewritten brief — iterates.

sections.dilemma: An output comes back and it is not right. You can press generate again and hope — the re-roll — or you can stop, critique the output, and carry the critique back into the brief. The re-roll takes ten seconds. The loop takes ten minutes and a rewritten document.
sections.choices: Re-roll until something you like appears, then select it. Or crit the output as you would a junior's drawing — what held, what drifted, what the brief never said — and revise the brief to v2 before running again.
sections.consequence: The re-roll treats the model as a slot machine and the designer as a picker. When something good arrives you cannot say why, and you cannot make it happen again. The loop treats every failure as information about the brief: the brief improves, the outputs converge, and the reasoning is on paper. A crit that only judges the image stalls. A crit that rewrites the brief turns generation into iteration.
sections.theCase: A student shows a courtyard house after forty generations and says the light "finally came right." Asked what changed between the thirty-ninth and the fortieth, they cannot say: same brief, different seed. A second student shows three images and three briefs — v1, v2, v3 — with the crit notes between them: "v1: light arrives from nowhere. Add north skylight, morning." The second student can do it again tomorrow, on another building.

sections.whenToUse: When you hand work to a system that will act over several steps — search, read, write files, call tools, come back — rather than answer once.
sections.method: Start with the six layers: intent, context, constraints, criteria, output form, iteration loop. Then add three. **Checkpoints:** where the process must pause and show you — "after the list of candidate sites, stop and wait." **Stop-conditions:** what ends the work — a count, a time, a finding, a failure. Written in the brief, a stop-condition tells the process when it ought to stop; it does not make it unable to continue. What enforces the stop is the system's own controls — an execution budget, a maximum number of steps, a timeout, a tool allowlist, a human approval gate — so set those where the tool lets you, and write the stop-condition as well. **Permissions:** what it may read, what it may change, and what it must never touch — the client folder, the sent mail, the live drawing. A permission in the brief asks; a permission set in the system is what holds. Write the three as plainly as constraints. Run a small version first, read the log of what it did, and only then give it the real job.
sections.watchForThis: A brief that states the goal and trusts the process to know when to stop — or trusts a sentence to stop it. A multi-step system that is wrong at step two carries the error through every step after it. One wrong answer from a chatbot is one wrong answer. One wrong answer inside a process is a chain.
sections.tryIt: Brief an agent-style tool to collect ten references on a topic and write a one-page note. Version one: goal only. Version two: goal plus a checkpoint after the references, a stop at ten, and a rule that it may read but not write outside one folder — and, where the tool allows, the same limits set in its settings, not only in the words. Compare the two logs, not just the two notes.
sections.proveIt: Show one process brief with all nine parts labelled and the log of a run, pointing to where a checkpoint or a stop-condition did its job — and to the system control (budget, step limit, approval gate, permission) that backed it.
sections.labNote: Six layers plus three is the Lab's extension of its own reasoning brief for systems that act. Vendors publish their own guidance on agents, and it agrees on the spirit — simple loops, human checkpoints, limits set in the harness rather than asked for in the prompt. The nine-part shape is ours, and it will be revised as the tools change.
sections.howItWorks: An agent is a model inside a loop: plan, act, observe, repeat. Each pass through the loop reads your brief again, so instructions that were clear for a single answer become ambiguous over twenty actions. What an agent can reach — files, mail, money — is set by its permissions, which someone configured, and how long it can run is set by its budget; those are the controls. The brief's stop-conditions and permissions ask; the configured ones enforce. The Studio Practice strand carries the responsibility side of that. Tool capabilities and safeguards change by the month, which is why this card is reviewed each edition.

card.oneLiner: A model does not use every part of its window equally well. Put load-bearing constraints at the top or in the latest turn, and state them again when the thread grows long.

sections.idea: A model holds a limited window of text and does not use every part of it equally well. Research on 2023 models found that material near the start and end was used more reliably than the middle. Newer models have narrowed that gap; how much remains depends on the model and the task. So a brief has a shape, not only a content. Put load-bearing constraints at the top, or in the latest turn, and state them again when the conversation grows long. A constraint stated once, forty exchanges ago, is still in the window and may be ignored.
sections.whyItMatters: "The model forgot my setback rule" is often a structure problem, not a memory problem. Once you know that placement matters on your model, the complaint becomes a decision about where to put the rule.
sections.inTheStudio: You set "every plan at 1:100, north up" at the start of a long session. Forty turns later a plan arrives at 1:50, north to the left. Nothing broke. The rule sank into a long middle. Say it again, close to where you need it, and ask whether the long thread is now costing you more than it is keeping for you.
sections.watchForThis: Treating a long thread as a free archive. Every earlier turn dilutes the attention available for the current one. Sometimes the right move is a fresh thread with a tightened brief that carries the constraints forward.
sections.tryIt: Take a constraint the model dropped deep in a long chat. Re-anchor it — state it again at the top of your next message — and run the same request. Then open a fresh thread with only the brief and the constraint and run it a third time. Compare all three.
sections.proveIt: Show a brief in which the load-bearing constraints sit where your model uses them best, and explain the placement in terms of the window — and of what you tested, not what you assumed.
sections.howItWorks: Models read the whole conversation every time they answer, through attention, and attention is a fixed amount of weight spread across everything in the window. The "lost in the middle" pattern was measured on 2023 models. Newer models have softened the curve a great deal — some now retrieve from very long contexts almost perfectly on the tests their makers publish — and products add memory or summaries on top, which changes how forgetting feels. That is why the card is EVOLVING: placement is a model- and task-dependent heuristic, not a law of language models. The habit costs nothing, and the warning against treating a long thread as a free archive holds whatever the curve does.

sections.whenToUse: When the client has given you three lines and a phone number, and you need a complete brief to design against. In practice this is more common than the long messy brief.
sections.method: Write down exactly what the client said: two or three lines, no more. Ask a reasoning model to draft a full brief from it — intent, user groups, spatial priorities, mood, constraints, success criteria, open questions. Add one instruction and never skip it: *distinguish what the client stated from what you are inferring; do not invent budget, deadline or site facts.* Then take a red pen to the draft. Mark every line as stated, inferred-and-useful, or invented. Strike the invented. Question the inferred. What survives is a brief you can take back to the client.
sections.watchForThis: Letting the generated brief stand because it reads well. It will read well. It will also have invented a budget, a plot size and a completion date from nothing, in the same confident tone as the parts that are true.
sections.tryIt: Generate a full brief from three lines of client context. Red-pen it. Count the inventions. Then sort the inferences into two piles: useful provocations that raised a question you should ask, and traps that would have quietly become facts.
sections.proveIt: Show a red-penned generated brief with the provenance of every line marked, and name which inferences were worth keeping as questions.
sections.labNote: We teach generation and decoding as a pair, and we insist on the red pen. Generation is a first draft of thinking. Editing is where authorship lives. Others treat the generated brief as a time-saver to be used as is; we think that is exactly where the invented budget enters the project.
sections.howItWorks: A model asked to complete a brief from thin context completes it the way it completes everything: with the most probable content. Probable budgets, probable plot sizes, probable deadlines. None of them are facts about your client. The "distinguish stated from inferred" instruction makes the model label where each line came from. That is the cheapest defence against invented facts, and it is only a request: a written instruction asks; the red pen is the control that enforces it.

card.oneLiner: Brief a grounded generator in what to keep, what to label, and what to return. The brief asks for the real input to be protected; a mask, a conditioning signal and your overlay check are what protect it.

sections.whenToUse: When you have a real input worth protecting — a drawn section, a plan, a site photograph, a page of text — and you want the model to edit, label, lay out or present it rather than invent past it. This is the grounded register.
sections.method: Start with what must not change: "preserve the geometry of the attached section; do not move walls, levels or openings." Then say what to add: labels, callouts, a title block, a layout. Then name the visual register as a drawing convention. Then the output format: size, proportion, file type. Last, state the instruction the whole brief exists for: "do not paraphrase any of the text" or "do not change the protected elements." Then reach for the control that enforces it: where the tool offers a mask, a locked region or a conditioning input — the drawing itself as a line or depth image — use it. A sentence such as "do not move walls" asks; the mask is what holds the wall. Run it. Check the protected elements first, before you look at anything the model added.
sections.watchForThis: Trusting the sentence. A preserve instruction is not a geometric constraint: a written instruction asks; the system's own controls enforce. And reading the output for what was added while missing what was changed. A grounded generator can redraw a wall half a metre over while adding a beautiful label to it. Check the fixed things against the input, element by element.
sections.tryIt: Write a grounded brief for one of your own drawings naming three things that must not change, two things to label, and the output format. Run it once with the preserve instruction alone and once with the instruction backed by a mask or a conditioning input. Overlay input and output for both and find every drift.
sections.proveIt: Show a case where a preserve instruction, backed by a mask or conditioning input, kept a real drawing from being redrawn: the input, the brief, the control you used, the output, and the overlay.
sections.labNote: You are not writing a prompt to produce the text. You are writing the text, then writing a prompt to protect it. That is our order of work for grounded tools: the real input comes first, the brief names what is guarded, and the tool's controls and your check do the guarding. Others use the same tools to generate from scratch, and that is legitimate. Our position is that the grounded register is most useful when it protects work that already exists.
sections.howItWorks: Grounded generators — image-reasoning models and conditioned diffusion — are built to follow instructions. They hold references, text, layout and constraints better than dreaming engines, and they surprise you less. Conditioning methods such as ControlNet let a supplied drawing steer the geometry directly; masks lock regions out of the edit. Those are the controls. The brief names what they protect, and the overlay check confirms that they did. None of this makes preservation automatic.

card.oneLiner: Directing a blend of references and owning it — authored synthesis, not a collage of borrowed parts.

sections.dilemma: You have three references that each carry something you want: the spatial pressure of one, the proportional discipline of another, the constructional clarity of a third. Some current image-reasoning models can blend several references into one new thing rather than pasting them side by side. The question is what you ask for, and what you accept when it comes back.
sections.choices: Ask for "a combination of these three" and accept what arrives. Or name what each reference is there to contribute, ask for a synthesis, and then read the result for which ancestor became too loud — and redirect.
sections.consequence: The first path gives you collage: three recognisable quotations in one frame, each borrowed, none yours. The second gives you synthesis — one new thing that carries what it inherited without becoming a muddle — and only if you did the curating, named what each reference contributes, and judged the blend. The difference is not in the model. It is in whether an author directed the blend and can say what each part owes to whom.
sections.theCase: A student brings four public-domain plates — Piranesi, Wagner, Viollet-le-Duc, Fergusson — and asks for a section of a colonial-era Indian courtyard in ruin. First pass: seventy per cent there, the Piranesi darkness swallowing the Fergusson clarity. The student's job at that moment is not to praise the image. It is to say "Piranesi up, Fergusson preserved," and to know why those are the right words. Four references that share a deep logic, and the synthesis starts to hold. Four that do not, and no instruction will save it.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student tell directed synthesis from collage in their own output, name what each ancestor contributed, and defend the result as authored rather than borrowed?
sections.position: The mood board has always been the prompt. AI has made the synthesis visible. The reference set is now brief input, the curation is the authorship moment, and a blend you cannot account for is a collage you happen to like.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Architects have always taken crosshatch density from one drawing and proportion from another and called it inspiration. Calling it synthesis, and insisting that the author can account for it, is what separates an authored plate from an averaged one. It is also the honest answer to the question of whose work is in the image.
sections.strongestObjection: A synthesis is still made of other people's work, and naming the ancestors does not settle the ethics. Public-domain plates are one thing; a living architect's photographs are another, and "directed synthesis" can be a respectable name for derivative work with better curation. The claim of authorship may be bigger than the provenance can support.
sections.revisionCondition: If the profession, or the courts, settle that blended reference output is derivative regardless of direction — or if our own students' synthesised work turns out, on inspection, to be one source in costume — we would retreat to "synthesis is a technique; authorship is a separate question," and send the reader to the provenance strand. Reviewed each edition.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: name files, folders and briefs so a colleague, your future self, or an agent can find and reuse them.

sections.position: Name files, folders and briefs so that a colleague, your future self, or an agent can find and reuse them without asking you. Being findable is a property of the work, not of the person searching. A brief called `final_v2_new.txt` in a folder called `stuff` is lost work, however good it was. A brief called `2026-08_courtyard-house_brief_v3.md`, beside `v3_output.png` and a one-line note, is reusable material — and increasingly, the next reader to open it will be a machine.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Architects already know this discipline under another name: wayfinding. Kevin Lynch spent five years in three cities learning what makes a place readable to someone who has never been there. A project folder is a place a stranger has to find their way through. What makes a city legible — clear paths, named districts, landmarks — makes a body of work legible too, to people and to agents.
sections.strongestObjection: Search is getting very good. If a retrieval system can find any file from a vague description of its contents, naming discipline is overhead; the machine will read the work and index it however it is named. Spending student hours on file hygiene may be teaching a habit that software is about to make unnecessary.
sections.revisionCondition: If, on real studio archives, content-based retrieval reliably surfaces the right brief from a vague query as well as a well-named one does — for agents and for people — we would teach naming as courtesy rather than necessity. We have not seen that on the messy archives we work in. Reviewed each edition.
sections.tryIt: Take a messy project of yours. Rename its files and briefs so that a newcomer, or an agent given only the folder, can find their way alone: date first, then project, artefact, version. Then ask a classmate to find "the brief that added the north skylight" without your help.
sections.takeItToCrit: Six months from now, could a teammate or an agent find and reuse this brief from its name and structure alone — and what in the naming makes that possible?
sections.howItWorks: Retrieval systems — the machinery under search and under agent memory — work on names and on content, and they work best when the two agree. A name that states date, subject, artefact and version is a summary the machine can trust before it opens the file. The Lab has written its own essay arguing that legibility to an agent is wayfinding in Lynch's sense. That argument is the Lab's own material and is carried here in prose.

grounding.ref: mt_ArVBEpMAPk, mt_5PgQB0QkWi (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: When you want to find out which change mattered, change one thing and keep the rest as steady as you can.

sections.whenToUse: Any time you want to know *which change* made the difference. A plant that grew taller. A paper plane that flew further. An AI picture that came out darker. If you changed five things before you looked, the answer is hidden inside the five.
sections.method: Pick one thing to change. Write it down. Keep everything else as steady as you can — same place, same time, same words, same tool. Run the test. Look at what changed. Now you can say "this caused that" and be believed. If you want to test a second thing, go back to the start and change only that one. One extra step with AI tools: they add a little randomness of their own, so run the same request twice before you trust a difference. If the two runs differ, that difference is the tool's, not yours.
sections.watchForThis: Changing one thing on purpose and a second thing by accident. You moved the plant to the window *and* watered it more. Now you have two suspects and no answer. Look for the accidental second change before you trust the result.
sections.tryIt: Ask an AI image tool for "a small house by a river." Then change one word only — "small" to "tall" — and ask again. Put the two pictures side by side. Everything that differs came from that one word. Now try changing three words at once and notice how much harder it is to say what did what.
sections.proveIt: Design a test with a friend. Say out loud the one thing you will change, and three things you will keep the same. Then say why keeping them the same matters.
sections.howItWorks: Scientists call this a controlled experiment. The thing you change is the variable; the things you hold steady are the controls. It is the test to use when the question is *which change did this?* Other good investigations work differently — watching many things at once and looking for patterns — and you will meet those later. Every honest test of an AI tool on this map — does this word matter, does this setting matter — is built on this one habit. Change one thing, look, write it down. The same rule comes back, for revising a brief, as ONE CHANGE AT A TIME on the Brief strand.

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: One result tells you almost nothing. The whole set, laid out together, tells you what happened.

sections.whenToUse: Any time you have a pile of results and someone asks "so what happened?" Ten test scores. Twenty thermometer readings from the classroom. A dozen pictures from the same AI request. The answer is never in one of them. It is in the whole pile.
sections.method: Lay all the results out where you can see them at once — a tally, a bar chart, a row of pictures on the table. Then ask three questions. What is typical? Most of the results sit around here. How spread out are they? Close together means the thing is steady; far apart means it is not. What stands out? One result far from the others is worth a second look, not a headline.
sections.watchForThis: Picking the one result you like and calling it "the result." A single good picture from an AI tool does not mean the tool is good. A single bad one does not mean it is bad. Neither one is the set.
sections.tryIt: Ask an AI image tool for the same thing ten times — "a courtyard with one tree." Lay all ten out in a grid. Now say what is typical (what did most of them do?), what is spread out (where did they disagree?), and which one stands out. You have just read a set.
sections.proveIt: Take any ten numbers from your week — marks, minutes, temperatures. Draw them as a chart. Point to what is typical and to what stands out, and say why a chart shows it and a single number cannot.
sections.howItWorks: In maths this is called data handling: tallies, bar charts, averages, range. On this map the same habit has a grown-up job. When a machine gives you twelve answers, the pattern across the twelve tells you what the machine *tends* to do. That is far more useful than any one answer. Later cards call the twelve a batch, and reading it a contact sheet.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Your mind can trick your choices
topics.description: Your brain takes shortcuts when it decides — and the shortcuts follow a pattern you can learn to spot. Your brain is fast because it takes shortcuts. Mostly that is useful.
evidence: Before you choose anything today — a snack, a game, a colour for a drawing — pause and ask: did I choose this because it came to mind first, because everyone else did, or because I looked at the options? Keep a tally for one day.
Name one shortcut your mind took this week. Then take one decision you made and draw a line through it: facts on one side, your own likes and values on the other.
topics.critPrompt: What might be nudging this choice without you noticing?

grounding.ref: Tversky & Kahneman, Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases (Science, 1974)

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: Your brain takes shortcuts when it decides — and the shortcuts follow a pattern you can learn to spot.

sections.idea: Your brain is fast because it takes shortcuts. Mostly that is useful. Sometimes it trips you. You trust the thing that came to mind first. You want the small reward now more than the bigger one later. You pick what everyone else picked. These are not silly mistakes. They are patterns, and everyone has them. Once you can name a shortcut, you can check it.
sections.whyItMatters: AI tools hand you answers that are fast and neat. That is exactly the kind of thing a shortcut-taking brain accepts without looking. Knowing your own tricks is the first protection.
sections.inTheStudio: The first picture the tool shows you is the one you keep comparing the others to. Not because it was best. Because it was first. Ask yourself: if picture four had come first, which would I like now?
sections.watchForThis: Mixing up a fact and a feeling. "This house is 9 metres wide" is a fact you can measure. "This house is nicer" is a value. It is yours and it is worth having, but it is not a fact. A good choice keeps the two apart.
sections.tryIt: Before you choose anything today — a snack, a game, a colour for a drawing — pause and ask: did I choose this because it came to mind first, because everyone else did, or because I looked at the options? Keep a tally for one day.
sections.proveIt: Name one shortcut your mind took this week. Then take one decision you made and draw a line through it: facts on one side, your own likes and values on the other.
sections.howItWorks: Psychologists call these shortcuts heuristics, and the tilts they cause biases. The first-thing-that-comes-to-mind trick has a name — availability. The first-thing-you-saw trick has one too — anchoring. You will meet anchoring again on this map, because AI images are very good at being the first thing you saw.

Before sharing any picture, say out loud the three moves and what each one found. Then name the feeling the picture was trying to give you.

grounding.ref: mt_tzMr83pS8v, mt_WtO50EZQkf (Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0)
IFLA, How to Spot Fake News

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: AI can make pictures, clips and text that look real but were invented. You can learn to check.

sections.whenToUse: Before you believe a picture, a video clip or a message — and always before you forward it. Especially when it makes you feel something strongly. That is exactly what a fake is built to do.
sections.method: Three moves, in order. First, check the source: who posted this, and would they know? Second, look sideways: does any other place — a newspaper, a known website, a person you trust — show the same thing? Third, notice your feelings: if the picture made you angry, scared or thrilled in one second, slow down. Real news rarely needs you to react that fast. Only after the three moves do you decide whether to trust or share.
sections.watchForThis: Trusting your eyes alone. Today some fakes still show tells — odd hands, melted writing, shadows going the wrong way. Tomorrow's fakes may not. Your eyes give you a hint. The source and the sideways look are the real check.
sections.tryIt: Take one surprising picture you saw online this week. Do the three moves. Write down who posted it, what else showed the same thing, and what it made you feel. Then decide: real, made, or not sure. "Not sure" is an honest answer.
sections.proveIt: Before sharing any picture, say out loud the three moves and what each one found. Then name the feeling the picture was trying to give you.
sections.howItWorks: Image and video tools learn from millions of real pictures, so their fakes look like real pictures. That is why the tells keep shrinking: each new model fixes the last one's mistakes. The card is marked EVOLVING for that reason. The eye-tricks change every year. The three moves do not, because they check the world around the picture rather than the picture itself.
