topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Heritage is not a prompt keyword

grounding.ref: Ploennigs & Berger, Generative AI and the History of Architecture

topics.description: The Lab's position: "Chettinad" in a prompt buys you a look; the building was a way of building, an answer to a climate, and somebody's money. Type "Chettinad house" or "Indo-Saracenic" into an image tool and you get a look: the colours, the columns, the arches, arranged the way the photographs usually arrange them. To the model a style is a pattern of pixels.
evidence: Generate "a Chettinad house", or any heritage style from your own region. Then find one photograph of a real one, and a plan if you can. Write down three things the real building does that the image does not show: where the rain goes, where the air moves, who paid for it and why.

When a student puts a heritage style on their board, ask them to name one reason the original was built that way — climate, construction or patronage — and to point to where that reason lives in their own scheme. If they can only name the look, the style is a keyword.
topics.critPrompt: When a student puts a heritage style on their board, ask them to name one reason the original was built that way — climate, construction or patronage — and to point to where that reason lives in their own scheme. If they can only name the look, the style is a keyword.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position: "Chettinad" in a prompt buys you a look; the building was a way of building, an answer to a climate, and somebody's money.

sections.position: Type "Chettinad house" or "Indo-Saracenic" into an image tool and you get a look: the colours, the columns, the arches, arranged the way the photographs usually arrange them. To the model a style is a pattern of pixels. The real building was several other things first. A Chettinad house was a way of building — lime plaster, Burma teak, a sequence of courtyards cut into a deep plan; an answer to a climate — the open court, the thick wall, the deep thinnai; a trade network — Nattukottai Chettiar merchants built with money made in Burma, Ceylon and Malaya and shipped the materials back along the same routes, teak, Italian marble, Belgian glass, so the house is a map of the Indian Ocean; and a social and ritual order — courtyards for weddings and funerals, a plan that ranks who enters where, a town grid and water tanks that belong to the same settlement. An Indo-Saracenic building was a colonial government's programme — British architects assembling Mughal and Hindu motifs onto a European plan for courthouses, railway stations and colleges, so that imperial rule would look native. The style exists because of that politics. A keyword carries none of it. Heritage is those reasons. The style is only what the reasons looked like on the day the photograph was taken.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A student who learns heritage as a keyword will design heritage as a costume: a jali stuck on a glass box, a Chettinad colour scheme on a flat with no court. The costume does nothing about the sun, which is exactly what the original was built to handle. A student who learns the reasons can use them in a new building that looks nothing like the old one, and it will still work.
sections.strongestObjection: Style is a legitimate analytical abstraction. Historians need categories, designers need shorthand, and search systems need labels. "Hoysala," "Art Deco," "Chettinad," "Indo-Saracenic" each carry real formal, temporal, geographic and political information, and a student who cannot use them cannot read a history book or a city. The error this card describes is not in the label. It is in treating the label as sufficient evidence of understanding — and a prompt keyword is no worse at that than a textbook chapter heading, only faster. Refuse the label and you lose the handle by which the reasons are found; a fifteen-year-old who has seen fifty generated "Chettinad" images may be more curious to visit Karaikudi, not less.
sections.revisionCondition: The objection is right about labels, and the card keeps them: the position is against the label as evidence, not against the label. We would revise the position itself if image tools began to return the logic with the look — a section through the court with the air path drawn, the tile named, the timber span given, a note on who paid and why — so that the keyword started to carry reasons; the card would then soften to "check what the keyword brought with it." We would also revise if students who began from generated styles went on to study the real buildings more often than students who began from books. We check both every edition.
sections.tryIt: Generate "a Chettinad house", or any heritage style from your own region. Then find one photograph of a real one, and a plan if you can. Write down three things the real building does that the image does not show: where the rain goes, where the air moves, who paid for it and why.
sections.takeItToCrit: When a student puts a heritage style on their board, ask them to name one reason the original was built that way — climate, construction or patronage — and to point to where that reason lives in their own scheme. If they can only name the look, the style is a keyword.
sections.howItWorks: This card is the heritage version of PATTERN ≠ PRECEDENT on Foundations. There, a pattern of courtyards is not a studied building; here, a pattern of a style is not a tradition. An image model learned each style from photographs, and photographs record surfaces. What held the roof up, where the water went and who commissioned the house are not in the pixels, so they are not in the model. A 2023 study tested generative models on architectural styles and found them accurate on the much-photographed styles and prone to invention on the rest. Many Indian regional traditions are in the rest (UNEVEN STYLES on this map). The argument that a region's architecture is a response to climate, material and culture, not a set of motifs, is called critical regionalism. The Lab keeps its own teaching note on it, and Frampton's essay is the reading behind that note.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: A green-looking render is not a green building
topics.description: The Lab's position on why leaves on a façade are a pattern and heat gain through it is physics. Image models learnt what "sustainable" looks like from photographs: timber, planting, louvres, a green roof, soft light. Whether they learnt anything about what those things do is contested; what is certain is that a picture of a louvre is not a measurement of the heat behind it.
evidence: Generate "a sustainable house in a hot climate." List every green-looking feature in the image. Next to each, write what it would actually do at your site — shade, cool, ventilate, nothing — and whether you can tell from the picture. Most rows will end in "cannot tell."
Point at one green-looking element in the student's render and ask what it does at 3 p.m. in April, and how they know. If the answer describes the picture, ask again.
topics.critPrompt: Point at one green-looking element in the student's render and ask what it does at 3 p.m. in April, and how they know. If the answer describes the picture, ask again.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position on why leaves on a façade are a pattern and heat gain through it is physics.

sections.position:
Image models learnt what "sustainable" looks like from photographs: timber, planting, louvres, a green roof, soft light. Whether they learnt anything about what those things do is contested; what is certain is that a picture of a louvre is not a measurement of the heat behind it. Visual plausibility is not performance verification. A render can carry every sign of a green building and still describe a glass box that cooks in April. Leaves on a façade are a pattern. Heat gain through that façade is physics. The machine never connected the two. A jury that takes the leaves as proof of low heat gain has been fooled by a look.
> The render shows what green buildings look like in pictures. It cannot show what this one will do in May.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A diffusion model makes images that look right. It does not model behaviour: it has no sun, no thermal mass, no wind. The photographs it learnt from were chosen to present sustainability well, not for measured performance, so the pattern it holds is the marketing pattern, not the building's. The general rule is the seductive-image test on this map; this card is that test applied to green-looking images.
sections.strongestObjection: Patterns are not empty. The features a model reproduces — deep overhangs, planting, shaded openings — are in the photographs because they worked, often enough, in real buildings. An image that shows them may steer a student toward sound moves before any simulation runs, and a tutor who dismisses the render as "only a pattern" may be throwing away the only environmental thinking the student has done so far.
sections.revisionCondition: An image tool wired to a physics engine — where the façade in the picture has been sized by a solar or thermal calculation the student can open — would close the gap this card names. When a mainstream tool ships a render with a checkable heat-gain figure attached, we rewrite this card from "pattern is not physics" to "read the physics behind the pattern." We check what the tools ship every edition.
sections.tryIt: Generate "a sustainable house in a hot climate." List every green-looking feature in the image. Next to each, write what it would actually do at your site — shade, cool, ventilate, nothing — and whether you can tell from the picture. Most rows will end in "cannot tell."
sections.takeItToCrit: Point at one green-looking element in the student's render and ask what it does at 3 p.m. in April, and how they know. If the answer describes the picture, ask again.
sections.howItWorks: This card is the environmental version of two cards on this strand. The seductive-image test (`dt_seductive-image-test`) asks of any image, "what decision does this let me make?" Pattern-is-not-precedent (`dt_pattern-vs-precedent`) separates a studied building from an average of many buildings. Here the average is of how green buildings are photographed. A diffusion model is trained on image–caption pairs. Captions with "sustainable" or "eco" sit beside photographs that share certain features, and the model learns those features. Whether the building in the photograph performed was never in the caption, so it was never in the training. The physics — solar gain through glass, mass that stores heat, openings that let wind through — lives in weather files, simulation and measurement. That is where the next cards take you.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Polish reads as truth

grounding.ref: IFLA, How to Spot Fake News

topics.description: Well-made sentences feel more true than they have earned. The feeling is in you, not in the sentence. A paragraph that reads smoothly feels more certain than its evidence. That is a fact about readers, not about truth.
evidence: Take one paragraph a model wrote for you. Rewrite it clumsily: same claims, worse sentences. Show both to a classmate and ask which they trust. Then check the claims. The trust and the truth will not line up.
Explain why polish tells you nothing about whether a claim is correct, and name the one thing that does.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain why polish tells you nothing about whether a claim is correct, and name the one thing that does.

card.oneLiner: Well-made sentences feel more true than they have earned. The feeling is in you, not in the sentence.

sections.idea: A paragraph that reads smoothly feels more certain than its evidence. That is a fact about readers, not about truth. Psychologists have repeatedly found that text which is easy to read tends to be judged more true and more familiar. A language model produces smooth text by construction, because it picks the most likely next word every time, so its polish costs nothing and proves nothing. The confidence you feel when you read it is yours. You lent it to the sentence.
sections.whyItMatters: The card CONFIDENT ≠ CORRECT describes the machine's end of this. This is your end. The trap closes only if you read polish as a reason to check less.
sections.inTheStudio: A junior asks a model for the fire rating of a partition system and gets three clean sentences with a number in them. They read like a manufacturer's data sheet. Nobody opens the data sheet. The number goes into the specification, and it is wrong by one hour.
sections.watchForThis: The small relaxation in your shoulders when an answer arrives tidy. Notice it. That is the moment when checking stops.
sections.tryIt: Take one paragraph a model wrote for you. Rewrite it clumsily: same claims, worse sentences. Show both to a classmate and ask which they trust. Then check the claims. The trust and the truth will not line up.
sections.proveIt: Explain why polish tells you nothing about whether a claim is correct, and name the one thing that does.
sections.howItWorks: The effect is older than machines, and it has its own literature. Experiments on what psychologists call processing fluency — Reber and Schwarz in 1999, and Alter and Oppenheimer's 2009 review of the field — found that statements which are easier to read are judged more likely to be true. Newspapers, brochures and confident speakers have always borrowed authority from it. What is new is the supply. A model generates finish for free, at any length, on any topic, including topics it has no reliable knowledge of. The studio end of this is only observational so far: one 2026 analysis of nearly ten thousand conversations between general users and one chat model found that when the model produced a finished artefact (a document, a piece of code), users were less likely to question its reasoning or notice missing context than in conversations where they kept refining. That analysis is about behaviour in a chat window, not about fluency as the psychologists mean it, and it cannot say why. The fix is a procedure. Decide what you will verify before you read, so the finish cannot lower the bar afterwards.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The machine did not invent the courtyard

grounding.ref: Archnet — Charles Correa (Concept Media / Aga Khan Trust for Culture, 1987), Kanchanjunga Apartments

topics.description: The passive moves of your own region are older than any dataset and better tested — but tested there is not proved here; the dilemma is a generated "eco" scheme against a plain courtyard house, and the simulation that decides between them. Passive first. Before any generated scheme, the design answers the climate with the moves its own region has tested for generations — in the Deccan the court, the deep verandah and the thick wall; in Kerala the sloping tiled roof, the nalukettu's inner court and the plan that lets the wind through; in Rajasthan the haveli's jaali and shaded chowk; in Ladakh the thick mud wall and the south-facing glazed room; in Assam the light, stilted house above the flood.
evidence: Draw the plan of one old house of your own region's type from a visit — the court or the inner court, the verandah depth, the wall thickness, the roof. Then brief an image tool with those three facts and "no green wall, no solar panels." Compare what it gives you with what it gave you before. Write down what the brief had to contain before the picture started to look like a building.

Ask the student which environmental moves in the scheme are passive — orientation, shade, mass, ventilation, the court — and which were supplied by the image tool's idea of "eco." Then ask them to strike the generated features on paper and say whether the house still works. If it does not, the scheme had no environmental design in it, only decoration.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student which environmental moves in the scheme are passive — orientation, shade, mass, ventilation, the court — and which were supplied by the image tool's idea of "eco." Then ask them to strike the generated features on paper and say whether the house still works. If it does not, the scheme had no environmental design in it, only decoration.

card.oneLiner: The passive moves of your own region are older than any dataset and better tested — but tested there is not proved here; the dilemma is a generated "eco" scheme against a plain courtyard house, and the simulation that decides between them.

sections.dilemma: Two schemes for a house in Vijayapura. One came from an image tool briefed "sustainable, eco, net-zero": a sculpted roof, a green wall, solar panels at an angle that looks right. The other is a plain courtyard house with deep verandahs and thick walls — the type the town has built for centuries. The jury is in an hour. The first looks like the future. The second looks like your grandmother's house. Which do you pin up?
sections.choices: Pin the generated scheme and argue for it from its features. Pin the courtyard and argue from the climate. Or do what a serious office does: take the passive moves of the region first — orientation, shade, mass, cross-ventilation, a court open to the sky — check them against this site with a weather file and a simple simulation, and only then ask whether anything in the generated scheme adds a move the courtyard lacks.
sections.consequence: Argue from features and you are defending a pattern you cannot explain. When the juror asks what the green wall does in a Vijayapura May, all you can do is describe the picture. Argue from climate and every element has a reason a juror can test, and a number from the simulation to test it with: the court loses its heat to the night sky, the verandah stops the sun before it reaches the wall, the thick wall slows the afternoon heat until the cooler night. Passive first does not forbid new ideas. It asks each new idea to prove it adds something the courtyard does not already do — and it asks the courtyard to prove itself on this plot too.
sections.theCase: A third-year student generates twelve "eco houses" for a plot in Belagavi. Eleven have green walls; none has a court. The tutor hands her Correa's writing on open-to-sky space and Baker's drawings of a rat-trap bond wall — bricks laid on edge with a cavity inside, fewer bricks and better insulation than solid brickwork. She rebuilds the scheme around a court and that wall, then runs the image tool again, briefed with those moves and nothing about "eco." The thirteenth image is the first one that would work in Belagavi.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student which environmental moves in the scheme are passive — orientation, shade, mass, ventilation, the court — and which were supplied by the image tool's idea of "eco." Then ask them to strike the generated features on paper and say whether the house still works. If it does not, the scheme had no environmental design in it, only decoration.
sections.position: Passive first. Before any generated scheme, the design answers the climate with the moves its own region has tested for generations — in the Deccan the court, the deep verandah and the thick wall; in Kerala the sloping tiled roof, the nalukettu's inner court and the plan that lets the wind through; in Rajasthan the haveli's jaali and shaded chowk; in Ladakh the thick mud wall and the south-facing glazed room; in Assam the light, stilted house above the flood. There is no one Indian repertoire. There is the one your site belongs to. Then the simulation: precedent says what worked there, simulation says whether it works here. The machine did not invent the courtyard, and it never learnt why the courtyard works.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A regional passive type is the only environmental evidence that comes with real, occupied buildings attached — a climate and a street address. Correa built open-to-sky space into housing at Belapur and into a Bombay tower, and wrote down why. Baker's rat-trap bond and filler slab are in many Kerala houses that can be visited. An image model's "eco" is a pattern from photographs. A passive type is a precedent. That is the pattern-is-not-precedent distinction, applied to heat, and it is why the type comes first and the simulation comes second — as the test of the type on this site, not as its rival. The Lab's own notes on Baker and on critical regionalism sit behind this card.
sections.strongestObjection: Precedent is evidence, not proof. "The vernacular did it" cannot establish that a courtyard will perform on this plot, in this geometry, at this density, for this household, in a city hotter than the village the type was built for. A jaali, a thick wall or a court is not passive-good in itself; its performance depends on orientation, proportion, occupancy and the hour, and a court on a six-metre plot can be an oven. Starting from the type can become starting from nostalgia, with "passive first" an excuse to skip the active systems a modern building needs and the measurement that would have shown the type failing.
sections.revisionCondition: We accept the objection's premise, which is why the position puts the simulation directly behind the type and not behind the generated scheme. We would revise the order if measured evidence, on Indian sites, showed schemes reached through generated imagery and simulation beating the regional type on comfort and energy without starting from it — the machine finding a move the repertoire did not have. We would also revise if the tools began to carry passive logic themselves: a generator that places a court because the weather file called for one. We look for both every edition.
sections.howItWorks: A passive building manages heat without fuel. It keeps the sun off the skin (orientation, shade), slows heat through the wall (mass, a cavity), lets heat out at night (the court open to the sky, cross-ventilation) and filters light and air (the jaali). These are physics, and a simulation can show them working — or not working, on this site, which is the point of running one. An image model has none of this. It has photographs, and in photographs "eco" is a look. So the order of work matters: the regional passive moves first, because they cost nothing to run; then the simulation that tests them here; then, if you want one, a picture. That order is why the surrogate and simulate-then-trust cards come after this one.
sections.tryIt: Draw the plan of one old house of your own region's type from a visit — the court or the inner court, the verandah depth, the wall thickness, the roof. Then brief an image tool with those three facts and "no green wall, no solar panels." Compare what it gives you with what it gave you before. Write down what the brief had to contain before the picture started to look like a building.

topics.description: A chat model tends to build on what you bring. That is agreement, not confirmation. A crit pushes back. A mirror cannot. Chat models are tuned to be helpful, and in practice that often means agreeable. Bring an idea and, in the chat models of 2026, the usual lean is to develop it, not to oppose it — a lean that changes with each version, system prompt and persona, which is why you set the terms yourself.
evidence: Present the same idea twice in two fresh conversations. Once: "Is this a good idea?" Once: "Give me the three strongest reasons a jury would reject this." Put the two replies side by side.
Show one place where the model's agreement would have let a flaw through, and the second question caught it.

card.oneLiner: A chat model tends to build on what you bring. That is agreement, not confirmation. A crit pushes back. A mirror cannot.

sections.idea: Chat models are tuned to be helpful, and in practice that often means agreeable. Bring an idea and, in the chat models of 2026, the usual lean is to develop it, not to oppose it — a lean that changes with each version, system prompt and persona, which is why you set the terms yourself. That agreement feels like confirmation. It is not. Validation comes only from something that could have said no: a tutor, a jury, a client, a calculation, a site. A system whose usual answer is yes cannot validate anything, however intelligent its yes sounds.
sections.whyItMatters: Design improves through resistance. A tool that removes resistance feels like progress and removes the mechanism by which work gets better.
sections.inTheStudio: A student pastes their concept note and asks, "Is this a strong idea?" The reply begins, "This is a compelling concept that…". The jury, a week later, does not begin that way. The note was never tested. It was complimented.
sections.watchForThis: Questions that can only be answered yes. "Is this good?" "Does this work?" The model will find a way to agree. Ask for the case against.
sections.tryIt: Present the same idea twice in two fresh conversations. Once: "Is this a good idea?" Once: "Give me the three strongest reasons a jury would reject this." Put the two replies side by side.
sections.proveIt: Show one place where the model's agreement would have let a flaw through, and the second question caught it.
sections.howItWorks: The agreeable streak tends to be trained in. Chat models are tuned on human ratings of their answers, and raters, being people, tend to rate agreeable answers well; how strong the lean is changes with each release, and makers have rolled back updates for being too agreeable. The same 2026 analysis of thousands of chat conversations between general users and one model found that people who kept refining an output were several times more likely to question the model's reasoning than people who accepted the first reply. So the questioning has to come from your side. The practical answer on this map is the sparring-partner card: instruct the model to attack, not to agree. This card is the reason that instruction is needed.

topics.description: People defer to a system's output even against their own eyes. This has been known for decades in cockpits and clinics. Now it is at every desk. When a system gives an answer, people tend to accept it over their own reading, and to skip checks they would otherwise have made. Researchers call this automation bias.
evidence: Ask a classmate to hand you a tool's answer to a task you can check by hand, such as five room areas from a plan, with one line quietly altered. You should not know which line. Notice whether you check, or defer. Then swap roles.
Describe one moment you deferred to an output against your own reading, and what it would take for you to notice next time.

card.oneLiner: People defer to a system's output even against their own eyes. This has been known for decades in cockpits and clinics. Now it is at every desk.

sections.idea: When a system gives an answer, people tend to accept it over their own reading, and to skip checks they would otherwise have made. Researchers call this automation bias. It has two forms: following a wrong suggestion, and failing to act because the system did not flag anything. It was studied in aircraft cockpits and hospital decision-support long before chatbots. It is a property of people working with machines, not of any one machine, which means it arrived at your desk with the first convenient tool.
sections.whyItMatters: The bias is in you. No update to the tool removes it. Only a habit does.
sections.inTheStudio: The area schedule a tool computed does not match your rough count. You assume you miscounted. Three weeks later the municipal submission carries the tool's figure, and the tool had read one room twice.
sections.watchForThis: The sentence "the software checked it." Software produced it. Checking is a separate act, and a person does it.
sections.tryIt: Ask a classmate to hand you a tool's answer to a task you can check by hand, such as five room areas from a plan, with one line quietly altered. You should not know which line. Notice whether you check, or defer. Then swap roles.
sections.proveIt: Describe one moment you deferred to an output against your own reading, and what it would take for you to notice next time.
sections.howItWorks: A 2012 systematic review of seventy-four studies of clinical decision-support found that wrong advice from a system raised the rate of wrong decisions, and that the effect shrank when people were trained for it, held accountable for their decisions, shown the system's confidence, and given information rather than a recommendation. Those four remedies transfer directly to a studio. A related 2025 observational study in one medical field found that clinicians' unaided performance fell after months of working with an AI assistant. That is nearby evidence that deference, kept up for long enough, becomes something worse. That is the next card.

topics.name: The batch is a contact sheet
topics.description: Read a set of outputs the way a photographer reads a contact sheet: the whole sheet first, never one frame on its own. The core skill in reading generated work is fast comparison across the whole set, before any single image pulls you in. Treat the batch as a contact sheet.
evidence: Scan a set of twelve to twenty images at thumbnail size. Mark three worth enlarging, each with a one-line reason. Then point to one thing a frame shows only when set next to its neighbours, and not alone.

Watch how the student moves through the batch. Do they read across the whole sheet before enlarging anything, or do they fall for the first strong frame and treat the rest as worse versions of it? Ask what the set agreed on. If they cannot say, they never read it.
topics.critPrompt: Watch how the student moves through the batch. Do they read across the whole sheet before enlarging anything, or do they fall for the first strong frame and treat the rest as worse versions of it? Ask what the set agreed on. If they cannot say, they never read it.

card.oneLiner: Read a set of outputs the way a photographer reads a contact sheet: the whole sheet first, never one frame on its own.

sections.dilemma: Sixteen images come back from one brief. The third one is strong. Your eye has already stopped on it, and the other fifteen are turning into background. Do you open the strong one now, or do you make yourself read the whole sheet before you look closely at any single frame?
sections.choices: Open the strong frame first and judge the rest against it. Or scan the whole set at one small size, frame beside frame, and only mark the few worth enlarging once the scan is done.
sections.consequence: Open the strong frame first and it becomes the anchor. Every other image is now "less like number three," and whatever the set as a whole was telling you is lost. Scan first and you see what the batch agrees on, where it disagrees, and which frames only mean something because of the frames beside them. Enlarging comes after, and it is quick, because the scan has already done the work.
sections.theCase: A second-year student pins up one beautiful image of a stepped ghat-side pavilion. The tutor asks to see the rest of the batch. Eleven of the twelve put the pavilion on the water's edge. The brief never asked for that. The one image the student chose was the only one that did not. That is interesting, and the student had not noticed it, because they never looked at the twelve together.
sections.takeItToCrit: Watch how the student moves through the batch. Do they read across the whole sheet before enlarging anything, or do they fall for the first strong frame and treat the rest as worse versions of it? Ask what the set agreed on. If they cannot say, they never read it.
sections.position: The core skill in reading generated work is fast comparison across the whole set, before any single image pulls you in. Treat the batch as a contact sheet. Until the sheet has been read, the one strong frame is a distraction.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The batch is the only evidence you have of what your brief actually asked for. A single frame shows you what the machine can do. The set shows you what it tends to do, and the tendency is the useful information. Photographers learnt this with a loupe over thirty-six frames. We have taken the habit and apply it to sixteen.
sections.strongestObjection: Reading in batches creates a bias of its own. At thumbnail size the most striking frame dominates the comparison and the subtle frame disappears, so the sheet trains you to select the loudest image, not to judge the set. The frames are not independent witnesses either: sixteen draws from one prompt share one set of habits, so "what the batch agrees on" may be the model's habit rather than a finding about your brief. And a contact sheet shows you only what was generated. It cannot show you what the brief should have produced and did not. Comparison trains selection. It does not train judgment of what is absent.
sections.revisionCondition: Workshop logs showing that scan-first students pick the loudest frame as often as frame-first students, and miss the absent idea as often. The scan would then be a ritual rather than a method, and the card would be rewritten around the harder question — what is missing from this set — with the sheet as one tool for asking it, not the first move. We run both methods in workshops and read the log.
sections.howItWorks: A contact sheet works because the frames are small and side by side. Small size stops the detail from seducing you. Side by side lets the pattern show. Look at the set and ask three things: what do most frames do, where do they disagree, and which frame stands out. It is the same reading you learnt on a chart of numbers, now on a grid of images. Only then pick the three worth opening, with a reason for each. This card is about seeing the set. The next one, DIAGNOSIS, is about reading what the set says about your brief.
sections.tryIt: Scan a set of twelve to twenty images at thumbnail size. Mark three worth enlarging, each with a one-line reason. Then point to one thing a frame shows only when set next to its neighbours, and not alone.

topics.description: Write what "acceptable" means before the first output arrives, or the outputs will write it for you. Write four lines on paper or in a note you can see. One: what the output must do for the project.

card.oneLiner: Write what "acceptable" means before the first output arrives, or the outputs will write it for you.

sections.whenToUse: Before any run longer than one shot: a render batch, an options study, a long text draft, an agent task. Before you open the tool, not after the first result.
sections.method: Write four lines on paper or in a note you can see. One: what the output must do for the project. Two: what must not move, the fixed things. Three: what would make you reject an output on sight. Four: how many you will make before you stop and judge. Then run. Hold every output against the four lines and nothing else. Mark pass or fail. Only then look at what you like.
sections.watchForThis: Writing the four lines after seeing the first output. The first output then becomes the definition of done, and everything after is judged by its resemblance to it.
sections.tryIt: Tomorrow's generation task: write the four lines first. After the run, count how many outputs you would have accepted without them. That number is the cost of not writing them.
sections.proveIt: Show one run where the four lines rejected an output you liked, and say what the lines caught that your eye missed.
sections.labNote: Defining done first is the Lab's recommended method, not the only one. RUBRIC FIRST, on this strand, is the criteria side of the same habit: must do, must hold, must avoid. This card adds the fourth line, the count — how many before you stop and judge — because "good enough" is a stopping threshold, what engineers call satisficing, and the threshold is the part the criteria alone do not set.
sections.howItWorks: Elsewhere on this map you give criteria to the model, inside the brief, so that it can test its own work. This card gives the criteria to you, and fixes the timing. The two are different moves. A criterion written into the prompt asks the model to check; it does not make the check happen — a written instruction asks, the system's own controls enforce, and the control here is on your side of the screen. A model reading your criteria still returns what is plausible. A person reading them before the flood still has a standard when the flood arrives. "Good enough" is a real engineering term, not a shrug. It means the point at which further generation buys images but not decisions. Defining it first is what makes stopping possible later.

topics.description: A plausible first output becomes the reference point, and the search narrows around it before your own idea has formed. Once a plausible answer is in front of you, it becomes the thing everything else is measured against. Your second question is shaped by it.
evidence: Run a brief once. Before writing the second prompt, write three questions that have nothing to do with the first result: about the site, the programme, the section. Then prompt from one of those. Compare where the session went against where it would have gone.
Show a session transcript and mark the exact prompt where the first answer set the direction for everything after.

card.oneLiner: A plausible first output becomes the reference point, and the search narrows around it before your own idea has formed.

sections.idea: Once a plausible answer is in front of you, it becomes the thing everything else is measured against. Your second question is shaped by it. You ask for "more like this, but…" instead of asking what else was possible — that is what the Lab sees in its studio logs. Psychologists call this anchoring, and it works on numbers, images and ideas alike. In design search it is expensive, because the first output arrives in seconds, before your own idea has had time to form. The search narrows before it has begun.
sections.whyItMatters: What you ask next decides what you find. If the machine's first draw writes your second prompt, the machine is steering the search and you are only holding the wheel.
sections.inTheStudio: A student asks for "a community library on a sloping site" and gets a cantilevered box with a glass front. Every prompt after that says "more like this, with…". Forty images later the slope has never been explored. The site's one real idea was abandoned in the first ten seconds.
sections.watchForThis: The word "more" at the start of your prompts. "More of this." "More like that." Each one is an anchor speaking.
sections.tryIt: Run a brief once. Before writing the second prompt, write three questions that have nothing to do with the first result: about the site, the programme, the section. Then prompt from one of those. Compare where the session went against where it would have gone.
sections.proveIt: Show a session transcript and mark the exact prompt where the first answer set the direction for everything after.
sections.howItWorks: Anchoring was described by Tversky and Kahneman in the 1970s. An initial value, even an arbitrary one, pulls later estimates towards itself. The design version has now been measured with generative tools. In a 2024 experiment with sixty participants in a visual ideation task, people who used an image generator while ideating fixated more on an initial example and produced fewer ideas, with less variety and lower originality, than people who worked without it. That study measured the fixation, not the wording of anyone's second prompt; the "more like this" pattern is the Lab's observation, and you can check it in your own logs. FIRST IMAGE, one ring up, takes the same finding to the studio day: when to let an image into the room at all. The counter is metacognition, watching your own thinking while you think, which is why this card sits beside the Lab's cards on prompting as thinking about thinking.

topics.description: A model can give you a stepwell's depth, date and function and still miss what the place means to the people who use it. card.oneLiner: A model can give you a stepwell's depth, date and function and still miss what the place means to the people who use it.

sections.position: A model can tell you a stepwell's depth, its date, its catchment and its function. It cannot tell you what it is like to go down into one in May: the temperature dropping step by step, the sound changing, what the place means to the town. AI processes information. It does not live experience. The felt, cultural meaning of a place is the layer you are there to carry, and no amount of information replaces having stood in it.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: "No site, no client" is the closed-world rule elsewhere on this map: the model has never stood anywhere. This card extends it one step. Even with every fact about a place, the model has no sense of what it *means*. In architecture, meaning is not decoration. It is the brief. The courtyard that is the centre of a family's life and the courtyard that is a leftover between blocks have the same dimensions. The difference is the thing a designer is hired to know.
sections.strongestObjection: Serious people disagree about whether this is a permanent boundary or a current one. Models now take in images, video and sound as well as text, and some researchers argue that systems trained on enough of the world's recordings will come to hold something like experience, or at least a working model of the physical and social world that is not "mere information." On that view, "AI does not live experience" is true of today's tools and unproven as a principle, and a card that states it as a principle may age badly.
sections.revisionCondition: If a model could tell a designer something about the *meaning* of a specific place (not its average, not the mood of its photographs) that the designer then confirmed by going there and that no text had recorded, the line between information and experience would need redrawing. We would also soften the card if the philosophical disagreement moved towards consensus. It is marked as a held position and reviewed every edition because the disagreement is live.
sections.tryIt: Take a place you know well. List what a model can state about it: dimensions, dates, materials, function. Then list what only lived experience holds: what it sounds like at dusk, who uses it and when, what it means to the street. Explain why "no site, no client" extends to "no lived meaning."
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student name the experienced meaning of a place that the model's information leaves out? Ask them about a place they have stood in. Then ask what of that made it into the brief.
sections.howItWorks: The card is marked as contested inside the Lab's own position because the disagreement is real. Today's models hold descriptions: text, images, recordings. They do not hold a body that was cold on the seventh step, and their account of what a place "means" is assembled from what people have written about places like it. That is information about experience. It is useful, and it is not the same thing. Whether future systems (embodied, continuous, learning from the world rather than from records of it) close the gap is an open question. This card names it rather than settles it.

topics.name: A real test hunts failure

grounding.ref: Goodfellow et al., Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples

topics.description: A demo shows the best case. A test goes looking for the worst one. A demo is chosen by the person selling the tool. It shows the inputs the tool handles best.
evidence: Pick one tool you use. Write five inputs designed to break it: a site photograph at night, a plan with labels in an Indian language, a façade with no windows, a brief that asks for two things that cannot both be true, a question about a building that does not exist. Run all five. Write down what happened.
Show the input that broke the tool, and say what that tells you about where the tool is safe to use.

card.oneLiner: A demo shows the best case. A test goes looking for the worst one.

sections.idea: A demo is chosen by the person selling the tool. It shows the inputs the tool handles best. A test is chosen by you, and it must include the cases the tool is likely to fail, not only the ones it is likely to pass. Feed it the awkward case, the torn scan, the brief that contradicts itself, the building it has probably never seen — alongside ordinary cases, so you learn where the edge is and not only that one exists. If you only confirm what you hoped, you have not tested. You have watched a second demo.
sections.whyItMatters: You will meet the worst case eventually. The only question is whether you meet it on purpose, in a test, or by accident, on a deadline.
sections.inTheStudio: A plan-reading tool counts every door on the vendor's sample plan. Your survey is hand-drawn, photographed at an angle, with room names in Kannada. Run that one first. If it holds, the clean plans will hold too.
sections.watchForThis: Testing with the same kind of input the demo used. Clean, typical, well-lit. That is not a test of your work. It is a test of their marketing.
sections.tryIt: Pick one tool you use. Write five inputs designed to break it: a site photograph at night, a plan with labels in an Indian language, a façade with no windows, a brief that asks for two things that cannot both be true, a question about a building that does not exist. Run all five. Write down what happened.
sections.proveIt: Show the input that broke the tool, and say what that tells you about where the tool is safe to use.
sections.labNote: Hunting for failure is the Lab's recommended way to start testing a tool, not the whole of testing. A full evaluation also runs ordinary, representative cases and counts the errors by kind — MISS OR ALARM on this strand — and, where it matters, checks how confident the tool was when it was wrong. The awkward five find the edge. The ordinary cases tell you how often you will meet it.
sections.howItWorks: Researchers formalised this in 2014 with adversarial examples: tiny, deliberate changes to an image that make a classifier confidently wrong, while the image looks unchanged to a person. The lesson spread. Modern systems are tested by teams whose whole job is to break them (the practice is called red-teaming), because the failures that matter are the ones nobody thought to look for. Your five awkward inputs are a small red team. The failure catalogue elsewhere on this map is where their findings go.

sections.idea: Skills are kept by practice. When a step is always handed to a tool, the practice stops and the skill can thin, because the tool covers for it. Researchers call the handing-over cognitive offloading. The evidence is early and uneven. In one clinical setting, clinicians' unaided detection rate fell after months with an AI assistant — one observational study. In higher education, over-reliance is the most reported risk in a 2026 review, which also finds structured use can strengthen reasoning. This card argues with the capstone on purpose: if judgment is the job, what happens to judgment never exercised?
sections.whyItMatters: The capstone says judgment stays yours. This card asks whether you will still have it. Both can be true, but only if you choose what not to offload.
sections.inTheStudio: A third-year student who has generated every section since first year is asked, on a site visit, to sketch a section of the existing building. They cannot. Not from lack of intelligence, but from three years of never needing to.
sections.watchForThis: "I'll learn that properly later." Later is when the tool is not there, and the tool is not there exactly when it matters: on the site, at the jury, at the client's table.
sections.tryIt: For two weeks, do one task unaided each day that you would normally hand over: a daylight sketch, a room count, an area calculation, a paragraph of the design statement. Then do the same task with the tool. Record where you have slipped, and where you have not.
sections.proveIt: State what in your own practice you refuse to offload, and why, with one piece of evidence from your own work that shows the skill is still there.
sections.howItWorks: Two kinds of evidence, and they do not point one way. The clinical study followed nineteen experienced endoscopists at four Polish centres and found that their adenoma detection rate in colonoscopies done *without* AI fell from 28.4 per cent before AI was introduced to 22.4 per cent after some months of using it. That is a retrospective, observational result, in one field, and the authors are careful about causation. The education review found generative AI acting as a cognitive amplifier under structured conditions and as a substitute under unguided use, with over-reliance, reduced analytical autonomy and cognitive offloading the three most reported risks. Its authors list their own limits: a single reviewer, English-language sources only, a two-year window. That is why this card is marked EVOLVING. The direction is clear enough to take seriously. The size of the effect, how permanent it is, and whether it transfers from detecting polyps to designing buildings are not settled, and we will revise as the evidence matures. The honest counterweight is this. The same review found that *structured* use amplifies rather than substitutes, and a small 2025 experiment found that a tool designed to provoke, by critiquing its own suggestions, restored critical thinking that unprovoked use had lowered. Atrophy is a tendency of unstructured use, not a law of the tool.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The model fills gaps it cannot know
topics.description: A generated "restoration" of a ruined façade is an invention wearing a plausible face — conservation keeps documented and conjectured apart, and an unconstrained model does not. Generation cannot turn missing evidence into known history. Restoration is limited by evidence; generation is limited only by likelihood.
evidence: Take one photograph of a damaged building. Produce a generated completion. Then produce a drawing in which documented fabric and conjectural fabric are visibly distinguished, with each conjecture's source — or the absence of one — noted. Explain in a paragraph why the second is a conservation document and the first is not.

When a student shows a "restored" view of a ruin, ask them to draw a line on it between what is documented and what is conjectured. If they cannot draw the line, the image is an invention, and the crit should be about where the evidence stopped.
topics.critPrompt: When a student shows a "restored" view of a ruin, ask them to draw a line on it between what is documented and what is conjectured. If they cannot draw the line, the image is an invention, and the crit should be about where the evidence stopped.

card.oneLiner: A generated "restoration" of a ruined façade is an invention wearing a plausible face — conservation keeps documented and conjectured apart, and an unconstrained model does not.

sections.dilemma: A photograph of a ruined gateway: the left half standing, the right half fallen. You give it to an image model and ask it to "restore the façade." Back comes a complete gateway, symmetrical, convincing, beautiful. Your tutor asks whether the right half looked like that. You do not know. Neither does the model. Do you put the image on the board?
sections.choices: Put it up as the restoration — it is the best image you have. Put it up labelled "conjectural reconstruction, AI-generated," and let the label carry the doubt. Or go back to the evidence first: what is documented about the fallen half — a drawing, an old photograph, the fallen stones themselves — and draw the documented part as documented and the conjectured part as conjecture, visibly different, and use the generated image only as a question to put to the evidence.
sections.consequence: The first choice puts an invention into the record with your name on it, and the record is what the next person restores from. The second is honest and still dangerous: a label is read once and the image is shared a hundred times without it. The third costs an afternoon in the archive and produces a drawing a conservation architect can act on, because it shows where knowledge stops. The charter the profession has worked to since 1964 says restoration "must stop at the point where conjecture begins." A model has no such point. Its whole method is to continue past it.
sections.theCase: A measured-drawing studio in a village near Gadag. A team documents a pillared hall whose roof is gone. For the jury one student generates a "restored" view with a full roof. A conservation architect on the jury asks which evidence gave the roof its slope. There was none — the model had given it a slope from a thousand other halls. The team's final sheet shows the standing columns in solid line, the roof in dashed line with the note "form conjectural; no evidence for pitch," and the generated image in a corner captioned as a hypothesis. The jury spent its time on the dashed line. That was the right place to spend it.
sections.takeItToCrit: When a student shows a "restored" view of a ruin, ask them to draw a line on it between what is documented and what is conjectured. If they cannot draw the line, the image is an invention, and the crit should be about where the evidence stopped.
sections.position: Generation cannot turn missing evidence into known history. Restoration is limited by evidence; generation is limited only by likelihood. A generated completion of a ruin, however the tool was driven, is conjecture that looks like documentation. It belongs in one place only: as a labelled hypothesis beside the evidence, never in the record.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The conservation charters exist because earlier generations invented freely and called it restoration. Venice (1964) drew the line at conjecture and asked that any new work be distinguishable from the original. An unconstrained model's output erases that distinction by the way it works: the documented half and the invented half come out in one surface, one light, one level of confidence. Putting the line back is the architect's job, and on a ruin it is most of the job.
sections.strongestObjection: Conservation has always drawn conjecture — the dashed line, the reconstruction drawing, the museum model — and it has been useful: it tells the public what a ruin was for and it makes a hypothesis testable. A model is a faster hypothesis engine. If students label its output as conjecture and test it against the evidence, the tool does what the reconstruction drawing always did, at a speed that lets you try ten hypotheses instead of one. Refusing it on principle may protect the record and starve the imagination.
sections.revisionCondition: Tools that carry the evidence boundary inside the output: the documented fabric rendered from the measured data, the conjectured fabric visibly different by default, the sources attached and still attached after the image is shared. When the distinction survives generation, the position softens to "generate, but keep the line visible." We would also revise if conservation bodies adopted generated reconstructions as accepted hypothesis drawings under stated rules. Reviewed every edition against the charters and the tools.
sections.proveIt: Take one photograph of a damaged building. Produce a generated completion. Then produce a drawing in which documented fabric and conjectural fabric are visibly distinguished, with each conjecture's source — or the absence of one — noted. Explain in a paragraph why the second is a conservation document and the first is not.
sections.howItWorks: The Venice Charter (ICOMOS, 1964) is exact on this. Article 9: restoration "is based on respect for original material and authentic documents. It must stop at the point where conjecture begins." Article 12: replacements of missing parts "must be distinguishable from the original so that restoration does not falsify the artistic or historic evidence." Article 15 goes further for ruins — "All reconstruction work should however be ruled out *a priori*," with only anastylosis, the reassembly of existing but dismembered parts, permitted. The Nara Document on Authenticity (1994) widens the frame: our ability to judge authenticity "depends, in part, on the degree to which information sources about these values may be understood as credible or truthful," and those sources — form and design, materials, use, traditions, setting — are judged within the culture the heritage belongs to. A model has no information sources about this building. It has a distribution over buildings. WHY IT MAKES THINGS UP on this map explains the mechanism; this card is that mechanism applied to a ruin. SCAN TO MODEL is where the documented half comes from; WHOSE HERITAGE is what happens when the invented half reaches the people who use the place.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Taste is trained
topics.description: Taste is a reference library, a set of positions, and a growing sense of what is yours and what is noise. It is built on purpose, not given. Taste is not a gift. It is a reference library you built, a set of positions you hold, and a growing sense of what is yours and what is noise.
evidence: Build a twenty-item reference library (buildings, drawings, photographs, texts) and write one line on why each item earned its place. Then state one position you hold that would change how you brief a model. "I distrust roofs that do not show their thickness," for instance, is a position, and it writes a line of every brief.
Ask what the student has cut from their references this term, and why. Taste shows in what gets cut. A library that only grows is just a feed in a folder.
topics.critPrompt: Ask what the student has cut from their references this term, and why. Taste shows in what gets cut. A library that only grows is just a feed in a folder.

card.oneLiner: Taste is a reference library, a set of positions, and a growing sense of what is yours and what is noise. It is built on purpose, not given.

sections.position: Taste is not a gift. It is a reference library you built, a set of positions you hold, and a growing sense of what is yours and what is noise. You build it on purpose: by looking at more than you are shown, by keeping what earned its place and cutting what did not, by being able to say why — and by asking who chose what you were shown. It is the one filter the machine cannot give you, because the machine's taste is the average of everyone's, and yours has to be the opposite of that.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Generated output is plentiful and arrives already looking good. The only thing that sorts it is a filter the person brings, and a filter is only as good as what it was trained on. A student with twenty references they can defend reads a batch differently from a student with a feed. The Lab teaches taste as a discipline (a library, positions, deletions) because the alternative is to inherit the model's.
sections.strongestObjection: Taste is not an individual library built "on purpose." What a student meets as good taste has already been filtered — by schools, publishers, awards, class, caste, wealth, colonial archives, the algorithms of the feed, and by who had the money to be photographed and remembered. A curriculum that says "train your taste" without saying so is teaching students to internalise the canon more efficiently, and to mistake the canon's filter for their own. In India that filter has left out most of what was built. And if generative tools raise everyone's floor — the research says they can, most of all for the less practised — the market may stop paying for a personal filter at all.
sections.revisionCondition: The first half of the objection we take as a correction to the card, not a refutation of it: a library built on purpose must include an account of who filtered what reached you, and the deletions must include inherited ones. We would revise the position itself on evidence from practice that offices stopped distinguishing, in hiring, in fees, and in who gets the room, between a trained filter and a good tool. If the market stops paying for the difference, the card moves from "the job" to "the craft." That is a real demotion and we would make it honestly. We watch practice, not only studios.
sections.tryIt: Build a twenty-item reference library (buildings, drawings, photographs, texts) and write one line on why each item earned its place. Then state one position you hold that would change how you brief a model. "I distrust roofs that do not show their thickness," for instance, is a position, and it writes a line of every brief.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask what the student has cut from their references this term, and why. Taste shows in what gets cut. A library that only grows is just a feed in a folder.
sections.howItWorks: Three parts, and each one can be built. The library: things you have looked at long enough to say why they matter, which is a different act from saving them. The positions: the few rules you hold that survive tool changes, and that can be written into a brief. The deletions: what you once kept and no longer do, which is the clearest record that the filter is moving. The Lab's own judgment register, which is internal material and not public, is built the same way, and this card is its student-facing form.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The polish disarms you
topics.description: When a machine hands you a clean, finished-looking artefact, your checking tends to drop. That is exactly when it should rise. We stay sharp while arguing with a machine and go slack the moment it hands us an artefact. We mistake how finished a thing looks for how true it is.
evidence: Catch one moment this week when a tidy, formatted output made you check it less than a messy one would have. Write down what you skipped. Then explain, in two sentences, why completeness and accuracy are not the same thing, and where in that output the gap was.
When a student is handed a neat, finished-looking deliverable, do they check it more, not less? Ask them what they checked in it, and what made them decide to check that.
topics.critPrompt: When a student is handed a neat, finished-looking deliverable, do they check it more, not less? Ask them what they checked in it, and what made them decide to check that.

grounding.ref: The Seduction of the Machine — the-seduction-of-the-machine-why
Anthropic, “AI Fluency Index”, Feb 2026 — in conversations where an artifact is created, users are less likely to spot missing context (−5.2pp), check facts (−3.7pp), or question reasoning (−3.1pp)

card.oneLiner: When a machine hands you a clean, finished-looking artefact, your checking tends to drop. That is exactly when it should rise.

sections.dilemma: Two outputs from the same model. One is a messy paragraph of half-formed reasoning. The other is a formatted document: headings, bullets, a summary table of site constraints. Which one do you check harder? Be honest. Now ask which one deserves it.
sections.choices: Let the finish set how hard you check: messy gets questioned, tidy gets pasted. Or turn it round on purpose. The more finished a thing looks, the more deliberately you check it, because finish is the cheapest thing a machine produces and the strongest signal your brain accepts.
sections.consequence: Let the polish decide and at some point you will paste a polished error into a client document: a site constraint that was never true, a byelaw clause that does not exist, set out in a table that made it look settled. Turn the reflex round and the tidy artefact gets the treatment a tidy junior's work gets. It is read line by line, precisely because it was easy to trust.
sections.theCase: A student asks a model for the setback rules for a plot in a Karnataka town. It returns a clean table (front, side, rear, by plot width) with a confident note on FAR. It looks like a page from the byelaws. She pastes it into her site analysis. The tutor asks which edition of the zoning regulations it came from. There is no edition. The table was simply the most likely-looking table, and looking likely was all the authority it had. A messy answer would have been checked.
sections.takeItToCrit: When a student is handed a neat, finished-looking deliverable, do they check it more, not less? Ask them what they checked in it, and what made them decide to check that.
sections.position: We stay sharp while arguing with a machine and go slack the moment it hands us an artefact. We mistake how finished a thing looks for how true it is. The Lab calls this the artefact paradox, and treats finished-looking output as the highest-risk kind of output, not the lowest. The position rests on an observed pattern and on what the Lab sees at the desk. The cause is not yet established.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Anthropic's February 2026 analysis of several thousand conversations with its own chat model reported that when the model produced an artefact (a document, a block of code, a formatted list), users showed less visible checking inside the conversation — noticing missing context, checking facts, questioning the reasoning — by a few percentage points each. The study is observational, covers one company's model, and sees only what happened inside the chat. It cannot say why the checking dropped, or whether people checked elsewhere. These were general users, not designers. We hold the position anyway, because the pattern matches what the Lab sees in studios, and because the artefact is also the thing most likely to be forwarded.
sections.strongestObjection: The evidence is correlational. "Conversations with artefacts contained less visible checking" does not show that the polish caused anyone to check less. The tasks that produce artefacts may simply be the tasks people check less — routine ones, or ones where the checking happens outside the chat, in a drawing or on a site the study could not see. Trained users may behave differently from the general users measured. Until somebody varies the polish and holds the task still, "the polish disarms you" is a hypothesis with a good story, not a mechanism.
sections.revisionCondition: A controlled study that varied how finished an output looked, held the task constant, and found no difference in checking — or found the difference vanished in trained users — would move this card from a standing position to a first-semester warning. The opposite result would make it a mechanism. Either way we review it against new studies every edition.
sections.howItWorks: Formatting is a pattern the model learnt like any other: what finished documents look like. It costs the model nothing and says nothing about whether the contents are true. Your brain, though, reads finish as effort and effort as care. That is a reasonable shortcut among humans, and a likely trap with a machine for which finish is free. The fix is a procedure, not an attitude. Decide *before* you read what you will verify in any artefact, so the polish cannot lower the bar afterwards.
sections.tryIt: Catch one moment this week when a tidy, formatted output made you check it less than a messy one would have. Write down what you skipped. Then explain, in two sentences, why completeness and accuracy are not the same thing, and where in that output the gap was.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Atmosphere is not information
topics.description: Some images carry mood, some carry buildable information, and few carry both. Ask what the image is for before you judge it. Atmosphere and information are two different jobs an image can do, and a designer must know which job each image on the wall is doing. The Lab's dreaming engines tend to produce the first.
evidence: Sort a set by whether each image carries mostly atmosphere or mostly information. Then take one atmospheric image and state exactly what buildable information it has, and what it does not. Be precise: "a window seat, depth unknown, sill height unknown, no structure shown."
When the student presents a beautiful image, ask what in it could be built. Watch whether atmosphere was standing in for information, and whether the student knew which one they were showing.
topics.critPrompt: When the student presents a beautiful image, ask what in it could be built. Watch whether atmosphere was standing in for information, and whether the student knew which one they were showing.

card.oneLiner: Some images carry mood, some carry buildable information, and few carry both. Ask what the image is for before you judge it.

sections.dilemma: A render of a reading room: dust in the light, a worn timber floor, a deep window seat. Everybody loves it. Is it good? You cannot answer that until you ask an earlier question: what is this image *for*? To set a mood, or to tell someone what to build?
sections.choices: Judge the image on feel. Or sort it first (is this mostly atmosphere, mostly information, or one of the rare images that is both?) and then judge it against its own job. An atmosphere image is judged on whether the mood is right and specific. An information image is judged on whether a contractor could act on it.
sections.consequence: Mix the two up and mood gets mistaken for finished design. The board goes to the client with feeling standing in for facts, and the facts get invented later by whoever builds it. Keep them apart and each image is allowed to be what it is. The mood image sets the direction, the information image gets drawn, and nobody takes measurements off the wrong one.
sections.theCase: A student presents a "final" image of a café in Mangaluru. Asked what in it could be built, she starts listing: the window seat (but how deep?), the floor (timber, but which timber, laid on what?), the ceiling (there is light, but no visible source). In two minutes the image has been sorted correctly: nearly all atmosphere, almost no information. It is a good atmosphere image. It was presented as something else.
sections.takeItToCrit: When the student presents a beautiful image, ask what in it could be built. Watch whether atmosphere was standing in for information, and whether the student knew which one they were showing.
sections.position: Atmosphere and information are two different jobs an image can do, and a designer must know which job each image on the wall is doing. The Lab's dreaming engines tend to produce the first. Grounded generators tend to serve the second. Neither is lesser. The error is confusing them.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Mood is where design starts. Information is where it ends up. Both are needed, and the damage happens at the handover, when a mood image gets read as a drawing. The Lab has watched that handover fail in practice often enough to teach the sorting before anything else about images.
sections.strongestObjection: The great architectural images carry both at once. A Binet photograph of a Zumthor interior is atmosphere and a lesson in construction in one frame. A strict sorting trains students to expect the split, and may lower their ambition for the image that refuses it. The rare "both" is the goal, not an exception to be filed away.
sections.revisionCondition: If generated images routinely began to carry reliable buildable information (dimensions that hold, junctions that resolve, light with a source), the sorting would become a check for the rare miss rather than the default reading. We test this every edition by measuring off the prettiest frame with a scale rule. So far the scale rule disagrees with the render.
sections.howItWorks: Image models learn from photographs, and photographs carry mood well and construction poorly, because the plan is not in the picture. So an engine tuned for evocative output produces atmosphere easily and information only by accident. Grounded generators, the ones that work from your own drawing, model or reference, hold information better because the information came from you. Knowing which engine made the frame tells you which job it is probably doing.
sections.tryIt: Sort a set by whether each image carries mostly atmosphere or mostly information. Then take one atmospheric image and state exactly what buildable information it has, and what it does not. Be precise: "a window seat, depth unknown, sill height unknown, no structure shown."

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The score is not your work
topics.description: A leaderboard measures performance on someone else's test, under lab conditions. Your site, your drawings, your deadline were not in the exam. A benchmark score says how a model did on a fixed, shared test: a set task, a set of inputs, and a scoring rule everyone uses — sometimes known answers, sometimes human raters, sometimes a hidden test set. That is useful.
evidence: Find the benchmark a tool you use quotes. Read what the test actually contains: the inputs, the answers, who judged. List three ways your work differs from it.
Explain what a benchmark can tell you and what it cannot, with one concrete example of each.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain what a benchmark can tell you and what it cannot, with one concrete example of each.

card.oneLiner: A leaderboard measures performance on someone else's test, under lab conditions. Your site, your drawings, your deadline were not in the exam.

sections.idea: A benchmark score says how a model did on a fixed, shared test: a set task, a set of inputs, and a scoring rule everyone uses — sometimes known answers, sometimes human raters, sometimes a hidden test set. That is useful. It is also narrow. Your studio has a particular site, drawings in a particular convention, a client who changes their mind, and a submission date. A high score proves the tool can do the test. Whether it can do your work is a separate question, and the only way to answer it is the five-input test on this map.
sections.whyItMatters: Marketing quotes scores. Your liability is your work. The two are not measured in the same place.
sections.inTheStudio: A model scores well on a document-reading benchmark built from clean PDFs. Your byelaw is a 1998 photocopy, scanned crooked, with a stamp across clause 7. The score did not include clause 7.
sections.watchForThis: The phrase "state of the art". It means "top of a particular table on a particular day". Ask which table, and what was on it.
sections.tryIt: Find the benchmark a tool you use quotes. Read what the test actually contains: the inputs, the answers, who judged. List three ways your work differs from it.
sections.proveIt: Explain what a benchmark can tell you and what it cannot, with one concrete example of each.
sections.howItWorks: Benchmarks are built from test sets with known answers, and the known answers are the limit. Whatever the set did not contain was not measured. The two benchmarks closest to your work show their scale honestly: fifty apartments in one, a hundred and twenty floor plans in the other. They also show how a serious test is made, which is why they appear on the previous cards. Two further cautions are standard in the field. A model may have seen data resembling the test during training, which inflates the score. And a score is a point in time. The next version moves it. Neither caution makes benchmarks useless. Both make them a starting point for your own test, not a substitute for it.
