topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Was the brief the failure?
topics.description: When a batch disappoints, the first suspect is your own brief, not the model. When a batch disappoints, the first suspect is your own brief — suspect, not convict. Reading your own brief critically is the mature user's first move, and it comes before any re-roll, any model switch and any complaint about the tool.
evidence: Take a failed batch and find the fault in the brief before you touch the model: the word that produced the wrong building. Then rewrite the brief to fix a failure you had first blamed on the engine, and run it once.

When the student's outputs miss, do they reach for the re-roll, or for the brief? Ask them to show the word in the brief that caused the miss. If they cannot find it, ask them to read the batch again.
topics.critPrompt: When the student's outputs miss, do they reach for the re-roll, or for the brief? Ask them to show the word in the brief that caused the miss. If they cannot find it, ask them to read the batch again.

card.oneLiner: When a batch disappoints, the first suspect is your own brief, not the model.

sections.dilemma: The batch is wrong. Not ugly, wrong: the wrong building, the wrong climate, the wrong idea. Your hand is already moving towards regenerate, or towards a different tool. Before it gets there, ask what the outputs show the brief really asked for.
sections.choices: Blame the engine and re-roll, or switch engines. Or read the batch as a faithful answer to your words, find the word that produced the wrong building, and rewrite the brief before you generate again.
sections.consequence: Blame the engine and you carry the same loose brief into the next batch and the next tool, and get the same wrongness in a different style, now convinced the tools are bad. Blame the brief first and most "model failures" turn out to be briefing failures you can fix in one line. That is cheaper than any re-roll, and it teaches you something about what you actually meant.
sections.theCase: Brief: "a contemporary house for a hot, humid coastal site, with local materials." Batch: twelve white boxes with floor-to-ceiling glass, two with palm trees. The student says the model does not understand the tropics. The tutor asks what *contemporary* usually looks like in the photographs the model learnt from. White boxes and glass. The brief asked for the wrong thing, and asked for it clearly. Rewritten as "deep overhangs, laterite walls, a Mangalore-tile roof, cross-ventilated, verandah on the windward side," the next batch is recognisably coastal Karnataka. The model did not change.
sections.takeItToCrit: When the student's outputs miss, do they reach for the re-roll, or for the brief? Ask them to show the word in the brief that caused the miss. If they cannot find it, ask them to read the batch again.
sections.position: When a batch disappoints, the first suspect is your own brief — suspect, not convict. Reading your own brief critically is the mature user's first move, and it comes before any re-roll, any model switch and any complaint about the tool.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The batch is the most honest reader your brief will ever have. It takes your words literally and answers with the most likely picture. Most disappointment is the gap between what you meant and what you typed, and that gap is yours to close. The Lab teaches this first because it is the move that makes every other card on this strand work.
sections.strongestObjection: Always suspecting your own brief first teaches user-blame. A failed batch belongs to the whole interaction — the brief, the model, its training coverage, the interface, the conditioning you gave it, the settings, the task — and blaming the brief by reflex is no more rigorous than blaming the machine by reflex. Worse, it breeds prompt superstition: if the machine fails, keep rewriting yourself until it behaves. Engines have blind spots no rewording closes (under-photographed regions, drawing conventions, dimensions), and the student sent back to the brief every time learns to doubt a brief that was fine, for a tool that cannot do the job.
sections.revisionCondition: The position is about the *first* suspect, and "diagnose the brief" is closer to what we mean than "blame" it. Read the batch, find the word; if there is no word to find, the tool goes to the bake-off. We would revise the card if workshop logs showed students spending more cycles rewriting briefs that were fine than they saved by catching loose ones. So far the loose brief has been the commoner cause, but the log is where that gets checked, not the slogan.
sections.howItWorks: A model answers the words you gave it, read through the habits of its training. "Contemporary" is a word with a strong default in the photographs. "Local materials" is a phrase with almost none, because captions rarely name the material. So the strong word wins and the weak phrase vanishes. Reading the batch tells you which of your words were strong and which were weak. The rewrite replaces the weak phrases with specific nouns the model has seen captioned: laterite, Mangalore tile, verandah.
sections.tryIt: Take a failed batch and find the fault in the brief before you touch the model: the word that produced the wrong building. Then rewrite the brief to fix a failure you had first blamed on the engine, and run it once.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Build your own test
topics.description: Five inputs you know cold, run before any real work. The designer who can test an unfamiliar tool beats the one who knows fifty products. Choose five inputs you know cold: a plan you drew, a site photograph you took, a specification you have checked, a question about a building you know well, and one deliberately awkward case. For each, write the expected answer before you run anything.
evidence: Build the five today, from what is on your desk. Make two of them the same plan twice — once annotated in English, once in Kannada script (ಅಡುಗೆಮನೆ, ಮಲಗುವ ಕೋಣೆ, ಹಜಾರ) — and see whether the tool reads the rooms in both. Run all five on two tools that claim the same job. Write the two score sheets.
Show the five inputs, the five expected answers, and the score sheets for two tools, and say which you would trust for what.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show the five inputs, the five expected answers, and the score sheets for two tools, and say which you would trust for what.

card.oneLiner: Five inputs you know cold, run before any real work. The designer who can test an unfamiliar tool beats the one who knows fifty products.

sections.whenToUse: Every time a new tool, model or version enters your workflow. Again after every update. Always before the deadline, never during it.
sections.method: Choose five inputs you know cold: a plan you drew, a site photograph you took, a specification you have checked, a question about a building you know well, and one deliberately awkward case. For each, write the expected answer before you run anything. Run all five. Score each: pass, partial, fail. Keep the five and the expected answers in one folder. Re-run the same five on every new version, and compare scores. Twenty minutes, once; five minutes, every time after.
sections.watchForThis: Testing with the vendor's sample. Their sample was chosen to pass. Your five were chosen because you know the right answer.
sections.tryIt: Build the five today, from what is on your desk. Make two of them the same plan twice — once annotated in English, once in Kannada script (ಅಡುಗೆಮನೆ, ಮಲಗುವ ಕೋಣೆ, ಹಜಾರ) — and see whether the tool reads the rooms in both. Run all five on two tools that claim the same job. Write the two score sheets.
sections.proveIt: Show the five inputs, the five expected answers, and the score sheets for two tools, and say which you would trust for what.
sections.labNote: The five-input test is the Lab's recommended method for meeting a new tool, not the only one. Larger evaluations exist and the next cards describe them; this one is sized to fit a desk and a Monday morning, and to be re-run without ceremony every time the product changes under you.
sections.howItWorks: This is what researchers do at scale. A benchmark is your five, multiplied. Blueprint-Bench asks models to turn photographs of fifty apartments into floor plans and scores them against the real plans. AECV-Bench asks them to count doors and windows on a hundred and twenty plans and to answer questions grounded in the drawings. The principle is identical: known inputs, known answers, a score. Your private benchmark has one advantage over theirs. It is made of your work, so a pass means something for your work. Products change under you. The five stay. That is why the test, not the product name, is the thing worth knowing.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Words for critiquing output
topics.description: To critique a generated image you need words that carry a fix, not a mood. "I like it" and "it feels off" are not yet critique. A feeling can start a critique; it cannot finish one.
evidence: Critique one output using only points a peer could act on in the next cycle. Then take three taste-verdicts ("nice," "off," "boring") and replace each with a named fault that can be fixed. Notice which of the three was hardest to convert. That is where your eye is least trained.
In crit, does the student name a fault the maker could fix, or only report a feeling? When they say "it doesn't work," ask: what, exactly, and what would you change?
topics.critPrompt: In crit, does the student name a fault the maker could fix, or only report a feeling? When they say "it doesn't work," ask: what, exactly, and what would you change?

grounding.ref: What Counts as Architectural Thinking After AI

card.oneLiner: To critique a generated image you need words that carry a fix, not a mood.

sections.position:
"I like it" and "it feels off" are not yet critique. A feeling can start a critique; it cannot finish one. Ask what in the work produced it, and which criterion it breaks. Critique of generated output needs words that carry a fix: *the light comes from nowhere* · *the scale is unbelievable, that door is two and a half metres* · *this material is wrong, laterite does not do that at a corner* · *the caption flattens the design into a style*. Precise critique is what makes the next cycle possible, because the next brief is written out of it.
> A fault you can name is a fault you can fix. A mood is just weather.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The studio crit has always worked this way. The useful juror names the fault and the useless one reports a taste. Generated output raises the stakes, because the next cycle is only as good as the words that describe what was wrong with the last one. A vocabulary of fixable faults (light, scale, material, structure, story) is the Lab's working critique register, and it is what lets a markup become a brief.
sections.strongestObjection: Some of the most important judgments do not break down into named faults. "This is the wrong building for this street" is true, can be acted on in the largest sense, and cannot be reduced to a light or a scale. A vocabulary that demands a fixable fault for every objection may train students to see only what the vocabulary can name, and to wave through a coherent, well-lit, believably scaled image of the wrong idea.
sections.revisionCondition: The vocabulary already includes *idea* and *story* as faults that can be named. "The idea is missing" is a sentence. We would revise the position if we saw critique-trained students becoming fluent at local faults and blind to the whole: cohorts whose crits got sharper at the detail and weaker at the scheme. That can be checked at jury, and we check it.
sections.tryIt: Critique one output using only points a peer could act on in the next cycle. Then take three taste-verdicts ("nice," "off," "boring") and replace each with a named fault that can be fixed. Notice which of the three was hardest to convert. That is where your eye is least trained.
sections.takeItToCrit: In crit, does the student name a fault the maker could fix, or only report a feeling? When they say "it doesn't work," ask: what, exactly, and what would you change?
sections.howItWorks: The Lab's critique register (light, scale, material, structure, idea, story) is its own working vocabulary, developed in teaching and kept as internal material. The words on this card are drawn from it. The register works because each word points at a layer of the image that can be checked on its own, and because each one maps onto something the next brief can say. Taste-words point at the viewer. Fault-words point at the image.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Coherence across a set
topics.description: Judging a visual family means judging how the images relate to each other, not each one alone. Coherence is a judgment made across the whole set, and it is where visual families quietly fall apart. No single image can pass or fail it.
evidence: Take a three- or four-image family and check it for consistent light, scale and material across the set. Find the one frame that breaks the family and say exactly what breaks it: the sun, the door height, the material. Then write the one brief line that would have prevented it.
Ask whether the images in the student's visual family belong to one project or only share a folder. Point at a material and ask them to find it in the next frame.
topics.critPrompt: Ask whether the images in the student's visual family belong to one project or only share a folder. Point at a material and ask them to find it in the next frame.

card.oneLiner: Judging a visual family means judging how the images relate to each other, not each one alone.

sections.dilemma: Four images for one project, each strong on its own. Together they go on a board. Do you judge them one at a time, in four passes, or do you ask the harder question: do these four belong to one building?
sections.choices: Approve each image on its merits. Or hold the four together and check three things across the set: is the light from the same sky, is the scale believable from frame to frame, is the same material actually the same material?
sections.consequence: Four individually good images with two different suns, a door that is 2.1 metres in one frame and 2.6 in the next, and a laterite wall that turns to brick between views do not read as a building. They read as a moodboard. The client senses it before they can say it. Checked as a family, the weak frame shows itself at once. It is usually the one made last, after the brief had drifted.
sections.theCase: A student's four-image family for a Coorg homestay. The main view has warm late-afternoon light from the west. The courtyard view has cool overcast light. The detail view has a roof tile profile that appears in neither. Each image was approved on its own. Laid side by side, the set falls apart in ten seconds. The fix is not a better image. It is one line in the brief, "the same 4 p.m. west light in every frame," carried through the whole set.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask whether the images in the student's visual family belong to one project or only share a folder. Point at a material and ask them to find it in the next frame.
sections.position: Coherence is a judgment made across the whole set, and it is where visual families quietly fall apart. No single image can pass or fail it. The Lab's five curation questions (mood or design, coherent, scale believable, materials consistent, what would need redrawing) are asked of the set, not of the frame.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A building is one thing. A set of images that claims to show it is claiming to show one thing, and generated images, each drawn fresh from the model's habits, do not keep that promise on their own. Somebody has to hold the sky still across the frames. That somebody is the designer.
sections.strongestObjection: Tools are catching up. Reference-image conditioning, consistent-character and consistent-scene features, and multi-view generation are being built precisely to keep light, scale and material stable across a set. If the machine holds coherence reliably, the designer's check becomes a glance, and this card overstates the work involved.
sections.revisionCondition: When a mainstream tool produces four-view families that pass the light, scale and material check without correction in most workshop runs, the card is rewritten from "coherence is your job" to "coherence is your check." We test this every edition on the same brief.
sections.howItWorks: Each generation is independent unless you make it otherwise. The model does not remember the sun it used in the previous frame. It draws a plausible sun again. So coherence has to be carried by the brief (the same light, the same material names, the same camera height, stated every time) and by the reading afterwards. A line in the brief asks for the same sun; it does not enforce it. What enforces it is the system's own controls — a reference image the tool conditions on, a fixed seed, a shared camera setting — and your check afterwards. Some tools now let you feed in a reference image to anchor the set. That helps, and it still needs checking.
sections.tryIt: Take a three- or four-image family and check it for consistent light, scale and material across the set. Find the one frame that breaks the family and say exactly what breaks it: the sun, the door height, the material. Then write the one brief line that would have prevented it.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Curation is diagnosis
topics.description: Reading a batch is not shopping. The batch shows you what your brief really asked for. The middle phase between generating and refining, which the Lab calls curation, is where the real learning happens, and it is the phase most people skip. Its job is to read the batch for what the brief actually said.
evidence: Sort a twelve-image batch into families. For each family write one line: what this family reveals about the brief. Then, using only the outputs, write the brief the model actually heard. Put it next to the brief you wrote. The gap is your next revision.
Ask the student what the batch taught them about their own brief, not which image they like. If the answer is a preference, ask again.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what the batch taught them about their own brief, not which image they like. If the answer is a preference, ask again.

card.oneLiner: Reading a batch is not shopping. The batch shows you what your brief really asked for.

sections.dilemma: Twelve images are on the table. You can treat them as a shop (which one do I want?) or as a report (what do these twelve say about the words I typed?). The first is quicker and feels like progress. The second is slower and tells you something about your own brief.
sections.choices: Shop: pick the closest one and move on. Or sort the twelve into families, name what each family has in common, and read each family as a sentence about the brief: "the brief said *open*, and the model heard *no walls*."
sections.consequence: Shopping leaves the brief exactly as vague as it was, so the next batch drifts the same way, and so does the one after that. Reading the batch as a report shows you the gap between what you meant and what the machine heard, and the next brief closes that gap. The first loop goes round in circles. The second one gets somewhere.
sections.theCase: The brief asks for "a light, open verandah house for Dharwad." Nine of twelve come back with glass walls and white floors. The student is about to pick the least glassy one. The tutor asks a different question: what did the model hear? It heard *light* as brightness, not as a light building. It heard *open* as transparent, not as shaded and ventilated right through. The next brief says "deep verandahs, filler-slab roof, shade first," and the batch changes character completely. The model did not change. The reading of the batch did.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student what the batch taught them about their own brief, not which image they like. If the answer is a preference, ask again.
sections.position: The middle phase between generating and refining, which the Lab calls curation, is where the real learning happens, and it is the phase most people skip. Its job is to read the batch for what the brief actually said. Everything else in the loop depends on that reading.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The Lab's workshop exercise is built around this phase, and the failure pattern is easy to spot in a log: three near-identical briefs, three near-identical sets, and a selection made on feel. The pattern the exercise wants is the opposite: a brief that changed because the previous batch exposed an assumption. The log shows which of the two happened, and the difference is obvious.
sections.strongestObjection: A trained eye shops well. An experienced designer looking at twelve images is already reading them. The diagnosis is happening silently, inside the choosing. Making the step explicit may help a beginner and only slow down an expert. A routine that helps novices is not a law for everyone.
sections.revisionCondition: Evidence that experienced practitioners who choose fast write second briefs as sharp as those who diagnose on paper. If their logs show the brief improving the same way without the written step, the step becomes training wheels: kept for the first year, dropped after that.
sections.howItWorks: CONTACT SHEET taught you to see the set before any frame. This card takes the next step: reading the set as a report on the words you wrote. A model answers the words you gave it, read through the habits in its training. So the batch records two things at once: your words, and the model's reading of them. Sorting the batch into families separates the two. Where every family agrees, the model read you clearly. Where the families split, your brief was ambiguous. Where every family does something you never asked for, you have found the model's habit, and now you can write against it.
sections.tryIt: Sort a twelve-image batch into families. For each family write one line: what this family reveals about the brief. Then, using only the outputs, write the brief the model actually heard. Put it next to the brief you wrote. The gap is your next revision.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Effort is not proof of thinking
topics.description: School treated visible effort as proof that thinking happened. AI makes convincing work appear without it, so the reasoning now has to be made explicit. Architectural education has run on a stand-in. Late nights, many drawings and iterations on the wall were read as evidence that a student was learning to think.
evidence: Show a piece of your work and, separately, state the thinking behind it: the framing you chose, the choices you made, the reversals, meaning what you would undo and why. Then explain why the polished output alone no longer proves that thinking took place.

When the work looks effortful, can the student still show where the actual thinking is? Ask for one reversal, something they undid, and the reason. A student who thought has one. A student who only assembled does not.
topics.critPrompt: When the work looks effortful, can the student still show where the actual thinking is? Ask for one reversal, something they undid, and the reason. A student who thought has one. A student who only assembled does not.

grounding.ref: What Counts as Architectural Thinking After AI — what-counts-as-architectural-thinking
What Counts as Architectural Thinking After AI
Systematic review: GenAI's impact on higher-order cognitive skills

card.oneLiner: School treated visible effort as proof that thinking happened. AI makes convincing work appear without it, so the reasoning now has to be made explicit.

sections.position: Architectural education has run on a stand-in. Late nights, many drawings and iterations on the wall were read as evidence that a student was learning to think. That stand-in was always fragile. AI breaks it cleanly. Convincing drawings, persuasive narratives and multiple options now appear without passing through the friction the studio relied on. This is not mainly a cheating problem. It is a structural one. Output is no longer proof of thinking. So the job shifts to making the reasoning explicit (the framing, the trade-offs, the reversals) rather than trusting what you can see.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The Lab's argument is that AI did not create this problem. It exposed it. Studios that rewarded recognisable patterns and visual confidence will keep doing so, only faster. The honest response is to change what is evaluated: decision logs, assumption maps, trade-off statements, and the question "what would you undo, and why?" If a student cannot explain why a solution exists, the solution does not count, however convincing it looks.
sections.strongestObjection: Friction was never just a stand-in. The late nights and the hundred drawings were also *where the thinking happened*. The struggle produced the understanding, not only the evidence of it. A teaching method that accepts frictionless output plus an explicit reasoning trace may be accepting a reasoning trace written after the fact, by someone who never did the thinking the trace describes. Effort may be a bad proof of thinking and a good cause of it.
sections.revisionCondition: This card does not say effort is worthless. It says effort is not *proof*. We would revise it if studios that moved to reasoning-based evaluation produced graduates who could explain decisions but not make them: fluent in trade-off language, weak in the room. That can be observed over a few cohorts, and the Lab's own workshop logs are one place to look.
sections.tryIt: Show a piece of your work and, separately, state the thinking behind it: the framing you chose, the choices you made, the reversals, meaning what you would undo and why. Then explain why the polished output alone no longer proves that thinking took place.
sections.takeItToCrit: When the work looks effortful, can the student still show where the actual thinking is? Ask for one reversal, something they undid, and the reason. A student who thought has one. A student who only assembled does not.
sections.howItWorks: A drawing used to carry its own evidence. It took hours, and the hours were visible. Generated output carries no such trace. It can be fluent, resolved and entirely unexamined. So evaluation has to ask for what the image no longer contains: the decision chain. The Lab's essay on this names four cognitive traces (decision logs, assumption maps, trade-off statements, reversals) and calls them architectural acts, not paperwork. The iteration log elsewhere on this strand is their working form.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Same brief, different engines
topics.description: Run one brief through different families of engine and read what each one rewards and what each one distorts. The same words make different worlds. You have one brief and two ways of generating, which the Lab calls a dreaming engine — producing evocative images from words alone — and a grounded generator — working from your own drawing, model or reference. Which one do you use for this phase?
evidence: Run one controlled brief across two engine families, changing nothing else. Name what each one kept and what each one lost, in a line each. Then take a stray output from a classmate and match it to the family that made it, going by its usual strengths and failures.
Can the student predict which family will serve a given phase, and show the comparison that taught them? Hand them a stray output and ask which family made it, and what in it gave that away.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student predict which family will serve a given phase, and show the comparison that taught them? Hand them a stray output and ask which family made it, and what in it gave that away.

grounding.ref: Prompt Personalities: How to Collaborate With ChatGPT and Claude

card.oneLiner: Run one brief through different families of engine and read what each one rewards and what each one distorts. The same words make different worlds.

sections.dilemma: You have one brief and two ways of generating, which the Lab calls a dreaming engine — producing evocative images from words alone — and a grounded generator — working from your own drawing, model or reference. Which one do you use for this phase? You can guess from the marketing, or you can find out.
sections.choices: Pick a tool by habit or by what your friends use. Or run the same controlled brief through both families, hold everything else still, and read the two batches side by side. What did each keep? What did each lose? What did each add that you never asked for?
sections.consequence: Pick by habit and you end up using a dreaming engine to produce a plan and a grounded one to find a mood, and blaming the tools for both. Run the bake-off and you learn each family's accent: the one that always adds drama, the one that holds your geometry and flattens your light. Then you can choose by phase. Dream early, ground late, and know which machine you are listening to.
sections.theCase: One brief, "a reading room in an old Dharwad wada, timber columns, a single north window," goes through both families. The dreaming engine returns atmosphere: dust in a shaft of light, a worn floor, columns too slender to be timber, a window twice the size the brief implied. The grounded generator, working from the student's own plan, returns the right column spacing and the right window, with light that is flat and a floor that looks new. Each kept something the other lost. The student now knows which to use on Monday and which on Thursday.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student predict which family will serve a given phase, and show the comparison that taught them? Hand them a stray output and ask which family made it, and what in it gave that away.
sections.labNote: "Dreaming engine" and "grounded generator" are the Lab's own names, not the industry's. Most tools now offer several modes in one product — text only, reference-conditioned, geometry-conditioned, retrieval-grounded — and the boundary the names draw is the Lab's way of teaching what to hold still, not the natural order of AI systems. The bake-off is the Lab's recommended method for learning a tool's accent. It is not the only one, and the names may change before the habit does.
sections.howItWorks: Engine families, as the Lab sorts them, differ in what they take as input and what they optimise for. A dreaming engine maps words to the most evocative likely image. It is tuned towards mood and is free to invent geometry. A grounded generator conditions on something you supply (a sketch, a plan, a photograph), so the geometry is held and the invention is confined to surface and light. Neither is better. They answer different questions. Reviewed every edition because the modes are converging: tools now offer both in one product, and the accents shift with every release. The bake-off is the durable part, the habit of testing rather than believing.
sections.tryIt: Run one controlled brief across two engine families, changing nothing else. Name what each one kept and what each one lost, in a line each. Then take a stray output from a classmate and match it to the family that made it, going by its usual strengths and failures.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Build a personal failure catalogue
topics.description: Keep a running record of the outputs that fooled you. It is the most honest map of how your eye is growing. One entry per failure, three lines. What fooled you: the output, kept as a thumbnail or a quote.
evidence: Start the catalogue this week with the last three outputs that got past you. For each, write the tell you missed. Then pick the one you suspect you repeat most and design one check that would have caught it.
Name one failure you repeat, straight from the catalogue, and show the check you now run for it. The answer should come from a record, not a guess.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what AI mistake they repeat most. The answer should come from a record, not a guess.

grounding.ref: Tankelevitch et al., The Metacognitive Demands and Opportunities of Generative AI

card.oneLiner: Keep a running record of the outputs that fooled you. It is the most honest map of how your eye is growing.

sections.whenToUse: Every time an AI output got past you: the image you believed, the brief that misfired, the polished answer you pasted before checking. Especially the ones that embarrassed you, because those are the ones you will otherwise forget.
sections.method: One entry per failure, three lines. *What fooled you*: the output, kept as a thumbnail or a quote. *The tell you missed*: what gave it away in hindsight. The shadow, the missing source, the too-neat table. *How you now catch it*: the check you added, in one sentence. Re-read the catalogue before every jury and every client meeting. Over a term, sort the entries. The tells that repeat are your blind spots, with names on them.
sections.watchForThis: Recording the machine's mistake instead of your own. "The model hallucinated a byelaw" is not an entry. "I pasted a byelaw table without asking for its edition" is. The catalogue is about your eye, not the tool's faults.
sections.tryIt: Start the catalogue this week with the last three outputs that got past you. For each, write the tell you missed. Then pick the one you suspect you repeat most and design one check that would have caught it.
sections.proveIt: Name one failure you repeat, straight from the catalogue, and show the check you now run for it. The answer should come from a record, not a guess.
sections.labNote: The catalogue is the Lab's method for turning a private thing, being fooled, into something that can be taught. It records what you did not yet know to distrust. We hold that a designer's eye grows fastest on its own written-down failures, and more slowly on anyone else's warnings, including ours.
sections.howItWorks: Knowing what you know, and noticing when you do not, is what psychologists call metacognition: monitoring your own thinking. Research on working with generative systems finds that much of the difficulty is metacognitive. The hard part is not the tool. It is judging the tool's output against your intent, and knowing how much to trust that judgment. A failure catalogue is a metacognitive aid. It keeps the evidence of where your confidence was wrong in one place, where it can correct you the next time the polish arrives.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Systematic beats spectacular

grounding.ref: Chatterjee et al., Getting it Right: Improving Spatial Consistency in Text-to-Image Models (SPRIGHT)

topics.description: One dramatic error teaches little. A pattern of small ones tells you where the tool reliably breaks, and why. A stair to nowhere, a hand with six fingers. Spectacular failures get shared and teach almost nothing, because they only tell you that the tool can fail, which you knew.
evidence: Write one prompt that states a spatial relation, such as "a window to the left of the door". Run it ten times. Count how often the relation is obeyed. Change the relation and run ten more. You now hold a pattern, with a number.
Name one reliable failure of a tool you use, with a count from your own runs, and your best guess at the cause — the diet, the settings, the interface, or the way you asked.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to name one reliable failure of a tool you use, with a count from your own runs, and your best guess at the cause — the diet, the settings, the interface, or the way you asked.

card.oneLiner: One dramatic error teaches little. A pattern of small ones tells you where the tool reliably breaks, and why.

sections.idea: A stair to nowhere, a hand with six fingers. Spectacular failures get shared and teach almost nothing, because they only tell you that the tool can fail, which you knew. What teaches is a pattern: the failure that comes back, under conditions you can name. Patterns can be predicted, and a pattern tells you where to look for the cause — the training diet is one common cause, not the diagnosis. A tool with a known pattern is a tool you can use safely around its edges. A tool with a funny story attached is just a tool you distrust vaguely.
sections.whyItMatters: "It gets left and right wrong about a third of the time" is a working rule. "It put the stair outside once" is a story.
sections.inTheStudio: Two students. One says the image tool is rubbish because it drew a door into a wall. The other says it reliably ignores "to the left of" and "above", so they never use it for adjacency and always use it for material. The second student has a pattern. The first has a grievance.
sections.watchForThis: Collecting funny failures instead of counting ordinary ones. The count is the knowledge.
sections.tryIt: Write one prompt that states a spatial relation, such as "a window to the left of the door". Run it ten times. Count how often the relation is obeyed. Change the relation and run ten more. You now hold a pattern, with a number.
sections.proveIt: Name one reliable failure of a tool you use, with a count from your own runs, and your best guess at the cause — the diet, the settings, the interface, or the way you asked.
sections.howItWorks: Spatial relations are the clearest measured case. Research in 2024 found that text-to-image models fail to follow spatial relationships in prompts with any consistency, and traced the cause to the diet. The captions these models train on rarely state where things are relative to each other. Re-captioning six million images to say so, and training on a small fraction of them, improved spatial accuracy noticeably. The failure was systematic, it had a cause, and the cause was fixable. Not every pattern traces to the diet: the settings, the interface, the conditioning you supplied and the way you phrased the ask all produce patterns of their own, and the count does not tell you which. That is what a pattern buys you that a one-off never does: a place to start looking. Your personal failure catalogue, elsewhere on this map, is where patterns build up.

evidence: Run five cycles on one brief. Change one named thing each time and write down the reason before you generate. Then explain, in your own words, why making a pile and picking one lands on the model's taste, not yours.

grounding.ref: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou & Velloso, 2024 (CHI; arXiv:2403.11164)
SCAPE: Searching Conceptual Architecture Prompts using Evolution

card.oneLiner: Making fifty images and picking the closest one is gambling, not iteration. Same machine, different discipline.

sections.dilemma: The deadline is Thursday. You can generate fifty images tonight and pick the closest one, or you can run five cycles, changing one named thing in the brief each time and writing down why. The first feels productive and is faster. The second feels slow, and it is the only one you can explain afterwards.
sections.choices: Pull the lever: generate in bulk, scroll, pick, upscale. Or iterate: treat the brief as a hypothesis, the image as the test, and the revision as the next brief. One change per cycle, each change with a reason in the log.
sections.consequence: Pull the lever and the image you pick is the one that happened to land nearest your taste. Really it is the model's taste, filtered through your mood at 1 a.m. You cannot say why it is right, so you cannot defend it, and you cannot do it again on purpose. Iterate and you end up with fewer images and a chain of decisions that made them. The chain is what a jury, a client and your future self can read. The image is only its last link.
sections.theCase: Two students, same brief: a primary school in Gadag, one courtyard, load-bearing brick. The first generates sixty images, picks number forty-one, and can only say that it "felt right." The second runs five cycles. The first brief is too generic and the model gives glass. The second adds "load-bearing brick, jack-arch roof." The third fixes the court proportion after the batch shows it too deep. The fourth moves the entrance after the batch puts it on the wrong street. The fifth adjusts the light. Five images on the wall, each with a line under it. The jury spends ten minutes with the second student and two with the first. Both walls have a good image on them. Only one wall has an argument.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student show the chain of decisions that made the image on the wall, cycle by cycle? Ask what changed between the third and fourth image, and why. If the answer is "I made more," it was a lottery.
sections.position: Generating fifty images and selecting the closest one is gambling, not iteration. Real iteration changes one thing in the brief each cycle and knows why. The casino and the studio use the same machine. The difference is the discipline, and the discipline can be taught.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: This is Sahil's founding position for the Lab's image teaching, and the one its image exercises are built on. Bulk-and-pick lands on the model's taste, because selecting from a random spread favours whatever the model tends to do. Brief revision lands on your taste, because each cycle moves the distribution towards your intent. The Lab's protocol calls the first one slot-machine prompting. It feels like progress and there is no thinking in it.
sections.strongestObjection: Wide sampling plus selection is a legitimate search method, and serious research builds on it. Evolutionary tools for architectural concept generation sample broadly on purpose, let the designer select, and breed from the selection, and they report more novel results than a single-prompt approach. When generation is nearly free, sampling a wide space *before* converging may be the more rigorous exploration, and "gambling" may be an insult aimed at a real method.
sections.revisionCondition: The objection describes sampling with selection *criteria stated in advance* and a record of what was selected and why. That is not what the card attacks. That is iteration at scale. We would rewrite the card if studio evidence showed undirected bulk generation, with no criteria and no log, producing schemes as defensible as logged iteration. The jury test has not gone that way yet.
sections.howItWorks: Each generation is a draw from a distribution the prompt has shaped. Fifty draws from one prompt sample that one distribution thoroughly. That is useful if you want to know what the prompt *means to the model*, and useless if you want to move it. Selecting from those fifty picks the draw closest to your preference, but the distribution never moved, so the next batch starts from the same place. Iteration moves the distribution. The research on fixation and generative tools supports the caution from the other side. In one controlled visual-ideation study with sixty participants, working with a stream of AI images narrowed ideas rather than widening them. That was a general ideation task, not an architecture studio, and it is one study.
sections.tryIt: Run five cycles on one brief. Change one named thing each time and write down the reason before you generate. Then explain, in your own words, why making a pile and picking one lands on the model's taste, not yours.

topics.name: The first image traps you
topics.description: Seeing AI images while you ideate can lock you in rather than free you up. The tool sold as fuel for divergence can be an anchor. Day one of a new brief. The blank page is uncomfortable, and an image tool will fill it in thirty seconds with something plausible.
evidence: Ideate on a brief twice: once with AI images from the start, once with none for the first hour. Count the distinct directions each way produced. Then name the moment a generated image narrowed your thinking instead of widening it. You will usually be able to point at the frame.

Can the student point to where an early AI image anchored the whole scheme, and say what they would do differently? Ask to see the ideas that came before the first image. If there are none, the image was the idea.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student point to where an early AI image anchored the whole scheme, and say what they would do differently? Ask to see the ideas that came before the first image. If there are none, the image was the idea.

grounding.ref: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou & Velloso, 2024 (CHI; arXiv:2403.11164)
Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI

card.oneLiner: Seeing AI images while you ideate can lock you in rather than free you up. The tool sold as fuel for divergence can be an anchor.

sections.dilemma: Day one of a new brief. The blank page is uncomfortable, and an image tool will fill it in thirty seconds with something plausible. Do you generate now, to get going, or later, after you have thought without pictures?
sections.choices: Generate first and ideate around what arrives. Or ideate first, with words, diagrams, the site and the programme, and bring images in only once you have several directions of your own to test them against.
sections.consequence: Generate first and the first plausible image becomes the anchor. Every later idea is measured as a departure from it, and the range of what you consider narrows without you noticing. Ideate first and the images arrive as tests of directions you already hold, where they can widen or sharpen your thinking without replacing it.
sections.theCase: Two sections of a first-year studio, same brief: a bus shelter for a village road near Dharwad. One section generated images on the first morning. The other drew and wrote for two days before touching a tool. At the pin-up, the first section's schemes were mostly variations on the first image the tool had produced that morning, a curved timber canopy on two legs. The second section had a stone bench under a tree, a wall with a roof, a lifted platform, a canopy, and then the curved timber one as well, arrived at as one option among five.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student point to where an early AI image anchored the whole scheme, and say what they would do differently? Ask to see the ideas that came *before* the first image. If there are none, the image was the idea.
sections.howItWorks: Anchoring is an old finding. The first value or form you see pulls every later judgment towards it. A 2024 controlled study at CHI tested this with image generators specifically. Sixty participants in a visual ideation task — not an architecture studio — were the subjects: those ideating with an AI image tool produced fewer ideas, less variety, and less original ones than those working without it. That is one study, in one setting, and it is why the card is marked EVOLVING. THE FIRST ANSWER ANCHORS, one ring down, describes the pull the first output has on your next prompt. This card is about the earlier decision: when to let an image into the room at all. The effect may depend on how and when the tool is introduced, and interface designs that delay or diversify the images may change it. Meanwhile the practical rule stands: ideate before you generate, and treat the first image as a suspect, not a seed.
sections.tryIt: Ideate on a brief twice: once with AI images from the start, once with none for the first hour. Count the distinct directions each way produced. Then name the moment a generated image narrowed your thinking instead of widening it. You will usually be able to point at the frame.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Is this tool any good?
topics.description: Every tool gets some things wrong. The question is which kind of wrong costs you more here: a false alarm or a miss. A tool claims to flag structural problems in a plan, or to check a drawing against a byelaw, or to spot generated images. It is right most of the time.
evidence: For a task you actually do, say whether a false alarm or a miss would cost more, and why. Then describe a simple check, with no maths, that would show whether a tool is good enough for that job: ten cases you already know the answer to, and a count.
Ask the student whether a false alarm or a miss would hurt more for this job, and how they would check. If they quote an accuracy number, ask what it is an accuracy at.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student whether a false alarm or a miss would hurt more for this job, and how they would check. If they quote an accuracy number, ask what it is an accuracy at.

card.oneLiner: Every tool gets some things wrong. The question is which kind of wrong costs you more here: a false alarm or a miss.

sections.dilemma: A tool claims to flag structural problems in a plan, or to check a drawing against a byelaw, or to spot generated images. It is right most of the time. Is "most of the time" good enough? That depends on a question the advert never asks. Which way does it fail, and which failure hurts you?
sections.choices: Trust the accuracy number. Or ask two sharper questions before relying on it. When it says "problem" and there is none (a false alarm), what does that cost me? When it says "fine" and there is a problem (a miss), what does that cost me? Then run a small test built around the costlier one.
sections.consequence: Trust the number and you can end up with a tool that is 95 per cent right and wrong in the one way you cannot afford: a byelaw checker that misses the clause that fails your approval, or a fake-detector that flags every real photograph. Ask which error costs more and you know what to test, how much to trust it, and where you must still look yourself.
sections.theCase: A student wants to use a tool that flags "structurally implausible" elements in generated images before they go into a presentation. False alarm: a sound cantilever gets flagged, which costs a minute to check. Miss: an impossible span gets waved through, which costs the client's trust. The miss is the expensive error. So the test is not "how often is it right?" but "of ten images with a real structural fault, how many does it catch?" Six of ten. The tool is useful as a first pass and useless as a last one. The student now knows which.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student whether a false alarm or a miss would hurt more for this job, and how they would check. If they quote an accuracy number, ask what it is an accuracy *at*.
sections.howItWorks: Testing a classifier means counting its two kinds of error separately. "How many of its alarms were real?" and "how many of the real problems did it find?" are different questions with different answers. A tool can score well on one while failing the other. A detector that flags everything finds every problem and is useless. Which question matters depends on the job. A check before a client meeting wants few misses. A check that interrupts your drawing wants few false alarms. Benchmarks for image models work the same way. They set controlled tasks (put the red cube left of the blue sphere; draw a plan that could be walked through) and count the failures by kind, which is why the benchmark cards elsewhere on this map report "at or near random" for spatial tasks rather than an overall score.
sections.tryIt: For a task you actually do, say whether a false alarm or a miss would cost more, and why. Then describe a simple check, with no maths, that would show whether a tool is good enough for that job: ten cases you already know the answer to, and a count.

topics.description: Faster than what? Better than what? A comparison has a baseline, or it is a feeling. Do the task once the unaided way, by hand or by your old method. Time it.
evidence: Pick one task this week you would normally hand to a tool. Do it both ways. Write the two sentences.
Show the pair, unaided and assisted, with the times, the criteria, and the two sentences.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show the pair, unaided and assisted, with the times, the criteria, and the two sentences.

card.oneLiner: Faster than what? Better than what? A comparison has a baseline, or it is a feeling.

sections.whenToUse: Whenever you are about to say a tool is faster, better, or worth the money. Before the claim, not in defence of it.
sections.method: Do the task once the unaided way, by hand or by your old method. Time it. Keep the result. Then do it with the tool. Time that. Judge both against the same four lines of "done" (written first, see GOOD ENOUGH, FIRST). Write one sentence with both numbers in it and one sentence on what each version had that the other lacked. That sentence is the only honest review of a tool you will ever write.
sections.watchForThis: Comparing against an imagined version of the old way, slower and worse than it really was. Memory flatters the new tool. Only a baseline you actually produced can be compared.
sections.tryIt: Pick one task this week you would normally hand to a tool. Do it both ways. Write the two sentences.
sections.proveIt: Show the pair, unaided and assisted, with the times, the criteria, and the two sentences.
sections.labNote: Producing your own baseline is the Lab's recommended method for judging a tool, not the only one. Published comparisons exist, and one in architecture is linked below; they tell you what happened to other people. The two sentences tell you what happened to you.
sections.howItWorks: This is the control group, borrowed from experimental science, where nothing counts as an effect without something to compare it to. The baseline also moves with the person. A 2026 study of thirty-six students, from architectural engineering and other disciplines, doing an architectural concept-design task found that generative assistance gave no overall performance advantage across the group but significantly improved the performance of novice designers, and lowered participants' confidence in their own creativity. So "faster than what?" has a second half: "for whom?" Your baseline is yours. It will change as you do, which is another reason to keep producing it.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: An image is not a proposal
topics.description: One frame can carry six different things (image, idea, geometry, buildability, atmosphere, story) and it can hold each one or fake it. A beautiful image is not a finished proposal. It is a frame that may contain parts of one.
evidence: Take one image and check it across all six: image, idea, geometry, buildability, atmosphere, story. Then find one case where the image is strong but the idea is missing, and one where the idea is strong and the image is weak. The second is the more valuable frame, and the harder one to defend in a room.

When the student pins up a render, ask which of the six layers it really holds. Watch whether they already know. A student who has checked will answer in order. A student who has not will defend the picture.
topics.critPrompt: When the student pins up a render, ask which of the six layers it really holds. Watch whether they already know. A student who has checked will answer in order. A student who has not will defend the picture.

card.oneLiner: One frame can carry six different things (image, idea, geometry, buildability, atmosphere, story) and it can hold each one or fake it.

sections.dilemma: A render arrives that makes the room go quiet. It looks finished. Do you treat it as a proposal, something that could go to a client, or as an image that may or may not contain a proposal?
sections.choices: Accept the frame as the scheme. Or take it apart into six layers and check each one. Is there an *image*? (Yes, obviously.) Is there an *idea*, a stance about how this place should work? Is there *geometry*: could this be drawn in plan and section? Is it *buildable*: would the structure stand, would the junctions resolve? Is there *atmosphere*, the feel of the light and material? Is there a *story*, something it says about who lives here and how? A frame can hold all six, or hold two and fake four.
sections.consequence: Treat a strong image as a proposal and the faked layers show up later: at coordination, at costing, in front of the client who took measurements off the render. Take it apart first and you know what you actually have. Perhaps a strong atmosphere and a story, with no geometry yet. That is useful. It tells you what to draw next.
sections.theCase: A client in Hubballi forwards an AI image on WhatsApp: "something like this." A cantilevered timber box over a stone base, golden light, a single tree. The student goes through the six. Image: yes. Atmosphere: yes, strong. Story: a retreat, a view. Idea: unclear. Why the cantilever? Geometry: the box has no depth that could be drawn. Buildability: nothing is holding the cantilever up. Two and a half out of six. The client's expectations were set by the three that are missing.
sections.takeItToCrit: When the student pins up a render, ask which of the six layers it really holds. Watch whether they already know. A student who has checked will answer in order. A student who has not will defend the picture.
sections.position: A beautiful image is not a finished proposal. It is a frame that may contain parts of one. The designer's job is to say which parts, and the six-layer check is how the Lab teaches that reading.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: This rule is older than AI. A hand-drawn perspective could always flatter an unresolved scheme. What has changed is the volume and the polish. Images now arrive looking finished before any thinking has been done, and they arrive from clients as well as from students. The check has to be explicit because the temptation is now constant.
sections.strongestObjection: Every proposal begins as an image, and the best designers have always worked backwards from the picture. Insisting on six layers before an image "counts" may kill the moment when a frame is genuinely ahead of its own geometry, when the sketch knows more than the person who drew it. A rigid check risks marking intuition as fraud.
sections.revisionCondition: This card does not forbid the image. It forbids calling the image a proposal. We would soften it if we saw students who had been taught the six layers become unable to start from an image, which would mean the check was producing caution where it should produce clarity. We watch for that in workshops.
sections.howItWorks: Image models learn what finished buildings look like in photographs. Atmosphere and story are in the photographs. Geometry and structure mostly are not, because a photograph does not contain the plan. So a model is strong on the layers a photograph carries and weak on the ones it does not. A render that scores high on the first and low on the second is not a flaw in the model. It is what the model was fed, showing through.
sections.tryIt: Take one image and check it across all six: image, idea, geometry, buildability, atmosphere, story. Then find one case where the image is strong but the idea is missing, and one where the idea is strong and the image is weak. The second is the more valuable frame, and the harder one to defend in a room.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Individual lift, collective sameness
topics.description: Generative AI can raise one person's output while flattening the variety across everyone. The tool seems to make your work better: a longer idea list, sharper images. The same seems true for everyone else in the studio, on the same tool.
evidence: Collect a class's AI-assisted outputs for one brief and measure how similar they became: sort them into families and count. Then explain, in two sentences, how a tool can help you individually and make the group more alike at the same time.
Can the student show where the class converged on one model's taste, and say what it would take to break out? Ask them which of their own moves they are confident nobody else in the room made.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student show where the class converged on one model's taste, and say what it would take to break out? Ask them which of their own moves they are confident nobody else in the room made.

card.oneLiner: Generative AI can raise one person's output while flattening the variety across everyone.

sections.dilemma: The tool seems to make your work better: a longer idea list, sharper images. The same seems true for everyone else in the studio, on the same tool. Walk the pin-up at the end of term and ask whether the room is richer or narrower than it was last year.
sections.choices: Judge the tool by what it does for you. Or judge it at two scales at once: what it does for one person, and what it does to the variety across the group. The two can move in opposite directions.
sections.consequence: Judge only the individual lift and a studio of thirty drifts towards one model's habits: the same roof, the same light, the same courtyard. Each student is a little better and the room is a lot more alike. Judge both scales and you can take the lift and protect the variety, with different models, different briefs, images introduced late, and precedent drawn from the real world rather than from the same feed.
sections.theCase: Picture an end-of-term exhibition in the first year a studio uses image tools widely. A visiting juror says the work is more polished than last year's. A minute later she says she cannot tell the projects apart. Both observations can be true at once. No single student did anything wrong. The room as a whole did.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student show where the class converged on one model's taste, and say what it would take to break out? Ask them which of their own moves they are confident nobody else in the room made.
sections.howItWorks: Two studies put numbers on the pattern. In one, writers given AI story ideas produced work that was rated better, and the lift was largest for the less practised writers, but the stories across the group were more similar to each other than the ones written unaided. In another, people generating ideas with a language model converged on a narrower set of ideas than people working without one. Both studies were on writing and idea lists, not on architecture studios. The studio drift described here is the Lab's inference from them and from what it has seen at pin-ups, and it should be read as that. EVOLVING, because the pull towards sameness depends on everyone using the same few models, and on interface choices that could change.

topics.name: The iteration log
topics.description: A steady record (brief version, output, judgment, next move) that lets you defend an AI process in a jury and improve it over time. Four columns, one row per cycle. Brief version: the exact words and settings you used, numbered.
evidence: Keep a full log across one design exercise: every cycle, all four columns. Then hand the log, and only the log, to a classmate and ask them to rebuild your decision chain from first brief to final frame. Where they get lost is where the log was thin.
Rebuild the whole decision chain for a reviewer using the log alone, with no talking and no extra images. If they can follow it, the process can be defended.

grounding.ref: What Counts as Architectural Thinking After AI

card.oneLiner: A steady record (brief version, output, judgment, next move) that lets you defend an AI process in a jury and improve it over time.

sections.whenToUse: Any time generated material is on its way into real work: a studio project, a portfolio, a client presentation. If the image will be on a wall, the log starts before the first generation.
sections.method: Four columns, one row per cycle. *Brief version*: the exact words and settings you used, numbered. *Output*: the image or text that came back, the one you kept, with a note on what the batch did. *Judgment*: what the output showed. What it got right, what it got wrong, what it revealed about the brief. *Next move*: the one change you will make, and why. Keep it short. A line per column is enough. The log is the artefact. The images are its evidence.
sections.watchForThis: A log written afterwards. A log written from memory is a story about a process, not a record of one, and it will smooth over the cycle where you changed three things at once and got lucky. Write the row before you generate, and finish it before the next one.
sections.tryIt: Keep a full log across one design exercise: every cycle, all four columns. Then hand the log, and only the log, to a classmate and ask them to rebuild your decision chain from first brief to final frame. Where they get lost is where the log was thin.
sections.proveIt: Rebuild the whole decision chain for a reviewer using the log alone, with no talking and no extra images. If they can follow it, the process can be defended.
sections.labNote: The log is the Lab's method, adopted from the first fifty-images test in 2026 and confirmed in every image workshop since. It is not the only way to keep a process honest. It is the one that turns "show your working" from a request into a habit, and it is the artefact a jury can read.
sections.howItWorks: The log works because it makes three invisible things visible: how the brief changed (which shows your thinking), the judgment column (which shows how you read the batch), and the next-move column (which shows the cause of every change). Together they are the trace of thinking that a finished image no longer carries on its own. The Lab's position that output is no longer proof of thinking leads straight here. If the work cannot show its reasoning, the reasoning has to be kept somewhere, and the log is where.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: The machine fixates too
topics.description: Generative models keep returning to familiar solutions. Re-rolling one model samples one set of learned habits, so the draws tend to cluster. You want more variety. The obvious move is to press generate again.
evidence: Re-roll one prompt twenty times and map how narrow the model's range really is: sort the twenty into families and count them. Then explain why switching models or reframing the brief beats re-rolling when you want real variety.
When a student wants more variety, do they re-roll the same model, or change the model or the brief? Ask them to show the re-roll batch and point at what did not change across it.
topics.critPrompt: When a student wants more variety, do they re-roll the same model, or change the model or the brief? Ask them to show the re-roll batch and point at what did not change across it.

grounding.ref: Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI (arXiv:2502.05870, 2025)
Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas (arXiv:2602.20408, 2026)

card.oneLiner: Generative models keep returning to familiar solutions. Re-rolling one model samples one set of learned habits, so the draws tend to cluster.

sections.dilemma: You want more variety. The obvious move is to press generate again. Twenty re-rolls later the images are all cousins. Is the problem your luck, or the machine's range?
sections.choices: Keep re-rolling, hoping the next draw leaves the neighbourhood. Or accept that a model has habits of its own (favourite forms, favourite palettes, favourite ways to resolve a corner) and get variety by changing the model, reframing the brief, or prompting deliberately against the habit.
sections.consequence: Re-roll and you spend an evening mapping how narrow one model's range is, without realising that is what you did. Switch the model or the brief and the range opens up, because you have moved to a different set of habits instead of sampling the same set again.
sections.theCase: A student needs three genuinely different roof strategies for a market hall in Davangere. Thirty re-rolls of "market hall roof, hot dry climate" give thirty variations on a long-span shed with clerestories. A reframed brief, "three roof strategies: vaulted, folded plate, and a field of small pitched roofs over a grid of columns," gets three in one batch. A second model with the same reframed brief gets a different three. The model had a favourite answer. The student had been asking it the same question thirty times.
sections.takeItToCrit: When a student wants more variety, do they re-roll the same model, or change the model or the brief? Ask them to show the re-roll batch and point at what did not change across it.
sections.howItWorks: Fixation, meaning a return to familiar solutions, was long studied as a human habit. Recent work finds the same pattern in generative models — measured so far in experimental studies of text and image models on idea-generation tasks, not in architecture. Repeated generations cluster around a small number of favoured forms, and the effect persists across prompts that a human would read as different. Work on idea lists from language models names two mechanisms: the model's own fixation around individual concepts, and the fact that it pools its knowledge into one average rather than holding many separate viewpoints. The same research shows that deliberate prompting strategies, such as asking for step-by-step reasoning first or assigning an ordinary persona, can widen the range substantially. That is the EVOLVING part. The narrowness is real and measured in those settings today, how wide one model's range is depends on the prompt, the settings and the model family, and the workarounds are improving. Test it rather than assume it.
sections.tryIt: Re-roll one prompt twenty times and map how narrow the model's range really is: sort the twenty into families and count them. Then explain why switching models or reframing the brief beats re-rolling when you want real variety.

topics.description: Too many options can tire the mind, and a tired mind can stop early. Stopping early and calling it a decision has a name of its own. Two different things happen here. The first is choice overload: under some conditions, a large set of options makes choosing harder, and people settle sooner or not at all.
evidence: When you feel done with an options study, write down the one question you have not yet asked of the chosen option. If you cannot answer it in a sentence, you stopped early. Ask it, then decide again.
For a finished set, show the moment you chose and the evidence that closed it. Then name what you would have needed to see to reopen the choice.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to for a finished set, show the moment you chose and the evidence that closed it. Then name what you would have needed to see to reopen the choice.

card.oneLiner: Too many options can tire the mind, and a tired mind can stop early. Stopping early and calling it a decision has a name of its own.

sections.idea: Two different things happen here. The first is choice overload: under some conditions, a large set of options makes choosing harder, and people settle sooner or not at all. It is real but not universal — it depends on how complex the options are and how sure you were of what you wanted. The second is premature closure: accepting an answer before it has been checked. That is an error of stopping, not of tiredness. A machine that can make fifty more options invites the first. The second is yours, with or without the machine.
sections.whyItMatters: Most decisions taken at two in the morning before a jury are closures. They get defended the next day as if they were decisions.
sections.inTheStudio: Forty massing options generated on Tuesday. By Thursday one is chosen — the one everybody stopped arguing about. Asked why, the team says "it felt resolved". Nobody can name what it resolved.
sections.watchForThis: Relief as the signal that you have decided. Relief is the signal that you have stopped. They are not the same event.
sections.tryIt: When you feel done with an options study, write down the one question you have not yet asked of the chosen option. If you cannot answer it in a sentence, you stopped early. Ask it, then decide again.
sections.proveIt: For a finished set, show the moment you chose and the evidence that closed it. Then name what you would have needed to see to reopen the choice.
sections.howItWorks: Premature closure appears in a 2003 catalogue of cognitive errors in medical diagnosis, alongside anchoring, with metacognition (stepping back to examine your own thinking) named as the main counter. Choice overload has a literature of its own: a 2010 meta-analysis of sixty-three experimental conditions found the average effect close to zero, with overload appearing only under certain conditions — complex options, no clear prior preference, a goal of choosing well rather than quickly. So "too many options" is a risk to check for, not a law. Its sibling on this map, THE FIRST ANSWER ANCHORS, sets where you look; closure decides when you stop. At the scale of many people a related pattern has been measured: a 2024 experiment in *Science Advances* with 293 short-story writers found that access to generated ideas raised the quality of individual work, most for the less creative writers, while making the collection of stories more similar to one another. That is writers, not designers, and it is convergence, not closure; we read it as what many people settling early on similar options can look like. The stopping-rule card is the practical answer: decide the stopping point before the run, so neither tiredness nor relief decides it for you.

topics.name: Prompting is thinking about thinking
topics.description: The struggle to prompt well is usually the struggle to state your own intent. Working with these systems is mentally expensive. You have to know what you actually want, judge what comes back against it, and decide how far to trust the result.
evidence: Take one failed prompt from this week. Before rewriting it, write in plain words what you actually wanted: what decision the output was supposed to help you make. Then rewrite the prompt from that sentence. Compare the two prompts. The second is usually shorter.
Explain why a vague prompt is often a sign of a vague intent, not a weak tool, with one example where stating the intent first changed what you asked for.

grounding.ref: Tankelevitch, Kewenig, Simkute, Scott, Sarkar, Sellen & Rintel, 2024 (CHI; arXiv:2312.10893)

card.oneLiner: The struggle to prompt well is usually the struggle to state your own intent.

sections.idea: Working with these systems is mentally expensive. You have to know what you actually want, judge what comes back against it, and decide how far to trust the result. Much of that is not about the tool. It is about you watching your own thinking, which psychologists call metacognition. Some of it is about the tool — limited control, hidden instructions, randomness — and the bake-off is where the tool takes its share. But a vague prompt is usually a sign of a vague intent. When the output disappoints, ask "what did I actually want?" before "how do I phrase this?"
sections.whyItMatters: Students add words to a failing prompt the way they add lines to a failing drawing. Naming the intent first saves both the words and the cycles.
sections.inTheStudio: A student types "make it more architectural" for the fourth time. The tutor asks what *architectural* means here. Heavier? More ordered? More like a building and less like a film set? The student pauses and says "I want the structure to show." That sentence is the prompt. It was also the intent, and it took four cycles to find because nobody asked for it first.
sections.watchForThis: Mistaking fluency for intent. A long, detailed prompt can still be vague about what the work is for. Length is not the same as clarity. One sentence that states the decision you are trying to make beats a paragraph of adjectives.
sections.tryIt: Take one failed prompt from this week. Before rewriting it, write in plain words what you actually wanted: what decision the output was supposed to help you make. Then rewrite the prompt from that sentence. Compare the two prompts. The second is usually shorter.
sections.proveIt: Explain why a vague prompt is often a sign of a vague intent, not a weak tool, with one example where stating the intent first changed what you asked for.
sections.howItWorks: Metacognition, meaning knowledge of your own thinking and the monitoring of it, was described by Flavell in 1979 and has been studied in learning ever since. A 2024 paper from Microsoft Research applied the idea to generative systems directly. It argues that the difficulty people have with these tools is largely metacognitive (knowing what you want, evaluating outputs, and calibrating confidence), and that interfaces could be designed to support that rather than leave it to the user. The Lab's reading is simpler. The prompt is a brief, and a brief is a statement of intent. Work on the intent and the prompt writes itself.

topics.description: Marking up AI output like a crit (what stays, what goes, what the next cycle must fix) is what turns generated material into authored work. The designer signs with the red pen, not with the prompt. Marking up AI output (what stays, what goes, what the next cycle must fix) is the act that turns generated material into authored work.
