grounding.ref: What Counts as Architectural Thinking After AI

card.oneLiner: Marking up AI output like a crit (what stays, what goes, what the next cycle must fix) is what turns generated material into authored work.

sections.dilemma: The output is good enough. You could accept it and move on, or you could mark it up (what stays, what goes, what must change) and send it round again. The first is faster. Only the second has your name on it.
sections.choices: Accept or reject the output whole. Or red-pen it like a junior's drawing, with ranked corrections that can each be acted on: "lose the second roof-light," "the plinth must be 600 higher," "keep the court, redraw the threshold." Then turn the markup into the next brief.
sections.consequence: Accept it whole and the work is the model's, with you as a client who said yes. Reject it whole and you have thrown away the parts that were right. Red-pen it and the decisions become yours. What was kept is now a choice, what was changed is now a design move, and the next cycle starts from your judgment rather than from zero.
sections.theCase: A student's generated elevation for a community hall in Bagalkot: good massing, a jarring glass entrance, too many openings on the west. The tutor hands over a red pen. Kept: the massing and the roof line, which are now a decision rather than an accident. Changed: the entrance becomes a deep stone porch, and the west openings are reduced to two, high and shaded. Ranked: the west wall first, because it governs comfort, and the porch second. The markup becomes the next brief, nearly word for word. Three cycles later the elevation is unmistakably the student's. The model drew every line of it.
sections.takeItToCrit: Is the student's markup a set of design decisions, or a list of complaints? Ask them to rank their corrections and say which one governs the others. A ranked markup is authorship. An unranked one is a mood.
sections.position: The designer signs with the red pen, not with the prompt. Marking up AI output (what stays, what goes, what the next cycle must fix) is the act that turns generated material into authored work. Prompting proposes. The markup decides. Authorship here means design authorship and creative responsibility — a teaching position, not legal advice; who owns the copyright in generated work is a separate question, taken up on the Ethics & Provenance strand.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Authorship in architecture has never been about who drew the line. It has been about who decided the line stays. Offices have run on this for a century: the principal's red pen over the junior's drawing. The Lab extends the same rule to the machine, because the alternative is a profession of people who say yes to plausible output and call it theirs.
sections.strongestObjection: A markup is only authorship if the person marking up could have made the thing. Red-penning a structure you do not understand, or a light you cannot draw, is editing for show. You are choosing among the model's offers without the knowledge to propose a better one. The pen may feel like authorship and be nothing more than taste with a red pen in its hand.
sections.revisionCondition: The objection is why the red pen sits beside the trace-over card and the forensics card. The markup has to be able to say *what* to draw instead, not only what to reject. We would revise the position if we saw students with strong markups and no drawing ability producing defensible work at jury. We have not. The jury finds them out.
sections.howItWorks: Each markup does two things at once. It records a judgment about this output, and it writes the next brief, because the ranked corrections *are* the revision. That is why the Lab's red pen and iteration log are one practice. The judgment column of the log is the markup, and the next-move column is its top-ranked correction. Ranking is the part students skip and the part that matters, because the top correction is the one that governs the scheme, and naming it is a design decision.
sections.tryIt: Red-pen one output: clear, ranked corrections the maker could act on in the next cycle. Then turn that markup into the next cycle's revised brief, and run it. Compare what came back with what you asked for.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Set the rubric before you generate
topics.description: Decide how you will judge the output before you make it. Otherwise the model's fluency decides for you. Three short lists, written before you press generate. Must do: what the image has to achieve.
evidence: Write a short rubric for the image you want: three lists, a line or two each. Generate. Hold the outputs to it. Then find the case where the rubric throws out an image your eye wanted to keep, and notice how that feels. That is the method working.
Show one case where the rubric you wrote first rejected a good-looking output, and say what the rubric saw that your eye did not.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student what criteria they set before generating. Did they hold to them when the pretty wrong answer showed up?

card.oneLiner: Decide how you will judge the output before you make it. Otherwise the model's fluency decides for you.

sections.whenToUse: Before any generation whose result you will have to choose between, defend, or show to someone else. If you are about to make more than one image, write the rubric first.
sections.method: Three short lists, written before you press generate. *Must do*: what the image has to achieve. "Show the court in afternoon shade," "read as load-bearing brick." *Must hold*: what cannot change. "The plan we drew," "a 3-metre floor-to-floor." *Must avoid*: what you will reject on sight. "Glass curtain walls," "anything the section cannot support." Then generate, and hold each output to the three lists in order. An image that fails *must hold* is out, however good it looks.
sections.watchForThis: Rewriting the rubric after the batch arrives, to let a beautiful wrong image in. That is the model's fluency deciding for you, one step removed. If the rubric was wrong, change it *before* the next run, and write down why.
sections.tryIt: Write a short rubric for the image you want: three lists, a line or two each. Generate. Hold the outputs to it. Then find the case where the rubric throws out an image your eye wanted to keep, and notice how that feels. That is the method working.
sections.proveIt: Show one case where the rubric you wrote first rejected a good-looking output, and say what the rubric saw that your eye did not.
sections.labNote: Criteria before generation is the Lab's method, and it is the twin of the criteria layer in the reasoning brief elsewhere on this map. It is not the only way to keep judgment honest. It is the one that turns "do I like it?" into a check you can defend to someone who does not share your taste.
sections.howItWorks: Without criteria, you judge an image by whatever stands out most, and in generated images what stands out most is polish. The model is good at polish, and polish tells you nothing about fit. A rubric written in advance moves the judgment to properties you chose for reasons, and it fixes the standard before the polish can lower it. The order matters. *Must hold* comes before *must do*, because an image that breaks a fixed constraint is not a candidate, however well it does everything else.

topics.name: Seduction is not quality
topics.description: The test is simple and hard: what decision does this image let me make? Many image models are tuned on human preference, which means they are built, in part, to flatter the eye. So is the performance of using them in public.
evidence: Reject a beautiful output because it answers no design question, and name the question it fails to answer. Then find two images that look equally good, one useful and one empty, and say what separates them. Being able to say that is the skill.

Ask the student what the prettiest image on their wall lets them decide. If the answer is "nothing," the wall is decoration. Ask them to take it down and see whether the scheme is weaker. Usually it is clearer.

grounding.ref: The Lexicon of Algorithmic Virtue — the-lexicon-of-algorithmic-virtue

card.oneLiner: The test is simple and hard: what decision does this image let me make?

sections.dilemma: The most cinematic image on your wall draws every eye, including yours. Someone asks what it is for. You realise you do not know. It is there because it is beautiful. Is that enough?
sections.choices: Keep it, because it makes the wall look better. Or put it to one question: what design decision does this image let me make? The court depth, the roof material, the way the street meets the door, anything at all. If the honest answer is "nothing," the image is decoration, however good it looks.
sections.consequence: Keep images that answer no question and the wall slowly becomes a performance of prompts, output and fluency with the tool, and the performance starts to feel like designing. Apply the question and the wall thins out. What remains is working material: fewer images, each of which moved something. That is a wall a juror can read.
sections.theCase: A student's review board for a weavers' cooperative in Ilkal: twenty-two images, three of them stunning. The tutor asks of each stunning one, "what did this let you decide?" The first: the decision to use a sawtooth roof. A real answer. The second: nothing. It was a "vibe." The third: nothing. It was the one the student's friends liked. Twenty-two images became nine, and the nine made the scheme readable for the first time.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student what the prettiest image on their wall lets them decide. If the answer is "nothing," the wall is decoration. Ask them to take it down and see whether the scheme is weaker. Usually it is clearer.
sections.position: Many image models are tuned on human preference, which means they are built, in part, to flatter the eye. So is the performance of using them in public. Neither is designing. The test of an image is what decision it lets you make. An image that answers no design question is noise, however cinematic.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The Lab has watched practitioners and students drift from design into display: feeds of outputs, prompt reveals, speed treated as a virtue. It is seductive because it looks like mastery. The decision test cuts through it with one question, and it is the question a client or a juror will ask eventually anyway.
sections.strongestObjection: Beauty *is* information. An image that makes the room go quiet has told you something about what people respond to, and a designer who files it as "noise" because it does not yet attach to a decision is throwing away evidence about what people want. Sometimes the decision an image enables is only discovered later. Applied rigidly, the test punishes the image that arrived early.
sections.revisionCondition: The test allows "not yet" as an answer, if the student can say what question they are holding the image against. We would rewrite the card if we found that decision-tested walls produced duller schemes than free walls across a cohort, which would mean the discipline was costing the work its ambition rather than its noise.
sections.howItWorks: Several image systems are fine-tuned using human ratings of which output looks better. Over millions of ratings, that training pushes the model towards whatever people click on: saturated light, dramatic angles, polished surfaces. The output is optimised to please, which is not the same as optimised to be useful. The same pull acts on the person using the tool. The reward for posting a striking output arrives faster than the reward for a resolved plan. The decision test is a deliberate counterweight to both.
sections.tryIt: Reject a beautiful output because it answers no design question, and name the question it fails to answer. Then find two images that look equally good, one useful and one empty, and say what separates them. Being able to say that is the skill.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Draw over the output
topics.description: Sketching over a generated image on trace is judgment made physical. What you redraw is what you rejected. Drawing over a generated image is judgment in its most physical form. When the hand decides what to fix, the designer is taking the frame back from the machine.
evidence: Lay trace over a generated image. Draw, marking every part you would redraw by hand, and leave untouched what you accept. Then explain what drawing over the image showed you that only looking did not. Keep the trace with the image in your log.

Ask to see the trace over the render. The marks are the student's real reading of the image, and more honest than anything they say about it. Ask what they did not redraw, and whether that was a decision.
topics.critPrompt: Ask to see the trace over the render. The marks are the student's real reading of the image, and more honest than anything they say about it. Ask what they did not redraw, and whether that was a decision.

grounding.ref: Pen-based scribble/annotation refinement of generated images with professional designers (arXiv:2602.08830, 2026)

card.oneLiner: Sketching over a generated image on trace is judgment made physical. What you redraw is what you rejected.

sections.dilemma: A render is on the desk. You could look at it and decide what is wrong. Or you could lay trace over it and draw, and find out that looking and drawing are not the same act.
sections.choices: Judge by eye and write notes. Or put trace over the image, redraw every part you would change, leave untouched what you accept, and read the trace afterwards as the record of your judgment.
sections.consequence: Judge by eye and you accept the parts you never tested. The eye is satisfied by likeness, and does not notice that the column has no base or the stair has no landing. Draw over it and the hand finds every place the image blurred or lied, because the pencil has to commit where the render did not. The trace is also a document. What you redrew is what you rejected. What you left alone is what you authored.
sections.theCase: A student is satisfied with a generated courtyard view of a school in Haveri. Trace goes over it. Within ten minutes the pencil has stopped four times. The verandah columns land on nothing. The court's far wall has no thickness. The stair rises to a level that does not exist in the section. The tree's shadow falls towards the sun. None of this was visible by looking, because the image was pleasant. All of it was visible the moment a line had to be drawn through it.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask to see the trace over the render. The marks are the student's real reading of the image, and more honest than anything they say about it. Ask what they did *not* redraw, and whether that was a decision.
sections.position: Drawing over a generated image is judgment in its most physical form. When the hand decides what to fix, the designer is taking the frame back from the machine. What you redraw is what you rejected. What you leave untouched is what you accepted — and accepting is a decision only if you can say why. The trace, with the reasons beside it, is the evidence.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Looking is passive and the eye is generous. Drawing is a commitment. Every line has to land somewhere, which is exactly what a generated image never has to do. The Lab holds this position because it has watched the pencil find, in minutes, faults that a morning of looking missed, and because the trace is the one artefact a jury can read as the student's own.
sections.strongestObjection: Moving a pencil is not proof of authorship. Leaving a generated column untouched does not mean you authored it; you may simply not have noticed it. Drawing over a stair does not mean you understood it; you may have redrawn the model's mistake in your own hand. The trace records where the hand went, not why, and a jury that reads it as "the student's own reading" may be reading a habit of mark-making. And the tools have absorbed the trace: refinement systems now take scribbles directly over the image (a study with thirty designers found visual markup more precise than text for spatial corrections), which makes drawing over a prompting method like any other. The physical paper version may be sentiment.
sections.revisionCondition: The value we claim is in the *deciding*, and the objection is right that the trace does not show the decision on its own. That is why the trace goes into the log with a line beside each mark saying what was wrong and what replaces it; a trace without the reasons is a drawing, not a judgment. If a tablet scribble fed straight to the model still forces the hand to commit and the reason to be written, the position survives the change of medium. We would revise it if students annotating directly in the tool produced readings as critical as those on trace, or if the research found their design thinking improving with in-tool sketching rather than what one recent study observed: students preferring text even when sketching served them better.
sections.howItWorks: A render satisfies the eye by likeness. A drawing has to answer different questions. Where does this edge go? What holds this up? What is behind that? Those are the questions a generated image most often leaves unanswered, and the pencil is the instrument that asks them. Two current lines of research bear on this. One, with thirty designers refining images, shows better spatial control from marking up images than from describing changes in text. Another, in an ideation study with students, finds that sketch-based input helps design thinking while students still reach for text. Both are small studies in design-tool settings rather than architecture studios, and both suggest the hand is doing work the eye and the keyboard are not.
sections.tryIt: Lay trace over a generated image. Draw, marking every part you would redraw by hand, and leave untouched what you accept. Then explain what drawing over the image showed you that only looking did not. Keep the trace with the image in your log.

topics.name: Make the machine argue back
topics.description: By default a model tries to please you. Tell it to attack your assumptions instead, and use it as a foil while you are still thinking. Set the terms before you ask. Tell the model its role: you are my foil; I will describe a design move; your job is to find the flaws in the material logic, the structural logic and the brief, and to push back on my assumptions.
evidence: Take one design decision you are confident about. Prompt a model to find the flaws in your material logic, with the role set as above. Write down the three strongest objections and act on at least one. Then note how different the exchange felt from asking "what do you think?"
Show one design move that changed because the model, told to push back, found a flaw you had not seen. Then explain why an agreeable answer would have been less useful than that disagreement.
topics.critPrompt: Does the student instruct the model to push back, or settle for the answer that flatters them?

grounding.ref: The Seduction of the Machine — the-seduction-of-the-machine-why
Anthropic, “AI Fluency Index”, Feb 2026 — users set the terms of the interaction in only ~30% of conversations, so most never tell the model how to behave
Prompt Personalities: How to Collaborate With ChatGPT and Claude

card.oneLiner: By default a model tries to please you. Tell it to attack your assumptions instead, and use it as a foil while you are still thinking.

sections.whenToUse: Whenever you are about to ask a model what it thinks of your idea. Especially when you are fond of the idea, and most especially when the model's first answer made you feel good.
sections.method: Set the terms before you ask. Tell the model its role: *you are my foil; I will describe a design move; your job is to find the flaws in the material logic, the structural logic and the brief, and to push back on my assumptions. Do not agree with me.* Then present the idea. Read the objections as a sparring partner's punches. Some will be wild, some will land. Act on the ones that land. Then ask it to argue the other side, and see which case is stronger.
sections.watchForThis: Ease. If the exchange feels effortless and the model keeps agreeing, either you have not set the terms or the model has slipped back into pleasing you. Many chat models lean that way. Reset the role. Friction is the sign it is working.
sections.tryIt: Take one design decision you are confident about. Prompt a model to find the flaws in your material logic, with the role set as above. Write down the three strongest objections and act on at least one. Then note how different the exchange felt from asking "what do you think?"
sections.proveIt: Show one design move that changed because the model, told to push back, found a flaw you had not seen. Then explain why an agreeable answer would have been less useful than that disagreement.
sections.labNote: The sparring partner is the second step of the Lab's friction protocol, dictate the terms of engagement, and it is a method, not a law. Other methods exist. This is the one that reliably turns a flattering assistant into a useful opponent, and the one most users never try. Anthropic's 2026 analysis found users setting the terms of the interaction in only around a third of conversations.
sections.howItWorks: Many chat models are tuned on human approval, and people tend to approve of agreement. So the default lean of such a model is towards your view, phrased well, which is the least useful thing it can give you when you are trying to think. Setting a role changes what "approval" looks like inside the conversation. You have told it that pushing back is the job. One limit to hold on to. Telling the model to argue is a written instruction: it asks, it does not enforce. The objections come from the same training as the agreement did, so the model can perform criticism — plausible reasons, no independent evidence — as easily as it performed praise. Treat the punches as questions for your own checking. Validation still comes from something that could have said no on its own account: a calculation, a site, a tutor (AGREEMENT ISN'T VALIDATION, on this strand). The card is reviewed every edition because model makers are actively working on this tendency, and the strength of the default lean changes with each release.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Where did this image come from?
topics.description: You do not prove an image is real by staring harder at the pixels. Ask where it came from, who made it, and what record it carries. A mixed set of building images lands in a precedent study: some photographs, some renders from practices, some generated. All of them are "references" now.
evidence: Take a mixed set of nine building images. For each, write three lines: where it came from, who made it, what record it carries — and mark any line you could not fill. Then sort the set by how much you could establish, not by how real it looks. Keep the one that fooled you in your failure catalogue, with the question that would have caught it.

Hand the student a mixed set. Can they say where each image came from, and what they could and could not establish about it? "I think it is generated" is a guess. "It appears nowhere earlier than this feed and carries no record" is a finding.
topics.critPrompt: Hand the student a mixed set. Can they say where each image came from, and what they could and could not establish about it? "I think it is generated" is a guess. "It appears nowhere earlier than this feed and carries no record" is a finding.

grounding.ref: IFLA, How to Spot Fake News
Diffusion: How AI Paints from Noise

card.oneLiner: You do not prove an image is real by staring harder at the pixels. Ask where it came from, who made it, and what record it carries.

sections.dilemma: A mixed set of building images lands in a precedent study: some photographs, some renders from practices, some generated. All of them are "references" now. You could sort them by eye, looking for the tells — melted text, a shadow going the wrong way. Or you could ask a different question of each one: where did this come from?
sections.choices: Trust your eye. Or trace each image. Who posted it, and where? Is there an earlier, larger copy somewhere else? Does a second, unconnected source show the same building? Does the file carry a record of how it was made — a content credential, a camera's data, a named photographer? Three questions, in order: where did it come from, who made it, what credentials does it carry. Only then decide what kind of thing it is.
sections.consequence: Sort by eye and you are betting on a skill that is failing. Studies of how well people tell generated images from real ones now put the score close to chance, and each new model removes the tells the last one left. Sooner or later a building that never existed enters your precedent study with the authority of one that does. Trace instead and the answer no longer depends on your eye. A photograph with a named photographer, a date and a place can be checked. An image that appears nowhere earlier than a design feed, with no maker and no record, is a likeness until proved otherwise — however good it looks.
sections.theCase: A precedent board on laterite houses of the Konkan coast: nine images. The tutor does not ask the class to spot the fakes. She asks for the source of each. Six trace to named photographers, a survey book and a practice's own site. One traces to a practice's portfolio page, where it is labelled as a render. Two trace no further than a design feed — no maker, no place, no earlier copy, no credential. One of those two had been cited by three students as "a house in Sindhudurg." Nobody had looked for the house. It was the best-looking image on the board.
sections.takeItToCrit: Hand the student a mixed set. Can they say where each image came from, and what they could and could not establish about it? "I think it is generated" is a guess. "It appears nowhere earlier than this feed and carries no record" is a finding.
sections.howItWorks: Three layers of evidence, from weakest to strongest. The pixels: the tells (melting text, shadows that disagree, brick coursing that changes module) still exist, but they shrink with every model release, and a 2024 meta-analysis of fifty-six studies put human detection of deepfakes close to chance, so the pixels are a hint at best. The trail: a reverse image search finds earlier and larger copies; a second, independent source confirms the building exists; a named maker can be asked. The record: some tools now attach a signed content credential to a file at the moment it is made, recording the tool, the maker and the edits — the open standard is C2PA. The card MARKED AT BIRTH, on the Ethics & Provenance strand, explains what these marks prove and what a missing mark does not. Two things to hold apart. Provenance is not truth: a genuine photograph can still mislead, and a generated image can be honestly labelled. And a missing record proves nothing: most real photographs carry no credential either. The card is EVOLVING because the tells and the marks both change by the month. The three questions do not.
sections.tryIt: Take a mixed set of nine building images. For each, write three lines: where it came from, who made it, what record it carries — and mark any line you could not fill. Then sort the set by how much you could establish, not by how real it looks. Keep the one that fooled you in your failure catalogue, with the question that would have caught it.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Knowing when to stop
topics.description: Iteration needs a stopping rule, or it turns back into gambling. Iteration without a stopping rule is gambling with better manners. Stop when changing the brief no longer changes the output, or when the output answers the question you actually asked.
evidence: Set the stopping point before an iteration run: the question to answer, or the convergence you will accept. Stop when you reach it, even if you are curious. Then, for a finished set, explain why the last useful cycle was the last one.
Ask the student why they stopped where they did. Could they have stopped three cycles earlier? Ask them to name the cycle where the question was answered, and what the cycles after it were for.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student why they stopped where they did. Could they have stopped three cycles earlier? Ask them to name the cycle where the question was answered, and what the cycles after it were for.

card.oneLiner: Iteration needs a stopping rule, or it turns back into gambling.

sections.dilemma: Cycle six gave you the image that answers the brief. Cycle seven might give you a slightly better one. So might eight. It is cheap to find out. When do you stop?
sections.choices: Stop when you run out of time or patience. Or set the stopping rule before you begin and keep to it: stop when changing the brief no longer changes the output, or stop when the output answers the question you actually asked. Either condition ends the run.
sections.consequence: Without a rule, iteration quietly turns back into the lottery it was meant to replace. You are no longer testing a brief. You are hoping for a better draw. With a rule, the run ends on a decision rather than on exhaustion, and the last cycle is the last *useful* cycle, which is something you can say out loud to a juror.
sections.theCase: A student is iterating a façade study for a housing block in Hubballi. Cycle five answered the question: how deep must the balcony be to shade the west wall at 4 p.m. in May? Cycles six to fourteen were "just seeing." By cycle fourteen the balcony depth had drifted back to a number that no longer shaded anything, because each cycle was chasing the previous image rather than the question. The tutor asked where the question had been answered. Cycle five. Nine cycles had bought images and lost a decision.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student why they stopped where they did. Could they have stopped three cycles earlier? Ask them to name the cycle where the question was answered, and what the cycles after it were for.
sections.position: Iteration without a stopping rule is gambling with better manners. Stop when changing the brief no longer changes the output, or when the output answers the question you actually asked. Going past that point buys images, not decisions.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Every cycle costs attention, and attention is the scarce resource in a studio, not images. The Lab's iteration log exists to make decisions visible. A run that continues past its last decision fills the log with noise and teaches the student that more is the same as better. It is not, and the jury can tell.
sections.strongestObjection: Discovery does not keep to rules. Some of the best moves in a project arrive in the cycle after the one that "answered the question," because the answer revealed a better question. A stopping rule set in advance can close the run at exactly the moment it was about to become interesting. Designers who stop when told to may be disciplined and dull.
sections.revisionCondition: The rule allows a new run with a new question. It forbids drifting on the old one. We would revise the card if logs showed that the cycles after the stopping point were reliably where the good ideas came from, which would mean drift is where design happens. In the Lab's workshops so far, drift is where balconies stop shading.
sections.howItWorks: Two signals tell you a run is done. The first is convergence: you change the brief and the output barely moves, which means the brief has stopped carrying new information and you are now sampling noise. The second is that the question is answered: the image now lets you make the decision you started the run to make. Either signal is enough. Both are easier to see if you wrote the question down before cycle one, which is why the stopping rule and the rubric live on the same page of the log.
sections.tryIt: Set the stopping point before an iteration run: the question to answer, or the convergence you will accept. Stop when you reach it, even if you are curious. Then, for a finished set, explain why the last useful cycle was the last one.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Styles known unevenly
topics.description: The model's grip on architectural history is uneven: fluent where the photographs were many, inventive where they were few. You ask for "a Gothic cathedral interior" and the result may pass a historian's glance. You ask for "a Hoysala temple mandapa" and you may get the right mood with the details wrong: the pillar count, the plinth, the way the ceiling is built.
evidence: Prompt a canonical style and a lesser-known regional one, and compare each result against a measured drawing or a good photograph. Then prompt the regional one three ways — in English ("Hoysala temple mandapa"), in Romanised Kannada ("Hoysala devalayada mantapa") and in Kannada script ("ಹೊಯ್ಸಳ ದೇವಾಲಯದ ಮಂಟಪ") — and compare the three. A name the model knows in one script and not another tells you which captions it learnt from. Then find one case where the model got the look of a style and missed the logic behind it: the structural reason, the climatic reason, the ritual reason.

Can the student tell where the model's style knowledge is solid and where it is bluffing, and prove it with a real building beside the output? Ask them which Indian traditions they would never use it for, and why.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student tell where the model's style knowledge is solid and where it is bluffing, and prove it with a real building beside the output? Ask them which Indian traditions they would never use it for, and why.

grounding.ref: Ploennigs & Berger, 2023 — Generative AI and the History of Architecture (arXiv:2312.15106)

card.oneLiner: The model's grip on architectural history is uneven: fluent where the photographs were many, inventive where they were few.

sections.dilemma: You ask for "a Gothic cathedral interior" and the result may pass a historian's glance. You ask for "a Hoysala temple mandapa" and you may get the right mood with the details wrong: the pillar count, the plinth, the way the ceiling is built. Same tool, same confidence. How much of its history do you trust? The only way to know is to test it.
sections.choices: Trust the model's style knowledge evenly, because it sounds even. Or test it. Prompt a heavily photographed style and a lightly photographed one, compare each against a real building, and map where the knowledge is solid and where it is bluffing.
sections.consequence: Trust it evenly and the under-photographed traditions, which include many of India's regional ones, get reinvented by the machine and passed off as reference. Students "learn" a regional style from a likeness of it. Test it and you know where the tool is a quick way into a tradition and where it is a confident stranger. Both are useful, as long as you know which one you are talking to.
sections.theCase: A history assignment: draw a comparative plate of a Chalukyan temple and a Palladian villa. A student uses an image model for both as a starting reference. The Palladian plate is close enough to correct the proportions against. The Chalukyan one has a stepped shikhara from the wrong region and a pillared hall with the wrong bay rhythm. Correcting it took the student longer than drawing from the survey book would have. The tutor's question was why the two results differed. The answer is the number of photographs.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student tell where the model's style knowledge is solid and where it is bluffing, and prove it with a real building beside the output? Ask them which Indian traditions they would never use it for, and why.
sections.howItWorks: How well a model knows a style depends on how many labelled images of it the model saw. Canonical European styles are photographed, captioned and written about in vast quantity. Many Indian regional traditions are not, or are captioned vaguely. Where the examples are thin the model does what it always does, which is produce the most likely image, and the most likely image of a rare style is a blend of nearby familiar ones. A 2023 study tested text and image models on architectural styles and asked where they distinguish correctly and where they fabricate. It also looked at how practitioners actually prompt these tools. What comes back is resemblance, not reasoning about why a style is the way it is. The Lab has not yet published a controlled run of this comparison on Indian traditions; the TRY IT below is that test, at your own desk. EVOLVING: better-captioned datasets and regional fine-tuning could change the map, and the card is reviewed as they appear.
sections.tryIt: Prompt a canonical style and a lesser-known regional one, and compare each result against a measured drawing or a good photograph. Then prompt the regional one three ways — in English ("Hoysala temple mandapa"), in Romanised Kannada ("Hoysala devalayada mantapa") and in Kannada script ("ಹೊಯ್ಸಳ ದೇವಾಲಯದ ಮಂಟಪ") — and compare the three. A name the model knows in one script and not another tells you which captions it learnt from. Then find one case where the model got the *look* of a style and missed the *logic* behind it: the structural reason, the climatic reason, the ritual reason.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Variation is not difference
topics.description: Two outputs can look different and still be the same idea in new clothes. Re-rolling gives you variation: the model's own range around one reading of your brief. Changing the brief is what gives you difference.
evidence: Sort a set into "only varies" and "truly differs," and defend where you drew the line. Then find two outputs that look different but carry the same design decision, and two that look alike but differ in intent. The second pair is harder to find, and more useful.
Ask the student which outputs are real alternatives and which are the same image in new clothes. Then ask them to draw the section of two "different" ones. The two sections will settle it.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student which outputs are real alternatives and which are the same image in new clothes. Then ask them to draw the section of two "different" ones. The two sections will settle it.

grounding.ref: Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI

card.oneLiner: Two outputs can look different and still be the same idea in new clothes.

sections.dilemma: You need alternatives for a jury: real ones, schemes that would take the project somewhere else. The tool gives you eight images that all look different: warmer, cooler, a taller roof, a wider court. Are these alternatives, or one idea dressed eight ways?
sections.choices: Count surface differences and call them options. Or test each pair with one question: if I chose this one instead of that one, would the project go somewhere else? A different section, a different structure, a different way of living in it? If not, it is variation. If yes, it is difference.
sections.consequence: Present variation as options and a sharp juror sees one scheme with a colour study attached. Worse, you believe you explored when you only went round in a circle. Find the real differences and you may have only two. But two genuine forks are worth more than eight versions of one idea, and now you know the next difference has to come from the brief, not from the re-roll button.
sections.theCase: A student brings five "options" for a hostel block in Belagavi. All five have the same double-loaded corridor. Only the skin changes. The tutor draws the section of each on the board: five identical sections. The student had been re-rolling. The sixth option, made after the brief was changed to "single-loaded, open to the west wind," was the first real alternative, and it took one cycle.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student which outputs are real alternatives and which are the same image in new clothes. Then ask them to draw the section of two "different" ones. The two sections will settle it.
sections.position: Re-rolling gives you variation: the model's own range around one reading of your brief. Changing the brief is what gives you difference. A set of variations is not a set of alternatives, and a jury should never be shown one as the other.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A generated image is a sample from the model's reading of your words. Sampling again gives you another point in the same neighbourhood. To leave the neighbourhood you have to change the words. That is how these systems work, and it is why the Lab teaches brief revision rather than seed-scrolling.
sections.strongestObjection: Variation is sometimes exactly what a project needs. Late in a scheme, when the parti is fixed and the question is material, proportion or light, the "same idea in new clothes" is the right output. Calling it lesser is a bias towards early-stage thinking. Difference is not always the more valuable thing.
sections.revisionCondition: This card already accepts the late-stage case. We would rewrite it if studio evidence showed students reliably telling the two apart without being taught, which would mean the distinction is obvious in practice and the card is solving a problem nobody has. So far the logs say otherwise.
sections.howItWorks: Each generation is a draw from a distribution shaped by your prompt and the model's training. Draws cluster. Eight draws from one prompt give you eight points in one cluster: different in detail, alike in what they assume. An experimental study of text and image models on design tasks found the same pattern: repeated sampling tends to narrow rather than widen. How far it narrows depends on the prompt, the settings and the model, so read it as a tendency to test, not a law. Changing the prompt moves the cluster. Changing the model moves it in a different way again.
sections.tryIt: Sort a set into "only varies" and "truly differs," and defend where you drew the line. Then find two outputs that look different but carry the same design decision, and two that look alike but differ in intent. The second pair is harder to find, and more useful.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Visual forensics
topics.description: Read an AI image for evidence: structure that cannot stand, light that comes from nowhere, materials that behave wrongly, joints that resolve nothing. Every generated image is a witness to be cross-examined, not a reference to be trusted. Visual forensics is the first stage of the Lab's working protocol, diagnosis before direction, and it exists to stop fantasy getting into the project.
evidence: Mark up a render. Point to every part of the structure and lighting that could not be real, with a reason for each. Then take three good-looking images and rank them by how much of each one would survive an engineer's first look.
Hand the student a beautiful image. Time how long it takes them to find the load path that is not there. Under a minute means they have the habit. Over five minutes means they were enjoying it.
topics.critPrompt: Hand the student a beautiful image. Time how long it takes them to find the load path that is not there. Under a minute means they have the habit. Over five minutes means they were enjoying it.

card.oneLiner: Read an AI image for evidence: structure that cannot stand, light that comes from nowhere, materials that behave wrongly, joints that resolve nothing.

sections.dilemma: An image is in front of you that you want to be true. A long span, a thin slab, a wall of glass meeting a stone roof with no visible frame. You can enjoy it, or you can cross-examine it. You can do both in the same minute. Only one of them is your job.
sections.choices: Ask "do we like this?" Or ask the Lab's forensic question, *what would fail first if we tried to build this?*, and go looking. Where is the load path? Where is the light coming from, and do the shadows agree? Is this material behaving the way that material really behaves? Does this junction resolve, or does the image go blurry exactly where the detail should be?
sections.consequence: Skip the forensics and the impossible enters the project as an expectation: the client's, the student's, sometimes the tutor's. It is discovered weeks later, at coordination or costing, by someone who never made the promise. Run the forensics and the image stays in its place: a useful witness, cross-examined, never allowed to sign anything.
sections.theCase: An image of a library in Mysuru: a stone vault, a roof-light running its full length, a reading balcony cantilevered from one side. The student goes looking. The vault has a roof-light where its compression ring should be. The balcony has no beam, no bracket, no thickening. Only the rendering is holding it up. The shadows say late afternoon. The roof-light says noon. Three findings in four minutes. The image is still beautiful. It is also now filed where it belongs.
sections.takeItToCrit: Hand the student a beautiful image. Time how long it takes them to find the load path that is not there. Under a minute means they have the habit. Over five minutes means they were enjoying it.
sections.position: Every generated image is a witness to be cross-examined, not a reference to be trusted. Visual forensics is the first stage of the Lab's working protocol, diagnosis before direction, and it exists to stop fantasy getting into the project.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Images now reach the studio before the brief does. Clients arrive with renders forwarded on WhatsApp. Those images set expectations, and a studio that cannot take them apart on sight will spend weeks trying to build something that should never have entered the work. The habit is a professional defence, not an academic nicety.
sections.strongestObjection: Running forensics on every image turns the studio into a checking department and trains students to look for failure before they look for possibility. The best early-stage images are *supposed* to be structurally impossible. That is what a dream is for. A forensic reflex applied too early can cost the project the idea it was about to have.
sections.revisionCondition: The Lab already separates dreaming from grounding, and forensics belongs at the boundary between them, not inside the dream. We would revise the card if we saw forensics-trained students producing timid early work (fewer risks, safer images) across a whole cohort. We watch the log for exactly that.
sections.howItWorks: Image models learn surfaces, not statics. They know what a cantilever looks like from a thousand photographs. They do not know why any of those cantilevers stood up. So the model produces the look of structure with no structure underneath, and it produces light by resemblance: a shadow where shadows usually go, not where this particular sun would put it. Those two facts predict the two commonest findings, missing load paths and light that contradicts itself. Junctions blur for a related reason. The photographs the model learnt from rarely show the detail, so the model goes vague where it has no pattern to draw from.
sections.tryIt: Mark up a render. Point to every part of the structure and lighting that could not be real, with a reason for each. Then take three good-looking images and rank them by how much of each one would survive an engineer's first look.

topics.subject: Judgment
topics.name: Friction is a feature
topics.description: Deliberate speed bumps (a challenge, a forced pause, a question before you accept) measurably bring critical thinking back into AI-assisted work. Every tool you use is being redesigned to remove friction: fewer clicks, faster output, less asking. Your studio is the opposite.
evidence: Add one deliberate friction step to an AI workflow (a written question before acceptance is the cheapest) and record what it caught over two weeks. Then name a place in your process where removing friction quietly removed a judgment.
Can the student point to the friction in their process that forces a decision, instead of waving the work through? Ask what it costs them, and whether they would keep it if nobody was checking.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student point to the friction in their process that forces a decision, instead of waving the work through? Ask what it costs them, and whether they would keep it if nobody was checking.

grounding.ref: "It makes you think": Provocations Help Restore Critical Thinking to AI-Assisted Knowledge Work (arXiv:2501.17247, 2025)

card.oneLiner: Deliberate speed bumps (a challenge, a forced pause, a question before you accept) measurably bring critical thinking back into AI-assisted work.

sections.dilemma: Every tool you use is being redesigned to remove friction: fewer clicks, faster output, less asking. Your studio is the opposite. A crit is friction by design. Which instinct do you carry into your own workflow: remove every speed bump, or keep some on purpose? And who decides which ones?
sections.choices: Optimise for smoothness and accept whatever arrives fastest. Or build friction in deliberately: a prompt that challenges the model's suggestion, a forced pause before accepting, a question you must answer in writing before the output goes anywhere. Be honest that each one costs time, and that you are choosing where to spend it.
sections.consequence: Strip all the friction out and the thinking goes with it. Not because you are lazy, but because the interface never gave judgment a place to happen. Keep friction in and you pay in speed, every time, and you get a workflow where decisions are made by someone rather than waved through. The trade-off is real. The only question is where you put it.
sections.theCase: A final-year student builds one speed bump into their workflow. Before any generated image enters the project folder, they write two lines: what this image lets me decide, and what in it I have not checked. Over a term the rule catches a floor plan that could not be walked through, a material that does not exist, and an image they had chosen because their friends liked it. It also costs them perhaps an hour a week. At jury, the question of which was worth more answers itself.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student point to the friction in their process that forces a decision, instead of waving the work through? Ask what it costs them, and whether they would keep it if nobody was checking.
sections.howItWorks: Two recent studies put evidence behind the idea. In one, brief "provocations" (short written challenges offering critiques and alternatives beside an AI suggestion) were found to prompt critical and metacognitive thinking in knowledge work. The effect depended on how urgent the task was, how expert the user was, and whether they felt responsible for the result. In another, prompts asking university students to reflect and consider other viewpoints during AI-assisted search broadened their exploration and improved how they evaluated the answers. Both are small studies in non-design settings, with twenty-four and forty participants, which is why the card is EVOLVING. The direction is clear. The size of the effect, and whether it carries over to studios, are not yet. The studio crit predates all of it, and is the same device.
sections.tryIt: Add one deliberate friction step to an AI workflow (a written question before acceptance is the cheapest) and record what it caught over two weeks. Then name a place in your process where removing friction quietly removed a judgment.

Presenting AI-assisted work to a jury means saying what is still a guess and what is settled, what was generated and what was drawn. You defend the chain of judgment, not the image.
evidence: Present an AI-assisted scheme to a classmate acting as juror. Under questioning, say what each image is (settled, guess, generated, drawn) and get it right. Then answer "is this real?" with the decision chain, not with a defence of the render.
Under jury pressure, does the student defend the image, or the judgment that made it? Ask "is this real?" and listen for whether the answer is a defence, a disowning, or an account.

card.oneLiner: You defend the chain of judgment, not the image. The pin-up is not the proof. The decisions behind it are.

sections.dilemma: A juror points at your best image and asks: "Is this real?" You have three possible answers. Defend the image: it is close, it is what I intended. Disown it: it is just AI, the real work is in the drawings. Or answer the question that was actually asked: say what this image is, what in it is settled and what is still a guess, what was generated and what was drawn, and what decision it carried. The first two are easier. Only the third survives the follow-up question.
sections.choices: Defend the render. Disown the render. Or defend the chain of judgment that made it, and be ready for the juror to find the one place in the chain where you cannot account for a decision, because that is what a good jury is for.
sections.consequence: Defend the image and the jury will find the load path that is not there, and the scheme will fall with it. Disown it and you have told the room that the most persuasive thing on your wall is not yours, and the room will believe you. Defend the chain and the image becomes what it always was, evidence of a decision, and the jury moves on to arguing about the decision, which is the argument you wanted.
sections.theCase: A student presents a housing scheme with six generated views. "Is this real?" The answer, practised: "This view is a mood study from cycle three. The court proportion in it is settled and matches the section. The balcony depth is not settled. I have since changed it, and the drawing on the left shows the current depth. The material in the image is wrong. The model gave me exposed concrete and the scheme is brick. I kept it because the light was what I wanted to test." The juror's next question is about the balcony depth. The jury has begun.
sections.takeItToCrit: Under jury pressure, does the student defend the image, or the judgment that made it? Ask "is this real?" and listen for whether the answer is a defence, a disowning, or an account.
sections.position: Presenting AI-assisted work to a jury means saying what is still a guess and what is settled, what was generated and what was drawn. You defend the chain of judgment, not the image. The pin-up is not the proof. The decisions behind it are. The student who can give that account has nothing to hide and nothing to apologise for.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A jury exists to test decisions. When the image is defended, the test is wasted on a likeness. When the image is disowned, the student has given up authorship of their most persuasive material. The account (settled, guessed, generated, drawn) is the only answer that lets the jury do its job, and it is the same account a client and a building authority will eventually require.
sections.strongestObjection: A narrated chain of judgment is evidence about a process. It is not the process. A fluent student can build an impeccable account after the fact — settled, guess, generated, drawn — around decisions that were never made in that order, or never made at all; a weaker speaker can have judged well and explain it badly. A jury that rewards the account rewards the narration, and the student who learns this card best may be the one who learns to rationalise best. Prejudice against generated images is the smaller problem, though it is real and it costs marks in rooms where it should not. The larger one is that the defence this card teaches can be manufactured.
sections.revisionCondition: The objection is why the account must rest on artefacts made at the time — the iteration log, the versioned briefs, the trace — and not on memory. A narrated chain with no contemporaneous record is a story, and a jury should treat it as one. We would revise the card if logged and unlogged accounts scored alike at juries over several cohorts, which would mean the record was not doing the work we claim. And we would revise the advice, not the position, if full accounts kept scoring below concealment: then the Lab would have to say so, and to work on the juries rather than on the students. It is reviewed every edition against what juries actually do.
sections.howItWorks: The account has four parts, and they can be rehearsed. *Settled*: what in this image matches a drawing or a decision you have made. *Guess*: what in it you have not yet resolved, and what you are doing about it. *Generated*: which elements the model supplied and which you directed. *Drawn*: what exists in your own hand, and where. A student who can give those four for every image on the wall has done the work this strand describes (forensics, the six layers, the log), and the jury becomes a conversation about the scheme. The wider argument, that the studio must now evaluate reasoning rather than output, is made in the Lab's essay on architectural thinking after AI.
sections.tryIt: Present an AI-assisted scheme to a classmate acting as juror. Under questioning, say what each image is (settled, guess, generated, drawn) and get it right. Then answer "is this real?" with the decision chain, not with a defence of the render.

card.oneLiner: The sharpest judgment is knowing when the machine should stay out. Refusal is a design move.

sections.position: The sharpest judgment in this strand is knowing when the machine should stay out. Sometimes a hand sketch, a site visit, or a conversation with the person who will live there is the right tool, and generation is the wrong one. Not because it would fail, but because it would succeed at the wrong thing: filling the moment with plausible output when the moment needed attention. Refusal is a design move. A confident "no", with a reason behind it, at the right moment, and defensible afterwards, is where taste shows most.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: A tool that is always available is always a temptation, and the cost of generating is now low enough that the only thing stopping you is judgment. The Lab holds that a designer's workflow should contain places where the machine is excluded on purpose (the first hour with a brief, the site, the client's kitchen), and that the student should be able to say where those places are and why. A workflow with no "no" in it has been designed by the tool.
sections.strongestObjection: Refusal can be habit dressed up as judgment. "I keep the machine out of early concept" is often a preference formed before the tools were any good, and the profession has a long record of refusing new instruments on principle and then adopting them late, in a hurry. Worse, a taught "no" becomes a ritual. Students exclude the tool at the stage they were told to, without ever testing whether that stage is where it actually fails them. Adoption data across the profession suggests the people refusing are not, on the whole, the people judging.
sections.revisionCondition: The position requires the "no" to be *reasoned*. The student must be able to say what the machine would have cost at that stage, and must have tested it at least once. We would revise the card if we found that students who excluded generation at a stage consistently produced weaker work at that stage than students who used it critically, which would mean the "no" was costing the work rather than protecting it. That is a comparison workshops can run, and the Lab runs it.
sections.tryIt: Name a stage of a real project where you kept the machine out on purpose, and defend that call. What would it have cost, and how do you know? Then take two tasks from the same project and separate the one where generation adds value from the one where it only adds noise.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student where in their project they refused to generate. Was that a reasoned call, or habit? Ask whether they tested the alternative. A reasoned "no" has a comparison behind it.
sections.howItWorks: Two kinds of evidence sit behind the position, and they point in slightly different directions, which is why this is a held position and not a rule. On one side, a study of AI assistance in vocational classrooms found lower-performing students offloading thinking rather than deepening it, and a 2025 retrospective, observational study in one clinical setting reported endoscopists' unassisted detection rates dropping after a period of AI-assisted work. That is early evidence of deskilling, in one field; the wider literature on offloading is mixed, and none of it is from architecture. On the other side, surveys of practice show adoption rising steadily, and the history of tools in this profession rewards early critical engagement over refusal. The card sits on the line between them. Exclude on purpose, test the exclusion, and keep the skill the machine would otherwise quietly take.

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: Every answer from an AI tool is made in a real building that burns real electricity — and often, not always, uses real water too.

sections.idea: An AI tool feels like it lives in your phone. It does not. Your question usually travels to a large building full of computers, called a data centre. Those computers need electricity to think. Many of them also use water to stay cool — often, not always; it depends on the building and the climate. So every answer has a small cost somewhere in the world. The same tools can also do real good — forecasting a cyclone, or cutting waste in a factory. So you weigh the help against the cost.
sections.whyItMatters: Anything that looks free is easy to waste. Once you know the cost is real, you start using the tool more carefully.
sections.inTheStudio: A student asks for fifty pictures of a house and keeps one. Forty-nine pictures were made, cooled, and thrown away. Nobody saw the bill, but there was one.
sections.watchForThis: Thinking "the cloud" is a cloud. It is a building with a roof, a car park, a power line, and often a water pipe.
sections.tryIt: Find out where the nearest large data centre to your city is. Look at it on a map. Notice what sits next to it — a power station, a river, a highway.
sections.proveIt: Explain to a friend where an AI answer is actually made. Name the one thing that building always uses up, and the one thing it often uses up.
sections.howItWorks: Data centres use electricity to run thousands of computer chips, and those chips get hot. Keeping them cool takes fans, chilled water, or both. Some data centres are cooled by air alone and use almost no water on site; others use a great deal; and water also goes into making the electricity at the power station. That is why this card says often, not always. A small model running on your own computer sends nothing anywhere — it still uses electricity. How much energy and water AI uses in total is still being measured, and the estimates change every year. So this card teaches that there is a cost, not how big it is. Later cards on this map put rough scales on it, and one of them treats the data centre as a building an architect may be asked to design.

topics.attribution: adapted from Marble Skill Taxonomy, CC BY-SA 4.0

card.oneLiner: If the examples lean one way, the machine usually leans that way too — and a person is still responsible.

sections.idea: A machine learns from examples. If the examples lean one way, the machine usually leans that way too. A toy case: show it a thousand photos of sloping roofs and ten of flat roofs, and it will think houses usually have sloping roofs. That lean is called bias. The machine did not choose it. The examples carried it in — and the goal it was trained toward, and later corrections, can add a lean or remove one. A machine cannot answer for any of this. A person has to: whoever picked the examples, and whoever uses the answer.
sections.whyItMatters: When a result looks unfair, do not stop at "why is the machine unfair?" Ask what it learned from, and who is responsible now.
sections.inTheStudio: Ask a drawing tool for "a house" and you may get a house from a country you have never visited. It is not ignoring you. It is showing you where most of its examples came from.
sections.watchForThis: Saying "the computer decided, so it must be fair." Biased examples can make a machine biased, and even good examples do not guarantee a fair result — and examples are gathered by people.
sections.tryIt: Ask an image tool for "a school" five times. Count how many look like your school. Then write one line on where the examples probably came from.
sections.proveIt: Take one lopsided result you have seen and trace it back: which examples would make a machine answer that way? Then name who should fix it.
sections.howItWorks: Bias in the examples is one of the most common reasons a machine treats two groups differently — not the only one. What the machine was told to aim for, how it was corrected after training, and how its answers are used all matter too. It shows up in faces it recognises badly, accents it mishears, and buildings it cannot picture. Fixing it means changing the examples, changing the goal, or correcting the answer, and all of those are jobs for people. The lean can even start at the desk where people tag the examples. An Indian film, *Humans in the Loop*, follows a woman in Jharkhand whose knowledge of the forest does not fit the labels the machine allows. A later card on this map, *The tilted mirror*, shows what the lean does to pictures of Indian streets and houses.

card.oneLiner: Many real ethical choices have strong points on more than one side — thinking them through beats grabbing a rule.

sections.idea: Some questions have one right answer. Is this wall 3 metres long? Measure it. Some ethical questions are clear too: do not fake a test result. But many hard ones are not. Should a school use face-recognition to take attendance? One side says it saves time. The other side says children should not be scanned every morning. Both sides have a point. That is what makes it a hard ethical question. Careful thinking means hearing the strongest point on each side before you decide, instead of grabbing a rule or going with whatever your friends feel today.
sections.whyItMatters: AI brings many new choices like this into your life at once. If you can hold two sides in your head, you will not be pushed around by whoever speaks loudest.
sections.inTheStudio: A design class votes on whether to let students use an AI drawing tool for homework. "Yes, it helps us learn faster." "No, we will stop learning to draw." A good class does not just vote. It writes both lists first.
sections.watchForThis: "Everyone thinks so" and "the rule says so" used as the whole answer. Neither one is an answer. Each is where your thinking should begin.
sections.tryIt: Pick one AI question from your week. Write the three strongest points for each side. Then write your own view in two lines, and say which point nearly changed your mind.
sections.proveIt: Argue one AI question from both sides out loud, then give your own answer and one reason that is your own, not borrowed from a rule or from the crowd.
sections.howItWorks: People who study ethics call this weighing values — speed against privacy, help against harm, my benefit against someone else's cost. Two honest people can weigh the same values differently. The aim is to see the whole scale, not to win. Not every question needs the scale: where one side has no real point, a long debate is a delay, not thinking. Many of the cards in this part of the map are weighing exercises, and they all need this habit.

card.oneLiner: Apps quietly collect things about you — and once you upload something to an online service, another organisation's computers may hold it.

sections.idea: Data about you is being collected all the time. The apps you tap, the videos you pause on, the words a smart speaker hears, the photos you upload. When you upload to an online service, another organisation's computers may receive it, use it, and keep it — to pick your ads, to improve their machine, or sometimes to sell. That is why it has value. Before you upload anything, ask two questions. What am I handing over? And is it only mine to hand over? A photo of your friends is not only yours.
sections.whyItMatters: You cannot take an upload back. Thinking for three seconds before it leaves your phone is the cheapest protection there is.
sections.inTheStudio: A student uploads a photo of a classmate's sketchbook to an AI tool "to see what it does." The classmate never agreed. The sketch is now on a company's computer, and may stay there.
sections.watchForThis: "It's a free app." Free apps are paid for somehow. Sometimes the payment is data — yours. Find out which before you trust one.
sections.tryIt: Open one app's settings and find the page that says what it collects. Write down two things on that list you did not expect.
sections.proveIt: Name two kinds of data an app collects about you without asking each time, and say one thing you would not upload without asking someone first.
sections.howItWorks: Most countries now have laws about personal data. India passed one in 2023, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and the rules that make it work, the DPDP Rules, 2025, are coming into force in stages. If you are under 18, the Act treats you as a child, and the rules about a parent's consent for your data are scheduled to start in May 2027 — the *You are a child in the data law* card on this map is about exactly that. The European Union has had a data law since 2018. These laws give you some rights over your data. But a law can only help after something has gone wrong. The habit of asking "what am I handing over?" helps before.

card.oneLiner: Know the rule for this assignment before you use AI in it. Declaring a use does not make a forbidden one allowed — and a permitted one may still need declaring.

sections.dilemma: Your studio submission is due tomorrow. A chatbot wrote the first draft of your design statement and an image tool produced two of your context views. Nobody asked you to declare anything, and you have not read the brief's AI clause, if there is one. Do you say what the machine did, and where?
sections.choices: Say nothing, and hope the question never comes. Add a one-line note — *AI was used for the first draft of the statement and for two context views, both reworked by me* — and let the tutor weigh it. Or go back to the brief first and find its rule: if any of these uses was forbidden, declaring it does not make it allowed; if the use is permitted, the brief may still require the note.
sections.consequence: Saying nothing works until the first question. After that the whole submission is under suspicion, including the parts that were yours. Declaring costs you one sentence and keeps every other sentence credible — where the use was allowed. The third route matters most: some briefs exist to test your own hand, and on those a declaration does not make the use acceptable. It only admits it. There is no rule of the form "using it is fine, hiding it is the offence". There is this assignment's rule, and you have to know it.
sections.theCase: A second-year jury in Bengaluru. A student's sheet carries a beautiful section. A juror asks how the stair was resolved. The student cannot answer, because the section was generated and never read. The problem was not that AI touched the drawing. The student submitted something they could not defend, and had not said so.
sections.takeItToCrit: If a juror asked right now how AI touched this submission, does the student have a truthful, specific answer ready? Ask it, and watch whether the answer is specific or vague.
sections.proveIt: Find the AI rule for one assignment you have already submitted. Write the honest one-line note for that work. Then sort the uses in it into three columns: *permitted, no note needed* · *permitted, needs declaring* · *forbidden, so a note would not have saved it*. The third column tells you what the brief was really testing.
sections.howItWorks: Schools and universities are writing their rules as you read this, and they differ: some ask for a declaration on every submission, some forbid generation in first-year studios, some permit a use without asking for a note, some say nothing yet. That is why this card is marked EVOLVING, and why the only rule that holds everywhere is to know the rule where you are. Two things are not changing. The person who signs a submission must be able to defend it. And a declaration does the same job as a citation: it tells the reader where the work came from. This card is the rule to find before you start; the *Disclosure* card on this map is the record you keep so that you can answer when asked.

card.oneLiner: A disclosure is a record of what the machine did in a piece of work — which tool, for what task, what you changed — and school, competition, client and publication each read it differently.

sections.idea: A disclosure is a record: what the machine did in a piece of work. Four kinds of reader ask for it, each for a different reason. A school wants to know what you learned. A competition wants to know what was generated, so entries are judged alike. A client wants to know what they can rely on. A publication wants to know what was made and found. The rules differ by place and get firmer every year; some require a disclosure, some do not, anonymous entries may forbid one. The record is the same: tool, task, what you did afterwards.
sections.whyItMatters: A record kept as you work can answer any of the four readers in a sentence. The same facts reconstructed after the question read as a confession. Same facts, very different position — and the Lab's advice, stated as advice, is to keep the record whether or not anyone has asked.
sections.inTheStudio: A jury asks, "Is that render generated?" Two answers. "Partly — the sky and the people are from an image model; the building is my model, the plan is mine, and I re-drew the ground floor after the render showed the entrance was wrong." Or: a pause. The first answer opens a conversation about the design. The second ends one.
sections.watchForThis: A disclosure that names the tool and nothing else. "Made with AI" tells a reader nothing they can use. Say the task, and say what you did afterwards. That is where your authorship shows.
sections.tryIt: Take one piece of your own work. Write its record once — model and version, what was generated, what you changed, which references, which decisions you kept and rejected. Then write the disclosure line four times from that record: for your school, for a competition, for a client, for a magazine. Note what changes between the four. Then find your school's actual policy and check whether your line would satisfy it, and whether it was required at all.
sections.proveIt: Produce the record for one real piece of work — tool, task, what you changed — and show how the disclosure drawn from it would need to differ for two different readers, including one who did not ask for it.
sections.howItWorks: Norms are forming from several directions at once: institutions' academic-integrity policies, competition rules that now carry AI clauses, publishers' author guidelines, and early labelling rules for generated content in some jurisdictions — the EU's from 2 August 2026. They do not agree with each other, and they change every year, which is why the card is EVOLVING and dated. The *Declaring AI* card on this map is the rule to find first: what this assignment allows and requires. This card is the record you keep so that, whatever the rule turns out to be, you can answer it. The part that does not change is older than AI: say what you did, in the place where it will be read.
