sections.takeItToCrit: Does the student treat AI's physical infrastructure as architecture they could be asked to design — with siting, cooling and water as design decisions — or as someone else's distant problem?

topics.description: Whether AI wears down your skill or builds it depends partly on what you delegate, what you still practise, and how your studio is set up — and the first two are decisions you make, usually without noticing. You can let the model draft every section and check them, or draft every section yourself and use the model to check you. The first is faster this semester.

sections.dilemma: You can let the model draft every section and check them, or draft every section yourself and use the model to check you. The first is faster this semester. The second is slower and you are not sure it matters. Which habit do you build in your first year?
sections.choices: Offload the whole task and review the output. Offload the drudgery — the repetitive, the already-understood — and keep the struggle that teaches. Or refuse the tool for the task altogether until the skill is yours.
sections.consequence: The first route produces a student who can judge a section only as well as their last hand-drawn one, and that was a long time ago. The second keeps the skill alive while still saving the hours that do not teach. The third is safest and slowest, and it leaves the student with no practice at the one thing a working office will demand: using the tool and staying sharp. The honest answer is usually the second. It needs you to know which parts of a task teach you something and which only take time. It is not purely your choice: a studio that wants five rendered alternatives by tomorrow has made part of the decision for you, and that is a decision for the people who set the brief.
sections.theCase: Two third-year students, same studio. One uses a model to generate every plan iteration and has never resolved a stair by hand. The other generates the tenth option only after drawing nine, and uses the model to find what the nine missed. At the jury both have good plans. Only one can redraw it under questioning.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student say which of their own skills their AI habits are exercising, and which they are outsourcing away? Ask for one of each, named.
sections.proveIt: Name one skill your AI use is building and one it is quietly letting fade. Then redesign one workflow so the AI removes drudgery but keeps the struggle that teaches you.
sections.howItWorks: The research describes this as a choice between structured, reflective use and passive offloading, which one 2025 study calls metacognitive laziness. The systematic review behind this card finds both gains and erosion, depending on how the tool is used, and the evidence is early. That is why the card is EVOLVING. topics.name: What the licence lets you do
topics.description: What you may do with an output is decided by the licence or terms you agreed to — not by whether the weights were free or the API was paid — so read them before a deliverable depends on the answer. Four steps, in order. Find the terms for the exact model or service you used — the licence file for open weights, the terms of use for an API or app.

card.oneLiner: What you may do with an output is decided by the licence or terms you agreed to — not by whether the weights were free or the API was paid — so read them before a deliverable depends on the answer.

sections.whenToUse: Before any AI-made output goes into something you will publish, sell, or hand to a client. Not after.
sections.method: Four steps, in order. **Find the terms** for the exact model or service you used — the licence file for open weights, the terms of use for an API or app. **Find the output clause**: what it says about who owns outputs and whether commercial use is allowed, and any conditions — attribution, revenue thresholds, restricted uses. **Find the input clause**: what the service may do with what you uploaded. **Record it** next to the deliverable: service, date, the sentence that permits the use. Terms change; the date is part of the record.
sections.watchForThis: Confusing *you own the output* with *the output is copyrightable*. A service can assign you whatever rights it has; it cannot create rights the law does not give. In the US, the Copyright Office holds that purely machine-generated material is not registrable. Indian law has a line for computer-generated works — Section 2(d)(vi) of the Copyright Act 1957: the author is "the person who causes the work to be created" — but whether a generative model's output is "computer-generated" in that sense is untested in Indian courts. Ownership and copyright are two different questions. And a second confusion: open weights are not open source. Published weights under a restrictive licence are still restricted; the Open Source Initiative's definition needs the freedom to use, study, modify and share, with enough of the code, the weights and the data information to do so.
sections.tryIt: For one model you use, find whether its terms allow commercial use of outputs and point to the exact sentence. Then compare two services — one open-weight, one paid — and show that your answer for each came from the licence text, not from the price or the download.
sections.proveIt: For two models you use, one open-weight and one paid, state whether their terms allow commercial use of outputs and where the terms say so; and explain why the download and the price told you nothing the text did not.
sections.howItWorks: Open-weight models ship with licences that range from fully permissive to use-restricted, and some add conditions above a certain scale of use; an open-weight licence can forbid commercial use. Paid services usually say in their terms that you own what you generate, subject to their policies; a free hosted service can grant the same. The variable is the text you agreed to. The licence covers your contract with the provider. Copyright covers your claim against everyone else. People mix the two up all the time. This card is EVOLVING because the terms change without notice and the copyright question is in court. Where a reference image or a dataset also carries a licence — the Creative Commons family is the most common — that licence travels with whatever you make from it.

Look for the documents, plural, because they are not always in one place: the model card, where there is one; the system card or technical report; the licence; the acceptable-use policy, where the use restrictions often live; and the privacy or data terms. On Hugging Face the model card is the README of the model's page; for commercial products it sits inside the documentation, in different shapes.

card.oneLiner: A well-documented model ships a card saying what it is, what it was trained on and what it may not be used for — read it where it exists, and where it does not, record the gap.

sections.whenToUse: Before a model enters a real workflow: before the first client upload, the first published image, the first invoice that depends on it. And again when the model updates.
sections.method: Look for the documents, plural, because they are not always in one place: the model card, where there is one; the system card or technical report; the licence; the acceptable-use policy, where the use restrictions often live; and the privacy or data terms. On Hugging Face the model card is the README of the model's page; for commercial products it sits inside the documentation, in different shapes. Some widely used models have no card worth the name — if so, that is the first line of your summary, and it changes what you may trust the model for. Read four things. **Intended use and limitations:** what the makers say it is for and where it fails. **Training data:** what they name, and what they decline to name. **Evaluation:** what it was tested on, and whether that resembles your work. **Licence and terms:** what you may do with outputs — commercial use, attribution, prohibited uses — and what the provider may do with your inputs. Write a five-line summary in the studio's own words and file it with the project. Where a field is missing, write "not stated". That is a finding.
sections.watchForThis: A card that is long and says nothing. Marketing pages and model cards can look alike. The test is whether it is specific: does it name datasets, give numbers, list failures? A card that names no limitations is a brochure.
sections.tryIt: Open the card for one open-weight model and one commercial model you use. Fill the four fields for each. Count the "not stated" entries. Then find the single sentence in each that matters most to a design studio — usually in the limitations or the terms.
sections.proveIt: Produce a filed one-page reading of one model's card and terms, with the four fields, every "not stated" marked, and the one clause that would change how the studio uses it.
sections.howItWorks: The model card as a form was proposed in 2018 by Margaret Mitchell and colleagues, as a standard way to report intended use, evaluation across groups, and limits. Hugging Face made it the default README of every model repository, with machine-readable fields for licence and datasets. Commercial providers publish less, in different shapes; many cards name categories of training data rather than an inventory; some use restrictions live only in an acceptable-use policy; and terms of service change even when the model does not. Where something you need is not disclosed, "not stated" is the finding — that is provenance literacy, and it is the sentence the filed summary most often turns on. That is why this card is EVOLVING: the habit lasts; the documents keep changing, and sometimes do not exist.

card.oneLiner: Some AI law now exists, it differs by country, and more is being written — know what has been passed, where, what remains open, and never invent what is in it.

sections.idea: There is no settled rulebook for AI in design practice, and there are real pieces. In India: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, with the DPDP Rules, 2025, coming into force in phases; the AI Governance Guidelines of 5 November 2025, principle-based, seven guiding principles, and, as the Lab reads them, no umbrella AI statute; and a first, interim court ruling on training. In the EU: the AI Act, with obligations in force from 2 August 2026. Each settles something and leaves more open. Know which exist, what each says, how to check; never invent what is in one.
sections.whyItMatters: "An AI law requires X" is now a sentence that can be true, false, or true only somewhere else. A designer who can say which, and give the source, is useful in the room. "The law requires X", said without a source, is how a studio talks itself into a bad decision. So is "there's no law, so anything goes."
sections.inTheStudio: A client in Bengaluru asks whether using an image model on their project photographs is "allowed under the AI law", and whether the generated views in the brochure must be labelled. The honest reply has four parts. India has no AI Act; its Governance Guidelines are principles, not a statute. India's data-protection law governs any personal data in those photographs. The copyright question is before the courts, with one interim ruling and no final answer. And in the EU, since 2 August 2026, certain AI-generated content must be marked — so a brochure that travels should say what its images are, and should say so anyway, because honesty does not wait for a law.
sections.watchForThis: A confident sentence about AI law with no date and no place attached. Law is local, and it is moving. A claim without a "where" and a "when" is not a claim about law — and the card you are reading carries a checked date for the same reason.
sections.tryIt: Find the primary text of one piece — the DPDP Act and its Rules, the AI Governance Guidelines, the EU AI Act's Article 50. Read the definitions section only. Write three lines: what it covers, where it applies, and one thing it does not address. Then write one way you would find out if it changed.
sections.proveIt: State, with sources, what AI-related law exists in one jurisdiction and what remains unsettled there, and say which of your own working habits it actually touches. Then explain why "an AI law requires X" without a primary source is a mistake.
sections.howItWorks: The law comes in layers. General laws — copyright, contract, privacy — apply to AI because they apply to everything. Then sector rules. Then AI-specific statutes, of which the EU's is the most complete so far. The dated layer, as of this edition: India's DPDP Act received assent on 11 August 2023; the DPDP Rules were notified in November 2025 and the provisions are being commenced in phases, the children's-data provisions scheduled for May 2027. MeitY published the India AI Governance Guidelines on 5 November 2025 — seven guiding principles, six pillars, a sector-by-sector approach; the Lab's reading is that they rely on existing law rather than creating a new statute, and that reading is ours, not the ministry's. On 24 July 2026 the Delhi High Court gave an interim — not final — ruling in *ANI v OpenAI*, treating training on news articles as prima facie fair dealing on the facts before it; the suit continues. A December 2025 DPIIT working paper proposed a mandatory licence for training; it is a proposal, not law. In the EU, the AI Act's Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026. UNESCO's 2021 Recommendation is not law, but 193 states adopted it, India among them, and national frameworks lean on it. Every sentence in this paragraph will need re-checking by the next edition, which is why the card is EVOLVING and why it carries a checked date. Read the primary text; do not cite a card about it.

topics.name: The render that lies
topics.description: A generated view can show a place that does not exist — presenting it as the real site condition is misrepresentation, not style. Showing a generated image as the real site condition is misrepresentation. It is not a style choice.
evidence: In a generated site image, spot one invented condition that could mislead a client or an authority. Then draw the line, in writing, between fair speculation and a false claim about what is really on the ground.
When a student shows a generated context view, do they flag what is real site and what the model invented — before anyone has to ask?
topics.critPrompt: When a student shows a generated context view, do they flag what is real site and what the model invented — before anyone has to ask?

grounding.ref: artificialintelligenceact.eu, A Practical Guide to Article 50
C2PA, Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity

card.oneLiner: A generated view can show a place that does not exist — presenting it as the real site condition is misrepresentation, not style.

sections.dilemma: Your context view is generated. It has quietly erased the neighbour's four-storey wall, flattened the slope, and added a heritage façade that is not there. It is the best image on the sheet. Do you show it as the site?
sections.choices: Show it as is and say nothing. Show it with a caption: *speculative view; neighbouring building and slope not as existing*. Or correct the image — restore the neighbour, the slope, the absence — and then show it.
sections.consequence: The first route makes a false claim about a real place to a client, a jury, or an approving authority, and the better the image, the bigger the lie. The second keeps the image and labels it honestly as speculation. The third costs an afternoon and produces a drawing that can be submitted anywhere. The first is the one that ends careers, slowly. A client who finds the neighbour's wall on site does not forget who hid it.
sections.theCase: A municipal submission in a hill town. The generated context view shows gentle ground and open sky to the north. The site falls three metres and the northern neighbour's house stands at the boundary. The authority's inspector has been to the site. The drawing is now a false statement to a public authority, and the architect signed it.
sections.takeItToCrit: When a student shows a generated context view, do they flag what is real site and what the model invented — before anyone has to ask?
sections.position: Showing a generated image as the real site condition is misrepresentation. It is not a style choice. Speculation is legitimate when it is labelled as speculation; a claim about what is on the ground is either true or false.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Renders have always flattered: bluer skies, thinner people, no cars. But a flattering sky has never moved a neighbour's wall. Generated context invents conditions that decisions will be made on — setbacks, light, views, approvals. The architect's signature on a drawing is a claim about the world, and the profession is trusted because that claim is true.
sections.strongestObjection: All renders lie, and always have. The profession has omitted the ugly neighbour, the overhead wires and the drain for decades and called it presentation. Singling out AI for a sin the discipline practised by hand is inconsistent — and a rule that every context view be as-existing would forbid most of the images the profession has ever shown.
sections.revisionCondition: If the profession adopts a labelling convention that makes an image's status explicit by default — content credentials on every file, a required *speculative / as-existing* tag on every sheet — the burden moves from the designer's sentence to the file, and this card is rewritten around reading the label rather than writing it. Reviewed every edition.
sections.proveIt: In a generated site image, spot one invented condition that could mislead a client or an authority. Then draw the line, in writing, between fair speculation and a false claim about what is really on the ground.
sections.howItWorks: Two things make the false site more than an ethical lapse. A drawing submitted for approval is a statement to a public authority, and a false one can carry consequences under whatever law governs such submissions where you practise. And in the EU, since 2 August 2026, AI-generated images that resemble real places and could pass as authentic fall under a disclosure duty, with exceptions for evidently artistic work. Neither of these is why the Lab holds the position. The position would stand with no law at all.

topics.name: Trained rarely, used constantly
topics.description: Training concentrates a large cost into model-building runs; everyday use spreads a small cost across billions of calls — and current analysis says the second is now the bigger bill. A model carries two bills. Training is a large cost concentrated in model-building runs, weeks of thousands of chips, and the runs repeat: models are retrained, fine-tuned, distilled and replaced.
evidence: Explain to a classmate, with a water bill as the analogy, how a connection charge paid each time the line is re-laid and a per-litre rate can both be large in different ways. Then map training and inference onto the two, and say why "per litre" is not one number when some calls are a sip and some are a tank.

Tell the concentrated cost of training runs apart from the repeating cost of everyday use, in plain words, and explain how "my one prompt is tiny" and "inference is the bigger footprint" can both be true at once.
topics.critPrompt: Can the student reason about the environmental cost at the right rough scale, without inventing a number or pretending the cost is zero?

card.oneLiner: Training concentrates a large cost into model-building runs; everyday use spreads a small cost across billions of calls — and current analysis says the second is now the bigger bill.

sections.idea: A model carries two bills. Training is a large cost concentrated in model-building runs, weeks of thousands of chips, and the runs repeat: models are retrained, fine-tuned, distilled and replaced. Inference is what happens every time anyone uses the model: a small cost per call, and "small" varies a hundredfold between a text reply and a minute of video. The small cost runs billions of times a day, and current analysis, including the IEA's 2025 report, points to inference as where most ongoing energy use now builds up. Keep this at rough scale. Nobody has a clean number per prompt.
sections.whyItMatters: Your prompt is small and the total is huge, and both are true at once. Seeing how the two fit together lets you judge the cost instead of just feeling bad about it.
sections.inTheStudio: "My one render is nothing" and "AI's footprint is enormous" said across the same table. Neither speaker is wrong. One is describing a single call; the other is describing the sum. The studio's share of the sum is its habits — how many calls, how loosely briefed.
sections.watchForThis: Inventing a number to win the argument. Per-prompt figures circulate widely, differ by a hundredfold, and mostly lack a source. Quote the IEA or quote nothing.
sections.tryIt: Explain to a classmate, with a water bill as the analogy, how a connection charge paid each time the line is re-laid and a per-litre rate can both be large in different ways. Then map training and inference onto the two, and say why "per litre" is not one number when some calls are a sip and some are a tank.
sections.proveIt: Tell the concentrated cost of training runs apart from the repeating cost of everyday use, in plain words, and explain how "my one prompt is tiny" and "inference is the bigger footprint" can both be true at once.
sections.howItWorks: Training adjusts the weights in each run; inference reads them on every call. Training's cost sits in one place and the company that paid it can measure it. Inference's cost is spread across every data centre that serves the model, and from outside it can only be estimated, not measured. The balance between the two shifts with model size, efficiency and usage, and the IEA's projections will be revised. That is why the card is EVOLVING. The *Two clocks* card on the Foundations strand is the same split seen from the learning side.

topics.name: Honest in the room
topics.description: Show AI-assisted work to clients, juries and the public with its status named — guess or resolved, machine-made or drawn. The duty of candour is the profession's; naming an image's status is how the Lab applies it. An AI-assisted image is shown with its status named before anyone asks: study, speculative, resolved, generated, drawn. Trust is the asset a practice keeps — that is the Lab's slogan, and its reason.
evidence: Present an AI-assisted study and name its status clearly: is it speculation or a real proposal? Then explain, in two sentences a client would understand, the risk of passing a generated image off as a finished design — and say which part of that is the profession's duty and which is the Lab's application of it.

grounding.ref: professional codes of conduct — the CoA 1989 Regulations carry general duties (standard of conduct, welfare of society, no advertising), not a clause on honest representation of images; the card states the duty in those terms
Council of Architecture, Architects (Professional Conduct) Regulations, 1989

card.oneLiner: Show AI-assisted work to clients, juries and the public with its status named — guess or resolved, machine-made or drawn. The duty of candour is the profession's; naming an image's status is how the Lab applies it.

sections.dilemma: The client meeting. On the screen is a generated interior that took four minutes and looks like a finished design. The client is delighted and asks when construction can start. The plan behind it does not exist yet. What do you say?
sections.choices: Let the delight stand and resolve the plan later, hoping it lands close to the image. Correct the status in the room — *this is a mood study, not a design; the plan will change it* — and risk deflating the meeting. Or change how you present: show the generated study beside an honest diagram of what is resolved, so the status is visible before anyone asks.
sections.consequence: The first route sells an image you cannot build, and you pay for it at the next meeting, when the client feels deceived. The second costs a moment of disappointment and buys a client who believes your next sentence. The third removes the moment altogether, because the sheet itself says what is speculation. The pressure in the room is real. The consequence of giving in to it is also real, and slower.
sections.theCase: A residential client in Pune forwards the generated view to her family group. Three relatives have opinions on the "finished design" by evening. The architect now has to un-design a building that was never designed, in front of an audience, because one image was shown without its status. Nobody lied. Nobody said what the image was either.
sections.takeItToCrit: In the mock client meeting, does the student's language keep the image's status honest even under pressure — when the client is pleased and asking the wrong question?
sections.position: An AI-assisted image is shown with its status named before anyone asks: *study*, *speculative*, *resolved*, *generated*, *drawn*. Trust is the asset a practice keeps — that is the Lab's slogan, and its reason.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The professional duty is the Council of Architecture's: the Professional Conduct Regulations, 1989, bind every Indian architect to a high standard of service and to the welfare of society. They say nothing about AI or images. The application — that an image's status must be said in the room — is the Lab's, not the Council's, and the card says so because a provenance curriculum cannot cite a rule its source never issued. We hold the application because a generated image is the fastest way yet invented to let a client believe a design exists, and the cost of that belief lands on the next meeting.
sections.strongestObjection: Every presentation image has always been partly aspiration, and clients know it; a mood study reads as a mood study to anyone who has commissioned a building before. Labelling every image by status treats the client as naive, slows the room, and adds a vocabulary the profession has not agreed — a "study" in one office is a "concept" in another. And a duty the Council has not written is not a duty. It is one studio's house rule, taught as if it were the profession's.
sections.revisionCondition: The Council, or a competition body, issuing a rule on the status of AI-assisted images — then this card teaches that rule and says where the Lab's differs. Or evidence that clients reliably read status without being told, in which case the position narrows to the cases where they do not. Reviewed every edition.
sections.proveIt: Present an AI-assisted study and name its status clearly: is it speculation or a real proposal? Then explain, in two sentences a client would understand, the risk of passing a generated image off as a finished design — and say which part of that is the profession's duty and which is the Lab's application of it.
sections.howItWorks: Two sources, kept apart. Professional duty: the Council of Architecture's 1989 conduct regulations, which bind every Indian architect to a high standard of service and to the welfare of society, and do not mention images, AI, or honest representation by name — they were written for a world without either. Application to AI visualisation: the Lab's, as stated above. The duty to represent things honestly is older and wider than any code; it is what a client is paying for when they hire a professional. Status words are the Lab's practical form of it. The *Render that lies* card on this map is the same duty at the site boundary.

topics.name: Disclosure in competitions
topics.description: Juries and publications increasingly ask what was AI-generated while the norms stay unsettled — write the disclosure line before you submit, not after you are asked. Disclose early, specifically, and in writing, whether or not the brief requires it. The disclosure line is part of the entry, drafted with it, not appended under pressure.
evidence: Draft the AI-use disclosure statement for a real or mock competition entry. Then argue, in a paragraph, why disclosing early protects the author more than staying silent — even when no rule forces it.
For work headed to a jury or a publication, has the student decided what to disclose and written it down — or are they hoping the question never comes up?
topics.critPrompt: For work headed to a jury or a publication, has the student decided what to disclose and written it down — or are they hoping the question never comes up?

grounding.ref: European Commission, Quick Facts: Transparency rules for AI systems

card.oneLiner: Juries and publications increasingly ask what was AI-generated while the norms stay unsettled — write the disclosure line before you submit, not after you are asked.

sections.dilemma: The competition brief says nothing about AI. Your entry used a model for massing studies and two of the four renders. Disclosing might count against you with a conservative jury. Staying silent might be discovered. The form has a box for "additional notes." What goes in it?
sections.choices: Say nothing — the brief did not ask. Write a disclosure so broad it says nothing: *digital tools were used*. Or write the specific line — *massing explored with [tool]; renders 2 and 3 generated from the author's model and edited; plans, sections and text by the author* — and let the jury weigh it.
sections.consequence: Silence works until a juror recognises a generated texture. Then the whole entry is suspect, including the plans you drew. The vague line protects nothing and reads as evasion. The specific line costs a sentence, may cost you a conservative juror, and makes every other claim on the sheet more credible. It also puts the record on your side if a later rule is applied backwards.
sections.theCase: A national student competition. Two shortlisted entries, both AI-assisted. One carries a specific disclosure; the other carries none. A juror asks both. The first entrant reads their line aloud. The second improvises, badly, and the jury's question becomes whether anything else on the sheet was theirs. The disclosure did not win the competition. The absence of one lost it.
sections.takeItToCrit: For work headed to a jury or a publication, has the student decided what to disclose and written it down — or are they hoping the question never comes up?
sections.position: Disclose early, specifically, and in writing, whether or not the brief requires it. The disclosure line is part of the entry, drafted with it, not appended under pressure.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Disclosure protects the author more than silence does. It turns something a juror might discover into something you have stated, and it makes the rest of the work more credible. The norms are being formed in public right now. The entrants who disclose are writing the norm. The ones who hide are setting up the scandal that will produce a harsher one.
sections.strongestObjection: Disclosure without a norm is a penalty on the honest. A conservative jury marks the discloser down while the silent peer advances. And because "AI-assisted" has no agreed boundary — is spell-check assistance? is a denoiser? — a specific disclosure can mislead by implying more machine than there was. Early disclosers may simply be early losers.
sections.revisionCondition: Evidence that juries systematically penalise disclosers and that the norm settles on not asking; or disclosure becoming mandatory everywhere, at which point this card stops being a position and becomes a procedure. Reviewed every edition against competition rules as they are published.
sections.proveIt: Draft the AI-use disclosure statement for a real or mock competition entry. Then argue, in a paragraph, why disclosing early protects the author more than staying silent — even when no rule forces it.
sections.howItWorks: Rules are arriving unevenly. Some competitions and journals now require a statement of AI use; many say nothing; a few forbid generated imagery outright. In the EU, since 2 August 2026, generated content that could pass as authentic carries a disclosure duty in some circumstances. In India no competition-wide rule exists that the Lab knows of as of this edition, and the Council's competition guidelines predate the question. The *Who is the author* card on this map supplies what the disclosure line describes; this card is where it gets written.

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Name, brief, audit, refuse
topics.description: When the model returns a placeless default, the literate response is four moves in order — and the fourth is the one that carries the weight. The default is not neutral; it is a placeless default — the model does not compute a cultural average, it leans where its data and its tuning lean. Name it, brief against it, audit what comes back, and refuse to ship the placeless image.
evidence: Take a flat default output and run all four moves, ending in a re-briefed, audited result. Then explain why refusing to ship the flat image is the move that carries the weight — not the styling.
Faced with a beautiful but placeless default, does the student run the four moves in order — or ship the pretty image and call it warm and modern? Ask to see the audit, not the final render.
topics.critPrompt: Faced with a beautiful but placeless default, does the student run the four moves in order — or ship the pretty image and call it warm and modern? Ask to see the audit, not the final render.

grounding.ref: Pishahang & Badiei, From Clay to Code

card.oneLiner: When the model returns a placeless default, the literate response is four moves in order — and the fourth is the one that carries the weight.

sections.dilemma: The guesthouse in Mysuru. You briefed for bamboo, lime-wash and afternoon light, and the model returned a beautiful room that could be in any hotel in the world. The client loves it. The deadline is Friday. Do you ship it?
sections.choices: Ship it and call it warm and modern. Re-prompt once, take whatever comes back, and ship that. Or run the four moves: **name** the flattening to the team and the client; **brief** against it with named typology, materials and climatic moves; **audit** the re-briefed output for what the default left behind; and **refuse** to ship anything that reads as anywhere-in-the-world when the project is specifically here.
sections.consequence: Shipping the default builds the bias into a real room, with your name on it. A single re-prompt usually keeps most of the default: the lime-wash still reads as gypsum, the jali is decoration, the eaves do nothing. Nobody audited it. The four moves cost a day and produce a room that belongs to its place. The fourth move is the one that carries the weight: without the refusal, the other three are styling.
sections.theCase: The Lab's own case, from the essay this card comes from. Brief: *warm, contextually grounded reception space, 4×4 m, bamboo and lime-wash, soft afternoon light.* Output: pale wood, white walls, raked light, low ceilings. You could find it in any global chain and nowhere in Karnataka. The deep eaves, the jali for privacy and air, the high ceiling, the cross-ventilation — the reasons the type exists — had all been lost. The image was not wrong. The neutrality was.
sections.takeItToCrit: Faced with a beautiful but placeless default, does the student run the four moves in order — or ship the pretty image and call it warm and modern? Ask to see the audit, not the final render.
sections.position: The default is not neutral; it is a placeless default — the model does not compute a cultural average, it leans where its data and its tuning lean. Name it, brief against it, audit what comes back, and refuse to ship the placeless image. The refusal is the authorship.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: For twenty years "globally minimal" was one designer's private taste. A model flattens by default, in seconds, every time. That makes it a built-in property of the tool: visible, and so something you can refuse. More data will not fix it from inside the model. The only thing that stops it is a designer who will not ship it.
sections.strongestObjection: "Brief against placelessness" can manufacture a new stereotype. If the remedy for the generic room is to demand that an Indian result look Indian, the model starts sprinkling jalis, courtyards, terracotta, carved stone, brass and arches onto contexts that never asked for them. A global language can be locally chosen; a conspicuously local one can be culturally fake — a jali added for a jury is no less decorative than pale wood added by a model. Specificity is not iconography, and the four moves do not say how to tell them apart. Add to that the practical objections: "refuse to ship" assumes a power most students and juniors do not have — in a firm the senior ships and the junior renders — and some clients genuinely want the global look, so refusing it is paternalism dressed up as ethics.
sections.revisionCondition: Models trained on well-documented regional corpora that stop producing the flat default by default. When the audit routinely finds nothing to refuse, the four moves become a checklist rather than a position, and the card is rewritten as procedure. And if the audit move cannot be made to distinguish specificity from costume, the position is rewritten around that distinction first. Reviewed every edition against what the tools actually return.
sections.proveIt: Take a flat default output and run all four moves, ending in a re-briefed, audited result. Then explain why refusing to ship the flat image is the move that carries the weight — not the styling.
sections.howItWorks: The four moves map onto the rest of this strand. *Name* is the *Tilted mirror* card, said out loud. *Brief* is the six-layer brief from the Brief strand, aimed against the corpus. *Audit* is provenance turned on the output: what did the default leave in — and what did the re-brief add that this place never had? *Refuse* is the judgment this whole map says is still yours. The *Documenting is representing* card is what you do so that the next designer has less to refuse.

topics.name: Clear the rights before shipping
topics.description: Before an AI-assisted image goes into a deliverable, someone clears at least three things — model terms, reference permissions, client agreement — and the person who spots the gap is you, by habit, even when the person who signs it off is not. At least three checks, recorded beside the file. Model terms: which model or service, what its terms say about commercial use of outputs, the date you read them.
evidence: Run the clearance pass on one AI-assisted output from the last month. Then list every reference image in that workflow and mark the ones you had no right to feed the model. Most students find at least one. Then add the fourth check the project actually needed — an NDA, a face, a logo — and say who in the studio had the authority to clear it.

Run an IP-clearance pass on one AI-assisted output — model terms, reference permissions, client consent, and whichever further checks the project calls for — point out which reference images in the workflow you had no right to feed the model, and say which gaps you could clear yourself and which you would have to escalate.
topics.critPrompt: Before the student ships, do they run the clearance pass by reflex, model, reference, client, or find the rights problem only when challenged?

grounding.ref: Creative Commons, the six licence types

card.oneLiner: Before an AI-assisted image goes into a deliverable, someone clears at least three things — model terms, reference permissions, client agreement — and the person who spots the gap is you, by habit, even when the person who signs it off is not.

sections.whenToUse: Every time an AI-assisted output leaves the studio: a client deliverable, a competition entry, a publication, a social post with the studio's name on it. Not when challenged. Before.
sections.method: At least three checks, recorded beside the file. **Model terms**: which model or service, what its terms say about commercial use of outputs, the date you read them. **Reference permissions**: every image you fed the model — whose is it, and do you have the right to use it that way? Your own site photographs, yes. A photographer's image from a magazine, no, not without permission. A client's existing drawings, only if the client agreed. **Client agreement**: does your contract or a written note cover AI use on this project, and the uploading of project material to third-party services? Three is the floor, not the list. Depending on the project, add: confidentiality and any NDA; personal data in the images; a real person's likeness; a trademark in frame; stock-image licences; who owns what an employee makes; where the provider stores what you uploaded. One line per check, per deliverable. If any line is blank, the deliverable waits. And if you are a student or a junior, "clearing" may not be yours to do: your job is to find the gap, write it down, and raise it with whoever signs.
sections.watchForThis: The reference image is where clearance most often fails. Students clear the model's terms and forget that the photograph they dropped in for image-to-image belongs to someone. "I only used it as a reference" is not a right the law recognises in most places. The output may carry that image's composition, and its owner's claim, into your deliverable.
sections.tryIt: Run the clearance pass on one AI-assisted output from the last month. Then list every reference image in that workflow and mark the ones you had no right to feed the model. Most students find at least one. Then add the fourth check the project actually needed — an NDA, a face, a logo — and say who in the studio had the authority to clear it.
sections.proveIt: Run an IP-clearance pass on one AI-assisted output — model terms, reference permissions, client consent, and whichever further checks the project calls for — point out which reference images in the workflow you had no right to feed the model, and say which gaps you could clear yourself and which you would have to escalate.
sections.howItWorks: At least three bodies of rules meet here. The model's terms are a contract between you and the provider. The reference image is governed by copyright, which in India is the Copyright Act 1957, and whether feeding a protected image to a model is infringement has not been settled by an Indian court as of this edition — the Delhi High Court's 24 July 2026 ruling in *ANI v OpenAI* was interim and concerned text. The client relationship is governed by your agreement and by confidentiality — a separate doctrine from privacy, with its own card on this map, *Client confidentiality is not privacy*. Personal data, likeness and trademarks each bring a fourth body of rules when they are in the frame. This card is EVOLVING because most of these are moving. The habit is not moving. The Lab treats the clearance pass as a studio reflex, like keeping a drawing register, learned early.

topics.subject: Ethics & Provenance
topics.name: Consent, community and the generated monument

grounding.ref: INTACH, Charter for the Conservation of Unprotected Architectural Heritage and Sites in India

topics.description: The people who still use a place have the first claim on how it is pictured — not the only claim — and a generated reconstruction shared online can fix a contested past in one image, so who is asked, who is shown and who decides comes before the prompt. Living heritage is decided with the people who keep it — not by a model, and not by the architect alone. Custodians, owners, trusts, the state's archaeology departments, scholars and the wider public all hold real claims on a place; the Lab's position is not that the users' voice is the only one, or always right, but that the architect may not be the one who decides by default.
evidence: Take one generated reconstruction of a place in use — yours or a published one. Write the caption it should have carried: author, method, what is documented, what is conjectured, who was consulted. Then list the people and bodies with a stake in that place and mark which of them saw the image before it circulated.

For any generated reconstruction of a place people still use, ask the student three questions in order: who was asked, who is shown, and who decides what counts as the heritage here? If the answers are "nobody, nobody, me," the project has not started.
topics.critPrompt: For any generated reconstruction of a place people still use, ask the student three questions in order: who was asked, who is shown, and who decides what counts as the heritage here? If the answers are "nobody, nobody, me," the project has not started.

card.oneLiner: The people who still use a place have the first claim on how it is pictured — not the only claim — and a generated reconstruction shared online can fix a contested past in one image, so who is asked, who is shown and who decides comes before the prompt.

sections.dilemma: A temple in a Karnataka town, still in worship, its outer mandapa altered in the 1970s with concrete and enamel paint. For a studio project you generate a "restored" view stripped back to an imagined twelfth-century state, and it is beautiful. The temple committee has not seen it. The priest's family has repainted that mandapa for three generations. A heritage group would like to use your image in a fundraising post. Do you let them?
sections.choices: Let it go out — it is your image and it argues for conservation. Hold it until the people who use the temple have seen it and said what they think of being shown their building without the parts they made. Or change what you make: generate nothing "restored" until you have been on site and asked what the building's keepers consider its heritage to be — which may include the 1970s mandapa.
sections.consequence: The image that goes out becomes the reference. Fundraisers, journalists and the next student will restore toward it, and the committee will be asked why their temple does not look like the picture. Holding the image costs a conversation, and the image may come back changed — the keepers may want the paint kept, the concrete gone, or neither. The third choice costs the most time and produces the only version with any standing: a proposal made with the people whose heritage it is, inside a tradition India's own conservation charter describes as living — master builders, sthapatis and raj mistris who "continue to build and care for buildings following traditions of their ancestors."
sections.theCase: A fourth-year elective on a town's heritage precinct. One team generates views of the bazaar street "as it was" — no signboards, no cables, no modern shopfronts — and the local paper runs them as how the bazaar should look. The shopkeepers whose fronts were erased were not asked; several had rebuilt those fronts with their own money after a fire. The tutor's question at jury was not about the images' quality. It was: who is in the picture, who was removed from it, and who decided?
sections.takeItToCrit: For any generated reconstruction of a place people still use, ask the student three questions in order: who was asked, who is shown, and who decides what counts as the heritage here? If the answers are "nobody, nobody, me," the project has not started.
sections.position: Living heritage is decided with the people who keep it — not by a model, and not by the architect alone. Custodians, owners, trusts, the state's archaeology departments, scholars and the wider public all hold real claims on a place; the Lab's position is not that the users' voice is the only one, or always right, but that the architect may not be the one who decides by default. A generated reconstruction of a place in use is circulated only after the people who use it have seen it and spoken, and it is captioned as a hypothesis with its author named. Consent comes before circulation.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The Nara Document (1994) says judgements of value and authenticity "may differ from culture to culture, and even within the same culture," and must be made "within the cultural contexts to which they belong." UNESCO's own definition of intangible cultural heritage says it "can only be heritage when it is recognized as such by the communities, groups or individuals that create, maintain and transmit it." India's INTACH charter (2004) recognises the living tradition of builders and the concept of jeernodharanam — renewal as a continuing practice — as part of conservation itself. A model has no community and no context. It has a distribution over photographs, most of them of monuments with no people in them. So a generated "restoration" is a claim about a contested past that nobody has made, and an image nobody made is the easiest thing in the world to pass around. The architect's job is to put a person back behind it: a name, a caption, a conversation.
sections.strongestObjection: "Ask the community" assumes there is one, and it assumes that whoever answers is the community. The body recognised as the temple's voice may be a dominant-caste trust, an all-male committee, the property-owning faction or the state department — and it may exclude the women who sweep the mandapa, the tenants against its wall, the lower-caste devotees, the migrants who use it, the dissenting descendants. Giving "the community" a veto can legitimise that hierarchy instead of protecting the heritage, and it can collide with statutory conservation duties and with legitimate scholarship and public interest. Consent from one is not consent from all; waiting for all is a veto on any proposal; and meanwhile the image tools are public and cheap — if the careful student does not make the reconstruction, a tourism board or a political campaign will, with less care. A position that hands the judgement to "the people who keep it" has to say which people, and it has not.
sections.revisionCondition: Evidence from real projects that consent-first practice prevents good conservation rather than improving it — proposals that died in consultation while the buildings fell. A settled Indian procedure for community consent on heritage imagery, at which point this card stops being a position and becomes the procedure. Or a workable method for hearing the voices a committee excludes — at which point the position is rewritten around that method, which is the revision the objection above is asking for. Reviewed every edition against what heritage bodies say and what the Lab sees in its own work.
sections.proveIt: Take one generated reconstruction of a place in use — yours or a published one. Write the caption it should have carried: author, method, what is documented, what is conjectured, who was consulted. Then list the people and bodies with a stake in that place and mark which of them saw the image before it circulated.
sections.howItWorks: FOUR PERMISSIONS on this map separates legal, contractual, institutional and ethical permission. This card is the ethical question at its hardest, because many people are affected and the harm is to memory, not to property. The Venice Charter's line at conjecture — RESTORED OR INVENTED — protects the record; Nara and the INTACH charter widen the question to whose judgement counts. India's protection frame — the Archaeological Survey of India for centrally protected monuments, state departments of archaeology for others, and a majority of architectural heritage that INTACH's charter notes "still remains unidentified, unclassified, and unprotected" — decides who may touch a building. None of it decides who may picture one, which is why this question sits in ethics and provenance rather than in law. SAYING YOU USED IT is where the caption gets written. The objection above is real: the Lab has no formula for which voice in a divided community prevails, nor for hearing the voices a committee leaves out — only the rule that the architect may not be the one who decides by default, and the practice of asking more than one body before the image moves.

sections.howItWorks: The grown-up name for this is media and information literacy. The persuasion part matters most. topics.description: A survey, a plan, a brief and a budget hold no "personal data", and all of them may still be forbidden to leave the office. Tuesday, eleven at night. The client's total-station survey and the structural consultant's forty-page report are open on your screen.

topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to name who owns each document in their project folder, and under what agreement. Then ask which of those documents they have already put into an outside tool. Watch whether they answer the privacy question when you asked the confidentiality one.

card.oneLiner: A survey, a plan, a brief and a budget hold no "personal data", and all of them may still be forbidden to leave the office.

sections.dilemma: Tuesday, eleven at night. The client's total-station survey and the structural consultant's forty-page report are open on your screen. A model could turn the report into a one-page summary by midnight. You have already removed the client's name and the plot number from the file. Nothing left in it is about a person. Is it now safe to upload?
sections.choices: Upload it: no personal data, no privacy problem, and the deadline is real. Or ask a different question first — not "is anyone's privacy in this?" but "whose file is this, and what did they agree to?" — and read the contract or the NDA before deciding. Or do the summary yourself tonight, and raise the question of an approved tool with the office tomorrow, so the next report has a route.
sections.consequence: Removing names answers the privacy question and leaves the confidentiality question untouched. A survey with its coordinates still identifies the site. A structural report still belongs to the consultant who wrote it and the client who paid for it. If the agreement says drawings and reports stay with the studio, the upload is a breach whether or not anyone ever finds out, and the breach is the studio's, not only yours. The second route costs ten minutes of reading. The third costs an evening and gives the office a rule it did not have.
sections.theCase: A small practice in Pune has a hospital client. The agreement says no project document goes to a third party without written consent. An intern anonymises the ward plans — no hospital name, no address — and uploads them to a free tool to get a room schedule. The plans still show the pharmacy store, the server room and the oxygen manifold. The hospital's security consultant finds out when the tool's output is pasted into a shared document with the tool's name in the header. Nothing personal was exposed. Something confidential was.
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student to name who owns each document in their project folder, and under what agreement. Then ask which of those documents they have already put into an outside tool. Watch whether they answer the privacy question when you asked the confidentiality one.
sections.tryIt: Take one live file from your own work: a survey, a plan, a client email. Write three lines. Does it hold anyone's personal data? Is it confidential by contract or by the plain duty of the job? Who would have to agree before it went into any outside service? If you cannot name that person, it stays in the office.
sections.howItWorks: The two duties come from two places. Privacy comes from data-protection law: India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 covers digital personal data — information about an identifiable person — and says nothing about a survey or a budget. Confidentiality comes from the agreement (a contract clause, an NDA) and from professional duty: the Council of Architecture's regulations, made under the Architects Act, 1972, bind a registered architect to the conditions of engagement and to integrity, and a breach of those conditions is a matter between the architect, the client and the Council, not the Data Protection Board. A practical test: anonymise the document, then ask whether you would still need permission to hand it to a stranger. If yes, the file is confidential, and removing names did nothing for it. THREE PILES on this map sorts what may go; this card explains why a clean-looking file can still belong in the "never" pile.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: From photographs to a measurable model

grounding.ref: Historic England, Geospatial Survey Specifications for Cultural Heritage (2024)
Kerbl et al., 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering

topics.description: A hundred overlapping photographs can become a model you can measure, if you give it control — and a splat you can walk through, which is a different thing. Two methods start from the same photo set and end in different places; decide which you need first. Photogrammetry gives a measurable model.
evidence: Photograph one small built thing with strong texture — a temple plinth, a brick gateway, a carved stone post — in forty to sixty overlapping frames, with a tape in the scene. Build the model in any free photogrammetry tool. Measure three dimensions on the model and the same three on site. Report the difference as a percentage.
Show one photogrammetric model beside its three on-site check measurements, with the error stated, and point to one surface in the model you know the camera never saw.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one photogrammetric model beside its three on-site check measurements, with the error stated, and point to one surface in the model you know the camera never saw.

card.oneLiner: A hundred overlapping photographs can become a model you can measure, if you give it control — and a splat you can walk through, which is a different thing.

sections.whenToUse: Before any decision about an existing building: a measured-drawing assignment, a conservation report, an addition to an old house, a record of a structure about to be altered. The scan is the documentation step that every later heritage decision rests on.
sections.method: Two methods start from the same photo set and end in different places; decide which you need first. Photogrammetry gives a measurable model. Walk the building and photograph it in overlapping passes. Historic England's metric-survey specification asks for at least 60 per cent overlap between adjacent images and 40 per cent between strips, and its own drone briefs ask for 80 per cent front-to-back; plan for the higher figure. Keep a steady distance and even light; an overcast morning is better than noon, because hard shadows and uneven light break the matching between frames. Give the model control, or it has shape but no dependable size: a scale bar or a measured distance for a small subject; for a building, surveyed control points on the fabric — the specification asks for at least four per elevation, plus check points it does not use in the adjustment. Run the set through a photogrammetry tool. It finds the same points across photographs, works out where each camera stood, and builds a point cloud — a cloud of measured points — and from that a mesh you can section and measure. Gaussian splatting is the other method. From the same kind of photo set it builds a view you can move through in real time. It is a view-synthesis representation, made to look right from any angle; a measurable surface is not what it produces by default, and pulling one out of it is a separate step that loses accuracy. Then check the photogrammetric model against the building: measure three things on site with a tape — a door width, a column spacing, a plinth height — and compare; those are your check points. Write the error down. If the model is two per cent out, every dimension you take from it is two per cent out.
sections.watchForThis: Trusting the surfaces the camera never saw. Photogrammetry invents nothing on purpose, but it smooths over gaps — the top of a cornice, the inside of a niche, a wall behind a tree — and the smoothed surface looks as solid as the measured one. Plain white walls, glass and polished stone also confuse it: the software needs texture to match points across frames.
sections.tryIt: Photograph one small built thing with strong texture — a temple plinth, a brick gateway, a carved stone post — in forty to sixty overlapping frames, with a tape in the scene. Build the model in any free photogrammetry tool. Measure three dimensions on the model and the same three on site. Report the difference as a percentage.
sections.proveIt: Show one photogrammetric model beside its three on-site check measurements, with the error stated, and point to one surface in the model you know the camera never saw.
sections.howItWorks: Photogrammetry is geometry, not machine learning. A method called structure from motion finds the same feature in many photographs and works out where the cameras were and where the points are; surveyed control gives the result its scale and its position, and check points measure its error. Machine learning comes in later. Gaussian splatting, published in 2023, represents a scene as a very large number of small soft blobs — 3D Gaussians — and adjusts them until views rendered from them match the photographs, which gives real-time walkthroughs at full HD. It is a rendering method first. A measurable surface has to be extracted from it, and that extraction is still a research problem: surfaces recovered from splats can be geometrically wrong where the photographs were ambiguous. Open projects such as Open Heritage 3D publish scan datasets of real monuments for anyone to download and section. EVOLVING because the methods change every year — what measures badly today may measure well by the next edition — and because phone-based capture is improving quickly. WORLD MODELS on this map is the frontier beyond this card; WHAT IT CAN TAKE IN covers how a photo set enters a model.

topics.name: Choosing the smaller model is a design decision

grounding.ref: The Hidden Layers: Compute, Energy, Labour, Bias

topics.description: Your own workflow has a footprint; the Lab treats model size and generation count as a budget line like any other. Four dials, set before you run. Model: the smallest model that does this job — a small model for a summary, a caption, a first sort; a large one only where the task has shown it needs one.
evidence: Take a task you did this week with a large model. Do it again with the smallest model you can access. Judge the two outputs blind. Then count the generations you ran last week on one project and write the number where you can see it.
Show one project log where the four dials were set before running and the actual spend recorded after — and say which dial you would move next time.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one project log where the four dials were set before running and the actual spend recorded after — and say which dial you would move next time.

card.oneLiner: Your own workflow has a footprint; the Lab treats model size and generation count as a budget line like any other.

sections.whenToUse: Every time you set up an AI step in studio work: which model, how many generations, at what resolution, and how many re-rolls before you stop and read what you have.
sections.method: Four dials, set before you run. Model: the smallest model that does this job — a small model for a summary, a caption, a first sort; a large one only where the task has shown it needs one. Count: decide the batch before you generate, and read the whole contact sheet before asking for more. Resolution: draft low, and render once at the size the deliverable needs. Re-rolls: decide how many you will allow before you go back and fix the brief. A re-roll usually means the brief is loose; it is not a free retry. Write the four settings at the top of the log beside the brief. At the end of the task, write what you actually spent: calls, images, hours.
sections.watchForThis: The "just one more" batch. If it takes fifty images to find one, you are not exploring; you have a loose brief, and you are paying for it in energy and time. Fix the brief, not the count. And read the model dial as a heuristic, not a carbon calculation: a small model that fails three times can cost more than a large one that succeeds once, hardware and provider efficiency move the figure more than size does, and providers publish almost nothing per task.
sections.tryIt: Take a task you did this week with a large model. Do it again with the smallest model you can access. Judge the two outputs blind. Then count the generations you ran last week on one project and write the number where you can see it.
sections.proveIt: Show one project log where the four dials were set before running and the actual spend recorded after — and say which dial you would move next time.
sections.labNote: Treating generation as a budget line is the Lab's method. Many studios treat it as free, because the invoice is small and the energy is spent somewhere else. We hold that an architect who prices a detail before drawing five hundred of them should price a batch before running fifty. Choosing the smaller model, when it does the job, is a design decision, because it is a decision about consequences.
sections.howItWorks: Every call runs in a data centre that draws electricity and, usually, cooling water; the footprint and not-free cards on this map hold the scale. The energy per call is argued over and depends on model size, hardware and load, which is why this card carries no figure and is reviewed each edition. What does not change is the direction: larger models cost more per call than smaller ones, more generations cost more than fewer, and higher resolution costs more than lower. The International Energy Agency's 2025 report on energy and AI is the reference for the scale at which this adds up across grids. The method here is the studio-sized version of the cost-and-latency budget card — the same discipline, with energy counted beside rupees.

topics.name: Verify before you build on it
topics.description: Treat an AI claim that carries weight as unverified until it is checked against evidence fit for the claim. In codes, bye-laws and specs, an unchecked claim becomes your liability. Treat the answer as a lead, not a finding. Take each claim that matters and find the evidence that settles it.
evidence: Ask a model three questions about the building bye-laws of your city — setbacks, floor area ratio, parking. Then find the actual bye-law document and check each answer. Sort the results: right, wrong, and right-for-a-different-city.
Show one confident AI claim you caught by checking it against its source, and the two-column notes that kept it out of your work.
topics.critPrompt: Ask which facts in the site analysis came from AI, and which of those the student actually checked. The ratio is the grade.

grounding.ref: IFLA, How to Spot Fake News

card.oneLiner: Treat an AI claim that carries weight as unverified until it is checked against evidence fit for the claim. In codes, bye-laws and specs, an unchecked claim becomes your liability.

sections.whenToUse: Whenever an AI answer is about to enter something that carries weight: a site analysis, a drawing, a specification, a report, a jury presentation. Especially anything with a number, a rule, or a product name in it.
sections.method: Treat the answer as a lead, not a finding. Take each claim that matters and find the evidence that settles it. For a rule or a figure that is usually the primary document: the bye-law text itself, the municipal record, the standard. For a product it is the manufacturer's datasheet, read knowing the maker wrote it. For a scientific question a good review may be stronger than any single paper. Where no one source settles it, find two that do not copy each other. Write the source next to the claim. Keep your notes in two columns: verified, with a source; unverified, still unchecked. Nothing from the second column goes into the work. If a claim cannot be verified, it stays unchecked, and you say so where it appears.
sections.watchForThis: Verifying by asking the same model again, or by asking a second model. That is a second guess, not a check. A check needs something outside the model: a document, a measurement, a person who would know.
sections.tryIt: Ask a model three questions about the building bye-laws of your city — setbacks, floor area ratio, parking. Then find the actual bye-law document and check each answer. Sort the results: right, wrong, and right-for-a-different-city.
sections.proveIt: Show one confident AI claim you caught by checking it against its source, and the two-column notes that kept it out of your work.
sections.labNote: The two columns are the Lab's method, and we hold it strictly: a claim without a source beside it does not enter the work. It is not the only way to verify. Some studios check by sampling; some trust a retrieval system that quotes the document it read. We keep the columns because they make the unchecked visible, and because the cost of a wrong setback is a rebuild.
sections.howItWorks: A model answering from its training produces the likeliest-sounding continuation, not a retrieved fact. The likeliest bye-law for "a city in Karnataka" can be an average of several cities' rules, and an average is not law. Systems with search or retrieval attached can quote real documents, and an answer drawn from a document you supplied is an extraction, not a guess. It still needs reading: a quoted page can be the wrong edition, a real-looking citation can point nowhere, and a primary source can be self-interested. Verification is not distrust of the tool. It is what lets you use the tool at all.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position on what a young architect should aim to be paid for as the tools spread.

sections.position: The tools are changing what a young architect is paid to do. The tasks that used to be the junior's ladder — rendering, drafting options, first-draft writing, research summaries — are increasingly done faster by machines under a senior's direction. Facing that honestly is part of the literacy. The answer is neither fear nor cheerleading; it is to aim. The value hardest for a machine to multiply is judgment, authorship and direction: deciding what the work is for, standing behind it, and steering the machine's output toward it. Aim there, early, on purpose.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: The ladder is changing shape, not disappearing. Production tasks taught judgment by repetition. If the repetition moves to machines, judgment has to be taught and claimed on purpose. Surveys of practice show the tools arriving before any settled answer: the profession is adopting faster than it is deciding. The RIBA's 2026 survey of UK practices puts use at 74 per cent, up from 59 per cent a year earlier. That is UK evidence about UK offices, and Indian fees, labour and procurement differ; the direction is the part we read across. A student who aims at direction now is not waiting for the profession to tell them where to stand.
sections.strongestObjection: "Aim at judgment" may be advice only a senior can take. Judgment was learned by doing the production work; the years of drafting taught the eye. If machines take the production, the route to judgment may close behind the people who already have it. And the problem is not one student's career. It is the profession's: if the production ladder goes, where does the profession manufacture its next generation of judgment? In the 2026 UK survey, 61 per cent of practices agreed that AI will make it harder for early-career professionals to acquire essential skills and experience. Telling a first-year student to aim at direction skips the very years that made direction possible, and no school has yet shown it can teach those years another way.
sections.revisionCondition: Evidence from studios and schools that students who skipped production work do not develop judgment — that the ladder cannot be replaced by deliberate teaching. Or evidence that judgment itself is being priced down as fast as production. Or an Indian survey, when one exists, showing a different shape here. We re-read the practice surveys, and watch our own studio's juniors, every edition.
sections.tryIt: List ten tasks a junior did in an architecture office in 2015. Mark which a machine does now, under direction. For each marked task, write what the junior learned by doing it, and where that learning has to come from now.
sections.takeItToCrit: Where do you want your value to sit once the tools are everywhere — and what in your work this semester is evidence that you are building it?

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: The blast radius of an error

grounding.ref: From Tool to System: RAG, Agents and the Studio Stack

topics.description: A chatbot gives one wrong answer. An agent uses one wrong answer to take fifteen wrong actions. A chatbot's error is one wrong answer in a box. You read it, you catch it or you do not, and it goes no further on its own.
evidence: Take one automated workflow you use or plan. Draw its steps as a chain. Mark the first step where a wrong output is consumed by the next. Count the steps from there to the first place a human looks. That number is your blast radius. Shrink it.
Explain why the same error rate means a different risk in a chatbot and in an agent, using one chain of steps from your own work.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain why the same error rate means a different risk in a chatbot and in an agent, using one chain of steps from your own work.

card.oneLiner: A chatbot gives one wrong answer. An agent uses one wrong answer to take fifteen wrong actions.

sections.idea: A chatbot's error is one wrong answer in a box. You read it, you catch it or you do not, and it goes no further on its own. An agent's error is different in reach, not in kind. The agent takes its wrong answer as the start of its next step, and the next, and nobody reads the middle. One misread level name becomes fifteen wrong sheets. Blast radius is the measure: how much a single wrong step can touch before a person looks. It grows with permissions, autonomy and the time before anyone checks.
sections.whyItMatters: The size of a mistake is not the size of the error. It is the size of everything the error could reach before it was seen.
sections.inTheStudio: An agent is asked to update every sheet that references the ground-floor level after a change. It reads the new level from the wrong drawing. Every referencing sheet is now consistently, tidily wrong — and consistency is what a checker looks for.
sections.watchForThis: Judging an agent by the quality of its answers. Judge it by the reach of its actions. A brilliant agent with a large blast radius is more dangerous than a mediocre one with a small one.
sections.tryIt: Take one automated workflow you use or plan. Draw its steps as a chain. Mark the first step where a wrong output is consumed by the next. Count the steps from there to the first place a human looks. That number is your blast radius. Shrink it.
sections.proveIt: Explain why the same error rate means a different risk in a chatbot and in an agent, using one chain of steps from your own work.
sections.howItWorks: Errors compound along a chain. If each step is right ninety-five times in a hundred, a chain of ten unchecked steps comes out right only about sixty times in a hundred. That is arithmetic, not opinion, and it is why the people building these systems recommend short workflows with checkpoints over long autonomous runs. Two things shrink the radius: shorten the chain before a human reads, and make a wrong step stop the chain rather than feed it. Neither needs a smarter agent. Both need the workflow to be designed.

grounding.ref: Risk-aware explainable multi-output workflow for early-stage screening of building heating and cooling load indicators
A machine-learning framework for daylight and visual comfort assessment in early design stages

topics.description: Sun, wind, heating, cooling, daylight — the assistance is real, the validity limits are real, and the tool must state them. One: name the question and the decision it feeds. Two: get the inputs right — orientation, glazing area, envelope, and a climate file for your city, not a default one.
evidence: Ask a language model for the cooling load of a simple room you describe. Then ask it which climate, which construction and which dataset its number assumes. Note whether it can say. Then find a climate file for your own city and see how many of those assumptions were wrong.
For one early-stage screening, show the inputs you gave, the validity limits the tool stated, and the confirmation step before the number drove a decision.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to for one early-stage screening, show the inputs you gave, the validity limits the tool stated, and the confirmation step before the number drove a decision.

card.oneLiner: Sun, wind, heating, cooling, daylight — the assistance is real, the validity limits are real, and the tool must state them.

sections.whenToUse: Early, when you want to rank options by heating, cooling, daylight or shading before a full model exists — and every time a fast number is about to drive a decision.
sections.method: One: name the question and the decision it feeds. Two: get the inputs right — orientation, glazing area, envelope, and a climate file for your city, not a default one. Three: use the fast tool — a surrogate model, or a script the language model helped you write — to screen and rank, not to size: a surrogate sizes nothing, and decides no compliance figure, until it has been validated against a full simulation for your kind of building. Four: ask what the tool was trained on and whether your building sits inside that range; a surrogate is only valid near the cases it learnt from. Five: confirm the chosen option with a full simulation or an engineer before it becomes a design decision. Screen fast, confirm properly.
sections.watchForThis: A surrogate's accuracy score describing its own training set, not your building. A 2026 workflow paper reports fit scores above 0.97 on a benchmark of 768 simulated configurations and then says plainly that these must be read as interpolation within the benchmark, not as evidence about real buildings or plant sizing. Read every accuracy claim that way.
sections.tryIt: Ask a language model for the cooling load of a simple room you describe. Then ask it which climate, which construction and which dataset its number assumes. Note whether it can say. Then find a climate file for your own city and see how many of those assumptions were wrong.
sections.proveIt: For one early-stage screening, show the inputs you gave, the validity limits the tool stated, and the confirmation step before the number drove a decision.
sections.howItWorks: A surrogate is a learning model trained on the outputs of a physics simulation, so that it can answer in milliseconds what the simulation answers in minutes. The 2021 daylight framework on this card trained a network on 2,880 simulations of a single-window shoebox room; the 2026 heating-and-cooling workflow trained on 768 simulated configurations with explicit validity gates and uncertainty bands. Both are useful for ranking; neither knows a courtyard in Hubballi unless one was in the training set. India has climate files for many cities, and the tools that accept them are changing quickly. That, with the pace of new surrogate research, is why this card is marked EVOLVING.
