topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Looking at decay with a machine

grounding.ref: Agrafiotis et al., Unsupervised crack detection on complex stone masonry surfaces
Ranieri et al., Automated Monitoring of Cultural Heritage Artifacts Using Semantic Segmentation

topics.description: Crack detection, change over time and stain mapping from images — where vision models genuinely help a conservation architect, and where a trained eye on site still decides. Photograph systematically: every bay, every elevation, the same positions and the same time of day on every visit, with the positions kept in a register, so that this year's set can be laid over last year's. Run a crack or defect detector over the set.
evidence: Photograph one old wall — a compound wall, a temple plinth, a railway building — in fifty frames. Run any crack-detection or image-tagging tool over them. Check every flag on site with a ruler and a note. Count true flags, false flags, and cracks you found that it missed. Those three numbers tell you how the tool behaves on your wall.
Show one wall's machine-flagged image beside your site notes, with every flag judged — crack, joint, stain, shadow — the three counts stated, and one flagged item you overruled, with the reason.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one wall's machine-flagged image beside your site notes, with every flag judged — crack, joint, stain, shadow — the three counts stated, and one flagged item you overruled, with the reason.

card.oneLiner: Crack detection, change over time and stain mapping from images — where vision models genuinely help a conservation architect, and where a trained eye on site still decides.

sections.whenToUse: A building that must be looked after rather than redesigned: a condition survey before a conservation plan, a periodic check on a monument, a comparison of this year's photographs with last year's. Use the machine to look everywhere. Use a trained eye to decide what it found.
sections.method: Photograph systematically: every bay, every elevation, the same positions and the same time of day on every visit, with the positions kept in a register, so that this year's set can be laid over last year's. Run a crack or defect detector over the set. Research models trained on masonry and monument imagery can flag and outline cracks on stone walls, and general vision models can sort photographs by visible damage. Treat the output as a list of places to look, not as a diagnosis. Compare across time: align this visit's photograph with the last one and ask the machine for differences. Change is one of the things a condition survey looks for — beside present condition, severity, cause and urgency — and change is what a machine compares well, provided the two photographs are registered: same position, same lens, similar light, a dry wall both times. A shifted viewpoint, a wet patch or new vegetation reads as change. Then go to site with the list. A trained eye decides whether a flagged line is a structural crack, a mortar joint, a lichen edge or a shadow, and whether a stain is rising damp, a leaking pipe or last week's rain; record that judgement against each flag. Write the survey as a human document — condition, cause, urgency — with the machine's output as an appendix and its error rate stated.
sections.watchForThis: A detector trained on one kind of masonry flagging everything that resembles its training set. A laterite wall's natural pitting, the crazing of old lime plaster, a chisel mark on a basalt pillar can all come back as "crack". You do not know the false-alarm rate on your building until you count it on your building. And the crack it did not flag is the more dangerous error.
sections.tryIt: Photograph one old wall — a compound wall, a temple plinth, a railway building — in fifty frames. Run any crack-detection or image-tagging tool over them. Check every flag on site with a ruler and a note. Count true flags, false flags, and cracks you found that it missed. Those three numbers tell you how the tool behaves on your wall.
sections.proveIt: Show one wall's machine-flagged image beside your site notes, with every flag judged — crack, joint, stain, shadow — the three counts stated, and one flagged item you overruled, with the reason.
sections.howItWorks: Crack detection is a vision task of the kind VISION on this map describes: a network trained on labelled images of damaged and undamaged surfaces learns to classify patches or outline pixels. Research on stone masonry has treated it as anomaly detection: learn what the undamaged surface looks like, then flag anything that departs from it. Part of the reason is that heritage rules often forbid the test interventions other surveys rely on, so a non-destructive method has real value. The strength is coverage: a machine looks at every square metre of a façade with the same attention. The weakness is meaning: it sees a line, not a cause. Cause — movement, water, salts, vegetation, an earlier bad repair — is diagnosed by someone who knows the construction, on site, often by touch and by tapping. SCAN TO MODEL is the geometry this survey sits on; WHERE A HUMAN SIGNS applies to the survey as it does to the drawing. EVOLVING because the models and the public datasets are improving quickly — segmentation models now generalise to monument surfaces they were never trained on — so the boundary between what the machine can flag and what the eye must decide moves with each edition. The signature does not.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Counting carbon before you build
topics.description: For many new buildings a large share of the carbon is spent before anyone moves in — how large depends on the type, the structure and the lifespan; early-stage tools can estimate it from a massing and a material list — and be wrong by the assumptions nobody typed. Carbon is spent twice in a building. Operational carbon is the electricity and fuel it uses once occupied.
evidence: Take one studio scheme. List its five heaviest materials by rough mass. Look each up in the ICE database, which is free for education. Multiply and rank. Then change one decision — a filler slab for a flat slab, fly-ash brick for fired brick — and see which line moves. You have just done what the early-stage tools do, and now you know what they assume.

Explain the difference between embodied and operational carbon, name the three parts of embodied carbon and the boundary a count must state, and show one early-stage estimate where you can list every assumption behind the number.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain the difference between embodied and operational carbon, name the three parts of embodied carbon and the boundary a count must state, and show one early-stage estimate where you can list every assumption behind the number.

card.oneLiner: For many new buildings a large share of the carbon is spent before anyone moves in — how large depends on the type, the structure and the lifespan; early-stage tools can estimate it from a massing and a material list — and be wrong by the assumptions nobody typed.

sections.idea: Carbon is spent twice in a building. Operational carbon is the electricity and fuel it uses once occupied. Embodied carbon is the rest, in three parts: upfront — quarrying, cement kilns, steel mills, transport, the crane; use-stage — maintenance, repair, replacement and refurbishment over its life, modules B1 to B5 in the whole-life carbon standards; and end-of-life — demolition, transport, waste. As grids get cleaner and buildings get tighter, the embodied share grows. It can be counted early, from a massing and a material list, using databases of carbon per kilogram. The count is only as good as the list.
sections.whyItMatters: The decisions that set embodied carbon — structure, span, material, how much building there is — are made in the first weeks. A count that arrives at tender stage is too late to change anything.
sections.inTheStudio: A student asks a model to estimate the embodied carbon of her hostel block. It returns a figure in kgCO2e per square metre with a confident paragraph. She asks what it assumed for the cement, the steel, the transport distance and the floor area. It assumed a European concrete mix, a generic steel, no transport, and a floor area it misread from her prompt. The figure was arithmetic done on a list she never wrote.
sections.watchForThis: A single figure with no boundary. "Cradle to gate" counts up to the factory door; "cradle to grave" counts the use stage and demolition too; a figure that does not say which one is not usable. A count that stops at practical completion has left out every replacement the building will need — the façade at thirty years, the services at twenty — and the RICS whole-life standard puts those inside embodied carbon. Ask where the count starts and stops before asking how big it is.
sections.tryIt: Take one studio scheme. List its five heaviest materials by rough mass. Look each up in the ICE database, which is free for education. Multiply and rank. Then change one decision — a filler slab for a flat slab, fly-ash brick for fired brick — and see which line moves. You have just done what the early-stage tools do, and now you know what they assume.
sections.proveIt: Explain the difference between embodied and operational carbon, name the three parts of embodied carbon and the boundary a count must state, and show one early-stage estimate where you can list every assumption behind the number.
sections.howItWorks: An early-stage embodied-carbon tool multiplies quantities by factors. Quantities come from your massing — area, storeys, structural type. Factors come from databases: the ICE database began at the University of Bath and, in its 2026 educational release, covers more than 200 materials; Environmental Product Declarations give factors for named products; EC3, from Building Transparency, searches them. A learning model in the loop can read your drawings for quantities, pick factors and write the report. Wherever you gave it nothing, it picks a default and does not tell you. The surrogate-model card explains why a fast answer stays confident outside its range. The targets are moving too. The RIBA's 2030 Climate Challenge (version 2, 2021) sets embodied carbon for new UK offices below 750 kgCO2e/m² by 2030 against a business-as-usual figure of 1,400, and for schools below 540 against 1,000, counted to the RICS whole-life boundary. Indian factors differ — our cement, our grid, our brick — and Indian product declarations are a young programme. Because the databases, the tools and the targets are all being re-issued, this card is marked EVOLVING.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: GIS meets the model

grounding.ref: Li & Ning, Autonomous GIS: the next-generation AI-powered GIS

topics.description: A map you look at is a picture. GIS is layers of data with coordinates — and a model reads the picture badly and the data well. What you need to know about a site does not live in a picture of a map. It lives in layers, of two shapes.
evidence: Get one open layer for your site — satellite imagery or a land-use layer from Bhuvan, ISRO's geoportal, or road and building outlines from an open map project. Ask a model to help you write the steps to compute the plot area or the slope across it. Run them. Check one number by hand against the survey.
Explain the difference between a map as a picture and a map as data, and say which of the two a model handles well today.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain the difference between a map as a picture and a map as data, and say which of the two a model handles well today.

card.oneLiner: A map you look at is a picture. GIS is layers of data with coordinates — and a model reads the picture badly and the data well.

sections.idea: What you need to know about a site does not live in a picture of a map. It lives in layers, of two shapes. Vector layers (plot boundaries, roads, drains, land use) are tables of records with geometry attached. Raster layers (elevation, satellite imagery, rainfall, land cover) are grids of cells, each holding a value. Every layer has a source and a date. That is a geographic information system. A language model can help you find the layer, write the query and run the script. Shown a screenshot, it guesses the slope. Given the elevation layer, it computes it.
sections.whyItMatters: "The site looks low" and "the site is 1.2 metres below the road, per the elevation layer dated 2019" are different sentences. Only the second one can be checked.
sections.inTheStudio: A student pastes a screenshot from a mapping app and asks a model whether the site floods. The reply is fluent and unsourced. Another student downloads the contour and drainage layers, asks the model to help write the steps to find the lowest point on the plot, and checks one number against the site survey.
sections.watchForThis: Asking a model to read a map image for numbers — area, slope, distance. Today's multimodal models read pictures of maps much as they read pictures of plans: for likeness, not measurement.
sections.tryIt: Get one open layer for your site — satellite imagery or a land-use layer from Bhuvan, ISRO's geoportal, or road and building outlines from an open map project. Ask a model to help you write the steps to compute the plot area or the slope across it. Run them. Check one number by hand against the survey.
sections.proveIt: Explain the difference between a map as a picture and a map as data, and say which of the two a model handles well today.
sections.howItWorks: The research direction is clear: a 2023 paper proposed the language model as the reasoning core of a GIS, writing and running the spatial analysis code from a question in plain language, and demonstrated a prototype doing so. That is the model as a programmer of spatial tools, not as a reader of maps. This card is marked EVOLVING because vision models are improving at reading map images and GIS tools are gaining language interfaces, so the line between picture and data is moving. The principle holds either way: a number you will act on comes from a layer with a source and a date, and the model's job is to get you to the layer.

topics.name: AI and the material choice

grounding.ref: EPD International — What is an EPD?

topics.description: A model can read a product declaration, compare carbon across options and summarise a datasheet; it cannot feel a wall or know your local kiln — use it to narrow, never to decide. One: gather the documents, not the adjectives — the EPD, the datasheet, the test report. Two: give the model the documents and ask for a table: embodied carbon with its boundary, the declared unit, strength or U-value, the distance from the named plant to your site, and the date of the declaration.
evidence: Find two EPDs for a material you use — two bricks, two cements, two tiles — from the Indian or the international EPD library. Ask a model to build the comparison table with boundary, unit and date in every row. Then find the one line where it quietly compared unlike with unlike.
Show one material decision with the model's comparison table beside it, the two lines that ruled options out, and the reason the final choice came from something the table could not hold.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one material decision with the model's comparison table beside it, the two lines that ruled options out, and the reason the final choice came from something the table could not hold.

card.oneLiner: A model can read a product declaration, compare carbon across options and summarise a datasheet; it cannot feel a wall or know your local kiln — use it to narrow, never to decide.

sections.whenToUse: When a material decision has more than two options and each comes with documents: a datasheet, a product declaration, a test certificate, a supplier's claim.
sections.method: One: gather the documents, not the adjectives — the EPD, the datasheet, the test report. Two: give the model the documents and ask for a table: embodied carbon with its boundary, the declared unit, strength or U-value, the distance from the named plant to your site, and the date of the declaration. Three: ask it to flag what each document does not say. Four: use the table to narrow to two or three options. Five: decide using what the table cannot hold — a sample in your hand, a visit to the kiln or the yard, the mason's word on what can be laid well here, and what the local supply will actually deliver in the monsoon. The model narrows. You decide.
sections.watchForThis: A comparison across declarations with different boundaries or units. One EPD counts cradle-to-gate per tonne; another counts cradle-to-grave per square metre. A model will put them in one column and not notice. Make it state boundary and unit in every row.
sections.tryIt: Find two EPDs for a material you use — two bricks, two cements, two tiles — from the Indian or the international EPD library. Ask a model to build the comparison table with boundary, unit and date in every row. Then find the one line where it quietly compared unlike with unlike.
sections.proveIt: Show one material decision with the model's comparison table beside it, the two lines that ruled options out, and the reason the final choice came from something the table could not hold.
sections.howItWorks: An Environmental Product Declaration is an independently verified, registered document that reports a product's environmental performance from a life-cycle assessment, under rules written for its product category. EPD International runs the global programme, and the Indian EPD programme is aligned with it. These documents are long, structured and numerical — exactly what a language model reads well. What the model cannot help with is the part of a material decision that has no document: how a stone weathers on this coast, which kiln near Dharwad fires evenly, whether the mason has laid a cavity wall before. The method ends with those on purpose. Declarations are being issued faster than they are read, and Indian product coverage is growing from a small base. That is why this card is marked EVOLVING.

topics.name: Minutes, mail, and the record

grounding.ref: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle

topics.description: Meeting notes and correspondence drafted with AI — speed set against confidentiality and the accuracy of the record. One: before anything is uploaded, decide what may leave the studio — client names, fees, unreleased drawings and anything under a non-disclosure agreement usually may not, and the confidential-inputs card on this map governs the call. Two: record with consent, transcribe, and let the model draft.
evidence: Record a site or studio meeting with everyone's consent — one that runs the way most meetings in Karnataka run, in Kannada and English mixed, with the numbers in one language and the reasons in the other. Draft the minutes with a tool. Then check every decision line against the recording. Count the lines that drifted — softened, merged, or misattributed — and count separately the lines that went wrong at a switch between languages, or where a Kannada name or place came back Romanised three ways. That count is the liability you would have circulated, and the second count is the one no English-language demo will show you.

card.oneLiner: Meeting notes and correspondence drafted with AI — speed set against confidentiality and the accuracy of the record.

sections.whenToUse: Any meeting note, mail or letter that someone will rely on later: a client decision, a consultant's instruction, a site instruction, a change in scope.
sections.method: One: before anything is uploaded, decide what may leave the studio — client names, fees, unreleased drawings and anything under a non-disclosure agreement usually may not, and the confidential-inputs card on this map governs the call. Two: record with consent, transcribe, and let the model draft. Three: mark every decision, figure, date and name in the draft, and check each one against the recording or your own notes — not against your memory of the meeting. Four: circulate as "draft minutes, as recorded by", with a correction window. Five: file the recording or notes beside the minutes, so the record has a source.
sections.watchForThis: Minutes that record what the model thought was said. A smooth summary drops the disagreement, and the disagreement is usually the point of the meeting. A long recording makes this worse: models recall the middle of a long transcript less reliably than its start and end.
sections.tryIt: Record a site or studio meeting with everyone's consent — one that runs the way most meetings in Karnataka run, in Kannada and English mixed, with the numbers in one language and the reasons in the other. Draft the minutes with a tool. Then check every decision line against the recording. Count the lines that drifted — softened, merged, or misattributed — and count separately the lines that went wrong at a switch between languages, or where a Kannada name or place came back Romanised three ways. That count is the liability you would have circulated, and the second count is the one no English-language demo will show you.
sections.proveIt: Show one set of minutes with each decision, figure, date and name ticked against its source, and the source filed beside it.
sections.howItWorks: Minutes are a record, and a record's value is that it can be checked later by someone who was not there. A model drafting minutes is predicting what minutes of such a meeting usually say, shaped by the transcript, which is why it smooths, merges and tidies. Long transcripts add a second failure: research on long contexts has measured that material in the middle of a long input is recalled less reliably than material at the ends. The method puts the checking on the items that carry consequence — decisions, figures, dates, names — and leaves the prose to the model.

card.oneLiner: On a document where every word carries responsibility, you write the words; the model only protects and lays them out.

sections.whenToUse: Any document where a changed word changes what you are promising: a bill of quantities, a fee proposal, a scope note, a specification clause, a letter to a client or a municipal office.
sections.method: Write the load-bearing text yourself, first. Then mark it: the quantities, the exclusions, the dates, the fee, and the small words that carry weight — "shall", "excluding", "subject to". Brief the model to keep the marked text exactly as written — no paraphrase, no tidying, no synonyms — and to work only on what surrounds it: layout, headings, a covering note, a table. When the model returns, compare the marked text against your original word by word. Anything changed is reverted, however much better it reads.
sections.watchForThis: The helpful paraphrase. "Excluding external works" becomes "external works to be discussed." The sentence reads better. The promise has changed. The model cannot tell which words are load-bearing, because to the model every sentence is just likely text.
sections.tryIt: Take one real document — a scope note from a studio, or a college project brief. Mark the load-bearing words. Ask a model to "improve the clarity" with no protection brief. Then run it again with the brief. Lay the three versions side by side and find where the meaning moved.
sections.proveIt: Show one responsible sentence a model paraphrased into a different promise, and the protection brief that would have stopped it.
sections.labNote: This is our method, from the studio's own documents: write the words, lock the words, let the model do everything else. Others let the model draft and then check. We find that checking a fluent paraphrase is harder than writing the sentence, because fluency hides the change.
sections.howItWorks: A model paraphrases because that is what it does: it continues text in the likeliest way, and the likeliest way is rarely your exact wording. An instruction to "preserve exactly" works most of the time, never every time. A written instruction asks; the system's own controls enforce. The controls here are simple: keep the protected text in a file the model never receives and paste it back yourself, or lock the cells and fields it must not touch, and then run a deterministic diff of the marked passages against your original. That is why the method ends with a word-by-word comparison rather than trust. The skill underneath is older than any tool: knowing which word cannot move. That is what a senior reads a junior's letter for.

card.oneLiner: Decide what kind of intelligence a task needs before you open any app.

sections.dilemma: A task arrives — say, a massing study for a tight corner plot. You know three apps well. Do you open the one you know best, or stop and ask what kind of engine this task actually needs?
sections.choices: Open the familiar app and bend the task to fit it. Or sort the task first into one of six families: reasoning (a model that plans and argues), dreaming (an image engine that explores freely), grounded (a generator that holds your geometry), data (tables, numbers, a spreadsheet brain), geometry (a modeller or a parametric tool), or cinema (a video engine). Then pick an app from the right family. The six families are the Lab's routing frame; the app names under them change every season.
sections.consequence: Route by brand and you get a dreaming engine doing a geometry job: beautiful massing that will not stand on the plot. Route by family and the app becomes replaceable, because the routing decision outlives every product launch. The same task often changes family as the project moves: dreaming at concept, grounded in design development, geometry at delivery.
sections.theCase: A student wants "options for the façade." In week two that is a dreaming job: explore widely. In week ten, with the structure fixed, the same words are a grounded job: hold the geometry, vary the skin. Same sentence, different engine. The student who routes by brand does week ten in a dreaming engine and drifts the structure without noticing.
sections.takeItToCrit: When the student reaches for a tool, first ask which family the task belongs to, and why that family at this stage. Do they choose by the goal, or by the brand they happen to know?

topics.description: Reversibility is the first test the Lab applies, not the only one: hand over what can be undone, hold what cannot — and then ask what else a wrong step could cost. An agent can now carry a task across many steps: rename the drawing set, update the register, draft the issue mail, send it. It is Friday evening.
evidence: Write ten tasks from your studio week on slips of paper. Sort them into two piles: undoable, not undoable. Then look at the second pile and name, for each, what a wrong version would cost and who would carry it. Those are the tasks a person signs. Now go back to the first pile and find the one slip that is undoable and still should not be delegated — there is usually one — and say which of the four further questions caught it.
For one task the student delegated this term: could it have been undone, and did they know that before they handed it over? If they cannot answer the first question, the second does not matter.
topics.critPrompt: For one task the student delegated this term: could it have been undone, and did they know that before they handed it over? If they cannot answer the first question, the second does not matter.

card.oneLiner: Reversibility is the first test the Lab applies, not the only one: hand over what can be undone, hold what cannot — and then ask what else a wrong step could cost.

sections.dilemma: An agent can now carry a task across many steps: rename the drawing set, update the register, draft the issue mail, send it. It is Friday evening. You can hand it the whole chain and go home, or hold the last step, or hold all of them and do the work yourself. Which steps are yours to give away?
sections.choices: Delegate everything repetitive and spot-check afterwards. Delegate nothing, because the agent might get it wrong. Or sort by a first question — can this step be undone? — and delegate the undoable steps while holding every step that cannot be reversed: sending, deleting, paying, submitting, overwriting the only copy. Then put the undoable pile through four more questions before it goes: what is the consequence if it is wrong; does the agent have the authority to do this at all; does the step touch anything sensitive; and would you notice if it went wrong. A reversible step that leaks a client's drawing to the wrong address is not safe because it can be re-sent.
sections.consequence: Delegate everything and one irreversible action slips through on the night the agent misreads a sheet number; the contractor now holds a wrong issue with your studio's name on it. Delegate nothing and you have bought an expensive tool and left it idle. Sort by reversibility and you get speed where a mistake is cheap and your attention where it is expensive. The renaming can be redone; the email cannot be unsent.
sections.theCase: Four hundred drawings to renumber under a new sheet convention, a drawing register to update, and an issue to the contractor due tonight. The agent proposes to do all three. A second-year hands over all three. A fifth-year hands over the renaming and the register, checks the register against ten sheets, and sends the issue mail from their own account after reading it.
sections.takeItToCrit: For one task the student delegated this term: could it have been undone, and did they know that before they handed it over? If they cannot answer the first question, the second does not matter.
sections.howItWorks: Practitioner guidance from the companies that build these systems says the same thing in their own words: keep agent workflows simple, and put a human checkpoint before any consequential action. Reversibility is the studio's first version of that rule, and it has a useful property: it does not require you to predict whether the agent will be right. It only requires you to know what happens if it is wrong. The next two cards take the idea further: how far a wrong step can reach, and what an agent can see and change.

topics.name: Site research with a fast assistant
topics.description: Let the AI draft the questions; let primary sources give the answers. Four moves. One: describe the site and the brief to a model and ask for the questions a thorough site analysis would answer — the questions, not the answers.
evidence: Pick a real plot you can visit. Get a model's question list. Walk the site with the list and answer what you can by looking. Count how many questions only the visit could answer, and how many the model had quietly answered wrong before you went.
Show one site dossier with a source cited for every fact the design leans on, and one AI-drafted question that genuinely changed where you looked.
topics.critPrompt: Does the dossier clearly separate what the AI suggested from what a real source confirmed?

grounding.ref: Whole Building Design Guide, Architectural Programming

card.oneLiner: Let the AI draft the questions; let primary sources give the answers.

sections.whenToUse: The first fortnight of any project — site, context, climate, programme — when the question list is long and you do not yet know what you do not know.
sections.method: Four moves. One: describe the site and the brief to a model and ask for the questions a thorough site analysis would answer — the questions, not the answers. Two: sort them — keep, merge, drop, and add the ones it missed, which will be the local ones. Three: answer each kept question from a primary source — the site visit, the survey, the municipal record, the meteorological data, the neighbour — and write the source beside the answer. A resident who has watched the lane flood every monsoon for thirty years is evidence, like the drainage layer; that a dataset is easier for a machine to read does not make it the stronger source. Four: build the dossier with two visible layers: what the AI suggested, and what a real source confirmed. Anything the model answered on its own stays marked as a lead until a source arrives.
sections.watchForThis: The model answering the questions it was asked only to pose. It will, fluently, with the climate of a city three hundred kilometres away. Take the questions; discard the answers.
sections.tryIt: Pick a real plot you can visit. Get a model's question list. Walk the site with the list and answer what you can by looking. Count how many questions only the visit could answer, and how many the model had quietly answered wrong before you went.
sections.proveIt: Show one site dossier with a source cited for every fact the design leans on, and one AI-drafted question that genuinely changed where you looked.
sections.howItWorks:
Models are strong at the shape of an enquiry — what a site analysis usually covers — because they have read thousands of them. They are weak at your site, because it was never in the data. Systems with search attached can fetch public documents, which shortens step three for some facts. It does not replace the visit, the survey, or the conversation with the person next door. This method was first taught in the Lab's own workshops and is kept there as a module.
Site research is also the first of several places where AI enters a studio without making any images. The same discipline — draft fast, then verify against a source — runs through scheduling and programme checks, specification drafting, the small scripts and code a studio needs, and the early-stage simulation surrogates that estimate daylight or heating and cooling loads before a full model exists. Each of those has its own card on this map with its own verification rules. The habit you are learning here is the one they all share.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Comparing drawings
topics.description: What changed between issues — where machine comparison helps, and where a vision model's reading of a drawing fails. One: if you have vector files, compare geometry — overlay the two issues, or run a drawing-comparison tool; geometric comparison is deterministic once the two files are correctly registered and normalised — same origin, same units, same layer states — and is only as good as that registration. Two: if you only have scans or rasters, overlay at the same scale and flick between them, or run an image difference; expect noise.
evidence: Take two issues of one plan. Ask a vision model what changed. Then overlay them yourself. Score the model: found, missed, invented. Keep the score; it is your own measurement of a moving capability.
Show one change register where every entry was confirmed against the two sheets, and say which entries the machine found and which it missed.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one change register where every entry was confirmed against the two sheets, and say which entries the machine found and which it missed.

card.oneLiner: What changed between issues — where machine comparison helps, and where a vision model's reading of a drawing fails.

sections.whenToUse: A new issue of a drawing arrives and you must know exactly what moved before anything downstream moves with it.
sections.method: One: if you have vector files, compare geometry — overlay the two issues, or run a drawing-comparison tool; geometric comparison is deterministic once the two files are correctly registered and normalised — same origin, same units, same layer states — and is only as good as that registration. Two: if you only have scans or rasters, overlay at the same scale and flick between them, or run an image difference; expect noise. Three: a vision model's "summary of changes" is a lead list, never a finding — ask it for suspected changes, then check every one yourself against both sheets. Four: record each confirmed change in the revision register, clouded on the drawing, with the issue date. Five: anything the model did not flag is not therefore unchanged.
sections.watchForThis: A multimodal model describing two plans as identical when a door swung the other way. Current benchmarks built from real drawings show these models counting doors, windows and rooms unreliably on plans; a door that moved is harder still.
sections.tryIt: Take two issues of one plan. Ask a vision model what changed. Then overlay them yourself. Score the model: found, missed, invented. Keep the score; it is your own measurement of a moving capability.
sections.proveIt: Show one change register where every entry was confirmed against the two sheets, and say which entries the machine found and which it missed.
sections.howItWorks: Drawings are a notation, and notation carries meaning in small marks — a swing arc, a hatch, a level tag. Image models trained mostly on photographs learn appearance, not notation, so they see a plan the way they see a picture of a plan. Vector comparison does not have this problem because it never looks; it subtracts coordinates. Its own failure is upstream: a shifted origin, a unit mismatch or a layer left off makes everything look moved, or nothing. That is why the method routes geometry to arithmetic and gives the model only the job it is good at: producing a list of places to look. EVOLVING because drawing-trained models are an active research direction and the benchmarks are re-run on every new model.

topics.name: Using AI does not lower the standard

grounding.ref: The Architects Act, 1972 — text, hosted by the Council of Architecture
Council of Architecture, Architects (Professional Conduct) Regulations, 1989

topics.description: The law and the Council set what a registered architect owes; a tool in the workflow changes none of it. In India the title "architect" belongs to the people on the register kept under the Architects Act, 1972. The Act lets the Council of Architecture set standards of conduct, and reprimand, suspend or remove an architect for misconduct.
evidence: Read regulation 2(1) of the 1989 conduct regulations; it is one page. For each duty an AI tool in your workflow could touch, write one line on how. Then pick one duty and describe the check you would add so that the tool's output meets it.
Take one AI-assisted deliverable and show, duty by duty, how it meets the standard the Council sets — and name the person who signs it.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to take one AI-assisted deliverable and show, duty by duty, how it meets the standard the Council sets — and name the person who signs it.

card.oneLiner: The law and the Council set what a registered architect owes; a tool in the workflow changes none of it.

sections.idea: In India the title "architect" belongs to the people on the register kept under the Architects Act, 1972. The Act lets the Council of Architecture set standards of conduct, and reprimand, suspend or remove an architect for misconduct. The Council's 1989 regulations say what the standard is: services of a high standard, a high standard of integrity, work that serves society's welfare. None of it mentions tools, because none of it depends on tools. A drawing made with AI is judged by the same standard as one made by hand. The person who signed it answers for it.
sections.whyItMatters: "The AI did it" is not a defence anyone has accepted for a bad drawing, and nothing in the law suggests it will be. The standard stays where it was. The tool only changes how fast you can fall below it.
sections.inTheStudio: A small office uses a model to draft the fire-escape schedule for a commercial building. The output looks complete and is wrong about travel distance in one wing. The sheet goes out under the architect's stamp. At approval the error is caught by the fire officer — or it is not. Either way, the question asked is not "which software?" but "who signed this, and did they check it?"
sections.watchForThis: Reading "AI does not lower the standard" as "AI must not be used". The duty is to the standard of the work, not to the method. A tool that helps you check more, faster, raises your ability to meet the standard. It cannot meet it for you, and it cannot take the blame.
sections.tryIt: Read regulation 2(1) of the 1989 conduct regulations; it is one page. For each duty an AI tool in your workflow could touch, write one line on how. Then pick one duty and describe the check you would add so that the tool's output meets it.
sections.proveIt: Take one AI-assisted deliverable and show, duty by duty, how it meets the standard the Council sets — and name the person who signs it.
sections.howItWorks: Two layers, kept apart on purpose. The duty is Parliament's and the Council's. The Architects Act, 1972 reserves the title to registered architects (section 37), lets the Council prescribe standards of conduct and a code of ethics and define what counts as professional misconduct (section 22), and provides the inquiry and the penalties (section 30). The 1989 regulations, made under the Act, are the code: high standard of service, integrity, fairness in administering a building contract, duties to clients, employees and consultants. How that duty applies to AI-assisted work is the Lab's reading, not the Council's text. Neither the Act nor the regulations mention AI. The Council has moved on AI in education — capacity-building programmes, curriculum — but, to the Lab's knowledge as of August 2026, it has issued no conduct guidance on AI in practice. Our reading is the plain one: the regulations bind the architect; the architect's output is the architect's whatever the method; so the standard of care is unchanged and the checking burden sits with the architect. Other professions are reading their own codes the same way — the RIBA's 2025 AI report is one example. The card is DURABLE because the duty is older than the tool, and a future Council guidance would add to this card, not reverse it. WHERE A HUMAN SIGNS is the procedure this principle rests on.

Draw the workflow you actually follow, not the one you would describe to a jury: every step from brief to submission, with who does it, what it produces, and how long it really takes. Mark the three hardest steps — the ones that eat nights.

Show a real workflow map with its three hardest steps marked and a defended yes or no for each.

card.oneLiner: Draw your real workflow, every step, before any AI enters it.

sections.whenToUse: Before adopting any AI tool into a project, a studio, or your own semester — and again whenever the way you work has drifted from the last map.
sections.method: Draw the workflow you actually follow, not the one you would describe to a jury: every step from brief to submission, with who does it, what it produces, and how long it really takes. Mark the three hardest steps — the ones that eat nights. For each, ask two questions: would an AI reduce the friction here, and would it replace the part that is the point? Only then place tools on the map. Mark the places where the answer is "no" as clearly as the places where it is "yes".

sections.tryIt: Map your last studio project honestly, hour by hour. Mark the three steps that hurt. Argue, in writing, which of them an AI actually helps with, and which it would hollow out.

sections.labNote: Map before tools is how we run every engagement, and the Lab keeps it as a standing rule in its own codex. The reason is not efficiency. No workflow is neutral. Every one carries a view of how design should happen, and the map is where that view becomes visible enough to argue with.
sections.howItWorks: Tools enter a process at its weak points, and you can only find the weak points in the real process. The map shows a second thing that is harder to see. A workflow that renders before it plans has already decided that the image comes first. Adding AI to that workflow speeds up that decision. The map lets you see it before it speeds up.

topics.description: Chatbot, custom assistant, agent, studio system — four points on one line, not four separate products. A chatbot answers when asked. A custom assistant answers with your studio's material loaded.

card.oneLiner: Chatbot, custom assistant, agent, studio system — four points on one line, not four separate products.

sections.idea: A chatbot answers when asked. A custom assistant answers with your studio's material loaded. An agent works through a sequence — searches, drafts, checks, files — inside a loop someone designed. A studio system is several of these with rules between them, running over time. Read the four as one line and each new product launch becomes a point on it, not noise. What changes along the line is not cleverness. It is how long the machine acts without you, and so who answers for what it did.
sections.whyItMatters: "Should I use AI?" is four different questions at four points on the line, and the fourth is a question about responsibility, not tools.
sections.inTheStudio: Asking a chatbot to summarise a bye-law is a one-off. A standing system that reads every new drawing against the bye-laws and flags possible breaches is a colleague who never sleeps and never signs. Who checks its flags? Who answers for the one it missed?

sections.tryIt: Take one task you do weekly — a precedent search, minutes, a drawing check. Write it four ways: as a chat question; as a question to an assistant holding your files; as an agent's sequence; as a standing system. Mark where a human must sign at each.

Published practitioner guidance recommends starting with the simplest loop that works and adding autonomy only where it earns its place. EVOLVING because the line is still being drawn. What counts as an "agent", and how far it runs unsupervised, shifts with each release, and the responsibility question is being settled in practice before it is settled anywhere else. topics.name: The structured building

grounding.ref: TU Delft, AI in Architectural Design
ResPlan: A Large-Scale Vector-Graph Dataset of 17,000 Residential Floor Plans

topics.description: Much of practice runs on structured building data, not renders — and where learning systems meet that data, progress is slower than the demos. A building information model holds walls, doors, levels and quantities as objects with properties and relationships, not as pixels. It is one substrate of practice, beside contracts, specifications and surveys, and the one an image generator lacks.
evidence: Open any building model. Pick one element — a door — and list every property it carries. Then sort the list: which of these could a learned system have filled from pattern, and which needed a person who knew the project? The second pile is the argument of this card.
Explain the difference between a system that sees pixels and one that reads structured objects, with one example of what each can do that the other cannot.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain the difference between a system that sees pixels and one that reads structured objects, with one example of what each can do that the other cannot.

card.oneLiner: Much of practice runs on structured building data, not renders — and where learning systems meet that data, progress is slower than the demos.

sections.idea: A building information model holds walls, doors, levels and quantities as objects with properties and relationships, not as pixels. It is one substrate of practice, beside contracts, specifications and surveys, and the one an image generator lacks. An image model conditioned on a depth or edge map is not blind to structure, but it carries no object semantics: it does not know a door from a gap. Systems that connect a language model to the IFC data read the objects directly. That work is slower than the demos: the data is messy, proprietary and shaped differently in every office.
sections.whyItMatters: A tool that handles the skin well and cannot read the body is a visualiser, not a design assistant. Knowing which of the two a tool works on tells you what it can really do.
sections.inTheStudio: An "AI plan generator" demo produces a handsome apartment layout in seconds. The studio's live model of a hospital wing holds tens of thousands of elements with fire ratings, levels and phases attached. The demo cannot open it. The two are not the same kind of thing, and the demo knows only one of them.
sections.watchForThis: "AI-powered BIM" on a product page. Ask two questions: what building data did the learning part train on, and what can it write back into the model? If the answers are "not disclosed" and "nothing", it is a viewer with a chatbot.
sections.tryIt: Open any building model. Pick one element — a door — and list every property it carries. Then sort the list: which of these could a learned system have filled from pattern, and which needed a person who knew the project? The second pile is the argument of this card.
sections.proveIt: Explain the difference between a system that sees pixels and one that reads structured objects, with one example of what each can do that the other cannot.
sections.howItWorks: Two different kinds of system meet the building. A pixel system — a diffusion model, with or without conditioning — learns appearance; conditioning on an edge map or a depth map holds the structure it is shown, but it never knows what the structure is. A structured system — a language model given the IFC file, or a rules engine over the model's objects — reads elements, properties and the relationships between them, and can be asked which doors on level three lack a fire rating. The first kind is trained on billions of photographs. The second is starved: a recent open dataset of residential plans as vector geometry with room-connectivity graphs and metric coordinates holds seventeen thousand, and it is large for its kind. Structured building data is scarce, proprietary and inconsistent, so the systems that read it are narrower and arrive later. The UK practice survey of 2025 showed the same shape — AI use most common in early visualisation and specification writing, with simulation and performance modelling less established; UK evidence, read as such. EVOLVING because the datasets are growing, the IFC-reading systems are new, and the vendors are moving; the gap between the two kinds of system is real today and is reviewed every edition.

topics.description: A client's "something like this" image is evidence to cross-examine, not an instruction to follow. The client arrives with a Pinterest board and three AI renders: "something like this." The images are glossy, the client is pleased, and the brief meeting has forty minutes left. Do you take the images as the brief, or take them apart?
evidence: Take a client’s reference image and list the un-buildable promises hidden in it
Turn a “something like this” image into the questions that recover the real brief
topics.critPrompt: Does the student cross-examine a client's image, or inherit it as an instruction? Ask for the list of un-buildable promises in one reference image, and the questions that recovered the brief.

grounding.ref: The AI Design Director Protocol — the-ai-design-director-protocol

card.oneLiner: A client's "something like this" image is evidence to cross-examine, not an instruction to follow.

sections.dilemma: The client arrives with a Pinterest board and three AI renders: "something like this." The images are glossy, the client is pleased, and the brief meeting has forty minutes left. Do you take the images as the brief, or take them apart?
sections.choices: Accept the image as an instruction and start designing toward it. Or read it as evidence of what the client wants, and question it: what does this picture promise that cannot be built on this plot, at this budget, in this climate? The cantilever with nothing under it. The floor-to-ceiling glass facing west in Hubli. The junction no material makes. Then turn each promise into a question that gets you to the real brief: is it the openness you want, or the glass?
sections.consequence: Take the image as the brief and you take on its promises. The day the engineer draws the column the client "was never shown", the disappointment is yours. Question it and the image becomes the most useful document in the room: a record of what the client wants, with the physics removed, which is exactly where a brief should begin.
sections.theCase: A couple bring an AI render of a "Kerala-style" house: a sweeping tiled roof, a double-height courtyard, a glass wall to the garden. The plot is thirty feet wide in a Bengaluru layout with a neighbour hard on each side. The roof cannot sweep, the courtyard eats a bedroom, the glass wall looks into the neighbour's bathroom. The student who asks "what in this picture do you love?" gets three answers — shade, a tree inside the house, light in the evening — and a buildable brief.
sections.takeItToCrit: Does the student cross-examine a client's image, or inherit it as an instruction? Ask for the list of un-buildable promises in one reference image, and the questions that recovered the brief.
sections.howItWorks: An image engine is built to make a building look right, not to make it stand. Spans, junctions and budgets are invisible to it, so its output is fluent exactly where a brief must be exact. The Lab's director protocol begins here, with diagnosis — reading the image for what it promises — before any reasoning or direction starts.

topics.name: Reading regulations with a machine

grounding.ref: Liu et al., Lost in the Middle
Whole Building Design Guide, Architectural Programming

topics.description: Byelaws and standards — extraction with page-true verification, because the stakes are legal. One: get the actual document — the edition in force for your city, because byelaws differ between cities and states and change between editions. Two: give the document to the model, as an upload, rather than asking its memory.
evidence: Ask a model a byelaw question cold, for your own city. Then give it the actual byelaw document and ask again, with clause references. Then open the clause. Three answers; count how many agree.
Show one extracted table of regulatory figures with a clause and page reference on every line, and every line ticked after you read the page.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one extracted table of regulatory figures with a clause and page reference on every line, and every line ticked after you read the page.

card.oneLiner: Byelaws and standards — extraction with page-true verification, because the stakes are legal.

sections.whenToUse: Any time a clause decides a number in the design: setbacks, floor-area ratio, fire separation, stair widths, accessibility, parking. Any time a regulation is about to be quoted in a document with your studio's name on it.
sections.method: One: get the actual document — the edition in force for your city, because byelaws differ between cities and states and change between editions. Two: give the document to the model, as an upload, rather than asking its memory. Three: ask for extraction with the clause number and page number beside every item. Four: open every page cited and read the clause yourself — page-true verification, every time. Five: record clause, edition and the date you checked it beside the figure in your notes. Six: anything the model gave you without a page reference is a guess, however fluent, and does not enter the drawing.
sections.watchForThis: A model answering a byelaw question from memory. Its memory is a blend of many cities and many editions, and the blend reads exactly like a clause. Mumbai's setbacks are not Bengaluru's; the National Building Code of India, published by the Bureau of Indian Standards, is a reference many local byelaws draw on but do not copy.
sections.tryIt: Ask a model a byelaw question cold, for your own city. Then give it the actual byelaw document and ask again, with clause references. Then open the clause. Three answers; count how many agree.
sections.proveIt: Show one extracted table of regulatory figures with a clause and page reference on every line, and every line ticked after you read the page.
sections.howItWorks: When the document is in front of the model, the answer comes from reading rather than recall — the grounding move this map calls bringing your own facts. It is much better and still not enough: models can mis-cite a page, merge two clauses, or quietly recall a figure from memory when the document is long, since material in the middle of a long input is recalled less reliably than its ends. The verification step exists because the figure ends up on a drawing that a registered professional signs, and a wrong setback means a rebuild, a penalty, or a refused permission. Opening the page costs minutes. Not opening it can cost the client and the contractor as well as you.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Read the competition's AI rules
topics.description: Find the competition's AI rule, follow it, and be able to point to the clause. Open the brief and the terms. For a competition in India, read them beside the Council of Architecture's Architectural Design Competition Guidelines, which set who may enter, how anonymity is kept and what a promoter must state; competition conditions are meant to be written under them.
evidence: Find a current architecture or illustration competition brief. Locate its AI clause, or confirm there is none. Summarise it in three lines and draft the disclosure statement an entry would need.
Before submitting, show the exact clause and the entry's disclosure beside it, and explain how the process met the rule, image by image.
topics.critPrompt: Before the student submits, ask where the competition's AI rule is, and whether the entry follows it. Can they point to the exact clause?

grounding.ref: Council of Architecture, Architectural Design Competition Guidelines
ASAI, Terms and Conditions for the Architecture in Perspective competitions

card.oneLiner: Find the competition's AI rule, follow it, and be able to point to the clause.

sections.whenToUse: Before you start an entry — not the night before submission — and again before you submit, when the entry has changed since you first read the brief.
sections.method: Open the brief and the terms. For a competition in India, read them beside the Council of Architecture's Architectural Design Competition Guidelines, which set who may enter, how anonymity is kept and what a promoter must state; competition conditions are meant to be written under them. Then search the brief for the words: AI, artificial, generated, originality, disclosure, authorship. Read the clause in full, including what it says about labelling and proof. Write three lines: what is allowed, what is forbidden, what must be disclosed. Plan the process to fit — if AI-assisted images must be labelled, decide now which images will carry the label. At submission, draft the disclosure statement the clause asks for, in the form it asks for. Keep the clause and your statement in the project folder.
sections.watchForThis: A brief with no AI clause at all. Silence is neither permission nor a ban. It is a question for the organiser, in writing, before you start. And if a clause reserves the right to ask for proof of originality, keep your process files: "proof" means showing the work.
sections.tryIt: Find a current architecture or illustration competition brief. Locate its AI clause, or confirm there is none. Summarise it in three lines and draft the disclosure statement an entry would need.
sections.proveIt: Before submitting, show the exact clause and the entry's disclosure beside it, and explain how the process met the rule, image by image.
sections.howItWorks: Competition terms are a contract, and entering accepts them. In India the frame above the contract is the Council of Architecture's competition guidelines: open competitions are for architects registered under the Architects Act, 1972; ideas competitions may admit students of architecture at the promoter's discretion; entries are assessed anonymously. As of this edition the guidelines say nothing about AI, so the AI rule, where there is one, sits in the individual brief. A growing number of briefs now carry one. One architectural-illustration society's terms for 2026, for instance, accept AI-assisted work but require it to be labelled, and reserve the right to demand proof of originality, with disqualification for refusal. Rules differ widely between organisers and change between years. That is why the card is EVOLVING and the method is "find and read", not "remember". Disclosure is also the professional habit this whole ring builds: say what was made, and how, before anyone asks. A competition's rule is not your school's rule; the academic-integrity card on this ring covers the submission you make for marks.

topics.name: What may be uploaded
topics.description: Decide what can go into an outside model — safe, anonymise first, never — before you paste. It is eleven at night, the client's drawing set is open, and a model could summarise the structural consultant's forty-page report in a minute. The drawings carry the client's name, the plot number, the budget and a consultant's stamp.
evidence: Sort a set of project materials into three piles: safe to upload, anonymise first, and never
Explain what a client contract or NDA means for feeding drawings to an outside model
topics.critPrompt: Before the student uploads a client's drawing, ask what in it should never leave the studio. Did they check the contract before pasting, and can they show the three piles?

grounding.ref: Press Information Bureau, Government notifies DPDP Rules to empower citizens and protect privacy
PRS Legislative Research, The Digital Personal Data Protection Bill, 2023

card.oneLiner: Decide what can go into an outside model — safe, anonymise first, never — before you paste.

sections.dilemma: It is eleven at night, the client's drawing set is open, and a model could summarise the structural consultant's forty-page report in a minute. The drawings carry the client's name, the plot number, the budget and a consultant's stamp. Paste, or stop?
sections.choices: Paste and hope. Or sort first, into three piles. Safe to upload: your own sketches, public information, generic questions. Anonymise first: drawings with names, addresses, budgets and identifiable people removed — then check whether what remains still identifies the project. Never: anything under a non-disclosure agreement, anything the contract says stays in the studio, anything that is another party's intellectual property, anything personal about a client or a user of the building. The third pile is decided by the contract and the law, not by convenience. Note that those are different reasons: personal-data law, a confidentiality clause, a non-disclosure agreement, copyright, security and the studio's own policy each forbid a different thing, and the four-risks card on this map takes them one at a time.
sections.consequence: A pasted drawing may be retained, reviewed, or used for training, depending on the provider's terms that week. Once out, it does not come back. It is a breach whether or not the client ever finds out. Sorting takes five minutes. A breach can end the relationship.
sections.theCase: An intern uploads a hospital's floor plans to get a room-schedule table. The plans show the pharmacy store and the server room. The hospital's agreement with the studio forbids sharing drawings with third parties. Nobody meant harm. The studio now has to tell the client.
sections.takeItToCrit: Before the student uploads a client's drawing, ask what in it should never leave the studio. Did they check the contract before pasting, and can they show the three piles?
sections.howItWorks: Providers' data terms differ — consumer and business tiers often differ inside one company — and they change, which is why this card carries a review date. India now has an enacted data-protection framework: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and the DPDP Rules, 2025, notified in November 2025 and commencing in phases over eighteen months, with the bulk of the obligations — the children's-data provisions among them — scheduled for May 2027. It concerns personal data: names, addresses, the people in the photographs. What it requires of a particular studio in a particular case is a question for a lawyer, not for this card. The habit comes before any law: know what you hold in trust, and treat every outside model as a third party, because it is one.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Quantities and schedules
topics.description: Bills of quantities and door schedules are tabular truth with money attached — trust nothing unchecked. One: counts and areas come from the building model's own schedule export, or from measured drawings by a person. A vision model's count of a PDF can start the list; it never prices it — no count from a vision model enters the bill until a person has recounted it.
evidence: Give a vision model a floor plan and ask it to count the doors, windows and rooms. Count them yourself. Compare. Then ask yourself what that error rate would cost across a forty-sheet set.
Show one bill-of-quantities extract in which every line names its source, and point to the five items you recounted.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one bill-of-quantities extract in which every line names its source, and point to the five items you recounted.

card.oneLiner: Bills of quantities and door schedules are tabular truth with money attached — trust nothing unchecked.

sections.whenToUse: Any bill of quantities, door or window schedule, finishes schedule or area statement: any table where a number becomes a rupee.
sections.method: One: counts and areas come from the building model's own schedule export, or from measured drawings by a person. A vision model's count of a PDF can start the list; it never prices it — no count from a vision model enters the bill until a person has recounted it. Two: use the language model for what it is good at — structuring the table, checking it for internal inconsistencies, flagging a door that appears in the schedule and not on the plan, formatting the output. Three: every figure traces to a source you can name: a schedule export, a measured sheet, a rate from a document. Four: spot-check — pick five items and recount them by hand; if one is wrong, recount all. Five: lock the words that carry responsibility, as the protect-the-text card sets out, and let the model move only the layout.
sections.watchForThis: A fluent bill with plausible numbers. Plausible is what these models produce, and plausible is not what a contractor prices. One wrong count in a schedule means a site instruction, a variation, and an argument about who pays.
sections.tryIt: Give a vision model a floor plan and ask it to count the doors, windows and rooms. Count them yourself. Compare. Then ask yourself what that error rate would cost across a forty-sheet set.
sections.proveIt: Show one bill-of-quantities extract in which every line names its source, and point to the five items you recounted.
sections.howItWorks: Counting on a drawing is exactly what the most recent benchmark built from real architectural plans tests — doors, windows, bedrooms, toilets, across a hundred and twenty floor plans — and the benchmark exists because the counts could not be assumed. A structured building model does not have this problem: its schedule is a query over objects, not a reading of a picture, which is why step one routes the number there. EVOLVING because drawing-reading models are being trained and re-tested on every release; the method does not depend on which way the scores move.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Digital twin means too much
topics.description: The label promises live data, simulation and AI. Ask which of those the thing in front of you actually has. "Digital twin" has no settled meaning. A study that read more than 15,000 scientific papers found that the capabilities people assume — real-time data, simulation, AI, two-way flow between building and model — are often not yet there in the twins of the built environment.
evidence: Find one built-environment project that calls itself a digital twin. List the capabilities the name implies. Check each against what the project actually documents. Write the gap down.
Ask three questions that separate a working twin from a label on a static model — and show them applied to one real example.
topics.critPrompt: When someone says 'digital twin', does the student ask which capabilities it actually has before believing it?

grounding.ref: Abdelrahman, Macatulad, Lei, Quintana, Miller & Biljecki, 2024–25 (arXiv:2409.19005)

card.oneLiner: The label promises live data, simulation and AI. Ask which of those the thing in front of you actually has.

sections.idea: "Digital twin" has no settled meaning. A study that read more than 15,000 scientific papers found that the capabilities people assume — real-time data, simulation, AI, two-way flow between building and model — are often not yet there in the twins of the built environment. The term is contested: serious people use it both for a live, sensing, simulating model and for a BIM file with a dashboard. Literacy here means asking which capabilities this particular twin has, and which ones it was sold with.
sections.whyItMatters: A client who buys "a digital twin" may be paying for a static model with a name. A student who can ask four capability questions protects both the client and the word.
sections.inTheStudio: A facilities manager shows you "the campus digital twin." Ask: does it receive live data from the buildings? Can it simulate — energy, crowds, failure? Does anything it computes flow back to control the building? How often is the geometry updated? Four questions, and the twin usually turns out to be a very good 3D record — useful, but not a twin in the sense promised.
sections.watchForThis: Arguing about the definition instead of the capabilities. The definition is contested and may stay so; the capabilities can be checked this afternoon.
sections.tryIt: Find one built-environment project that calls itself a digital twin. List the capabilities the name implies. Check each against what the project actually documents. Write the gap down.
sections.proveIt: Ask three questions that separate a working twin from a label on a static model — and show them applied to one real example.
sections.howItWorks: The survey used language processing over the full text of the articles to map how the term is used, and found its promised features less mature in buildings than in manufacturing, where the word began. CONTESTED because the disagreement over meaning is real and unresolved; reviewed because the gap it measures is closing in places.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Drafts, minutes and specs, verified
topics.description: Draft the studio's writing fast with AI; check every fact strictly before it leaves the studio. Give the model the raw material — your notes, the recording's transcript, the previous version — and ask for a draft. Then change roles, from writer to checker.
evidence: Draft minutes of a real meeting with AI from your rough notes. Before sending, mark every fact verified or unverified. Count the unverified. Then find the one figure it stated confidently and wrongly — there is usually one.
Show one AI-drafted document with every actionable claim marked and sourced, and the line you struck.
topics.critPrompt: For a document the student drafted with AI, ask which lines they checked, and against what. The unchecked lines are the liability.

card.oneLiner: Draft the studio's writing fast with AI; check every fact strictly before it leaves the studio.

sections.whenToUse: Minutes, specification clauses, letters, schedules, tender notes: the writing a studio produces every week that is shaped like prose but carries facts.
sections.method: Give the model the raw material — your notes, the recording's transcript, the previous version — and ask for a draft. Then change roles, from writer to checker. Mark every claim in the draft that a reader could act on: a date, a quantity, a product, a decision, who agreed to what. Check each against its source — your notes, the datasheet, the drawing — and mark it verified, or strike it. Nothing unmarked leaves the studio. For minutes, the checked draft goes to the people who were in the room before it goes anywhere else.
sections.watchForThis: The invented specific. Draft minutes record "the client approved the 150 mm slab" when the client said "that sounds fine" about nothing in particular. The model fills gaps with likely detail, and in a specification likely detail is a wrong number that looks right.
sections.tryIt: Draft minutes of a real meeting with AI from your rough notes. Before sending, mark every fact verified or unverified. Count the unverified. Then find the one figure it stated confidently and wrongly — there is usually one.
sections.proveIt: Show one AI-drafted document with every actionable claim marked and sourced, and the line you struck.
sections.howItWorks: The draft is fast because the model knows the shape of minutes and specifications from thousands of examples. The facts are unreliable for the same reason: it knows what minutes usually say, and fills your gaps from the usual. The method separates what the model is good at — form, completeness, plain sentences — from what only you can supply. The load-bearing-words card on the core ring is the sharper case: text the model should not draft at all.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Making, not just drawing

grounding.ref: Pishahang & Badiei, From Clay to Code

topics.description: CNC, robotic fabrication, and the point where a generated output meets physical tolerance. Between a generated form and a made thing stands tolerance. Materials move, tools have limited reach, joints need to fit, and a millimetre matters.
evidence: Take one generated pattern. Cut or print a hundred-millimetre piece of it. Measure the deviation between the file and the object. Write down everything the file did not know that the machine needed — the kerf, the material thickness, the minimum feature the tool could cut.
Explain where tolerance enters between file and object, and why an image model cannot hold it, with one measurement from your own test.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to explain where tolerance enters between file and object, and why an image model cannot hold it, with one measurement from your own test.

card.oneLiner: CNC, robotic fabrication, and the point where a generated output meets physical tolerance.

sections.idea: Between a generated form and a made thing stands tolerance. Materials move, tools have limited reach, joints need to fit, and a millimetre matters. No single file carries all of that. The chain runs: design geometry; fabrication constraints — tool, stock, kerf, tolerance; toolpaths from both; a simulation to check them; post-processing into one machine's instructions; then the object, measured. An image holds none of these, because an image has no ruler. Digital fabrication is where generative outputs meet the physical world, and the physical world does not negotiate. A render fails on a screen. A panel fails on site.
sections.whyItMatters: The last metre between file and object is where most of the knowledge lives. A student who can generate a pattern and cannot get it made has learnt the cheap half.
sections.inTheStudio: A generated brick screen, beautifully lit. The mason asks the bond, the module, how the corner turns, what holds the perforated course. Nobody asked the image, because the image could not have answered. The same pattern laser-cut at model scale comes back with every slot a kerf too wide.
sections.watchForThis: Treating a mesh exported from an image-to-3D tool as a fabrication file. It is a likeness of a surface. It has no thickness you chose, no tolerance, no knowledge of the material it will be cut from — and material behaviour is never "in the file": it enters as the feeds, speeds, offsets and allowances a person sets when the toolpaths are made, and it is checked on the bench.
sections.tryIt: Take one generated pattern. Cut or print a hundred-millimetre piece of it. Measure the deviation between the file and the object. Write down everything the file did not know that the machine needed — the kerf, the material thickness, the minimum feature the tool could cut.
sections.proveIt: Explain where tolerance enters between file and object, and why an image model cannot hold it, with one measurement from your own test.
sections.howItWorks: Robotic and CNC fabrication in architecture is a research field in its own right — ETH Zurich's Gramazio Kohler Research has spent two decades on it — and its central lesson is that the geometry and the making are designed together, with the machine's constraints inside the design from the start, and the toolpaths, the simulation and the post-processed machine code treated as stages of the design rather than an export at the end. Generative image models sit outside that loop: a 2025 study that tested three diffusion models on vernacular pigeon towers found they reproduced geometric pattern reliably and misread material and climatic reasoning — the look of a construction without its logic. Tools that feed fabrication constraints back into generation are active research, which is why this card is EVOLVING; the tolerance itself does not change.
