topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Render to reel, and when not to
topics.description: Image-to-video is cheap. The question is whether the motion serves the design or polishes a scheme you have not resolved. Start from a locked still rather than from text alone; that is the Lab's rule, and the note below says why. Ask the honest question first: does this project need atmosphere in motion, or does it need something else that motion is standing in for — a walkthrough, a section, a decision not yet taken?
evidence: Take one approved still. Make a short motion study and write the design idea the motion serves. Then name one still you chose not to animate, and say why.
Show one motion study with its one-sentence purpose, and one deliberate refusal with its reason. If the only thing the clip shows is "it moves", the exercise failed.
topics.critPrompt: Ask what the video shows that the still could not. If the only answer is 'it moves', the exercise failed.

grounding.ref: OpenAI, Video generation models as world simulators

card.oneLiner: Image-to-video is cheap. The question is whether the motion serves the design or polishes a scheme you have not resolved.

sections.whenToUse: When the project needs atmosphere in time — light moving through a room, a figure crossing a threshold, a slow push through a doorway — and the still it starts from is already approved. Not for navigation, not for construction, not for a scheme still changing.
sections.method: Start from a locked still rather than from text alone; that is the Lab's rule, and the note below says why. Ask the honest question first: does this project need atmosphere in motion, or does it need something else that motion is standing in for — a walkthrough, a section, a decision not yet taken? If it is the second, stop. If it is the first, write in one sentence the design idea the motion serves, before any engine opens. Generate short variants, change one thing at a time, then curate: one motion gesture, usually the slowest. Keep a note of what you chose not to animate, and why.
sections.watchForThis: Motion used to hide a problem. An unresolved elevation looks resolved for six seconds with drifting light. The client approves the feeling, but the drawing has not moved. Motion spreads a problem across more frames; it does not solve it.
sections.tryIt: Take one approved still. Make a short motion study and write the design idea the motion serves. Then name one still you chose not to animate, and say why.
sections.proveIt: Show one motion study with its one-sentence purpose, and one deliberate refusal with its reason. If the only thing the clip shows is "it moves", the exercise failed.
sections.labNote: Image-to-video is the Lab's method, not the only one. Text-to-video is a legitimate way to make a clip, and for some work — a mood piece with no fixed geometry — it is the faster one. We start from a locked still because in architectural work the still is where the geometry was decided, and a clip that starts from text decides it again without you. That is a rule about authorship, not a fact about the engines.
sections.howItWorks: Video engines extend a still into time by predicting plausible motion. The Lab's playbook on AI video — its own material, taught in its workshops — sets the workflow as image-to-video: the still is the score, the motion is the performance. Atmosphere is the dependable use today. Consistent multi-shot sequences are the moving frontier. The card is reviewed because the engines improve every few months and what they can hold steady changes with each release. The discipline does not change.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Discipline when time is short
topics.description: Deadline pressure is when iteration turns into fifty-image gambling — unless you change one thing per cycle and keep a log. The jury is at nine tomorrow. The render is not right.
evidence: Run a timed iteration that changes one named variable per cycle and still lands the result
Explain why churning out volume and picking feels faster under deadline, but is usually slower
topics.critPrompt: Under a mock deadline, watch whether the student tightens the brief or floods the engine. The panic move is the tell. Ask for the log.

grounding.ref: iteration discipline matters most when time and cost are tight
Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI

card.oneLiner: Deadline pressure is when iteration turns into fifty-image gambling — unless you change one thing per cycle and keep a log.

sections.dilemma: The jury is at nine tomorrow. The render is not right. You can run fifty variations in an hour and pick one, or run five, changing one named thing each time, and know why the fifth is better. Which?
sections.choices: Flood the engine: fifty images, scroll, pick the one that feels right, hope it holds at nine. Or hold the discipline: name the variable that is wrong — light direction, material, camera height — change only that, judge fast, log the change, go again. Fifty feels faster. Five usually is.
sections.consequence: Flooding produces a pick you cannot explain and cannot reproduce; the jury asks "why this one?" and the honest answer is "it came up." One-variable cycles produce a result with a reason attached, and a log that lets you go back to cycle three when cycle five overshoots.
sections.theCase: One in the morning, a courtyard render, the shadow is wrong. The student generates forty, scrolls, picks the warmest. At the jury the shadow is right, but the courtyard's proportion has quietly changed between generations — the engine drifted the geometry while the student was judging light. Nobody noticed, because nothing was held constant.
sections.takeItToCrit: Under a mock deadline, watch whether the student tightens the brief or floods the engine. The panic move is the tell. Ask for the log.
sections.howItWorks: Each generation is a draw from a range. Change one input and you learn what that input controls; change five and you learn nothing you can use next time. The log is the studio's memory of the search. Studies of designers using generative tools report fixation — settling early on what the engine shows — as a real cost. So the discipline here guards against fixation under pressure, not only against waste.

sections.method: Treat the folder as a place a stranger has to find their way through. One entry point: a short read-me at the top that says what the project is, where the live files are, and where not to look. A software lab reached the same conclusion from the other side: an agent working in a codebase needs "a map, not a 1,000-page instruction manual" — a short entry file that points onward, not an encyclopaedia. topics.name: Lock what must not move
topics.description: Every grounded generation needs a written statement of what must not change. Before the prompt says what to make, write what to keep. List it plainly: preserve all geometry exactly; preserve the typography; do not add objects; do not change the light direction; preserve the figure's identity; preserve the material palette; preserve the aspect ratio.
evidence: Add a preservation block to one grounded prompt. Generate. Remove the block and generate again. Lay both beside the source and circle every difference. List the parts of the scene that drift most — you will find they are edges, counts and faces.
Show one grounded generation with its preservation block, and the drift that appeared when the block was removed.
topics.critPrompt: When a generation drifts, ask which preservation line was missing. The drift is usually a 'do not change' that nobody wrote down.

grounding.ref: state what must not change — the preservation block

card.oneLiner: Every grounded generation needs a written statement of what must not change.

sections.whenToUse: Any grounded generation, image or video, that starts from something you have already decided: a massing, a plan, a material palette, a person's face, a frame proportion.
sections.method: Before the prompt says what to make, write what to keep. List it plainly: preserve all geometry exactly; preserve the typography; do not add objects; do not change the light direction; preserve the figure's identity; preserve the material palette; preserve the aspect ratio. Paste that block at the end of every prompt in the execution phase. Then give the block teeth, because a written instruction asks; the system's own controls enforce. Where the geometry must hold exactly, protect it with a control the engine cannot argue with: a mask that keeps the engine out of the regions that must not change, a conditioning input — a depth map, an edge map, your own line drawing — that holds the structure, or a deterministic composite that pastes the decided parts back over the generated ones. After generation, check the block line by line against the output — did the geometry hold, did the palette hold — before you look at whether the image is good.
sections.watchForThis: Drift you did not notice because you were looking at what changed. A preservation block only works if you check it: the engine honours it more often than not, never always. "Preserve all geometry exactly" is a brief, not a lock; emphatic wording does not become a guarantee.
sections.tryIt: Add a preservation block to one grounded prompt. Generate. Remove the block and generate again. Lay both beside the source and circle every difference. List the parts of the scene that drift most — you will find they are edges, counts and faces.
sections.proveIt: Show one grounded generation with its preservation block, and the drift that appeared when the block was removed.
sections.labNote: Naming what to keep is as much a design act as naming what to make. This is the Lab's standing rule for grounded work, from its own playbook on AI video. Others rely on reference strength alone. We write the block, because a decision that is not written down is a decision the engine makes for you.
sections.howItWorks: A generator does not know which parts of your reference are decisions and which are accidents. Conditioning methods — the family of techniques behind holding a reference — pull the output toward the reference, but the pull is statistical, and a conditioned diffusion model is still a generator, not a CAD constraint solver. A written preservation instruction narrows the draw further; a mask or a composite removes the draw from the parts that must not move; and a visual check, or an overlay diff against the source, closes the rest of the gap. When a generation drifts, the missing line is usually a "do not change" nobody wrote down, and the missing control is usually a mask nobody drew.

card.oneLiner: Scopes, keys and logs — the permissions an agent holds are design decisions somebody made, and they reach your files, your mail, your money.

sections.whenToUse: Before any agent is connected to anything the studio owns: a project folder, a mailbox, a calendar, a drive, a payment account. Again whenever the task changes.
sections.method: Two columns. Left: what the agent can *read*. Right: what it can *write or act on*. For every connection — every tool, connector or integration the agent is given — record three things. The scope: which folders, which mailbox, which accounts, not "the drive". The key: whose credentials it acts under, because an agent acting under your login acts as you. The log: where each action it takes is recorded, so that a wrong action can be found and undone. Grant the least that does the job. Review the two columns when the task changes, because permissions granted for one task quietly outlive it.

sections.proveIt: For one agent setup, show the scope, the key and the log for every connection — and name the one you narrowed after writing it down.
sections.howItWorks: Agents reach the world through tools, and an open standard now exists for connecting a model to tools and data sources — files, databases, search, calendars — so that the same agent can be plugged into many systems. That is what makes agents useful and what makes this card necessary: the connection is standardised, the permission decision is not. It remains a choice someone makes at setup, usually in a hurry. card.oneLiner: Develop mood on one track and massing on another, and combine them on purpose.

sections.whenToUse: Early design, when you are tempted to ask one image for everything — the feeling and the form — and whenever a generated study keeps changing shape between versions.
sections.method: Two tracks, run separately. The atmosphere track: light, material, season, hour of day, register — explored in a dreaming engine with no geometry held, then curated to a small set. The geometry track: massing, plan logic, section, the position of openings — fixed in a modeller or a drawing, where they can be measured. Only when both are clear do you combine: a grounded generation that holds the geometry from the second track and applies the atmosphere from the first. Write down which decisions belong to which track. A decision on the wrong track is how drift begins.
sections.watchForThis: The beautiful study whose courtyard is a different width in every version. The engine was asked to hold form while exploring mood, and it traded one for the other without telling you. Form has to be directed; you do not stumble into it.
sections.tryIt: Run one study on two tracks — a mood set and a massing model — then produce the directed image the two generate together. Write which decisions you took on each track.
sections.proveIt: Show the two tracks and the combined result, and name which decisions belong to atmosphere and which to geometry.
sections.labNote: This is the Lab's director protocol in one move: anchor the geometry, develop the mood, let the picture emerge only when both are clear. Others work image-first and work the form out backwards from the picture. We find that route produces drifting geometry and proposals that do not hold together, so we teach the separation from the first week.
sections.howItWorks: Image engines hold atmosphere well and geometry poorly, because they were trained on photographs. Ask one for both and it solves the easy half and approximates the hard half. Separating the tracks gives each to the tool that can hold it — the engine for light, the model for measure — and keeps the combining step a decision you make, on the day you are ready to make it.

topics.name: A surrogate answer needs a real simulation behind it

grounding.ref: Risk-aware early-stage heating/cooling surrogate workflow with explicit validity limits
A machine-learning framework for daylight and visual comfort assessment in early design stages

topics.description: Surrogates to explore a hundred options fast, a physics engine for the three you will defend, and the surrogate re-checked against it — never a surrogate number alone in a submission. A physics engine does not make an answer true; it makes it checkable. Three stages and a rule. Explore: use the surrogate — the fast model trained to imitate a simulation — to rank many options in minutes; this is what it is for.
evidence: Take one scheme with three massing options. Rank them with any fast daylight or energy tool. Then run the top one through a full simulation with your city's weather file. Compare the two figures and write one sentence on what the difference tells you about the other two. Then run the simulation twice more with your two least certain inputs moved to their plausible extremes, and report the result as a range, not a number — "between 41 and 58 kWh/m², most likely 47" — with the assumption that drives the width named.
Show one submission sheet where every performance number carries its source — surrogate or simulation — its inputs and its date, and where no surrogate figure stands alone.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one submission sheet where every performance number carries its source — surrogate or simulation — its inputs and its date, and where no surrogate figure stands alone.

card.oneLiner: Surrogates to explore a hundred options fast, a physics engine for the three you will defend, and the surrogate re-checked against it — never a surrogate number alone in a submission. A physics engine does not make an answer true; it makes it checkable.

sections.whenToUse: Any time a fast performance number — daylight, heating, cooling, wind — is about to move from your screen into a drawing, a jury sheet, a client report or a submission.
sections.method: Three stages and a rule. Explore: use the surrogate — the fast model trained to imitate a simulation — to rank many options in minutes; this is what it is for. Defend: take the two or three options you would actually argue for and run them through a physics engine with your site's weather file — EnergyPlus, Radiance, a CFD run, or an engineer's model. Re-check: for those three, put the surrogate's figure and the simulation's figure side by side. The gap between them is the surrogate's error on your building, and it tells you whether the ranking from the explore stage can be trusted. Then check the simulation itself: change the two inputs you are least sure of — the occupancy, the infiltration, the glazing g-value — and see how far the answer moves. That range is the number's honest width, and it goes on the sheet beside the number. The rule: a number that leaves the studio carries the simulation's name, its inputs and its date — never the surrogate's alone. If the simulation has not been run, the sheet says "indicative, not yet simulated."
sections.watchForThis: A surrogate figure that survives into a later drawing because nobody tracked which numbers were fast and which were real. Mark them differently from the first day — a colour, a suffix — so the provenance is on the sheet, not in your memory.
sections.tryIt: Take one scheme with three massing options. Rank them with any fast daylight or energy tool. Then run the top one through a full simulation with your city's weather file. Compare the two figures and write one sentence on what the difference tells you about the other two. Then run the simulation twice more with your two least certain inputs moved to their plausible extremes, and report the result as a range, not a number — "between 41 and 58 kWh/m², most likely 47" — with the assumption that drives the width named.
sections.proveIt: Show one submission sheet where every performance number carries its source — surrogate or simulation — its inputs and its date, and where no surrogate figure stands alone.
sections.labNote: This is the Lab's method. It is a rule about what may leave the room, not a view on which tool is better. Surrogates are good; we use them. But a number a client will act on needs physics behind it, because a surrogate is just as confident outside the range it learnt from as inside it, and it cannot tell you which is which. The physics does not make the number true — the weather file, the boundary conditions, the occupancy, the material properties and the mesh can all be wrong — but it makes the number checkable, input by input, which a surrogate is not. A surrogate figure standing alone is the first thing this strand tells a student not to put in a submission.
sections.howItWorks: A surrogate is a regression model trained on the outputs of a simulation; the surrogate-model card explains why it is fast and why it is silent outside its training range. Recent building-performance research shows what good practice looks like: an early-stage heating-and-cooling surrogate that reports an explicit validity domain and an uncertainty band with each prediction, and states that its fit scores describe interpolation within its own benchmark, not real buildings. The daylight surrogate on this card was trained on 2,880 simulations of a single-window shoebox room — useful for ranking options, and nothing like a courtyard. The method here is the studio's version of that discipline: the validity check is done by running the physics on the options that matter, rather than by the tool. It extends the climate-numbers card — screen fast, confirm properly — to the moment of handover. And it points at the checkpoint card: the simulation is where a human signs a performance claim.

topics.name: The deliberate no
topics.description: Choosing, on purpose, not to use AI at a step — to protect the part of the work that is the point. The tool is open, it is fast, and the step in front of you is the one where the design actually gets decided — the first plan sketch, the site walk, the conversation with the client's mother about where she will sleep. Use it, because you can?
evidence: Name a step in a real project where AI was kept out on purpose, and defend the choice
Tell apart refusing AI on purpose from simply never thinking about it
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student where in this project they refused AI on purpose, and why. Then ask them to distinguish that refusal from a step where they simply never thought about it.

grounding.ref: reduce friction, not judgment — know when to refuse
Willems, Khan, Huang, Camburn, Sockalingam & Poon, 2025 (arXiv:2510.19342)

card.oneLiner: Choosing, on purpose, not to use AI at a step — to protect the part of the work that is the point.

sections.dilemma: The tool is open, it is fast, and the step in front of you is the one where the design actually gets decided — the first plan sketch, the site walk, the conversation with the client's mother about where she will sleep. Use it, because you can? Or keep it out, because of what the step is for?
sections.choices: Use AI everywhere it works; speed is speed. Or refuse it at chosen steps, for one of two reasons: this step is the point of the work — where your judgment is formed, not applied — or another tool does the job better: a pencil, a tape, a walk. The refusal is a design decision, written down with its reason.
sections.consequence: Use it everywhere and you may end up with a fluent scheme you cannot explain, because the step that formed it was skipped. A workflow map with no "no" on it was never really examined. Refuse AI on purpose at a few steps and the "yes" steps get stronger, because you know what they are protecting.
sections.theCase: A final-year student keeps AI out of the first week of a housing project: site walks, hand sections, conversations. From week two it runs everywhere — research, options, drafts. At the jury the student can say why the plan is what it is. A classmate who generated from day one presents beautifully and cannot answer "why this plan?"
sections.takeItToCrit: Ask the student where in this project they refused AI on purpose, and why. Then ask them to distinguish that refusal from a step where they simply never thought about it.
sections.howItWorks: A workflow is a sequence of decisions about where effort goes. Friction is effort that produces nothing. Judgment is effort that produces the designer. AI removes both alike unless it is told where to stop. The "no" is how you tell it.

topics.name: Checkpoints in automation

grounding.ref: From Tool to System: RAG, Agents and the Studio Stack

topics.description: Approval gates — the drawing goes out when a named person approves it, and the approval is recorded, whatever produced it. Trace the workflow from first input to last output. Mark every point where the work crosses to the outside or cannot be undone.
evidence: Pick one workflow in your studio that ends outside it. Draw it. Mark the crossings. For each mark, write the name of who signs. If you wrote "whoever is there", you have found the hole.
Show one workflow in which the gate is structural — the work genuinely cannot proceed without a named person's sign-off — and say what the agent does up to that point.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student to show one workflow in which the gate is structural — the work genuinely cannot proceed without a named person's sign-off — and say what the agent does up to that point.

card.oneLiner: Approval gates — the drawing goes out when a named person approves it, and the approval is recorded, whatever produced it.

sections.whenToUse: When designing any workflow that ends in something leaving the studio or becoming irreversible: an issue, a submission, a payment, a published image, a deleted set.
sections.method: Trace the workflow from first input to last output. Mark every point where the work crosses to the outside or cannot be undone. At each mark, a named, authorised person approves the step and the approval is recorded — a person, not "the team", and not the agent. Where the law or the contract requires an actual signature, it is a signature; elsewhere it is a recorded approval, and the word "signs" on this card is shorthand for that. Make the gate structural: the workflow cannot proceed past it without the sign-off, rather than a reminder someone can dismiss. Record who signed and when. Then count the gates. Too few and errors escape; too many and people start signing without reading, which is worse than no gate because it looks like one.
sections.watchForThis: A gate a rushed person can skip. On the night before a submission, a reminder is not a gate. Only a step that will not run is a gate.
sections.tryIt: Pick one workflow in your studio that ends outside it. Draw it. Mark the crossings. For each mark, write the name of who signs. If you wrote "whoever is there", you have found the hole.
sections.proveIt: Show one workflow in which the gate is structural — the work genuinely cannot proceed without a named person's sign-off — and say what the agent does up to that point.
sections.labNote: A named person at every crossing is the Lab's rule. Other studios gate by role, by committee, or by a logged acknowledgement, and some gates genuinely need a review rather than a signature. We name a person because a name is what turns a reminder into a gate: "whoever is there" is the hole on every workflow map we have seen.
sections.howItWorks: In India the Architects Act, 1972 governs who may call themselves an architect, and the Council of Architecture's Professional Conduct Regulations set the duties of a registered architect; which drawings a local authority accepts, and under whose signature, is set by that authority's own rules. Where a submission carries a registered professional's signature, the liability attached to it does not move because a machine drew the lines or an agent assembled the set. That reading of what automation leaves untouched is the Lab's; the standard-of-care card on this ring carries the framework itself. The signature is where responsibility has long lived; automation changes what happens before it, not what it means. Builders of agent systems say the same from their side: put a human checkpoint before consequential actions. The studio version is older than the technology: a checking signature on every sheet that leaves. The production card on this map, verify loops in production, builds the machinery around the gate; this card fixes where the gate must be.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: AI across the project arc
topics.description: The Lab's position on where AI belongs across a project: wherever it reduces friction, never where it replaces judgment. AI fits differently at each stage — research, brief, massing, iteration, drawings, communication — and one rule decides where it goes. The real risk is not being replaced by the machine.
evidence: Draw your project's arc, stage by stage. Place each AI use you actually made on it. Mark each: friction reduced, or judgment replaced? Then name one stage where you keep AI out on purpose.
Can the student say where in their project AI works for them, and where it would replace the very part that is the point?
topics.critPrompt: Can the student say where in their project AI works for them, and where it would replace the very part that is the point?

grounding.ref: The AI Design Director Protocol — the-ai-design-director-protocol

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position on where AI belongs across a project: wherever it reduces friction, never where it replaces judgment.

sections.position:
AI fits differently at each stage — research, brief, massing, iteration, drawings, communication — and one rule decides where it goes. The real risk is not being replaced by the machine. It is working with one that nobody is directing. Direct it like a brilliant, tireless junior: fast, visually impressive, and with no regard for structure, budget or human use unless you supply them. This is a friction map, not a tool list.
> Reduce friction, not judgment.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Because the failures we see in studios are failures of direction, not of tools: a stunning render of a scheme nobody decided, a research dossier nobody verified, an option set nobody curated. A friction map puts the tool where the nights are lost and keeps it out of where the design is decided.
sections.strongestObjection: Friction is sometimes the safety mechanism. Checking a dimension twice, reading a clause slowly, drawing the section by hand, reconciling two schedules that should agree: these feel like friction precisely because they force the mind through the work, and that forcing is where errors get caught and understanding gets made. "AI wherever it reduces friction" risks automating away the process that creates the judgment the map says it protects. The line between friction and judgment is not fixed, and from the inside it may not be findable: what feels like friction to a student — the hand section — may be the judgment being formed. A small study of thirty-six architecture students found generative AI helped novices in conceptual design and gave experienced designers no measurable gain; it is too small to make a law of, but it points the same way — where AI helps depends on who is sitting there, and a map drawn for a studio may be wrong for the people in it.
sections.revisionCondition: If the tools begin carrying design decisions end to end — brief to scheme — with results clients and juries accept, "reduce friction, not judgment" stops describing a boundary and starts describing a preference. If studies keep finding the benefit lives entirely with novices, the map becomes a map of expertise rather than of project stages, and we redraw it. And if we find, in our own workshops, that the steps we mapped as friction were the steps where the checking happened, the map gets a third mark beside yes and no: friction that is doing a job. Reviewed every edition.
sections.tryIt: Draw your project's arc, stage by stage. Place each AI use you actually made on it. Mark each: friction reduced, or judgment replaced? Then name one stage where you keep AI out on purpose.
sections.takeItToCrit: Can the student say where in their project AI works for them, and where it would replace the very part that is the point?

topics.description: A studio's own drawings, specs, photos and debriefs are the material its future systems search — and, one day, learn from. A finished project looks like storage: a folder closed, a drive filled. It is actually infrastructure.
evidence: Take one finished project. Write the debrief a search system would need: problem, site condition, what was tried, what held, what failed. Then ask: could a stranger find this by design intent in a year?
Explain how a studio archive can be searched by intent rather than by filename, and name what a debrief written today would teach a system next year.

card.oneLiner: A studio's own drawings, specs, photos and debriefs are the material its future systems search — and, one day, learn from.

sections.idea: A finished project looks like storage: a folder closed, a drive filled. It is actually infrastructure. A studio system that answers "what did we do about west light on a narrow plot?" searches the studio's own archive — but only if the archive can be searched by what things mean, not just by what they are called. The debrief you write today is the answer a system gives next year. What is never written down cannot be found. What is filed as clutter is lost.
sections.whyItMatters: Every studio has ten years of judgment in files nobody can search. The difference between a studio with a memory and one without is classification, not software.
sections.inTheStudio: A senior remembers that the 2019 school project solved a monsoon-drainage problem beautifully. The junior searches "drainage" and finds forty files named by sheet number. The solution exists and cannot be found. Had the debrief said "monsoon drainage, sloped site, open channel", the archive would have answered.
sections.watchForThis: Believing that uploading the archive creates intelligence. It creates a pile. Retrieval quality depends on someone having described what each piece means — which precedent, which stage, why it was kept.
sections.tryIt: Take one finished project. Write the debrief a search system would need: problem, site condition, what was tried, what held, what failed. Then ask: could a stranger find this by design intent in a year?
sections.proveIt: Explain how a studio archive can be searched by intent rather than by filename, and name what a debrief written today would teach a system next year.
sections.howItWorks: Retrieval systems turn documents into searchable meaning and return the closest matches to a question. What comes back can only be as good as the description that went in. Whether a material enters the archive because it was explored, specified, procured, or weathered well is an architectural judgment no software makes for you. Training a model on a studio's own work is a further step, with questions of consent and ownership that the provenance strand takes up.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position on what remains yours when machines multiply everything else.

sections.position:
AI multiplies options faster than any designer can inspect them. That makes judgment the bottleneck: deciding what matters, which evidence deserves trust, what gets rejected, what gets developed, and who carries the consequences. That decision chain — not the volume of generated material — is where a designer's authorship lives.
> This is not a consolation prize. It is the job.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Every earlier tool shift in this profession — drafting to CAD, CAD to BIM — moved production and kept responsibility exactly where it was. Nothing in the current shift moves the signature. Someone still decides, and someone still answers for the decision.
sections.strongestObjection: Judgment in architecture does not belong to one designer. It is distributed: the client decides the budget and the brief, the structural engineer decides what stands, the services consultant what breathes, the contractor what can be built on Tuesday, the regulator what is permitted, the community what is tolerated, the code what is lawful, and the users decide, years later, what the building was. Some decisions are not yours to make. Some are negotiated. Some are statutory. So if authorship lives in "the decision chain", whose chain is it? The card risks replacing the fear of the machine with the old heroic-author picture of architecture, in which one person decided everything, when the honest description was always a chain with many hands on it. And a second objection follows: as models improve, some links in that chain may be automated, and "judgment" shrinks to whatever machines cannot yet do — a retreating territory, not a standing one.
sections.revisionCondition: If the chain is the right picture, then our position should say which links are the architect's, not claim the chain. We revise the card the day we can no longer name, on a real project, the decisions that were the architect's to make and answer for. We revise it further if clients, juries and regulators come to accept a machine's justification as accountability — a system that can not only make the call but *answer for it* when it goes wrong. The day responsibility transfers, this card changes. We review it every edition.
sections.takeItToCrit: What did you decide that AI could not have decided for you — and where is the proof in the work?

Show the five steps as artefacts — the locked still, the brief, the variants, the curation note, the final clip — and say what the clip shows that the still could not.

grounding.ref: the still is the score, the motion is the performance

card.oneLiner: Lock the still. Write what moves, how fast, how long, what stays. Explore, pick one gesture, lock the deliverable.

sections.whenToUse: Every time a still is going to become motion for a client, a presentation, or a channel — after the still is approved and before any video engine opens.
sections.method: Five steps. One: lock the still. If the still is unresolved, motion spreads the problem across more frames. Two: write the motion brief as a separate document answering four questions: what moves (the camera, the light, a figure, a drape); how fast (as slow as the purpose allows: a house or a gallery reads slowly, but a railway station, a bazaar lane or a festival street may need the opposite, and the brief says which); how long (match the platform; six seconds with locked motion beats twenty with drift); what stays still (the architect's hardest decision — geometry, type, a figure's identity). Three: generate short exploratory variants, one parameter changed at a time, and do not pick yet. Four: curate — watch each twice, choose the one gesture that carries the still without overpowering it, and write down why. Five: lock the deliverable — the curation note becomes the final prompt, with the preservation block, at production quality.
sections.watchForThis: Opening the engine before the brief is written. The engine will invent a motion, and you will spend the evening editing its idea instead of directing yours. Two moving elements per clip is the ceiling; three is noise.
sections.tryIt: Write a full motion brief for one approved still before you open any video engine. Make the clip. Show the note that explains why you chose its one motion gesture.
sections.proveIt: Show the five steps as artefacts — the locked still, the brief, the variants, the curation note, the final clip — and say what the clip shows that the still could not.
sections.labNote: The still is the score; the motion is the performance. The five steps are the Lab's own playbook on AI video, taught in its workshops and built to survive engine releases. Engines rotate. The directing vocabulary does not. Our preference for slow motion is a preference, from the kind of work we mostly show; it is not a principle of architecture, and a clip of a terminal at rush hour that drifts slowly has got the building wrong.
sections.howItWorks: A video engine predicts plausible motion from a frame and a prompt. Given no brief, it predicts the average motion for that kind of image, which is rarely the right one for this building. The brief narrows the prediction to a direction you chose. The curation step is the one nobody talks about, and it is what separates authored motion from a clip that merely moves.

sections.dilemma: Your best spread has a generated hero image. The jury — or the employer — will ask how it was made. Hide the process and let the image speak, or show the brief, the iterations, and what you decided?
sections.choices: Present the final image alone and hope nobody asks. Or build the spread to show the judgment: the brief you wrote, the option set, the rejected ones and why, the one decision the machine could not make — and carry a one-line authorship note that says what was generated, what was drawn, and who directed it.
sections.consequence: A hidden process reads as deception the moment it is discovered, and it does get discovered — by a question, a reverse image search, a senior's eye. A shown process reads as authorship: the image becomes evidence of a chain of decisions, and the decisions are yours. Honesty is not a cost on the work. It is what makes the work yours.

sections.howItWorks: The authorship note is a small discipline with a large effect: it forces you to know, for each image, what you decided. The competition clause elsewhere on this ring is the same discipline imposed from outside. The portfolio is where you impose it on yourself first. Disclosure settles what you did. It does not settle who owns the result: in India the Copyright Act, 1957 counts drawings, plans and works of architecture as artistic works, has a line on computer-generated works written long before these tools, and says nothing yet about what a provider's terms grant you in an image the model made — and the Delhi High Court's July 2026 ruling on training was interim and concerned text. When a studio wants more than the apps give, the choices run along a spectrum, not between two doors. At one end, build: a custom tool, coded for one job, owned outright, maintained forever.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position on the choice every studio meets beyond off-the-shelf apps: where on the spectrum from building custom tools to running agentic workflows on general systems a small studio should sit.

sections.position: When a studio wants more than the apps give, the choices run along a spectrum, not between two doors. At one end, build: a custom tool, coded for one job, owned outright, maintained forever. At the other, run: an agentic workflow on general-purpose systems — a model, a set of permissions, a library of briefs, a few connectors — orchestrated rather than built. Between them sit buying software as a service, configuring a platform, scripting around one, fine-tuning a model, self-hosting an open one, commissioning a system from someone else, and combining several of these. This is a way to decide, not a list of products to buy. For most small and mid-sized studios we hold that the run end is the right default: it bends as the models improve, and it fails in ways a non-programmer can see and fix.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Because the thing that changes fastest is the model, and a custom tool freezes today's model into tomorrow's liability. Orchestration opens selective points of access to what the studio already has — its drawings, its files, its spreadsheets — and asks "what should the system be allowed to touch?" rather than "can it connect to everything?" A principal can answer that question. A principal cannot fix the code.
sections.strongestObjection: Build versus run is not the axis that matters. Who owns the code, where it is hosted, which model it uses, whether the model's weights are open, how deep the integration goes, how much is customised, where the data lives and who maintains it are separate dimensions, and a studio can sit anywhere on each. "Build" does not mean owned outright: a custom tool usually rents its model through an API and its hosting from a cloud. "Run" does not mean rented ground: an agentic workflow can run on an open model on a machine in the studio. Collapse eight dimensions to one and the decision looks simpler than it is, and the real objection to orchestration — that a studio on a provider's general system controls neither pricing, nor terms, nor data handling, nor the day the model is retired — is an objection to one hosting choice, not to a path. For anything load-bearing — a compliance check, a fee calculator — the studio may need to hold some of those dimensions tightly whichever end it starts from.
sections.revisionCondition: If the dimensions stop moving together — if, say, self-hosted open models make ownership cheap without losing adaptability — the spectrum stops being a useful shorthand and this card becomes a matrix: one row per dimension, the studio's choice in each. Evidence from small studios that orchestrated workflows broke more often, or cost more over three years, than built tools of the same scope, or a provider event — a retirement, a terms change — that damaged studios at the run end in a way the build end would have survived, would move our default. Reviewed against what we run ourselves.

topics.name: Verify loops in production
topics.description: Build verification into a running system — self-checks, limits it cannot route around, and a human sign-off it cannot skip. Design three things before the system runs. A verify step: the system checks its own output against a source or a rule and marks what it could not confirm.

card.oneLiner: Build verification into a running system — self-checks, limits it cannot route around, and a human sign-off it cannot skip.

sections.whenToUse: The moment a studio task becomes a standing system: anything that runs without someone watching every step — a drawing checker, a minutes writer, a research agent, a filing routine.
sections.method: Design three things before the system runs. A verify step: the system checks its own output against a source or a rule and marks what it could not confirm. A limit: permissions the workflow cannot exceed — read but not write, draft but not send, flag but not decide — and the closer a step sits to money, liability, authorship or an irreversible change, the harder the limit. A gate: a named human who must say yes before the work passes a stated point, with the system unable to proceed otherwise. Then test the gate by trying to get around it. If you can, the system can.
sections.watchForThis: Decorative guardrails. A rule the system is "told" to follow is a request. A guardrail is a limit it cannot cross. If the answer to "what can the work not do until a human says yes?" is "nothing", there are no guardrails — only intentions.
sections.tryIt: Take one automated studio task. Design its verify step, its hard limit, and its human gate. Then play the system: find a way past the gate. Redesign until you cannot.
sections.proveIt: Show one system where you can point to what it checks, what it cannot do, and where a human must sign — and explain why a limit the workflow can slip past does not constrain it.
sections.howItWorks: Verification is not the last step of agentic work; it is part of its architecture. Graduated permissions — read differs from write, draft from send — are how that architecture is built. Practitioners' guidance on agents says the same: add autonomy only where it earns its place, and keep humans at the points of commitment. The Lab's own essay on legible environments — its own material, not yet published — adds the reason the gate must be visible: a stranger, human or machine, has to be able to find it.

card.oneLiner: The Lab's position on what the fee is for when production accelerates.

sections.position:
Clients have paid for lines — drawings are a defined deliverable in every appointment, and a fee has been charged for them for as long as the profession has existed. Our position is about where the value underneath that fee is migrating: the lines were paid for because they were where the responsible thinking could be seen and the liability was carried, and as production gets cheap, what the client is really buying becomes visible. If production speeds up, the fee does not vanish. It moves to what it was always for: decisions, coordination, and carrying risk under a signature. A practice that prices itself by drawing hours will be priced against the machine and lose. A practice that prices judgment, responsibility and the transfer of risk, and says so in the proposal, has something the machine cannot invoice.
> The fee follows the signature, not the hours.
sections.whyWeHoldIt: Earlier tool shifts in this profession — drafting to CAD, CAD to BIM — cut production time without ending the profession. In our reading of practice, fees did not rise with productivity in those shifts; they were competed down. What held its value was what could not be competed away: who answers for the building. The 2025 survey of UK practices found well over half using AI, most of it in early visualisation and specification writing, and two-thirds worried about their work being imitated; that is UK evidence, and Indian fees are set in a different market. Production is already moving, and value is already contested. Nothing in the current shift moves the signature — though what the signature is worth in India needs stating, and the objection states it.
sections.strongestObjection: The objection is pure economics. Productivity gains do not have to migrate into a new billable category at all. They can be captured by the client as lower fees, by the largest firms as scale, or by the software providers as rent, and nothing in the history of this profession's tool shifts says the architect keeps them. Clients buy outcomes, not virtues: if a system can deliver a coordinated, permitted, buildable set, the client pays the lowest fee that gets an accepted drawing, responsibility is insured rather than bought, and the value moves to whoever owns the tool. And in India the signature is a weaker moat than the position assumes. The Supreme Court held in 2020, in *Council of Architecture v Mukesh Goyal*, that the Architects Act, 1972 protects the title "architect" but does not make the practice of architecture the exclusive preserve of registered architects; local building rules and particular appointments add their own requirements. "Risk under a signature" cannot be treated as the universal economic foundation of practice here. The premise is shaky too: a 2026 study of architecture students found generative assistance gave no overall performance advantage across the group. If production is not speeding up as claimed, the fee is not moving; it is only being squeezed.
sections.revisionCondition: Two checkable signals. Fee benchmarks, in India or abroad, showing fees falling in step with production time even at practices that price judgment and liability explicitly in their proposals. Or professional indemnity for machine-produced drawing sets becoming cheap and routine, which would mean the market had found a way to carry the risk without the signature. Either one, sustained across editions, and this card changes. If Indian fee data, when it exists, shows the value migrating to the client or the vendor rather than to the practice, the position is wrong for here and we will say so. We check every edition.
sections.tryIt: Take one real fee proposal, anonymised. Split the fee into four parts: production hours, decisions, coordination, liability carried. Then ask what the client believed they were buying. The gap between your split and their belief is the conversation this card is about.
sections.takeItToCrit: If every drawing in your project could be produced in an hour, what in it would a client still pay you for — and can you point to it in the work?
sections.howItWorks: A fee is a price for a bundle: time, expertise, coordination, and the transfer of risk from client to professional. Automation shrinks the first part and leaves the others untouched. That is why the Lab's position is that the fee moves rather than disappears. The objection is serious because bundles can be taken apart: a client who can buy production elsewhere may try to buy only production, and find out later what was in the rest of the bundle. In India the bundle's legal part is thinner than in some countries — the title is protected, the practice is not reserved — so the risk-transfer argument has to be made in the appointment, not assumed from the register. This card is EVOLVING within its positional frame: the position is held, the evidence is young, and the revision conditions are watched.

topics.subject: Studio Practice
topics.name: Stage a studio's adoption
topics.description: A small studio takes on AI in stages — audit, a few tools, a pilot on a real project, keep what worked, review every quarter. Three months, three stages. Month one, literacy: audit the workflow (the map from the core ring), choose a small set of tools by engine family, and write down what is safe to use them on.
evidence: Draft a staged adoption plan for a small studio you know, with a milestone at each month. Name the pilot project. Write the agenda of the first quarterly review, including what would make you drop a tool.
Show a plan where a reader can point to the audit, the pilot, the review date, and the rule for dropping what failed.
topics.critPrompt: Ask the student where the plan says 'stop and review'. A plan with no point to pause and drop what failed is a shopping list, not a plan.

card.oneLiner: A small studio takes on AI in stages — audit, a few tools, a pilot on a real project, keep what worked, review every quarter.

sections.whenToUse: When a studio — or a student's own practice — decides to adopt AI deliberately rather than one download at a time.
sections.method: Three months, three stages. Month one, literacy: audit the workflow (the map from the core ring), choose a small set of tools by engine family, and write down what is safe to use them on. Month two, workflow: use them on real work — briefs, moodboards, research, presentations — on one pilot project, not across the studio. Month three, studio habits: turn what worked into a brief library, a file protocol, a review checklist and internal examples, and drop what did not. Then a standing rule: review every quarter, and at each review name one thing to stop.
sections.watchForThis: A plan with no "stop and review" in it. A list of tools with dates is a shopping list. The pilot project and the quarterly review are what make it a plan: they are where failure gets noticed and dropped.
sections.tryIt: Draft a staged adoption plan for a small studio you know, with a milestone at each month. Name the pilot project. Write the agenda of the first quarterly review, including what would make you drop a tool.
sections.proveIt: Show a plan where a reader can point to the audit, the pilot, the review date, and the rule for dropping what failed.
sections.labNote: Three months and three stages is the Lab's roadmap, not a law of practice. Another studio might stage it over six months, or by project rather than by month. What we hold to is the shape — audit, pilot, review, a rule for stopping — because the plans we see fail lack one of those, and the calendar is only there to make sure the review happens.
sections.howItWorks: Adoption usually fails by scatter: five tools, no pilot, nobody whose job it is to review. The staging exists to make dropping a tool routine rather than embarrassing. This is the Lab's own ninety-day roadmap — its own material, shared in workshops as a single page. Surveys of UK practice show adoption running ahead of policy in many studios, which is exactly the scatter the staging prevents; the Indian picture is not yet surveyed.

topics.name: Teach juniors the judgment
topics.description: A senior builds support around a junior, then removes it as the standard takes hold — and knowing when to remove it is the art. The Lab holds that a senior's job is to pass on judgment, not tool tricks. The method is old.
evidence: Coach a junior — a first-year, a classmate — through one AI-assisted task. Write down where you chose to step back, and what you left them to decide alone. Then tell apart, in one paragraph, teaching the tool from teaching the judgment that governs it.
Name what you left the junior to decide alone, and why that was the moment the teaching happened.

grounding.ref: Collins, Brown & Newman, Cognitive Apprenticeship (ERIC, Technical Report 403)

card.oneLiner: A senior builds support around a junior, then removes it as the standard takes hold — and knowing when to remove it is the art.

sections.idea: The Lab holds that a senior's job is to pass on judgment, not tool tricks. The method is old. Show the work being done. Coach the junior through it. Build support around them — checklists, templates, a review before anything leaves — and then take the support away piece by piece as the junior can hold the standard alone. Builders call that last move striking the formwork. Knowing when to strike — too early and the work sags, too late and the junior never learns to stand — is the whole art, in the studio as in the classroom.
sections.whyItMatters: AI has made tool tricks cheap and judgment scarce. Teach a junior the tool and you have taught something the next release will make obsolete. Teach the judgment and you have taught what governs the tool.
sections.inTheStudio: A senior hands a junior an AI-assisted site-research task with a checklist: sources required, a verification column, three questions to add that the model will miss. Week one, the senior reviews every line. Week four, only the unverified column. Week eight, the checklist goes; the junior keeps the habit. The stepping back was the teaching.
sections.watchForThis: Demonstrating instead of stepping back. A senior who does the judging in front of the junior every time has modelled it, not transferred it. Transfer happens at the moment the senior leaves something to be decided alone — and says so.
sections.tryIt: Coach a junior — a first-year, a classmate — through one AI-assisted task. Write down where you chose to step back, and what you left them to decide alone. Then tell apart, in one paragraph, teaching the tool from teaching the judgment that governs it.
sections.proveIt: Name what you left the junior to decide alone, and why that was the moment the teaching happened.
sections.labNote: This is the Lab's method for bringing a junior up, and it is addressed to whoever is doing the bringing up: a senior, a teacher, a final-year student with a first-year beside them. It is a position about what is worth teaching. The research behind it describes how support is built and removed; it does not prove that judgment matters more than tools, which is our claim, and which a studio that hires for tool skill would dispute.
sections.howItWorks: Education research named this cognitive apprenticeship: modelling, coaching, scaffolding, and fading — the deliberate removal of support. The Lab's own essay on the subject — its own material, not yet published — reads the same sequence off a building site: formwork holds the slab until the slab can hold itself, and then it is struck. The AI labs have lately rediscovered the move in their own harnesses: build a temporary structure around a model's weakness, then remove it as the model improves.
